A homogeneous linear equation c_1 x_1 + c_2 x_2 + ... + c_k x_k = 0 with integer coefficients is partition regular over the positive integers if for every finite coloring of the positive integers N, there exists a solution (x_1, ..., x_k) in N^k where all x_i have the same color.
c_1, ..., c_k are non-zero integers
k >= 2

body: [Example 2.7 of arXiv:2110.05374, 'When Janson meets McDiarmid: Bounded difference inequalities under graph-dependence'] Let (X_1, X_2, X_3) be dependent random variables with K_3 as their dependency graph, and let (X_i)_{4≤i≤9} be independent random variables that are also independent of (X_1, X_2, X_3). Then the vertex-disjoint union G of K_3 and 6 copies of K_1 is a dependency graph for (X_i)_{i∈[9]}. If every X_i takes values in a real interval of length c ≥ 0, then for every t > 0 Janson's inequality (Theorem 1.4 of the paper, with χ_f(G) = 3) gives P(Σ_{i∈[9]} X_i − E[Σ_{i∈[9]} X_i] ≥ t) ≤ exp(−2t²/(27c²)), while Corollary 2.6 gives the better bound P(Σ_{i∈[9]} X_i − E[Σ_{i∈[9]} X_i] ≥ t) ≤ exp(−8t²/(81c²)). The second bound uses the fractional forest vertex cover with weight 1/2 on each of F_1 = {1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7}, F_2 = {1, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9} and F_3 = {2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9}: each G[F_k] is K_2 plus 4 copies of K_1, so (Σ_k w_k √(Σ_{{i,j}∈E(G[F_k])} (c_i + c_j)² + Σ_{T∈T(F_k)} c_{min,k,T}²))² = ((3c/2)·√(2² + 1 + 4))² = 81c²/4.

OPEN per arXiv:2609.02820v1 (Theorems 1.5–1.6, PDF pp.5–6); bounded later-work check found no settlement. In the critical iid particle–hole model on Z^4, particles take synchronous discrete-time simple random-walk steps and settle permanently into stationary holes. After immediate cancellation the iid integer-valued excess η is nonconstant, has mean zero and an exponential moment. Does P(the origin is strictly closer in ℓ1 distance to an unfilled hole than to an active particle at time t) tend to zero for every such law? The source proves yes for d≤3 and exhibits counterexamples for d≥5 with P(η=1)=P(η=−1)=p and P(η=0)=1−2p. It explicitly says simulations suggest this counterexample extends to d=4. This general particle–hole question is distinct from the original binary one-car-or-one-spot parking initial law. Novelty: KNOWN source gap; current openness not certified by zero indexed citations.

body: For any integers r, s >= 1, every sequence of more than (r-1)(s-1) distinct real numbers contains either an increasing subsequence of length r or a decreasing subsequence of length s. The bound is sharp: there exist sequences of exactly (r-1)(s-1) distinct reals with no increasing subsequence of length r and no decreasing subsequence of length s. Every target-dependent slot depends on at most three consecutive entries of

[Proposition 1 (Dynamical fluctuation expansion) of arXiv:2604.04100, '\LARGE Learning Equilibrium Fluctuation Expansions from Overdamped Langevin Dynamics'] Let  $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$ and assume that $X_\varepsilon$ is the solution of \eqref{SDE-0}  with initial data $\xi_{\varepsilon}$ satisfying Assumption \ref{A1}. Let $(\bar{X}_m)_{0\leq m\leq n}$ be the solution of \eqref{eq-barX0-intro}, \eqref{eq-barX1-intro}, \eqref{eq-barXm-intro}, respectively. We define the remainder terms as $$
w_{\varepsilon,m}(t)
:=\frac{X_\varepsilon(t)-\sum_{k=0}^{m}\varepsilon^{k/2}\bar X_k(t)}{\varepsilon^{m/2}},
\qquad 0\le m\le n,\,\,t>0.
$$ 
Then for each $p\ge1$ and $t>0$, there exists a constant $C(p,t,n)>0$, independent of $\varepsilon$, such that for all $m=0,1,\cdots,n$,
\begin{equation*}
	\mathbb{E}\bigl|w_{\varepsilon,m}(t)\bigr|^{2p}\leq C(p,t,n)\varepsilon^{p}.
\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Dynamical fluctuation expansion

[Lem taylor-expansion of arXiv:2607.05097, 'Asymptotics of Lyapunov Exponents and Phase Transitions for Fluids with Degenerate Forcing'] Let $K \in \mathbb{N}$, $m \in \mathbb{N}_0$, $M \geq \delta > 0$, and $f:\Delta^K(1) \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be smooth and such that
    $$\|D^m f(0)\| \geq \delta \quad \text{and} \quad \sup_{t \in \Delta^K(1)} \|D^{m+1} f(t)\| \leq M\,.$$
    
    Then there is some $C(K,m)$ (independent of $f$) such that
    $$\|f\|_{L^2(\Delta^K(1))} \geq C(K,m)\delta^{K/2+m+1}M^{-K/2-m} \,.$$

body: PROVED (separable case of the bounded-density quadratic-form conjecture, 2026-09-22). If Q(X)=sum_j lambda_j X_j^2 is diagonal in the independent coordinates X_j (densities <=1) and has at least three eigenvalues with |lambda_j|>=1, then Q(X) has a density bounded by pi, and pi is attained (X1^2+X2^2, uniforms). Proof: among three eigenvalues of modulus >=1, two share a sign (pigeonhole); each squared term lambda X^2 has density <= y^{-1/2}; two same-sign terms convolve to a density <= B(1/2,1/2)=pi (Beta integral); convolving the remaining independent terms cannot increase the sup (Young). Sharpness: one large eigenvalue gives density y^{-1/2} (unbounded); two opposite-sign give a logarithmic singularity (unbounded). The GENERAL non-separable case remains OPEN: it reduces to a uniform L1 bound on the characteristic function, but the per-direction oscillatory decay integral e^{isx^2}f dx = O(|s|^{-1/2}) is NOT uniform over densities <=1 (for each s there is an admissible f with |integral|>=1/2), so the coupled case needs the joint oscillatory-integral analysis (resolution of singularities). Paper: Downloads/Quadratic_Form_Bounded_Density_paper.pdf.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). A probability measure mu on R is moment-determinate if it is the unique probability measure sharing its full sequence of moments (m_k)_{k>=0}. The Carleman condition gives a simple sufficient criterion: if sum_{k=1}^infinity m_{2k}^{-1/(2k)} = infinity, then mu is moment-determinate. In practice this is most often invoked via a stronger, easier-to-check sub-condition, such as subgaussian or lighter tails, for instance P(|X|>t) <= C exp(-ct^2), which implies the even moments grow at most at Gaussian rate and hence satisfy Carleman's sum divergence; a common proof strategy in random matrix theory and random measure convergence is to show convergence of all moments to those of a known moment-determinate limit, such as the compactly supported semicircle law, and then invoke Carleman's condition, or compact support directly, to upgrade moment convergence to convergence in distribution. It does not hold automatically for every measure with finite moments of all orders: the classical log-normal distribution is the standard counterexample, having finite moments of every order yet failing to be moment-determinate, so other measures share its entire moment sequence, meaning that verifying Carleman's sum diverges, or invoking compact support, is a genuinely necessary step, not a formality. Typical failure: Assuming that finiteness of all moments, or even termwise convergence of a sequence's moments to a limit's moments, is sufficient to conclude convergence in distribution, without checking that the limit measure is itself moment-determinate; the log-normal-type failure of moment determinacy is the standard cautionary example, and in random matrix or random measure contexts, using the method of moments toward a limit whose determinacy has not been separately established, as happens for some heavy-tailed spectral limits, can produce a plausible-looking but invalid convergence claim. Canonical reference: Carleman, 1926, Les Fonctions Quasi Analytiques, Gauthier-Villars; Akhiezer, The Classical Moment Problem, 1965, Hafner Publishing; Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices, 2010, Cambridge University Press.

$$

$$

\[
\Sigma\ :=\ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{n_N}\sum_{i=1}^{r(N)}\frac{m_i^{(N)}\bigl(m_i^{(N)}+1\bigr)}{2}
\]

\[
\phi(z)\ :=\ \int_0^1 \log\Bigl(\frac{e^{tz}-1}{tz}\Bigr)\,dt,

domain $\mathscr{D}=\{z\in\C:\ \frac{e^{tz}-1}{tz}\notin(-\infty,0]\ \text{for all }t\in[0,1]\}$, and limiting function

body:
[Theorem thm:introduction-lattice-induction of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] The following assertions hold.

\begin{enumerate}
\item
For every $d\geq 1$, each lattice-induced
probability-preserving Borel $\mathbb R^d$-space admits a
generating stealthy Delone cross-section.

\item
Let $\eta$ be an ergodic translation-invariant point process on
$\mathbb R$ with positive intensity and local second moments. If
\[
    \int_{0<|\xi|<1}
    \frac{1}{\xi^2}\,d\sigma_\eta(\xi)
    <
    \infty,
\]
then the translation action on its configuration space has a
nonzero eigenvalue and is lattice-induced.
\end{enumerate}

Consequently, an ergodic probability-preserving Borel
$\mathbb R$-space is lattice-induced if and only if it admits a
generating stealthy Delone cross-section. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Stealthy cross-sections and lattice induction

body:
Load-bearing hypothesis: the equivalence 'admissible shock ⇔ Lax inequalities f'(u_-) ≥ σ ≥ f'(u_+)' requires the flux to be convex (genuinely nonlinear) on the range of the data. For a nonconvex flux one must use Oleinik's full chord condition, which involves f at every intermediate state, not only the two endpoint derivatives. Counterexample: f(u) = u^4 - 5u^2 (so f'(u) = 4u^3 - 10u), left state u_- = 2, right state u_+ = -2. Since f(2) = f(-2) = -4, Rankine-Hugoniot gives the stationary shock σ = 0, and the Lax inequalities hold strictly: f'(2) = 12 > 0 > f'(-2) = -12. Yet the shock is NOT admissible: the chord joining (-2,-4) and (2,-4) is the constant -4, while f(0) = 0 lies ABOVE it, so Oleinik's condition fails; equivalently the Kruzhkov inequality with k = 0 requires σ(k - u_-) ≥ f(k) - f(u_-), i.e. 0 ≥ 4, which is false. The correct entropy solution of this Riemann problem is read off the least concave majorant of f on [-2,2] (the hull construction for a decreasing jump u_l > u_r): a shock from u_- = 2 down to u* = (√7 - 2)/3 ≈ 0.2153, the point at which the line through (2, f(2)) is tangent to the graph of f, then an attached rarefaction from u* down to -u*, then, by symmetry, a shock from -u* to u_+ = -2. The two shock speeds are -(16 + 14u*)/9 ≈ -2.113 and +(16 + 14u*)/9 ≈ +2.113, and the rarefaction sweeps the speeds between them. Auditor's check: whenever a proof calls a jump admissible using only characteristic speeds, verify convexity of the flux on the interval spanned by the two states; otherwise test the whole chord.
Counterexample flux f(u) = u^4 - 5u^2 with states u_- = 2, u_+ = -2, shock speed σ = 0
Lax inequalities compare σ only with f'(u_-) and f'(u_+)
Oleinik's condition requires the graph of f between the two states to lie on the correct side of the chord at EVERY intermediate value
For nonconvex flux the Riemann solution is generally a composite of shocks and rarefactions given by the convex (or concave) hull construction
title: Pitfall: Lax's Shock Inequalities Are Not Sufficient When the Flux Is Not Convex

body: Theorem (campaign status: audited-pass): Under affine spanning, projective simplicity, and coordinate-full homogenization, an affine fibre of density greater than 27/512 cannot have old geometric distance three. Structure: homogeneous compression yields an optimal residual plane; if it descends with any slack the old distance is ≤ 2; otherwise it has the saturated shared-h pattern, the balanced local relation reduces the old support to three or five coordinates, and long directions, flag estimates, planar spectra, the m = 8 exact normal forms, and the m ≤ 7 intrinsic enumeration cover every possible effective size. In each case either the density is ≤ 27/512 or an old rank-two residual certificate contradicts distance three. Notes: Quantifier: under the distance-three hypothesis EVERY optimal homogenized plane must be exceptional, so excluding any selected one suffices. Density threshold 27/512 ~ 0.0527. Finite components certified per p.27; this is a deterministic local theorem, not the determinant conjecture.

In the F_2 long-power family, G_1=G_2=Z, the b factor has chi_b=(1+p)/(1-p), and this specializes to p(2chi_N(p)-1)=1. The union-of-factor-generators assumption is essential; this formula is not asserted for arbitrary prescribed generating sets. Source: Kozakova arXiv:math/0611668v3, Theorem 1.

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.02257, 'Aperiodic random walks: uniform estimates, local limits and invariance principles'] We prove uniform endpoint estimates, killed local limits, and conditioned-bridge invariance principles for triangular arrays of centered, aperiodic, integer-valued random walks with uniform exponential tails. The endpoint estimates cover all nonnegative heights, while the local limits treat positive diffusive and zero endpoints. The increment law may vary with the scaling parameter.
title: Abstract of arXiv:2609.02257: Aperiodic random walks: uniform estimates, local limits and invariance principles

[Proposition 510 of arXiv:2411.15485, '\bf\Large Stochastic Volterra Equations for Local Times of Spectrally Positive L\'evy Proc'] For each $p\geq 2$, there exists a constant $C>0$ independent of $n $ and $t $ such that 
 \begin{eqnarray}
  n^2\theta_n  \int_0^\infty    \Big(t\wedge \frac{y}{n}  \Big)^p    \Lambda_n(dy) 
  \!\!\!&\leq\!\!\!& C\cdot (1+t)^{p-1}, \\
  n^2\theta_n   \int_0^\infty  \Big(t\wedge \frac{y}{n}  \Big)^p  \boldsymbol{e}_{c}*d\Lambda_n(y)\, dy 
  \!\!\!&\leq\!\!\!& C\cdot \Big(\frac{\theta_n}{n^{p-2}}  +  (1+t)^{p-1} \Big). 
 \end{eqnarray} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Fluctuations of preferential-attachment distances and diameter structural reduction Result: If integer-valued X_n is centered by real c_n, every centered value lies in Z-c_n. Along a subsequence with fractional parts c_n tending to r, any weak limit is supported on Z-r. Two subsequences whose fractional parts have different limits can therefore have incompatible translated-lattice limits. Check: For an open set G at positive distance from Z-r, mu_n(G) is eventually 0, so the portmanteau inequality mu(G) <= liminf mu_n(G) gives mu(G) = 0; countably many such open intervals cover the complement of Z-r, so any weak limit lives on Z-r. The deterministic example X_n=floor(c_n) gives centered value minus the fractional part. Own-work draft, proof (unaudited), kind route-failure, Target 3. For a probability space of absolutely continuous characteristic paths theta=(a,b,w), assume finite integrated squared Euclidean speed, original w learning rate one, nonnegative loss with integral_0^t E||theta_prime||^2 <= L0-Lt, L0<=E, and rotationally invariant p0=w0/sqrt(d) with E||p0||^2<=R^2. For fixed unit u and gamma_t=<w_t,u>/sqrt(d), ||gamma_t||_2 <= (R+sqrt(t*(L0-Lt)))/sqrt(d) <= (R+sqrt(t E))/sqrt(d). If P(|gamma_t|>=h)>=m>0, necessarily t E >= [sqrt(d)*h*sqrt(m)-R]_+^2. If Law(gamma_t)>=ell Lebesgue on [l,r], then replace h sqrt(m) with sqrt(ell*(r^3-l^3)/3). Hence bounded initial loss and normalized second moment exclude fixed positive unweighted mass of order-one scales in t=o(d), without pointwise bounds on parameters. This standard action-displacement application does not control amplitude-weighted exponential features, does not rule out an O(d) alignment phase, and does not prove Target 3. Concrete smooth flows need the explicitly stated differentiation and energy hypotheses; global existence is not asserted.
Characteristic paths absolutely continuous with finite integrated squared Euclidean speed
Nonnegative loss and energy dissipation inequality as explicitly stated
Initial loss <=E independent of d
Initial normalized weights rotationally invariant with second moment <=R^2

[Proposition PropSubMart of arXiv:2608.11178, 'A submartingale for the probability of avoiding the origin in one-point interaction ground'] Fix \(d\in\{2,3\}\), \(T,\gamma>0\), and
\(x\in\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}\). The process
\(\mathbf S^{T,\gamma}=\{\mathbf S_t^{T,\gamma}\}_{t\in[0,T]}\), defined by
\[
\mathbf S_t^{T,\gamma}
:=
S_{T-t}^{\gamma}(X_t),
\qquad
t\in[0,T].
\]
is a bounded, continuous
\(\mathbb P_x^{T,\gamma}\)-submartingale with respect to
\(\{\mathcal F_t^{T,x}\}_{t\in[0,T]}\). Moreover, if
\(\mathbf S^{T,\gamma}
=
\mathbf M^{T,\gamma}+\mathbf A^{T,\gamma}\)
denotes its Doob--Meyer decomposition, then the increasing component
\(\mathbf A^{T,\gamma}\) is constant during the excursions of \(X\) away
from the origin, while the martingale component satisfies
\(\mathbf M^{T,\gamma}\in L^2(\mathbb P_x^{T,\gamma})\) and is given by
\begin{align}
\mathbf M_t^{T,\gamma}
=
S_T^\gamma(x)
+
\int_0^t
\nabla S_{T-s}^\gamma(X_s)\cdot dW_s^{T,\gamma},
\qquad
t\in[0,T].
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: A series of real or complex terms sum a_n converges iff for every eps > 0 there is N such that |a_{n+1} + ... + a_m| < eps for all m > n >= N. In particular a convergent series has a_n -> 0, and absolute convergence implies convergence.

For a connected finite plane honeycomb graph with f bounded faces and compatible prescribed boundary midpoint values, the homogeneous vertex-relation kernel has complex dimension f. Fewer than f additional complex linear conditions cannot determine interior midpoint values uniquely. Exactly f suffice: orient each internal edge, put J_e=(v-u)F(p_e)/2, and impose c_i^T J=0 on the real signed cycle vectors of the bounded faces. These constraints give a unique solution to the algebraic boundary problem; they are not claimed to hold for the actual SAW observable or to prove a scaling limit. This is an author-proved auxiliary result, pending full independent review.

Let mu be a nonnegative Borel measure on R such that every polynomial is absolutely integrable and integral q(t)^2 dmu(t)>0 for every nonzero real polynomial q. Let p_k be its degree-k monic orthogonal polynomials, with p_0=1. Fix n>=1 and alpha in R, and write r_1<...<r_n for the n distinct real roots of p_n+alpha p_(n-1). There are strictly positive real numbers lambda_1,...,lambda_n such that integral f(t)dmu(t)=sum_(i=1)^n lambda_i f(r_i) for every real polynomial f of degree<=2n-2. These weights are unique. The parameter alpha is arbitrary real; no support-location restriction on the roots is added. The asserted exactness degree is2n-2, not2n-1 for arbitrary alpha. This is Lemma3.6 of Cohn-Kumar.

Lemma (L_Fs of the paper). Suppose that, for some $e$ in $\langle A\rangle_H\setminus A$,

we have

v(F_e)/e(H)
\leqslant v(F_f)<v(F_e).
\]

[Proposition 2 (Probabilistic representation and error decomposition) of arXiv:2604.23133, 'High-Precision Framework for Expected Hitting Times Analysis in the Dice-Sum Process'] For every \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) and \(s \ge 0\), define
\[
F(s) := \mathbb{E}_s\big[\min(T,\omega_N)\big].
\]
Then, \(F\) satisfies the same recursion and boundary conditions as~\eqref{eq:ENdef}, and hence provides a solution of the truncated recursion.
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
E(s) - F(s)
\;=\;
\mathbb{E}_s\!\big[(T - \omega_N)\,\mathbf{1}_{\{\omega_N < T\}}\big].
\end{equation}
In words, \(\min(T,\omega_N)\) represents the truncated stopping time, and
\((T-\omega_N)\mathbf{1}_{\{\omega_N<T\}}\) is the additional waiting time incurred along paths that overshoot the cutoff \(N\) before hitting the target set~\(\mathcal{H}\).

	\begin{equation}

	\end{equation}
	holds for some $\alpha \in (0,1)$. Let $(X_\epsilon)_{\epsilon\in (0,1)}$ be a family of $Y_\alpha$-valued random variables  that is uniformly tight in $ Y_0$ and has uniform tail estimates in $Y_1$, i.e., 
	\[\biggl(\sup_{\epsilon\in (0,1)} \mathbb{P} ( \|X_\epsilon \|_{Y_1} \ge N) \biggr)\,\to\, 0,
	\]
	as $N\to\infty$. Then $(X_\epsilon)_{\epsilon\in (0,1)}$ is also tight in $Y_\alpha$.

[Theorem 2.7 (van den Berg) of arXiv:2507.06186, '2507.06186'] Suppose that $D$ is simply connected and that $\partial D$ is Minkowski nondegenerate with
Minkowski dimension $\msf d_M(\partial D)\in[1,2)$. That is,
\[0<\liminf_{r\to0}\frac{\msf{A}(\partial D_r)}{r^{2-\msf d_M(\partial D)}}\leq
\limsup_{r\to0}\frac{\msf{A}(\partial D_r)}{r^{2-\msf d_M(\partial D)}}<\infty,\]
where we define
\[\partial D_r=\left\{x\in\mbb R^2:\inf_{y\in\partial D}|x-y|<r\right\}.\]
There exists constants $c\in(1,\infty)$ and $\th>0$ such that
\begin{align}

c^{-1}t^{1-\msf d_M(\partial D)/2}\leq\msf{A}(D)-\msf M_0(t)\leq ct^{1-\msf d_M(\partial D)/2},\qquad t\in(0,\th).
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma lem:d_P_bound of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] \noindent{\nf(a)} Let $\bm\xi$ be a random vector in $L^q$, i.e. $\mathds{E}[|\bm\xi|^q]<\infty$, for some $q\in(0,1]$. Then, 
$$\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{\xi},a\bm{\xi})\geqslant |1-a^q|\mathds{E}\big[|\bm\xi|^q\big] \quad \text{ for any constant }a \in(0,\infty).$$

\noindent{\nf(b)} Assume that the random vectors
$\bm\xi_1, \bm\xi_2, \bm\zeta_1, \bm\zeta_2$ are in $L^q$, for some $q\in(0,1]$, and that 
$(\bm{\xi}_1,\bm{\zeta}_1)$ and $(\bm{\xi}_2, \bm{\zeta}_2)$ are independent. Then the following inequality holds:
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{\xi}_1+\bm{\xi}_2,\bm{\zeta}_1+\bm{\zeta}_2)
\leqslant \mathcal{W}_q(\bm{\xi}_1,\bm{\zeta}_1) + \mathcal{W}_q(\bm{\xi}_2,\bm{\zeta}_2).
\end{equation*}

body:
[Lemma 2605211341 of arXiv:2609.02626, 'Comparison principles and symmetry for subquadratic fractional $p$-Laplacian equations'] Let $N\ge 1$, $s\in (0, 1)$ and $p>1$. Suppose that $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ is a bounded open set, and $u\in \widetilde{W}^{s,p}(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of
\[
(-\Delta)_p^s u= g\quad \mbox{in } \Omega,
\]
for some $g\in L^1_{loc}(\Omega)\cap W_0^{s, p}(\Omega)'$. Let $v\in L^1_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^N)$  satisfy
\[
{\rm dist}({\rm supp}(v), \Omega)>0, \quad \int_{\Omega^c}\frac{|v(x)|^{p-1}}{(1+|x|)^{N+sp}} {\rm d}x<\infty.
\]
Define
\[
h(x)=2\int_{{\rm supp} (v)}\frac{J_{u+v}(x, y)-J_u(x, y)}{|x-y|^{N+sp}} {\rm d}y, \quad \mbox{for a.e. }x\in \Omega.
\]
Then $u+v\in \widetilde{W}^{s,p}(\Omega)$ and it solves weakly $(-\Delta)_p^s (u+v)= g+h$ in $\Omega$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
PROOF (UNAUDITED); novelty unverified. For deterministic x in R^d with d>=1 and s=||x||^2/d in (0,1], take independent standard Gaussian U(n by d), W(n by n), v(n), with n>=1. Define h=Ux/sqrt(d), a=tanh(h), H=Wa/sqrt(n), f=v^T tanh(H)/sqrt(n). With all raw U,W,v trainable and no biases, the diagonal NTK Theta_n=||grad_U f||_F^2+||grad_W f||_F^2+||grad_v f||^2 satisfies ||Theta_n-Theta_infty||_2<=37/sqrt(n). Here F(q)=E tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2, R(q)=E sech(sqrt(q)Z)^4 and Theta_infty=F(F(s))+(F(s)+s R(s))R(F(s)). This is also a W2 bound to the deterministic NTK point mass.
Two hidden layers of common width n; one fixed nonzero input, normalized squared norm <=1; independent Gaussian initialization; tanh; raw-parameter NTK scaling as stated; no trainable biases. Uses unaudited C021 and reviewed C002 v2 scalar kernel shape.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:2e54f669559ce1276dfe40f4e7ccfcb607ea68e74c8a28015756a0133b6fdbad","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/2e/2e54f669559ce1276dfe40f4e7ccfcb607ea68e74c8a28015756a0133b6fdbad.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:f3aeefd89b9bd0bd89a56e7f3aa2fc2ce4fb878722b532ee4aa00190646ee9e0","bundle_entry_key":"t250_w712_c022","bundle_id":"population.w712-t250-c021-c022-transpose-tanh-ntk","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"Quantitative Tensor Programs and Gaussian shared-weight conditioning","draft":"w712/bundle_016.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.neural_networks:two-hidden-tanh-diagonal-ntk-rate","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C022 v1: n^(-1/2) rate for one initial two-hidden-layer tanh NTK program

Kind: narrowed. Target: 2, one transpose-using program.
Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty unverified. This is a one-input
diagonal NTK result, not the entire NTK matrix on multiple inputs or
a quantitative Master Theorem for arbitrary transpose programs.

## Model and statement

Let x in R^d be deterministic, with d>=1 and s=||x||^2/d in (0,1].
Let U in R^(n by d), W in R^(n by n) and v in R^n have independent
standard Gaussian entries, mutually independent, with n>=1. Define

    h=Ux/sqrt(d), a=tanh(h), H=Wa/sqrt(n),
    f(x)=v^T tanh(H)/sqrt(n).

All nonlinearities are coordinatewise. Train the raw parameters U,W,v
with the displayed scaling retained in the computational graph; there
are no bias parameters. The scalar diagonal empirical NTK is

    Theta_n(x,x)=||grad_U f||_F^2+||grad_W f||_F^2+||grad_v f||^2.

For Z standard Gaussian put

    F(q)=E tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2,
    R(q)=E sech(sqrt(q)Z)^4,
    q1=F(s), q2=F(q1), r1=R(s), r2=R(q1),
    Theta_infty=q2+(q1+s r1)r2.

Then, for all n>=1,

    ||Theta_n(x,x)-Theta_infty||_2 <=37/sqrt(n).     (1)

Equivalently, W2(Law(Theta_n(x,x)),delta_(Theta_infty)) is at most
37/sqrt(n), since coupling to a deterministic point has exactly that
L2 cost. The constant is universal on 0<s<=1 and deliberately loose.
The program genuinely uses W and W^T together; the quantitative shared-
weight step is C021, not an independent-backward-weight replacement.

## 1. Differentiate the exact finite-width program

Set qhat=||a||^2/n, D=diag(sech(h_i)^4), rhat=tr(D)/n,
g_j=sech(H_j)^2, b_j=v_j g_j and Rhat=||b||^2/n. Direct differentiation
with respect to the raw parameters in the stated parametrization gives

    ||grad_v f||^2 = Qhat2:=mean_j tanh(H_j)^2,
    ||grad_W f||_F^2 = qhat Rhat,
    ||grad_U f||_F^2 = s T,
    T=b^T W D W^T b/n^2.

For the last line grad_(U_ik) f=x_k sech(h_i)^2(W^Tb)_i/(n sqrt(d));
summing its square over i,k supplies exactly s, not an additional n.
Hence

    Theta_n=Qhat2+qhat Rhat+s T.                    (2)

Conditional on h, a,D are fixed with 0<=D<=I, and a!=0 almost surely
because s>0 and tanh vanishes only at zero. W,v are still fresh independent
Gaussians. C021 with g(t)=sech(t)^2 therefore gives, conditionally and
then unconditionally,

    ||T-rhat Rhat||_2<=9/sqrt(n).                   (3)

This is the only new transpose-conditioning input, and is unaudited.

## 2. Scalar forward and derivative moments

The h_i are iid N(0,s). Since tanh^2 and sech^4 lie in [0,1],

    ||qhat-q1||_2<=1/sqrt(n),
    ||rhat-r1||_2<=1/sqrt(n).                       (4)

Given h, the H_j are iid N(0,qhat). Thus

    ||Qhat2-F(qhat)||_2<=1/sqrt(n).

The independently reviewed C002 establishes that F is increasing and
concave, with F(0)=0 and F'(0+)=1. Consequently it is 1-Lipschitz on
[0,1]. Equations (4) give

    ||Qhat2-q2||_2<=2/sqrt(n).                      (5)

Given h, the pairs (H_j,v_j) are iid and E Rhat=R(qhat). Their individual
second moment is E[v_j^4 sech(H_j)^8]<=3. Conditional variance and total
expectation therefore give

    ||Rhat-R(qhat)||_2<=sqrt(3)/sqrt(n).             (6)

We also need a Lipschitz bound for R, proved here without an inverse
variance denominator. Let psi(t)=sech(t)^4. Its second derivative is

    psi''(t)=16 sech(t)^4 tanh(t)^2-4 sech(t)^6,

so |psi''|<=20 on R. If 0<=p<=q, take independent standard Gaussians
Z,Z'. The random variable sqrt(p)Z+sqrt(q-p)Z' has variance q. Taylor's
theorem, with a pointwise remainder at most 10(q-p)(Z')^2, and conditional
centering of the first-order term in Z', show

    |R(q)-R(p)|<=10(q-p).                          (7)

All expectations of the remainder are finite; psi' is bounded, so the
centered linear term is integrable. This includes p=0 and does not move
an uncontrolled derivative or limit through an integral.

## 3. Assemble the NTK rate without factoring dependent errors

Put Ahat=qhat+s rhat and A=q1+s r1. Both lie in [0,2]. From (2)--(3),

    ||Theta_n-[Qhat2+Ahat Rhat]||_2<=9/sqrt(n).      (8)

Expand the remaining product in the following exact order:

    Ahat Rhat-A r2
       =Ahat[Rhat-R(qhat)]
        +Ahat[R(qhat)-R(q1)]+(Ahat-A)r2.

Bounding Ahat pointwise by 2, r2 by 1, and using (4), (6), (7),

    ||Ahat Rhat-A r2||_2
       <=[2sqrt(3)+20+2]/sqrt(n).                  (9)

Neither Ahat nor qhat is assumed independent of Rhat. Triangle
inequalities with pointwise bounds suffice. Combine (5), (8), (9):

    ||Theta_n-Theta_infty||_2
       <=[33+2sqrt(3)]/sqrt(n)<37/sqrt(n),

using sqrt(3)<2. This proves (1).

## Scope, prior work, and remaining question

This is an explicit bounded-smooth-activation, diagonal, single-input
example of Target2. It does not control the NTK at two distinct inputs,
the full backward row distribution, growing depth, or reuse in a general
Tensor Program. The next mathematical extension is the off-diagonal
kernel: joint forward conditioning then has rank two and may become
ill-conditioned when the input features align.

Primary-source prior-work check: Hanin--Nica, arXiv:1909.05989v1,
Theorem1, PDF page4, treats ReLU diagonal NTK moments with zero-initialized
but trainable biases and two-sided second-moment comparability. That
comparability alone is insufficient to subtract the squared mean and
deduce a variance O(1/n); no such inference is used here. This is not a
claim that an n^(-1/2) tanh NTK rate is new in the literature. Independent
novelty assessment remains pending. The elementary Gaussian conditioning
mechanism itself is standard and is not claimed new.

Load-bearing checks: the precise raw-parameter normalization in section1;
the conditional independence required by C021; qhat>0 almost surely;
bounded derivatives for (6)--(7); and pointwise rather than independence
estimates in (9). At n=1 the conditioning still includes the rank-one
term, and (1) remains valid. There is no s=0 cancellation in the proof;
that case is outside the stated range. All checks are author checks only.
Formalization remains UNVERIFIED; no independently checked proof or

body: Let X be a Banach space and A: D(A) subset of X -> X a linear operator. There exists a strongly continuous semigroup (T(t))_{t >= 0} of bounded linear operators on X with ||T(t)|| <= 1 for every t >= 0 (a contraction semigroup) whose infinitesimal generator is A if and only if: (i) A is closed and D(A) is dense in X; and (ii) every lambda > 0 lies in the resolvent set of A, with ||(lambda I - A)^{-1}|| <= 1/lambda for every lambda > 0. [standard, e.g. Pazy, Semigroups of Linear Operators and Applications to Partial Differential Equations]

[Theorem thm:explicit_current_1 of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] Let $(X_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be an ergodic diffusion with invariant measure $\mu$ whose
symmetric part $\mathcal{L}_S$ satisfies the Poincar\'e inequality~(equation eq:poincare of the paper)
with spectral gap $\lambda_\mathrm{gap}>0$ (Assumptions~(ass:dynamics of the paper)). 
Let $\overline{J}_t(U)$ denote the empirical current according to Definition~(def:empirical_current of the paper)
with ergodic mean $\E^\mu[\overline{J}_t(U)]=\E^\mu[v_{\textrm{s}}\cdot U]= \E^\mu[W]$,
and let $\nu\ll\mu$ with $\mathrm{d}\nu/\mathrm{d}\mu\in L^2(\mu)$.
Then for all $t > 0$ and $a > 0$,
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(\overline{J}_t(U) - \E^\mu[\overline{J}_t] \geq a\right)
  \leq
  \left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}
  \exp\left[-t\frac{\tilde\sigma_{J,1}^2}{c_{J,1}^2}h\left(\frac{c_{J,1} a}{\tilde\sigma_{J,1}^2}\right)\right],
  
\end{align}
where $h(u) \equiv 1 + u - \sqrt{1+2u}$ and we define
\begin{align}
  \tilde\sigma_{J,1}^2 \equiv
  \frac{2\mathrm{Var}_\mu(W)}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}} + 2\|Q\|_{L^\infty(\mu)},
  \qquad 
  c_{J,1} \equiv \frac{\|W-\E^\mu[W]\|_{L^\infty(\mu)}}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}}.
\end{align}

[Lem uniform-exp-lower-bound of arXiv:2607.05097, 'Asymptotics of Lyapunov Exponents and Phase Transitions for Fluids with Degenerate Forcing'] For every $\tilde z_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d$, $\eta \in (0,\eta^*(\tilde z_0))$, and $\delta, c > 0$ there are $\rho, C > 0$ such that for all $z_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with $\|z_0-\tilde z_0\| \leq \rho$, $\epsilon < \rho$, $v \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and $t \geq C$
    $$\|P_\eta(z_0)v\| \geq \delta \|v\| \implies \|P_{\eta}(z_0)e^{t A^\epsilon(z_0)}v\| \geq e^{(\lambda(A^\epsilon(z_0))-c)t}\|v\| \,,$$
    where $P_\eta(z_0)$ is as in (def:proj-eta of the paper).

body: Theorem (campaign status: audited-pass): Choose an independent dominating set U in C_n of size d = ceil(n/3) whose cyclic gaps have (edge-)length two or three. Put L_u = A + B_u and R = span{L_u : u in U}; the L_u are independent. Orient the cycle: in a length-two gap u-v-u' take basis forms B_v, C_v; in a length-three gap u-v-w-u' take B_v, C_v, C_w. Together with A these are exactly n+1 full-dual forms, linearly independent by backward substitution through each gap. Modulo R: B_u = -A, C_u = B_v, B_w = C_w in the relevant gap cases, so every full-dual form has a signed basis representative with residual in R. Hence dcb(A_n) = dgeo(A_n) = ceil(n/3). Notes: Explicit optimal certificate, not just an existence bound. Form count checks: sum of gap lengths = n edges, so d gaps contribute n forms, plus A = n+1.

[Theorem intro-fredi of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] (Theorem (fredi of the paper))
  
  Let $n$ be a fixed integer. Let $A$ be a random Hermitian matrix of size $N$ and assume
  that for every finite $r$ one has
  \begin{equation}
    \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} N^{n \varepsilon} \left( \frac{1}{N} \log
    \mathbb{E}[H \text{} C (x_1, \ldots, x_r, 0^{N - r} ; \lambda_1 (A),
    \ldots, \lambda_n (A))] - \sum_{j = 0}^{n - 1} \sum_{i = 0}^r
    \frac{1}{N^{j \varepsilon}} \Psi_j (x_i) \right) = \sum_{i = 1}^r \Psi_n
    (x_i), 
  \end{equation}
  where $\Psi_0, \ldots, \Psi_n$ are smooth functions in a complex neighborhood of
  $0$, the above convergence is uniform in a complex neighborhood of $0^r$, and $0 <
  \varepsilon < n^{- 1}$. Then the $1 / N^{n \varepsilon}$ correction of the
  average empirical distribution of $N^{- 1} A$ is given by
  \begin{equation}
    \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} N^{n \varepsilon} \left( \frac{1}{N^{k + 1}}
    \mathbb{E}[\ensuremath{\operatorname{Tr}} (A^k)] - \sum_{j = 0}^{n - 1} \frac{1}{N^{j
    \varepsilon}} \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{(j)}_k \right) =\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_k^{(n)},
    
  \end{equation}
  where for every $j \in \{0, \ldots, n\}$
  \[ \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{(j)}_k := \sum_{b_1 + 2 b_2 + \cdots + j \text{} b_j
     = j} \sum_{m = 0}^{k - b_1 - \cdots - b_j} \frac{k!}{m! (m + 1) ! (k - m
     - b_1 - \cdots - b_j) !b_1 ! \ldots b_j !} \text{{\hspace{8em}}} \]
  \begin{equation}
    \text{{\hspace{14em}}} \times \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi'_0
    (x))^{k - m - b_1 - \cdots - b_j} (\Psi'_1 (x))^{b_1} \ldots (\Psi'_j
    (x))^{b_j}) \right|_{x = 0} . 
  \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Defn local_multiple_radial_SLE_kappa of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] The locally commuting $n$-radial $\mathrm{SLE}(\kappa)$ is a compatible family of measures 
\[
\mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, q\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n\right)}
\]
on $n$-tuples of continuous, non-self-crossing curves $\left(\gamma^{(1)}, \gamma^{(2)}, \ldots, \gamma^{(n)}\right)$ for all simply connected domains $\Omega$ with marked points $\left(z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, q\right)$ and target sets $\left(U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n\right)$. These measures satisfy the following conditions:

\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] \textbf{Conformal invariance}: If $\varphi: \Omega \to \Omega^\prime$ is a conformal map, then the pullback measure satisfies
    \[
    \varphi^* \mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega^\prime; \varphi(z_1), \varphi(z_2), \ldots, \varphi(z_n), \varphi(q)\right)}^{\left(\varphi(U_1), \varphi(U_2), \ldots, \varphi(U_n)\right)} 
    = \mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n\right)}.
    \]
    It suffices to describe the measure when $\left(\Omega; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, q\right) = \left(\mathbb{D}; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, 0\right)$. The definition for arbitrary $\Omega$ with a marked interior point $q$ can then be extended by pulling back via a conformal equivalence $\varphi: \Omega \to \mathbb{D}$ mapping $q$ to $0$.

    \item[(ii)] \textbf{Domain Markov property}: Let $\left(\gamma^{(1)}, \gamma^{(2)}, \ldots, \gamma^{(n)}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\mathbb{D}; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, q\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n\right)}$, and parametrize $\gamma^{(j)}$ by their own capacity in $\mathbb{D}$. For stopping times $\mathbf{t} = (t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n)$, define
    \[
    \tilde{U}_j = U_j \setminus \gamma^{(j)}_{[0, t_j]}, \quad 
    \tilde{\gamma}^{(j)} = \gamma^{(j)} \setminus \gamma^{(j)}_{[0, t_j]}, \quad 
    \tilde{\Omega} = \mathbb{D} \setminus \bigcup_{j=1}^n \gamma^{(j)}_{[0, t_j]}.
    \]
    Then, conditionally on the initial segments $\bigcup_{j=1}^n \gamma^{(j)}_{[0, t_j]}$, we have
    \[
    \left(\tilde{\gamma}^{(1)}, \tilde{\gamma}^{(2)}, \ldots, \tilde{\gamma}^{(n)}\right) 
    \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\tilde{\Omega}; \gamma^{(1)}_{t_1}, \gamma^{(2)}_{t_2}, \ldots, \gamma^{(n)}_{t_n}, q\right)}^{\left(\tilde{U}_1, \tilde{U}_2, \ldots, \tilde{U}_n\right)}.
    \]

    \item[(iii)] \textbf{Absolute Continuity with respect to independent SLE($\kappa$)}: Let $\left(\gamma^{(1)}, \gamma^{(2)}, \ldots, \gamma^{(n)}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\mathbb{D}; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, 0\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n\right)}$. Let $z_j(t) = e^{i \theta_j(t)}$, the capacity-parametrized Loewner driving function $t \mapsto \theta_j(t)$ for $\gamma^{(j)}$ satisfies
    \[ 
    \begin{aligned}
    \mathrm{d} \theta_j(t) &= \sqrt{\kappa} \, \mathrm{d} B_j(t) + b_j\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}(t)\right) \, \mathrm{d} t, \\
    \mathrm{d} \theta_k(t) &= \cot\left(\frac{\theta_k(t) - \theta_j(t)}{2}\right) \, \mathrm{d} t, \quad k \neq j,
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    where $B_j(t)$ are independent standard Brownian motions, and $b_j(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ are $C^2$ functions on the chamber 
    \[
    \mathfrak{X}^n = \left\{(\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid \theta_1 < \theta_2 < \cdots < \theta_n < \theta_1 + 2\pi \right\}.
    \]
\end{itemize}

body: [Theorem thm: main dual of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] The process $(V(-r)+r,\, r\ge 0)$ is a homogeneous Feller process starting from $0$. For any $r>0$, $\frac{V(-r)+r}{r}$ has distribution ${\mathcal B}(\frac{\widehat{\delta}}{2},\frac{\delta}{2})$. Conditionally on $V(0)=z>0$,  the  process $V$ stays constant then jumps at time $\mathrm{x}$ where  $\frac{z}{z+{\mathrm x}}$ has distribution ${\mathcal B}(\frac{\delta}{2},1)$. Conditionally on ${\mathrm x}=x$, $\frac{V(-x)+x}{x+z}\sim {\mathcal B}(\frac{\widehat{\delta}+\delta}{2},1)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.12839, 'Spiking Neural Networks with Elephant Reinforcement'] Let \(N<\infty\). Consider the process
\[
Y_t=(V_t,S_t,K_t)
\in \mathbb N^N\times\mathbb Z^N\times\mathbb N^N.
\]
Assume that site \(i\) fires with rate
\[
\lambda_i(V,S,K)
=
\mathbf 1_{\{V_i>\alpha S_i^+\}},
\qquad
S_i^+=\max\{S_i,0\},
\]
and leaks with rate
\[
\gamma\mathbf 1_{\{V_i>0\}},
\qquad \gamma>0.
\]
When site \(i\) fires, \(V_i\) is reset to \(0\), its two neighbours receive
one unit of potential, and
\[
S_i\mapsto S_i+\xi_i,
\qquad
K_i\mapsto K_i+1.
\]
Then the process is non-explosive. More precisely, if \(N_t\) denotes the
number of events up to time \(t\), then
\[
\mathbb E[N_t]\leq (\gamma+1)Nt<\infty.
\]

DRAFT concept backed by an author derivation, not a promoted theorem. Let mu_omega be random probability Borel measures, I a bounded open interval, 1<p<infinity, and eta_n>0 a deterministic sequence tending to zero. Set F_n(omega,E)=integral eta_n/((t-E)^2+eta_n^2) dmu_omega(t), jointly measurable. If sup_n E integral_I F_n^p <= C<infinity, then almost surely mu_omega|I=rho_omega dE with rho_omega in Lp(I), and E integral_I rho_omega^p <= C/pi^p. For 0<p<=1, integral_I F_eta^p <= |I|^(1-p)pi^p holds for every probability measure, including atoms; those power bounds alone cannot imply ac. p>1 is sufficient, not necessary for ac, and the criterion may yield zero mass on I.

[Corollary 11 of arXiv:2608.18834, 'The Parabolic Anderson Model's Total Mass at Small Times: Geometry, Fluctuations, and Reno'] Suppose that Assumption \ref{Assumption} holds,
and let $\ka>0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $H_0>1/2$ or $\partial D$ is sufficiently irregular, then the deterministic
heat diffusion mechanism dominates $u_\ka$'s total mass asymptotics. More specifically:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $H_0>1/2$ and \eqref{Equation: Regular Heat Content} holds, then
\[\lim_{t\to0} t^{-1/2}\big(|D|-\msf M_\ka(t)\big)=\frac{\sqrt{2}|\partial D|}{\sqrt{\pi}}\qquad\text{in probability}.\]
\item If \eqref{Equation: Fractal Heat Content} holds for any $\msf m\in(d-1,d)$, then
\[\lim_{t\to0}\frac{1}{\log t}\log\big||D|-\msf M_\ka(t)\big|=\frac{d-\msf m}{2}\qquad\text{in probability}.\]
\end{enumerate}
\item If $H_0=1/2$ and \eqref{Equation: Regular Heat Content} holds, then as $t\to0$, one has
\[\mbf E\big[|D|-\msf M_\ka(t)\big]\sim\frac{\sqrt{2}|\partial D|}{\sqrt{\pi}}t^{1/2}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\sqrt{\mbf{Var}\big[|D|-\msf M_\ka(t)\big]}\sim\ka\mf c\,t^{1/2}.\]
In particular, the noise now has an impact on the first-order total mass asymptotic via $\ka$ and the constant $\mf c$ in \eqref{Equation: c Constant}.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 11 of arXiv:2608.18834

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Analyse M(1,1) on Z^2 through the range of the first-coordinate walk. Result: In M(1,1) the first coordinate moves only at first visits and the second at later visits; the set of visited vertices is the range, and the first-coordinate process is a simple random walk on Z run at the rate of new visits. Recurrence of M(1,1) would follow if the walk returns to the origin infinitely often; since the second coordinate performs a simple random walk on the column above the current first coordinate whenever the vertex was visited before, the walk behaves in each column like a 1D random walk (recurrent) until it hits an unvisited vertex, at which time the first coordinate steps. The number of new visits up to time n is the range R_n; the first coordinate after n steps is a simple random walk at time R_n, so |X^1_n| is of order sqrt(R_n), and the range of a planar walk-like process is at most n, giving |X^1_n| <= sqrt n; a return to the origin requires both coordinates to vanish. A heuristic: if R_n ≍ n/log n as for planar simple random walk then the first coordinate is diffusive at the slower clock, and the walk is 'more recurrent' than planar simple random walk, supporting the conjecture; but the range of M(1,1) is not that of simple random walk because the exploration is column-wise. A rigorous partial fact: M(1,1) is recurrent if and only if the first coordinate returns to 0 infinitely often at times when the second coordinate is 0; since within a column the second coordinate is a recurrent 1D walk that keeps returning to 0 until it finds a new vertex, and new vertices in a column are found at the ends of the visited interval, the question is whether the first-coordinate walk (which is a simple random walk in the clock of new visits) visits 0 infinitely often, which it does a.s. (1D recurrence), and whether at those visits the second coordinate is 0 - not automatic. So recurrence of M(1,1) reduces to: at the (infinitely many) times the first coordinate is 0, the second coordinate, which then performs a 1D walk in the column of 0 with the visited interval of that column, returns to height 0 before finding a new vertex - which has probability bounded below by a constant each time if the visited interval around height 0 in column 0 has length bounded... the visited interval in column 0 grows, and the probability of returning to 0 from the boundary of an interval of length L before exiting is of order 1/L... summing over the visits to column 0 gives a divergent series only if the interval lengths grow slowly enough. This is the crux and I did not settle it; the reduction is recorded. Key identity: M(1,1) recurrent iff, at the infinitely many returns of the first coordinate to 0, the second coordinate returns to 0 in column 0 before finding a new vertex; the return probability is of order 1/(visited interval length). Obstruction: Growth rate of the visited interval in column 0 not controlled.

For any centered law Q of support diameter D, with a=E X^2 and b=E X^4, a<=D^2/4 and b+3a^2<=D^2*a. Let A be a linear operator on a Banach space X, and let M ≥ 1, ω ∈ ℝ. The following are equivalent: (a) A generates a C_0-semigroup (T(t))_{t ≥ 0} with ‖T(t)‖ ≤ M e^{ωt} for all t ≥ 0; (b) A is closed, densely defined, every real λ > ω lies in ρ(A), and ‖(λ − A)^{-n}‖ ≤ M/(λ − ω)^n for all λ > ω and all n ≥ 1; (c) A is closed, densely defined, every λ with Re λ > ω lies in ρ(A), and ‖(λ − A)^{-n}‖ ≤ M/(Re λ − ω)^n for all such λ and all n ≥ 1. Contraction case (M = 1, ω = 0): A generates a contraction C_0-semigroup iff A is closed, densely defined, (0, ∞) ⊂ ρ(A) and ‖(λ − A)^{-1}‖ ≤ 1/λ for all λ > 0; here the single power n = 1 suffices. When M > 1 the estimates on all powers n cannot be dropped: the n = 1 bound alone is a strictly weaker (Kreiss-type) condition.
X is a Banach space
A is a linear operator, closed and densely defined in (b),(c)
the resolvent power estimates hold for every n ≥ 1 when M > 1

[Definition 14 (Square well model (SWM)) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Fix $d\in\Z_{\geq 1}$ and $\beta\in\R_{\geq 0}$.
    For any domain $\Lambda$ and $\zeta:\Z^d\to[-1,1]$,
    the \emph{square well model} (SWM) on $\Lambda$ with boundary condition $\zeta$
    at inverse temperature $\beta$ is the probability measure  on $\alpha\in[-1,1]^\Lambda$ given by
    \[
        \diff\mu_{\SWM,\Lambda,\beta}^\zeta(\alpha) = \frac1{Z_{\SWM,\Lambda,\beta}^\zeta} e^{-\beta H_{\SWM,\Lambda}^\zeta(\alpha)} \diff\alpha,
    \]
    where $Z_{\Lambda,\beta}^\zeta$ is the normalising constant,
    $\diff\alpha$ the Lebesgue measure, and
    \[
        H_{\SWM,\Lambda}^\zeta(\alpha) := \sum_{\substack{\{x,y\}\subset\Lambda\\x\sim y}} (\alpha_x-\alpha_y)^2 + \sum_{\substack{x\in\Lambda,\,y\in\Lambda^c\\x\sim y}} (\alpha_x-\zeta_y)^2.
    \]
    The label $\SWM$ is omitted when no confusion is likely to arise.
title: Square well model (SWM)

[Thm 5 of arXiv:2606.07194, 'Survival Probability of Markov Linear Reccurence Sequence in a Random Environment: Subcrit'] Let $\{Y_n\}$ be a strongly subcritical positive zero-absorbing MRSRE with $\rho\in (0,1)$. Assume that~(\ref{BnCond}) and ${\bf E}^{(h)}\kappa<\infty$ holds for some $h>h^*_+$. Then 
\begin{enumerate}
\item \begin{equation}

{\bf P}(Y_n>0|Y_0=i)\sim f^*_i \rho^n,\quad {\bf P}(Y_n=k|Y_n>0)\to p_k^*,\ n\to\infty,
\end{equation}
where $\{p_k^*\}$ is a distribution, and $\{f^*_i\}$ is a bounded sequence such that
$$
\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} p_{i,j} f^*_j=\rho f^*_i,\ i>0,\
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} p_i^* p_{i,j}=\rho p^*_i,\ j>0,\
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} p_i^* f^*_i=1;
$$
\item for any $h>h^*_+$ 
$$
{\bf P}(Y_n>0|Y_0=i)\le c i^h \rho^n,\ i>0,
$$
where $c=c(h)$ is some constant.
\item For any positive $h$ such that $R(h)<\rho$ and~(\ref{BnCond}) holds, the distribution $\{p_k^*\}$ has a finite $h$-th moment.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary cor:inv of arXiv:2505.14012, 'Ergodicity for stochastic neural field equations'] Suppose that
Assumptions (assu:space of the paper), (assu:noise of the paper), (assu:hat of the paper), and (assu:inv of the paper) hold.
Then, for
\[\eta:=\sqrt{2}|f(0)|\|\rho\|_{L^1(U)}^{1/2}+\tilde{\tilde{C}}_B,\]
and for any $u_0\in H_1$, and any $t\in [0,T]$, it holds that,
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{ess\,sup}\displaylimits_{0\leq s\leq t}\mathbb{E}\left(\|u(s)\|^2_1\right)+(2\alpha-\beta)\mathbb{E}\int_0^t\|u(s)\|_1^2\,ds \leq \|u_0\|^2_1 + \eta t,
\end{align*}
where $\beta\ge 0$ is as in Assumption (assu:inv of the paper).
In particular, for $u_0\in H_1$, $u\in L^\infty([0,T];L^2(\Omega;H_1))\cap L^2([0,T]\times\Omega;H_1)$.

body:
For unit vectors v,w in C^n, let P=vv* and Q=ww*. Their determinantal laws are single-site laws with probabilities |v_i|^2 and |w_i|^2. The optimal coupling cost for normalized Hamming distance on subsets of {1,...,n} equals (1/n)sum_i ||v_i|^2-|w_i|^2| and is at most trace|P-Q|/n. If both laws are invariant under a finite permutation group, averaging yields an invariant coupling of the same cost. This is a finite rank-one result, with no general equivariant approximation theorem asserted.

[Thm 4 of arXiv:2512.05687, '$L^p$-Boltzmann-Gibbs principle \\ via Littlewood-Paley-Stein inequality'] Assume
\begin{align} 
V\in C^2(\R) \quad \text{and} \quad 0<c_-\le V''\le c_+<\infty,
\end{align}
for some positive constants $c_+$ and $c_-$.
Let $\ell_0 \ge 1$, $p\ge 4$, and let $f$ be a local $L^{p'}(\mu_{u_0})$ function 
on $\mathcal{X}_N=\R^N$ for some $p'>p$
depending only on $\eta_{\La_{\ell_0}}=(\eta(x))_{x\in \La_{\ell_0}}$
such that $ \tilde{f}(u_0)  =0$ and 
$\tilde{f}' (u_0)=0$.  Then, there exists a constant $C=C(u_0,\ell_0)>0$, 
which is uniform in $N, \ell, \ga\in \R$, such that, for $T>0$, 
$\ell\geq \ell_0$ and a function $h$ on $[0,T]\times \T_N$, we have
\begin{align}  
& E_{\mu_{u_0}}\bigg[ \; \sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\Big| \int_0^t ds \; \sum_{x\in\T_N} 
   h(s,x)  r_s^{N,\ell;2}(x)  \Big|^p\; \bigg]\\
& \hskip 3mm \notag
    \le  C \Big( T^{(p-2)/2} N^{-p/2}\ell^{p/2} +T^{p-1} N^p \ell^{-3p/2}\Big)
        \|f\|^p_{L^{p'}(\mu_{u_0})} \int_0^T \frac{1}{N}\sum_{x\in{\T_N}}|h(t,x)|^p dt,
\end{align}
where 
\begin{align}  
r_s^{N,\ell;2}(x)=f(\tau_x \eta^{N}_s)  - \frac{1}{2} \tilde{f}''(u_0)
\Big\{\Big(\big(\eta^{N}_s\big)^{(\ell)}(x)-u_0\Big)^2    
  -\frac{{\rm var}(u_0)}{2\ell+1} \Big\}.
\end{align}
and 
${\rm var}(u)=u'(\la(u)) = E^{\mu_u}[(\eta(0)-u)^2]$ is the variance of $\mu_u$;
see \eqref{eq:u-deri}.
Recall \eqref{eq:eta-ell-B} for $\eta^{(\ell)}(x)$ and we take $\eta_s^N$ 
for $\eta$.
On the other hand, when only $\tilde{f}(u_0)=0$ is known, we have
\begin{align}  
& E_{\mu_{u_0}}\bigg[\; \sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\Big| \int_0^t  ds \; \sum_{x\in{\T_N}} 
  \; h(s,x) r_s^{N,\ell;1}(x)\Big|^p\; \bigg]\\
&\hskip 3mm \notag
  \le  C \Big( T^{(p-2)/2} N^{-p/2}\ell^{p} +T^{p-1} N^p \ell^{-p}\Big)
        \|f\|^p_{L^{p'}(\mu_{u_0})} \int_0^T \frac{1}{N}\sum_{x\in{\T_N}}|h(t,x)|^p dt,
\end{align}
where
\begin{align}  
r_s^{N,\ell;1}(x) = f(\tau_x \eta^{N}_s) 
  - \tilde{f}'(u_0)\Big\{\big(\eta^{N}_s\big)^{(\ell)}(x) - u_0\Big\}.
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Theorem 39 (Stegall's variational principle) of arXiv:2606.16636, 'Free energy of non-convex multi-species spin glasses with centered Ising spins'] Let $\mcl K$ be a convex and weakly compact set in a separable Hilbert space $\mcl H$, and let $g:\mcl K\to\R$ be an upper semi-continuous function bounded from above. [Prop P:properties-elpp of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Fix $\rho \in \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty\}$, and let $\mathcal{Q}^\rho$ be a subsequential limit in law of $\mathcal{Q}_n^{\rho_n}$ along a sequence $\rho_n \to \rho$. Then $\mathcal{Q}^\rho$ satisfies the following properties. In what follows, $c> 0$ are universal constants, and we define
		$\mathcal{G}^\rho(x, s; y, t) = \mathcal{Q}^\rho(x, s; y, t) + \frac{(x-y)^2}{(t-s)}$ for any $(x,s;y,t)\in \mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow$.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item \textup{(Independent increments)} For any disjoint collection of time intervals $(s_i, t_i), i\in\llbracket1, k \rrbracket$, the increments
		$\mathcal{Q}^\rho(\cdot, s_i; \cdot, t_i)$
		are independent.
		\item \textup{(Metric composition)} For any fixed $r < s < t$ and $x, y \ge 0$, we have
		$$
		\mathcal{Q}^\rho(x, s; y, t) = \max_{z \ge 0} \mathcal{Q}^\rho(x, s; z, r) + \mathcal{Q}^\rho(z, r; y, t).
		$$
		\item \textup{(KPZ scaling)} Fix $q > 0$, and consider the rescaled field
		$$
		\mathcal{Q}^{\rho, q}(x, s; y, t) := q^{-1} \mathcal{Q}^\rho(q^2x, q^3 s; q^2 y, q^3 t).
		$$
		Then $\mathcal{Q}^{\rho, q}$ is a subsequential limit of the sequence $\mathcal{Q}^{q \rho_n}_n$.
		\item \textup{(One-point tail bounds)} For $u = (x, s; y, s + t) \in \mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow$, and all $a > 0$,
		\begin{align*}
			\mathbb{P}( \mathcal{G}^\rho(u)< - a t^{1/3}) &\le 2\exp(-c a^3), \\
			\mathbb{P}( \mathcal{G}^\rho(u) > a t^{1/3} + t (\rho\vee 0)^2) &\le 2\exp\left(-c a^{3/2} \left(1 \wedge \frac{\sqrt{a}}{(\rho \vee 0) t^{1/3}}\right)\right).
		\end{align*}
		Furthermore, for $u = (0, s; 0, s + t)$ on the diagonal, we have the following Gaussian lower bound: for all $0 < a < t (\rho\vee 0)^2$,
		\begin{align*}
			\mathbb{P}( \mathcal{G}^\rho(u) < -a + t (\rho\vee 0)^2) &\le 2\exp\left(- \frac{ca^2}{(\rho\vee 0)t}\right).
		\end{align*}
		\item \textup{(Two-point spatial tail bound)} 
        There is a universal constant $C_0>0$, such that for any $u = (x, s; y, s+t), u' = (x, s; y + z, s+t)  \in \mathbb H^2_\uparrow$, and 
        $a>C_0\max(z^{3/2}/t, \sqrt{z}|x-y|/t, \sqrt{z} (\rho\vee 0))$,
        we have:
		\begin{equation}
			
\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{G}^\rho(u) - \mathcal{G}^\rho(u')| \ge a\sqrt{z}) \le 2 \exp(- c a^2).
		\end{equation}
		\item \textup{(Two-point temporal tail bound)} There is a universal constant $C_0>0$, such that for any $u = (x, s; y, s + t), u' = (x, s; y', s+t + r)  \in \mathbb H^2_\uparrow$, where $0<r<t$ and $(x, s), (y, s+t), (y', s + t + r)$ are all collinear, and $a > C_0\max(r^{2/3}(x-y)^2/t^2, r^{2/3}(\rho\vee 0)^2)$, we have:
		\begin{equation*}
			\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{G}^\rho(u) - \mathcal{G}^\rho(u')| \ge a r^{1/3}) \le 2 \exp(- c a^{3/2}).
		\end{equation*}
		\item \textup{(Basic parabolic shape estimate)} For any $(x, s; y, s + t) \in \mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow$ and $a, \delta > 0$ we have:
		\begin{equation*}
            \begin{split}
                \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}^\rho(x, s; y + z, s+ t) &\le t(\rho\vee 0)^2  + a t^{1/3} + \delta z^2 \text{ for all } z \in [-y, \infty)) \\
                &\ge 1 - 2\exp\left(-c_\delta a^{3/2} \left(1\wedge \frac{\sqrt{a}}{(\rho\vee 0) t^{1/3}}\right)\right),
            \end{split}
		\end{equation*}
        where $c_\delta$ is a constant depending on $\delta$.
		\item \textup{(Time stationarity and reversal)} For any $r \in \mathbb{R}$, we have

\mathcal{Q}^\rho(x, s; y, t) \stackrel{d}{=} \mathcal{Q}^\rho(x, s + r; y, t + r) \stackrel{d}{=} \mathcal{Q}^\rho(y, -t; x, -s),
        $$

[Corollary cor:sharp of arXiv:2608.25279, 'Provable Non-Acceleration of Standard Strang\\ Splittings of Kinetic Langevin Dynamics'] \begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm(i)] For the tuning
\begin{equation*}
 h=\frac1{4\sqrt\kappa},
 \qquad
 \gamma=4\sqrt\kappa,
 \qquad
 Q=Q_{1/(4\sqrt\kappa),\,4\sqrt\kappa}^{U},
\end{equation*}
there is a universal
constant $C_1<\infty$ such that, for every $\kappa>1$, $d\ge1$,
$U\in\mathcal U_\kappa^d$, every initial state $z$, and every
$\varepsilon\in(0,1)$,
\begin{equation*}
 t_{\mathrm{mix}}(z,\varepsilon;Q,\pi)
 \le C_1\kappa\log\!\left(\frac{C_1\kappa(1+W_2(\delta_z,\pi))}{\varepsilon}\right),
\end{equation*}
where $\pi$ is the unique invariant law of $Q$.
\item[\rm(ii)] Let $\mathfrak t$
be any numerically
stable fixed-parameter OBABO tuning rule, let $C,c>0$ and $a,b\ge0$
be constants, let $\tau:(1,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ satisfy
$\tau(\kappa)=o(\kappa)$ as $\kappa\to\infty$, and let
$\kappa_0>1$. Then there exist $\kappa\ge\kappa_0$ and
$U\in\mathcal U_\kappa^2$ such that $Q_{h_\kappa,\gamma_\kappa}^U$ has a
unique invariant law $\pi$, and there are $z\in\mathbb R^4$ and
$n\in\mathbb N$ for which
\begin{equation}
 \norm{\delta_z(Q_{h_\kappa,\gamma_\kappa}^U)^n-\pi}_{\mathrm{TV}}
 >C\kappa^a\bigl(1+W_2(\delta_z,\pi)\bigr)^b
   \exp\!\left(-\frac{cn}{\tau(\kappa)}\right).
\end{equation}
In particular, no such bound holds with $\tau(\kappa)=\kappa^\alpha$
for any $\alpha<1$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def:scaleFunction of arXiv:2412.05030, 'Characterization of Subordinate Symmetric Markov Processes'] For constants $0 < \alpha_1 \le \alpha_2$, 
  we say a continuous function $\psi : [0,\infty) \to [0,\infty)$ satisfies $LU(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$
  if $\psi$ is strictly increasing, $\psi(0) = 0$, $\psi(1) = 1$  and 
  there exists constants $C \ge 1$ such that
  \begin{align}
    C^{-1} \left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^{\alpha_1} \le \frac{\psi(R)}{\psi(r)} \le C \left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^{\alpha_2}, \qquad 0 < r \le R.
  \end{align}
  We call such function $\psi$ a scale function.
title: Scale function

$f\in C^{1+\beta}_0([0,1];\mathbb R^d)$ with

        s^{2\alpha}D_{0^+}^{\alpha}(s^{-\alpha}f_s)
    \right\|_{C^1([0,1];\mathbb R^d)}
    \le C\|f\|_{1+\beta}.
\end{equation}

body:
[Theorem 22 (Two-parameter rough integral on rectangular domains) of arXiv:2605.08844, 'Signature Kernel and Schwinger-Dyson Kernel Equations as Two-Parameter Rough Differential '] Let 
\[
Z \in \mathcal{D}^{p, q}_{\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}}\big([a, b] \times [c,d], \mathrm{Hom}(V \boxtimes W, F)\big).
\] 
Then the limit
\[
\int_{[a,b] \times [c,d]} Z_{s, u} \, d(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y})  
   :=  \lim_{\left|\mathcal{P} \times \mathcal{D}\right| \to 0} 
   \sum_{\mathcal{P}\times \mathcal{D}} \Omega^Z
\]
exists and satisfies the estimate
\begin{align*}
\Bigg|
\int_{[a,b]\times[c,d]} Z_{s,u}\, d(\mathbf{X}_s,\mathbf{Y}_u)
- \Omega^Z\begin{pmatrix} a, b \\ c, d \end{pmatrix}
\Bigg|
&\le C_{p,q,T}\Big[
      A(\theta,T,\mathbf{R})\,
      \omega_{\mathbf{X}}(a,b)^{\theta}\,
      \omega_{\mathbf{Y}}(c,d)^{\theta} \\
&\qquad
      + B_X(c,d)\,\omega_{\mathbf{X}}(a,b)^{\theta}
      + B_Y(a,b)\,\omega_{\mathbf{Y}}(c,d)^{\theta}
\Big].
\end{align*}

where $\theta = \min(\frac{\floor{p} + 1}{p}, \frac{\floor{q} + 1}{q})$ and 
\begin{align*}
&A(p, q, \mathbf{R}) 
= \left( \sup_{j \in [0:\kappa)} \| \mathbf{X}^{(j+1)} \|_{p_j} \right)
  \left( \sup_{k \in  [0:\lambda)} \| \tilde{\mathbf{X}}^{(k+1)} \|_{\tilde{p}_k} \right)
  \left( \sup_{(j,k)\in [0:\kappa) \times [0:\lambda)} \| \mathbf{R}^{(j,k)} \|_{(q_j,\tilde{q}_k)} \right),\\
&B_{X}(c,d)
= 
\sup_{(j,k)\in [0:\kappa) \times [0:\lambda)}\left[ 
  \|\mathbf{X}^{(j+1)}\|_{\frac{p}{j+1}}\,
  \|\mathbf{Y}^{(k+1)}\|_{\frac{q}{k+1}}\,
  \big\| R^{1, (j,k)}
       \big\|_{\frac{p}{\kappa - j}}\,
  \omega_{\mathbf{Y}}(c,d)^{\frac{k+1}{q}}
\right],\\
&B_{Y}(a,b)
= \sup_{(j,k)\in [0:\kappa) \times [0:\lambda)}
\left[
   \|\mathbf{X}^{(j+1)}\|_{\frac{p}{j+1}}\,
  \|\mathbf{Y}^{(k+1)}\|_{\frac{q}{k+1}}\,
  \big\| R^{2,(j,k)}\!
       \big\|_{\frac{q}{\lambda - k}}\,
  \omega_{\mathbf{X}}(a,b)^{\frac{j+1}{p}}
\right].
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Two-parameter rough integral on rectangular domains

\|\bar{z}'(t)\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \|v(t)\|_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}(t)$}}}^2,

[Lemma 47 (Long-range order implies positive frequency) of arXiv:2504.02435, 'Poisson-Voronoi percolation in higher rank'] Let $\omega_p^{(\lambda)}$ be Poisson-Voronoi percolation with parameters $\lambda>0$ and $p\in(0,1]$ such that
    $$
    \inf_{x,y\in X} \mathbb P_{p}^{(\lambda)}\big( x \leftrightarrow y \big) \geq \delta
    $$
    for some $\delta>0$.
    Let $\tilde{\beta}$ be the map from Theorem~\ref{thm:ClusterFrequency}. Then

body:
[Thm 4 of arXiv:2608.13208, 'Universality in dimension $1$ of kinetically constrained lattice gases'] KCLGs in one dimension divide in three universality
classes:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $c(-1,0,\bone_{(-\infty,-1]})\neq0$ and $c(-1,0,\bone_{[0,\infty]})\neq0$,
then $q_{c}=0$. In this case the model is \emph{noncooperative} (see
\cite{Shapira2024Noncooperative} and Section \ref{subsec:noncooperative}
below).
\item If $c(-1,0,\bone_{(-\infty,-1]})=0$ and $c(-1,0,\bone_{[0,\infty)})=0$,
then $q_{c}=1$. We say in this case that the model is \emph{blocked}.
\item If $c(-1,0,\bone_{(-\infty,-1]})\neq0$ and $c(-1,0,\bone_{[0,\infty)})=0$
or vice versa, then $q_{c}\in(0,1)$. We call such models \emph{one-sided}.
\end{enumerate}
By $\bone_{(-\infty,-1]}$ (respectively $\bone_{[0,\infty)}$) we
mean the configuration filled in $(-\infty,-1]$ (respectively $[0,\infty)$)
and empty elsewhere. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 4 of arXiv:2608.13208

body:
[Lemma 24 of arXiv:2608.18557, 'Randomly Permuted Orthogonal Products and Fast Dimension Reduction'] There exist couplings of an ORA walk \(Q_T^{\mathrm O}\) and an
	S-ORA walk \(Q_T^{\mathrm S}\), both of length \(T\), such that,
	possibly under different couplings,
	\[
	Q_T^{\mathrm S}
	=
	G_T^{\mathrm L}Q_T^{\mathrm O},
	\qquad 
	Q_T^{\mathrm S}
	=
	Q_T^{\mathrm O}G_T^{\mathrm R},
	\]
	where \(G_T^{\mathrm L}\), \(G_T^{\mathrm R} \in \mathcal H_d\) are signed
	permutation matrices. Consequently, for every $I\subseteq [d]$ and every $X\subseteq \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, we have
	\[
	\norm{Q_T^{\mathrm S}}_\infty
	\stackrel{\mathrm d}=
	\norm{Q_T^{\mathrm O}}_\infty,
	\qquad
	\kappa_I(Q_T^{\mathrm S})
	\stackrel{\mathrm d}=
	\kappa_I(Q_T^{\mathrm O}),
	\qquad
	\Theta_{Q_T^{\mathrm S}}(X)
	\stackrel{\mathrm d}=
	\Theta_{Q_T^{\mathrm O}}(X).
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 24 of arXiv:2608.18557

[Thm eq:RootDecomp of arXiv:2506.18207, 'Cartan's Path Development, the Logarithmic Signature and a Conjecture of Lyons-Sidorova'] Let $\Delta$ be the set of
all nonzero roots with respect to a given Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak{h}.$
Then $\mathfrak{g}$ can be written as the direct sum 
\begin{equation}
\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{h}+\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}\mathfrak{g}^{\alpha}.
\end{equation}
In this decomposition, one has $\dim\mathfrak{g}^{\alpha}=1$ for
each $\alpha\in\Delta$. Moreover, if $\alpha,\beta,\alpha+\beta\in\Delta$
then $[\mathfrak{g}^{\alpha},\mathfrak{g}^{\beta}]=\mathfrak{g}^{\alpha+\beta}.$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem VEV of arXiv:2609.02409, 'Membranes and Maps'] [OP06:GW-H]
    The connected vacuum expectation value $\langle \mathcal{E}_{k_1}(z_1) \cdots \mathcal{E}_{k_n}(z_n) \rangle^{\circ}$ vanishes for $n>1$ whenever $k_1\leq 0$, $k_n\geq 0$, or $\sum_j k_j\neq 0$. If $k_1 > 0$, it satisfies the recursion
    \begin{equation}
        \left\langle \mathcal{E}_{k_1}(z_1) \cdots \mathcal{E}_{k_n}(z_n) \right\rangle^{\circ}
        =
        \sum_{i=2}^n
        \varsigma\Bigl(
            \det\begin{psmallmatrix} k_1 & k_i \\ z_1 & z_i \end{psmallmatrix}
        \Bigr)
        \left\langle
            \mathcal{E}_{k_2}(z_2) \cdots
            \mathcal{E}_{k_i+k_1}(z_i+z_1) \cdots
            \mathcal{E}_{k_n}(z_n)
        \right\rangle^{\circ} \,,
    \end{equation}
    with initial condition $\langle \mathcal{E}_{k}(z) \rangle^{\circ} = \frac{\delta_{k,0}}{\varsigma(z)}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem VEV of arXiv:2609.02409

Let a<b be finite, f in C-infinity([a,b]), t_1,...,t_m distinct nodes in [a,b], m>=1, and k_1,...,k_m positive integers. Put D=sum_i k_i and g(t)=product_i(t-t_i)^(k_i). There is a unique polynomial p of degree<D with p^(j)(t_i)=f^(j)(t_i) for 0<=j<k_i. For t in [a,b] outside the nodes, there exists xi strictly between min(t,t_1,...,t_m) and max(t,t_1,...,t_m) such that f(t)-p(t)=f^(D)(xi)g(t)/D!. At a node the error is zero; no strict-interior witness is asserted for a collapsed interval. In particular, if every k_i is even and f^(D)>=0 on [a,b], then p(t)<=f(t) throughout [a,b]. Derivatives at endpoints are understood one-sided.
a<b finite; f smooth on the closed interval
distinct real nodes inside [a,b]; all multiplicities positive integers
the strict-interior remainder assertion is for nonnodes

[Proposition 209 (The main below-top-order a priori estimates for the transport variables and the modified fluid variables) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] Let $N = \Ntop$ and let $\fluxcontrolVort_N(\ubar,u),  \dots, \bulkcontrolDivGradEnt_N(\ubar,u)$ be the $L^2$-transport-controlling quantities as defined in Def.\,\ref{D:FUNDAMENTALTRANSPORTL2CONTROLLINGQUANTITIES}. 
	Under the parameter size-assumptions of Sect.\,\ref{SS:PARAMETERSIZEASSUMPTIONS}, the data-assumptions of Sects.\,\ref{S:ASSUMPTIONSONTHEDATA}, 
	and the bootstrap assumptions of Sect.\,\ref{S:BOOTSTRAPEVERYTHINGEXCEPTENERGIES},
	there exists a constant $C > 0$
	such that the following estimates hold for 
	$(\ubar,u) \in [\leftubar,\ubarboot) \times [\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]$: 
\begin{subequations} 
	\begin{align}
		\fluxcontrolVort_{\le N} (\ubar,u) + \bulkcontrolVort_{\le N} (\ubar,u)
		& \leq C \initialsmalldoublenull^2,  \\
		\fluxcontrolGradEnt_{\le N} (\ubar,u) + \bulkcontrolGradEnt_{\le N} (\ubar,u)& \leq C \initialsmalldoublenull^2,  \\
		\fluxcontrolVortVort_{\le N-1} (\ubar,u) + \bulkcontrolVortVort_{\le N-1} (\ubar,u) & \leq C \initialsmalldoublenull^2,  \\	
		\fluxcontrolDivGradEnt_{\le N-1} (\ubar,u) + \bulkcontrolDivGradEnt_{\le N-1} (\ubar,u) & \leq C \initialsmalldoublenull^2.  
	\end{align}
\end{subequations}	
In addition, let $\toricontrolVort,\toricontrolGradEnt,\toricontrolVortVort, \toricontrolDivGradEnt$ denote the $L^2$-controlling quantities on the double-null tori  defined in Def.\,\ref{D:FUNDAMENTALTRANSPORTL2CONTROLLINGQUANTITIES}. Then, the following a priori estimates hold:
\begin{subequations}
		\begin{align}
			\toricontrolVort_{\le N - 1}(\ubar,u), 
			\,
			\toricontrolGradEnt_{\le N - 1} 
			& 
			\leq C \initialsmall^2, 
			 \\
			\toricontrolVortVort_{\le N - 2}(\ubar,u),
			\,
			\toricontrolDivGradEnt_{\le N - 2}(\ubar,u)
			& \leq C \initialsmall^2.
			
	\end{align}
\end{subequations} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: The main below-top-order a priori estimates for the transport variables and the modified fluid variables

[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2605.17494, 'Generalized intersection exponents and local cut points for three-dimensional Brownian loo'] Fix $\alpha_*$ in $I_0$. Let $\Lc^{\alpha}$ be the subcritical Brownian loop soup in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Controlled generators, exact finite-state diagnostic, coupling, renewal reward or capacity comparison Result: A two-job calculation isolates the value of probing. Job A has size 0.01 with probability 0.9 and 100 with probability 0.1; job B has known size 2. SERPT initially selects B because E[A]=10.009. Completing B before A gives expected sum of completion times 14.009. Serving A for 0.01, then serving B if A survives, gives 0.9*(0.01+2.01)+0.1*(102+2.01)=12.219. The Gittins stopping ratio at probe duration 0.01 is 0.01/0.9, smaller than B rank 2. Any approximation proof based only on expected residual size loses this probing advantage. Check: In the long-A branch, total A completion time is 102 after the intervening two units for B; omitting those two units would give a false larger improvement. Both strategies are enumerated by the two possible A sizes. Obstruction: This finite instance does not establish a stationary approximation factor, nor distinguish the full worst-case ratios of SERPT and M-SERPT.

Let X, Y, Z be Banach spaces, T in B(X,Y) and S in B(Y,Z) both Fredholm. Then S T in B(X,Z) is Fredholm and ind(S T) = ind S + ind T. In particular, composing with an invertible operator does not change the index, and if S T is a compact perturbation of the identity then ind S = -ind T.
X, Y, Z are Banach spaces
T in B(X,Y) and S in B(Y,Z) are both Fredholm

\[
\iota_X\colon X \to  S,
\qquad
\iota_Y\colon Y \to  S
\]
be smooth representable morphisms.
Assume that \(X\) and \(Y\) are HT-split over \(S\).
Then
\[
Z \defeq X\times_S Y
\]
is HT-split over \(S\).

[Theorem theo.generalcluster of arXiv:2411.19145, 'On the intersection of critical percolation clusters and other tree-like random graphs'] Assume that $\mathcal G$ satisfies the BK inequality and (equation Halpha of the paper), for some $\alpha\in (d/2,d)$. Let $(\mathcal C_0^i)_{i\ge 1}$ be independent copies of the connected component of $0$ in $\mathcal G$. 
\begin{itemize}
\item[$(i)$] If $\alpha \in (\frac{(k+1)d}{2k},\frac{kd}{2(k-1)})$, for some $k\ge 2$, then there exists $\kappa>0$, such that  
$$\mathbb E\left[\exp\left(\kappa \cdot |\mathcal C_0^1 \cap \dots\cap \mathcal C_0^k|^{\frac{2\alpha}{d}-1}\right)\right]<\infty.  $$
\item[$(ii)$] If $\alpha = \tfrac{kd}{2(k-1)}$, for some $k\ge 3$, then there exists $\kappa>0$, such that for any $t>e$, 
$$\mathbb P(|\mathcal C_0^1 \cap \dots\cap \mathcal C_0^k|>t)\le \exp\Big(-\kappa (\frac t{\log t})^{\frac {2\alpha}d-1}\Big).$$
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let Gamma be a C^2 embedded (D-M)-dimensional manifold of local minima of a C^3 function L on R^D, with rank(Hess L(x))=M for every x in Gamma. Let U be an open neighborhood of Gamma such that gradient flow from each point in U exists for all t>=0 and converges to an endpoint Phi(x) in Gamma. Assume Phi:U->Gamma is C^2. Then for x in Gamma, D Phi(x) is the Euclidean orthogonal projection onto T_x Gamma. In particular, ker(Hess L(x))=T_x Gamma, range(Hess L(x)) is its normal space, D Phi(x) is identity on tangent vectors, and it vanishes on normal vectors. This derivative assertion is at x in Gamma; it does not say Phi agrees with the nearest-point projection away from Gamma. Source: Li, Wang and Arora, Lemma 4.3, PDF p7, proof PDF pp29--30.
Gamma is a C^2 embedded manifold of local minima of L in Euclidean R^D
L is C^3 and Hess L has constant rank equal to codimension M on Gamma
U is an open neighborhood of Gamma with globally existing convergent gradient flow
The endpoint map Phi:U->Gamma is C^2

body: Let U subset R^n be open. A function u: U -> R is harmonic if it is twice continuously differentiable on U (u in C^2(U)) and satisfies Laplace's equation Delta u = sum_{i=1}^n partial^2 u/partial x_i^2 = 0 at every point of U.
title: Harmonic Function

[Theorem intro:1-d continuum T>0:FRSB of arXiv:2605.05631, 'Wandering Exponents and the Free Energy of the High-Dimensional Elastic Polymer'] Let us assume that $(B''(x))^{-1/3}$ is strictly concave and fix $\beta,t>0$. If ((eqn:Larkin equation of the paper)) has a solution and $\mu<\mu_{Lar}(\beta;t)$ then the model is FRSB. Otherwise the model is RS. Moreover, when the model is FRSB, the Parisi pair is given by 
		\[
		\zeta_c([0,s])=\begin{cases}
			\beta^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{t}\right)^{1/3}\frac{-B'''(2(q_c-s))}{3\left(B''(2(q_c-s))\right)^{4/3}};\quad s\in [q_0,q_*)\\
			1;\quad s\in [q_*,q_c]\\
			0;\quad s\in [0,q_0)
		\end{cases},
		\]
		where $(q_0,q_*,q_c)$ is the unique triple with $0\le q_0<q_*<q_c$ which satisfies:
		\[q_c-q_*=\frac{1}{\beta\sqrt{\mu_{Lar}(\beta;t)t}},\;\;\; 2B''(2(q_c-q_0))=\sqrt{\mu^3t},\;\; -B'(2(q_c-q_0))=\frac{q_0}{\mu^3t}. \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem intro:1-d continuum T>0:FRSB of arXiv:2605.05631

Own-work draft; proof (unaudited). CLASSICAL METHOD, own presentation; proof (unaudited), not a novelty claim. Let B be an invertible real dxd matrix,K=B*(c+closed Euclidean ball of radius r),r>=0,contained in an open differentiability domain. Let F_theta be C1 there for every admissible parameter theta. Suppose Z encloses every B^-1 F_theta(Bc),an exact new center c_new has distance at most e from every point of Z,and ||B^-1 DF_theta(y)B||2<=q for all y in K and all admissible theta. Then every x in K satisfies ||B^-1 F_theta(x)-c_new||2<=q*r+e. For a real matrix C,one may certify its Euclidean operator norm by ||C||2^2<=max_i sum_j |(C^T C)_ij|. Outward-rounded interval bounds on the derivative and central image therefore give r_next=up(q*r+e),including midpoint rounding. The domain test and invertibility must be verified; a floating-point center alone gives no error bound.

body: A space is a Baire space if every countable intersection of dense open sets is dense. Baire category theorem: every complete (pseudo)metric space - hence every Banach space - is a Baire space, and so is every locally compact Hausdorff space. It underlies the uniform boundedness principle, the open mapping theorem, and the closed graph theorem.
title: Baire category theorem

If X_N has a circular-law limit and P is a fixed complex polynomial, spectral mapping gives mu_(P(X_N))=P_pushforward(mu_(X_N)) exactly, including algebraic multiplicities. The continuous mapping theorem therefore yields the pushforward of the circular law. The Brown measure of P(c) is the same pushforward, by factorizing P(z)-lambda and using multiplicativity of the Fuglede-Kadison determinant. Check: For each test function h bounded and continuous, h composed with P is bounded and continuous, so weak convergence passes through P. At the logarithmic-potential level, P(c)-lambda factors into commuting(c-root_j) terms, and determinant multiplicativity gives the same transformed Brown measure. Existing real-Gaussian and Bernoulli circular laws supply the initial one-matrix convergence. Obstruction: For several noncommuting input matrices there is no joint eigenvalue spectral mapping. [Lemma 18 (Tail flow from general initial data) of arXiv:2608.10992, '2608.10992'] Let $\mu$ be a probability law on $\N$. There exists a unique family
$q^\mu=(q_k^\mu)_{k\geq1}$ such that $q_1^\mu\equiv1$,
$q_k^\mu\in C^1([0,\infty))$ for $k\geq2$,
$q_k^\mu(0)=\mu([k,\infty))$, and
\begin{equation}

        (q_k^\mu)'
        =
        \sum_{u=1}^{k-1}q_u^\mu
        (q_{k-u}^\mu-q_k^\mu)
        +q_k^\mu(1-q_k^\mu),
        \qquad k\geq2.
\end{equation}
For every $t\geq0$,
\[
        1=q_1^\mu(t)\geq q_2^\mu(t)\geq\cdots\geq0,
\]
and each $q_k^\mu$ is non-decreasing in $t$. Consequently,
$q^\mu(t)$ is the tail of a unique probability law $\mu_t$ on
$\N\cup\{\infty\}$, with
\[
        \mu_t(\{\infty\})
        =
        q_\infty^\mu(t)
        :=
        \lim_{k\to\infty}q_k^\mu(t),
\]
and $(\mu_t)_{t\geq0}$ is non-decreasing in stochastic order.

Cards are drawn from the bottom of the deck and placed on a shelf uniformly at random. Once a shelf is chosen, the card is placed at the top of the existing pile or at the bottom with probability $1/2$.

\[
 \|\mathscr L(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger\mathscr L^*\|\le d^2.
\tag{3.2.4}
\]
The mixed blocks satisfy
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|\mathscr D(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger\mathscr G^*\|&\le\sqrt2,
 &\|\mathscr G(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger\mathscr D^*\|&\le\sqrt2,\\
 \|\mathscr L(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger\mathscr D^*\|&\le d,
 &\|\mathscr D(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger\mathscr L^*\|&\le d,\\
 \|\mathscr L(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger\mathscr G^*\|&\le\sqrt2\,d,
 &\|\mathscr G(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger\mathscr L^*\|&\le\sqrt2\,d.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.2.4a}
\]
All these bounds remain true after tensoring by $I_V$.  They also hold,
with the same constants, when $(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger$ is replaced
everywhere by a finite Green kernel
$R_s=\sum_{\ell=0}^s\mathcal K^\ell$ acting between centered channels.

body: Record of an outside reading, 14 October 2026, of Y. Shmalo, The relaxation time does not control the normal approximation of stationary additive functionals (repository yspennstate/relaxation-time-normal-approximation, commit 40395f256c67), which answers Aldous-Fill Open Problem 4.30 negatively. The reader (a Claude model, fresh clone, no access to the author's internal reviews) found it correct: the construction answers the question as printed (Aldous-Fill p. 137; 'Open Problem 30' of the 1994 chapter, p. 26), and because it evaluates the distribution function at x = 0 the answer holds under any normalization; the parameter the question omits is sigma^2/tau_2, with sigma^2 of order 2b^2/s^2. All five findings are presentational: display (1.2) is a weakening of Lezaud's Theorem 3.1, and Remark 2 lacks one limsup line. An independent sampler gives P(S_8 <= 0) = 0.8838 +- 0.0051 at b = 2 against the repository's 0.8844, and the bound P(S_s <= 0) >= 1 - 4/s held on all 25 (b, s) pairs tried. A second independent reading (a Codex model) was still in progress on 14 October. Not refereed.
title: Outside reading of the answer to Aldous-Fill Open Problem 4.30, 14 October 2026: found correct, a second reading in progress

[Lemma Approximate capacity additivity of arXiv:2606.23025, 'Spectral-Capacitary Bounds for Homological Recovery from Reflected Brownian Trajectories'] Let
\(A_{i},A_{j} \subset M\) be targets, each comparable to an
intrinsic \(\varepsilon\)-ball, whose intrinsic distance is at
least a separation parameter \(\varrho > 0\) with
\(\varepsilon < \varepsilon_{0}\varrho\). Then there exists
\(\theta = \theta(\varepsilon/\varrho) \in \lbrack 0,1)\), with
\(\theta(t) \rightarrow 0\) as \(t \rightarrow 0\), such
that

\[(1 - \theta)\left( \operatorname{Cap}_{N}\left( A_{i} \right) + \operatorname{Cap}_{N}\left( A_{j} \right) \right) \leq \operatorname{Cap}_{N}\left( A_{i} \cup A_{j} \right) \leq \operatorname{Cap}_{N}\left( A_{i} \right) + \operatorname{Cap}_{N}\left( A_{j} \right).\]

Consequently, by the comparison of Proposition 5.1, the killed
eigenvalues satisfy, for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\),

\[\lambda_{A_{i} \cup A_{j}} \geq c_{ce}\, C_{ce}^{- 1}(1 - \theta)\left( \lambda_{A_{i}} + \lambda_{A_{j}} \right).\]
