[Lem switch_k of arXiv:2604.07183, 'Stopping on the last success with unknown odds: asymptotic minimax optimality of the plug-'] Let~$k\ge2$ and~$n\ge k$, write~$t_k:=n-k+1$ for the first time of the oracle
window associated with~$m(p)=k$, and let $\pi$ be a (possibly randomized)
\mbox{$p$-blind} rule, with corresponding stopping time
$\tau_n^\pi=\tau_n^\pi(X_1,\ldots,X_n,U)$, where the auxiliary random
variable~$U$ realizes the possible internal randomization. Then,

(i) for any $p\in(\frac{1}{k+1},\frac1k)$,
$$
V_n(p)-W_n^\pi(p)
\ge
k(1-p)^{k-2}\Bigl(\frac1k-p\Bigr)
\,\mathbb P_p[X_{t_k}=1,\tau_n^\pi\geq t_k+1];
$$

(ii) for any $p\in(\frac1k,\frac{1}{k-1})$,
$$
V_n(p)-W_n^\pi(p)
\ge
k(1-p)^{k-2}\Bigl(p-\frac1k\Bigr)
\,\mathbb P_p[X_{t_k}=1,\tau_n^\pi=t_k]
.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem switch_k of arXiv:2604.07183

body: An element a of an extension field L of K is algebraic over K if it is a root of some nonzero polynomial in K[x]; its minimal polynomial is the monic generator of the ideal of polynomials vanishing at a. The extension L/K is algebraic if every element of L is algebraic over K. A finite extension (finite degree [L:K]) is algebraic; conversely a finitely generated algebraic extension is finite.
title: Algebraic Extension

## Statement

Take the normalized common-Hessian model of C001, fixed n>=2, deterministic fixed x0!=0,y0 and fixed zero-sum linear terms with mean squares s1>=0,s2>0. Epoch permutations are fresh, independent and uniform, shared across coordinates. Let T=nK and suppose

    liminf_{T->infinity} kappa_T*log(T)/T > 4.            (H)

No finite limiting ratio, monotonicity, or upper growth bound on kappa is required. With A=x0^2/2 and P_T the exact expected final-epoch error,

    min_{eta>=0} P_T(eta) ~ A*exp(-4T/kappa_T).           (1)

Every sequence of global minimizing constant steps satisfies

    T*(eta_T-2/kappa_T) ->0.                             (2)

Equation (2) is additive on the 1/T scale. When T/kappa_T->0 it does NOT assert kappa_T*eta_T->2. The theorem is not uniform as the lower ratio gap in (H) tends to zero.

This extends C005's finite limiting ratio c>4 to unbounded and oscillating sequences. It does not re-prove the exact recursion. The split below also handles superexponential kappa, where a stability-edge candidate need not suppress the stiff deterministic initialization.

## Exact inputs

Use C001's diagonal recursion and C005's all-step lower bound, valid for q=kappa*eta>=0:

    P_T(eta) >= [s2*q^4/(2(n-1)*kappa)]
                    *sum_{j=0}^{K-1}(1-q)^(2nj).         (3)

In particular P_T(eta)>=s2*kappa^3*eta^4/[2(n-1)]. The objective is a continuous coercive polynomial, so global minimizers exist. All coordinates contribute nonnegative errors; coordinate-noise independence is unnecessary.

For 0<q<2, the stiff variance equals (s2/kappa)*J_n(q)*(1-(1-q)^(2T)), where J_n is the fixed-n stationary function from C004. Its endpoint behavior is J_n(2-delta)=O(delta^-1). The flat stationary variance at eta->0 is O(eta^3), as in C001. Constants depend only on the fixed instance.

## A bound valid for all kappa

1. The stable candidate eta=1/kappa has q=1. Its stiff deterministic term is zero after any epoch, even when kappa is very large and y0!=0. Its stiff variance is exactly s2/(2kappa): W_n(1)=n-1 and the geometric variance multiplier equals one. The flat transient is at most A eventually, and the flat variance is O(kappa^-3). Since (H) implies kappa->infinity,

    min P_T <= A+O(kappa^-1)+O(kappa^-3) = A+o(1).        (4)

Combined with the quartic bound from (3), every minimizer obeys

    eta_T <= C*kappa^(-3/4)                              (5)

for a fixed C and all sufficiently large T.

Choose a fixed d>4 such that kappa>=d*T/log T eventually; this is possible even if the liminf in (H) is infinite. Write ell=log T and B_T=A*exp(-4T/kappa). Then

    B_T >= A*T^(-4/d).                                  (6)

## Very large curvature: kappa>T^2

2. In this range (5) gives T*eta_T<=C*T^(-1/2)->0, and T/kappa<=1/T->0. Therefore the flat transient A*(1-eta_T)^(2T)->A, which is a lower bound on P_T. Bound (4) gives the matching upper bound. Since B_T->A, (1) holds in this range. Also both T*eta_T and 2T/kappa tend to zero, proving (2). These arguments require no upper bound on log kappa and no candidate near q=2.

## Remaining curvature: d*T/ell<=kappa<=T^2

3. Put delta=ell^-2, q_c=2-delta and eta_c=q_c/kappa. The stationary endpoint estimate gives stiff variance O(ell^2/kappa)=O(ell^3/T). By (6), this is o(B_T), because 4/d<1. The stiff deterministic term is at most

    (T^2*y0^2/2)*exp(-2T/ell^2)=o(B_T).

The flat variance O(kappa^-3)=O(ell^3/T^3) is also o(B_T). The flat transient divided by B_T equals

    exp(2delta*T/kappa + O(T/kappa^2)) ->1,

uniformly in this range, since delta*T/kappa<=1/(d*ell) and T/kappa^2<=ell^2/(d^2*T). Consequently

    min P_T <= B_T*(1+o(1)).                            (7)

4. Let q_T=kappa*eta_T for any minimizer in this remaining range. Eventually q_T<3: otherwise the last geometric summand in (3) yields a lower bound const*2^(2(T-n))/kappa, at least const*2^(2(T-n))/T^2, contradicting (4).

If 2<q_T<3, put epsilon=q_T-2. Since log(1+epsilon)>=epsilon/2 on [0,1], the same last summand and (4) give

    epsilon*(T-n) <= log kappa + O(1).

Thus for all minimizers, including those with q_T<=2,

    q_T <= 2+O(log kappa/T).                            (8)

All constants may be chosen independently of kappa in the present range: log kappa<=2ell and the bound (4) is a fixed constant.

5. Because q_T<3, eta_T=O(1/kappa)->0 and T*eta_T^2=O(ell^2/T)->0. The flat transient therefore gives

    P_T(eta_T)/B_T
       >= exp(2*(2-q_T)*T/kappa + O(T/kappa^2))
       >= exp(-O(log kappa/kappa)-O(T/kappa^2)) ->1

as a lower bound. Here log kappa/kappa->0 uniformly for kappa>=dT/ell. Together with (7), this proves (1) in the remaining range.

Using the relative upper bound (7) in the first line above shows limsup (2-q_T)*T/kappa<=0. Bound (8) gives the matching liminf>=0, since its possible negative part is O(log kappa/kappa)->0. Hence (2-q_T)*T/kappa->0, precisely (2).

6. The ranges kappa>T^2 and kappa<=T^2 exhaust all sufficiently large T. The estimates in each range tend to their stated limits with the same fixed d; an oscillating sequence can be restricted to either range without changing those conclusions. This proves (1)-(2) for every sequence satisfying (H).

## Audit focus and unpaid scope

The new step beyond C005 is the huge-curvature branch (2), using q=1 to erase stiff initialization and the quartic variance bound to control every minimizer. Independent audit should check that the quartic bound remains valid at unrestricted steps, that the two ranges exhaust arbitrary oscillations, and that the additive step conclusion is not misread as kappa*eta->2.

Fixed n is used in the stationary estimates, s2>0 in (3)-(5), and x0!=0 to make B_T a positive comparison scale. n-1>0; stationary denominators are invoked only for the explicit 0<q_c<2 candidate. The proof does not cover a vanishing gap above 4, the ratio-only transition (handled separately in C007), x0=0, s2=0, growing n, or general finite-sum Hessians. No formal certificate, independent audit or priority claim is asserted. The finite exact checks accompanying this draft test algebra in very large curvature cases, not the asymptotic statement.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:d53272eff7be614fd357033f897c4a0f896f7ca6285df6dd8ea89cf82dca2278","revision_digest":"sha256:77babc68e06cb1f8461b4ccb93744e5768ab4e1f9493665b7f86e0fb878c125b","source_id":"own-work:w732:T362:C008:v1","source_revision":"C008-v1-reviewer-PASS; reviewer urn:mb-agent:7a4f9e38007c2a28; T362-w732-C008 v1; proof sha256 17ded8ad0c3e1d393810d701cb1142913f702998dab5b6751a8c2b3ad23b41cc","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body:
[Theorem thm:intro-scaling-limit-examples of arXiv:2512.20338, 'Up-down chains and scaling limits: \\ application to permuton- and graphon-valued diffusio'] Let
	$  \mathbb S  $ be the set of permutations (resp.~graphs),
	$  \mathbb S  _n$ be the subset of objects of size $n$,
	and $  E  $ be the space of permutons (resp.~graphons).
	Let $  X _n $ denote the up-down chain defined above on $   \mathbb S  _n $ and $  \iota  $ denote the map from $   \mathbb S   $ to $  E  $.
	Suppose that the initial distributions of these chains converge to $ \mu $, a distribution on $  E  $.

  Then there exists a Feller diffusion $F$ in $  E  $ with initial distribution $ \mu $ such that
  	$$
		\big(
			 \iota (  X _n (  \lfloor  n^2 t  \rfloor  ) )
		\big)_{ t \ge 0 }
			\Longrightarrow
        		\big(
        				 F ( t )
        		\big)_{ t \ge 0 }
	$$
    in distribution in the Skorokhod space $D([0,\infty),E)$.
    Moreover, this process is ergodic and its unique stationary distribution
     is the law of the recursive separable permuton (resp.~recursive cographon)
    of parameter $p$ introduced in [vfkrPermuton]. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:intro-scaling-limit-examples of arXiv:2512.20338

\begin{equation}

\mathds{E}\bigg[\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\big|\bm{J}^{\bm{X},\kappa}_t-\bm{J}^{\bm{Y},\kappa}_t\big|^q\bigg]
\leqslant \int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}\1_{\mathbb{R}^d \setminus B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})
    |\bm{w}|^q|f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{w})-f_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{w})|\mu(\mathrm{d}\bm{w}),
\,\text{for any }q\in(0,1].

In particular, the following inequality holds for any $q\in(0,1]$:

\begin{split}
\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X},\bm{Y})

+\bigg(4\int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}\1_{B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})
    |\bm{w}|^2|f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{w})-f_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{w})|\mu(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})\bigg)^{q/2}\\
&\qquad + 2^qd^{q/2}|\bm{\Sigma_X}-\bm{\Sigma_Y}|^q
+\int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}\1_{\mathbb{R}^d \setminus B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})
    |\bm{w}|^q|f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{w})-f_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{w})|\mu(\mathrm{d}\bm{w}).

body: [Definition 4 of arXiv:2604.05138, 'Convergence rate of $H$-property for step-graphons'] [Skeleton graph] To a step-graphon $W$ with a partition $\sigma = (\sigma_0, \ldots, \sigma_q)$, we assign the undirected graph $S$ on $q$ nodes, with $V(S) = \{u_1, \ldots, u_q\}$ and edge set $E(S)$ defined as follows: there is an edge between $u_i$ and $u_j$ if and only if $W$ is nonzero over $[\sigma_{i-1}, \sigma_i) \times [\sigma_{j-1}, \sigma_j)$. We call $S$ the {\bf skeleton graph} of $W$ for the partition $\sigma$.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Locate the rate bottleneck in the Hermitisation argument. Result: The Hermitisation proof controls the log-potential U_n(z) = (1/n) log|det(n^{-1/2}M_n - z)| through the singular-value distribution of the shifted matrix; the error has three parts: (a) the rate in the Marchenko-Pastur-type convergence of the singular-value distribution, of order n^{-1/2}-ish under four moments and degrading to n^{-c(eps)} under 2+eps moments through the truncation at level n^{1/(2+eps)}; (b) the smallest singular value lower bound, which contributes only a log-factor to the log-potential error; (c) the conversion from log-potential convergence to weak convergence of the ESD, which costs a power through the smoothing of the Laplacian. The truncation in (a) is the eps-dependent bottleneck: entries are truncated at n^{1/(2+eps)}, the truncated variance differs from 1 by O(n^{-eps/(2+eps)}), and this variance error propagates to the singular-value distribution as a shift of the same order, giving delta of order eps/(2+eps) times the conversion loss in (c). So one expects delta(eps) = c eps/(2+eps) for small eps with c < 1 from step (c), and a plateau at the four-moment rate for eps >= 2. This is a heuristic scaling, not a theorem; the exact constant c requires the sharpest version of (c), which is the Kolmogorov-distance version of the log-potential-to-measure conversion. Key identity: Truncation at n^{1/(2+eps)} induces a variance error n^{-eps/(2+eps)}, which caps delta(eps) at a constant times eps/(2+eps) for small eps. Obstruction: Sharp conversion constant from log-potential to Kolmogorov distance.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Attempt the non-amenable direction through the spectral radius criterion of Benjamini-Schramm and Hutchcroft's p_c <= 1/spectral radius... type bounds. Result: Known route: if p_c < 1/rho where rho is the spectral radius of simple random walk, then at p slightly above p_c the expected number of open paths of length n to distance n grows slower than the number of returns... this gives p_c < p_u for graphs where p_c(G) < 1/(rho ... ) and is the content of the Benjamini-Schramm 1996 criterion p_c < 1/(1 + spectral gap)?; the general conjecture needs p_c < p_u even when p_c is close to 1/rho... For groups with p_c(G) < 1/rho(G) the conjecture holds; the remaining case is groups with a Cayley graph where p_c >= 1/rho, and the Pak-Smirnova trick replaces the generating set to make p_c small relative to rho. So the conjecture in its generating-set-free form (some Cayley graph) is settled by Pak-Smirnova, while the conjecture for EVERY Cayley graph reduces to showing p_c(G) < 1/rho(G)^{?}... I checked the inequality p_c <= 1/(1 + h) where h is the Cheeger constant... Benjamini-Schramm prove p_c <= 1/(1+h) and p_u >= 1/(1+h)?? no. The honest reduction: for every Cayley graph, p_c < p_u would follow from p_c < 1/rho (Benjamini-Schramm criterion) and the open question is whether every non-amenable Cayley graph satisfies p_c < 1/rho, which fails? For the free group with the standard generators p_c = 1/(2d-1) and 1/rho = (2d-1)/(2 sqrt(2d-1)) > p_c, consistent. No counterexample and no proof. Obstruction: Need p_c(G) < 1/rho(G) or another uniform criterion for every Cayley graph of every non-amenable group.

body:
Let Omega in R^n be open and A measurable with lambda|xi|^2 <= A(x)xi.xi and |A(x)xi.eta| <= Lambda|xi||eta| for a.e. x (0 < lambda <= Lambda). Let u in H^1_loc(Omega) be a weak solution of div(A grad u) = 0 in Omega. Then for every ball B_R(x0) contained in Omega, every 0 < r < R and every real constant k, integral over B_r(x0) of |grad u|^2 <= (16 Lambda^2 / (lambda^2 (R - r)^2)) times integral over B_R(x0) of |u - k|^2. The same inequality holds with u replaced by (u - k)^+ on both sides when u is only a weak subsolution (div(A grad u) >= 0), and with (u - k)^- when u is a supersolution. This is a reverse Poincare inequality: it bounds the energy of a solution by its oscillation in L^2, and it is the engine of both De Giorgi's and Moser's iterations.

[Lem 24 of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] Recall the definition of $Y$ in Definition \ref{def:prior_factor}. Define
\beq 
	X_2 := \sum_{\gamma \in \caG_C^2} \frac{1}{N^{m^\gamma/2}} Y (\gamma) Z(\gamma)
\eeq
and
\beq 
	R_2 := \sum_{\gamma \in \caG_C^2} \frac{1}{N^{m^\gamma/2}} Z(\gamma).
\eeq
Then, $\E[(X_2 - R_2)^2] = o(1)$.

In the normalized second Ray-Knight identity on a finite symmetric network pinned at a base vertex, the field identity in law is {L_(tau(t))^x + phi_x^2/2}_x =_d {(phi_x+sqrt(2t))^2/2}_x, with the left Gaussian field independent of the walk. It does not assert L_(tau(t))^x =_d (phi_x+sqrt(2t))^2/2. When Var(phi_x)=g>0 and t>0, the local-time marginal has mean t and an atom exp(-t/g) at zero, whereas the shifted Gaussian square has mean t+g/2 and no atom at zero. The omitted term in the earlier C0011 attempt invalidates that transfer step. This correction does not decide present openness of the full planar level-set problem.

body:
Own work, proof (unaudited), novelty unestablished.

U in R^(N by M), V in R^(P by M), N,P>=2,M>=1, have independent
iid real entries within each array; the arrays are independent.
Their fixed scalar laws u,v are centered with variance one and
finite fourth moments u4,v4. Assume measurable scalar functions
tau_U,eta_U,tau_V,eta_V,zeta_V satisfy, for bounded C1 functions h
with bounded derivative, including their bounded smooth compositions
in the proof,

 E[u h(u)]=E[tau_U(u) h'(u)],
 E[(u^2-1)h(u)]=E[eta_U(u) h'(u)],
 E[v h(v)]=E[tau_V(v) h'(v)],
 E[(v^2-1)h(v)]=E[eta_V(v) h'(v)],
 E[(tau_V(v)-1)h(v)]=E[zeta_V(v) h'(v)].             (1)

Assume |tau_U|<=T_U, |tau_V|<=T_V almost surely and
E eta_U^2,E eta_V^2,E zeta_V^2 finite. No differentiability of
these five functions and no posterior independence is assumed.
Bounded truncation of h(x)=x gives E tau_U=E tau_V=1.
Define the finite scalar constants

 t_U=E tau_U^2, t_V=E tau_V^2,
 e_U=E eta_U^2, e_V=E eta_V^2, z_V=E zeta_V^2,
 a_U=E[tau_U u^2], a_V=E[tau_V v^2],
 b_U=E[tau_U u], b_V=E[tau_V v],
 h_U=E eta_U, h_V=E eta_V,
 L_N=N-2+2*a_U^2+2*b_U^4.

Let independent Z have iid standard Gaussian entries, X=UV^T/sqrt(N),
Y=sqrt(s)X+Z, d=NP, alpha=P/N, beta=M/N, v_s=1+beta*s.
Set g=beta/v_s, m_N=E||X-E[X|Y]||^2/d and
B_N=log(v_s)/2-I(X;Y)/d, with natural logs.

## Explicit constants and result

Put A=beta^2*(N-1)*(P-1)/N^2 and

 E3=6*(N-1)*(P-1)*M*(t_U^2*t_V-1)/N^4,
 Ec=6*(N-1)/N^4 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^2*(v4+2*(P-1))+M*(M-1)*a_V^2],
 Eeta=2/N^3 * [M*P*e_U*T_V^2+M*(M-1)*h_U^2*b_V^2],
 Ezeta=2*N*M*z_V/N^3,
 E4=24*(N-1)*(P-1)/N^5 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^2*e_V*N+2*M*(M-1)*b_U^2*h_V^2],
 W=120*(N-1)*(P-1)*(P-2)/N^6 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^6*N*(N-1+u4)+M*(M-1)*L_N],
 F2=2*(Eeta+Ezeta), F3=2*(E3+Ec), F4=E4.            (2)

All constants are nonnegative. For all s>0,delta>0,

 g-m_N <= (1+delta)*s^3/v_s^2*(sqrt(A)+s*sqrt(W))^2
       +3*(1+1/delta)/v_s^2*(s^2*F2+s^3*F3+s^4*F4). (3)

For the exact R_N in038(10), define

 a=(N+u4-3)/N, b=(P+v4-3)/N,
 Q(s)=v_s^3+beta*(a+b)*v_s*s^2+beta*a*b*s^3,
 D(s)=v_s^2*Q(s), delta_N=1/floor(sqrt(N)),
 eps_N=delta_N*A+3*(1+1/delta_N)*(F2+F3+F4),
 K_N=A*(Q(1)-1)+(1+delta_N)*(A+2*W).

For 0<=s<=1 the requested estimate and its integral are

 0<=R_N(s)<=eps_N*s^2+K_N*s^4,                      (4)
 half integral_0^s R_N(t)dt<=eps_N*s^3/6+K_N*s^5/10. (5)

In particular the full finite-N two-sided information bound is

 -A*(D(1)-1)*s^5/10
 <= B_N(s)-A*s^4/8
 <= eps_N*s^3/6+K_N*s^5/10.                         (6)

For fixed priors with positive aspect ratios bounded above,
F2,F3,F4=O(1/N), W,A,Q(1) are uniformly bounded,
eps_N=O(N^(-1/2)), and K_N is uniformly bounded.
If alpha_N->alpha>0,beta_N->beta>0, every limiting information
envelope therefore satisfies

 B(s)=alpha*beta^2*s^4/8+O(s^5), 0<=s<=1,            (7)

with the explicit remainder constants in (6). Existence or uniqueness
of the information limit is not required. The finite-N error in (6)
is additive O(N^(-1/2)*s^3), not a pure uniform Taylor remainder
after dividing by s^4 arbitrarily close to zero.

Equivalently the normalized mutual information has the explicit
finite-N polynomial

 P4_N(s)=beta*s/2-beta^2*s^2/4+beta^3*s^3/6
                              -(beta^4+A)*s^4/8,

and

 -eps_N*s^3/6-K_N*s^5/10
 <= I(X;Y)/d-P4_N(s)
 <= [beta^5+A*(D(1)-1)]*s^5/10.                     (6a)

The elementary identity log(1+x)=x-x^2/2+x^3/3-x^4/4
+integral_0^x t^4/(1+t)dt, valid for all x>=0, pays the log remainder.
Thus the limiting quartic term in I/(NP) is
-(beta^4+alpha*beta^2)*s^4/8, and no prior fourth cumulant enters
at that order within this class. The channel parameter is s=1/Delta;
I(UV^T;Y)=I(X;Y) because deterministic nonzero rescaling of the
input is invertible.

## Non-Gaussian example and whole-family scope

Both priors may independently be uniform on [-sqrt(3),sqrt(3)].
For either law take tau(x)=(3-x^2)/2, eta(x)=x-x^3/3;
for the V law take zeta(x)=-eta(x)/2. Their endpoint values vanish,
and their negative derivatives are x, x^2-1, and tau(x)-1,
respectively. Ordinary one-dimensional integration by parts proves
(1), without a Gaussian prior or a boundary contribution.
Exact constants are T=3/2, fourth moment9/5, t=6/5,
e=8/35, z=2/35, a=3/5, b=h=0.
Gaussian priors also satisfy (1) with tau=1,eta=x,zeta=0.
The result applies to every fixed law satisfying the stated kernel
conditions, not just these examples. Discrete Rademacher priors do
not satisfy (1) for arbitrary smooth tests and are not covered.
Specifically choose a compact smooth cutoff of (3*x-x^3)/2 which
equals that polynomial near {-1,1}. At a Rademacher input, h(u)=u
and h'(u)=0, so E[u*h(u)]=1 while E[tau(u)*h'(u)]=0 for every
finite function tau on its support. This is an obstruction to
applying the present derivative-transfer route to that law, not a
counterexample to quartic universality for discrete priors.

More concretely, each of U and V may have any standardized beta
law, with its own arbitrary fixed positive shape parameters p,q.
Let k=p+q, C=1/k, B=(q-p)*sqrt(k+1)/(k*sqrt(p*q)), and
x=(t-p/k)/sqrt(p*q/[k^2*(k+1)]) for t~Beta(p,q). Then

 tau(x)=1+C+B*x-C*x^2,
 eta(x)=tau(x)*(x+B)/(1+C),
 zeta(x)=B*tau(x)-C*eta(x).

The beta density times tau vanishes at both endpoints, including
when the density itself is unbounded there, because p,q>0.
Direct integration of its derivative proves E[x h]=E[tau h'].
Writing Q=x^2-1, the identity tau-1=B*x-C*Q and applying this
first identity to x*h(x) give
(1+C)E[Q*h]=E[tau*(x+B)*h']; this proves the eta identity.
The zeta identity follows by the same linear relation tau-1.
All kernels are bounded on the compact standardized support, so
every hypothesis of (1) is paid. This covers two asymmetric beta
priors as well as the symmetric subfamily. For an asymmetric exact
check, Beta(2,3) standardized as x=5*t-2 has
tau=(6+x-x^2)/5, eta=tau*(1+5*x)/6, zeta=tau*(1-x)/6.
Independent arrays and standard Gaussian channel noise; N,P>=2,M>=1; X=UV^T/sqrt(N)
Fixed centered unit-variance factor laws with finite fourth moments; bounded tau_U,tau_V
E[u h]=E[tau_U h'], E[(u^2-1)h]=E[eta_U h']; corresponding V identities and E[(tau_V-1)h]=E[zeta_V h'] for bounded C1 h with bounded derivative
Square-integrable eta_U,eta_V,zeta_V; precise constants and all rate bounds are in proof Eqs2,13
Positive finite convergent aspects only for limiting coefficient; no information-limit existence assumed

class; it is not the full finite-moment Target1 or its first
prior-dependent coefficient.

## Hypotheses

U in R^(N by M), V in R^(P by M), N,P>=2,M>=1, have independent
iid real entries within each array; the arrays are independent.
Their fixed scalar laws u,v are centered with variance one and
finite fourth moments u4,v4. Assume measurable scalar functions
tau_U,eta_U,tau_V,eta_V,zeta_V satisfy, for bounded C1 functions h
with bounded derivative, including their bounded smooth compositions
in the proof,

 E[u h(u)]=E[tau_U(u) h'(u)],
 E[(u^2-1)h(u)]=E[eta_U(u) h'(u)],
 E[v h(v)]=E[tau_V(v) h'(v)],
 E[(v^2-1)h(v)]=E[eta_V(v) h'(v)],
 E[(tau_V(v)-1)h(v)]=E[zeta_V(v) h'(v)].             (1)

Assume |tau_U|<=T_U, |tau_V|<=T_V almost surely and
E eta_U^2,E eta_V^2,E zeta_V^2 finite. No differentiability of
these five functions and no posterior independence is assumed.
Bounded truncation of h(x)=x gives E tau_U=E tau_V=1.
Define the finite scalar constants

 t_U=E tau_U^2, t_V=E tau_V^2,
 e_U=E eta_U^2, e_V=E eta_V^2, z_V=E zeta_V^2,
 a_U=E[tau_U u^2], a_V=E[tau_V v^2],
 b_U=E[tau_U u], b_V=E[tau_V v],
 h_U=E eta_U, h_V=E eta_V,
 L_N=N-2+2*a_U^2+2*b_U^4.

Let independent Z have iid standard Gaussian entries, X=UV^T/sqrt(N),
Y=sqrt(s)X+Z, d=NP, alpha=P/N, beta=M/N, v_s=1+beta*s.
Set g=beta/v_s, m_N=E||X-E[X|Y]||^2/d and
B_N=log(v_s)/2-I(X;Y)/d, with natural logs.

## Explicit constants and result

Put A=beta^2*(N-1)*(P-1)/N^2 and

 E3=6*(N-1)*(P-1)*M*(t_U^2*t_V-1)/N^4,
 Ec=6*(N-1)/N^4 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^2*(v4+2*(P-1))+M*(M-1)*a_V^2],
 Eeta=2/N^3 * [M*P*e_U*T_V^2+M*(M-1)*h_U^2*b_V^2],
 Ezeta=2*N*M*z_V/N^3,
 E4=24*(N-1)*(P-1)/N^5 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^2*e_V*N+2*M*(M-1)*b_U^2*h_V^2],
 W=120*(N-1)*(P-1)*(P-2)/N^6 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^6*N*(N-1+u4)+M*(M-1)*L_N],
 F2=2*(Eeta+Ezeta), F3=2*(E3+Ec), F4=E4.            (2)

All constants are nonnegative. For all s>0,delta>0,

 g-m_N <= (1+delta)*s^3/v_s^2*(sqrt(A)+s*sqrt(W))^2
       +3*(1+1/delta)/v_s^2*(s^2*F2+s^3*F3+s^4*F4). (3)

For the exact R_N in038(10), define

 a=(N+u4-3)/N, b=(P+v4-3)/N,
 Q(s)=v_s^3+beta*(a+b)*v_s*s^2+beta*a*b*s^3,
 D(s)=v_s^2*Q(s), delta_N=1/floor(sqrt(N)),
 eps_N=delta_N*A+3*(1+1/delta_N)*(F2+F3+F4),
 K_N=A*(Q(1)-1)+(1+delta_N)*(A+2*W).

For 0<=s<=1 the requested estimate and its integral are

 0<=R_N(s)<=eps_N*s^2+K_N*s^4,                      (4)
 half integral_0^s R_N(t)dt<=eps_N*s^3/6+K_N*s^5/10. (5)

In particular the full finite-N two-sided information bound is

 -A*(D(1)-1)*s^5/10
 <= B_N(s)-A*s^4/8
 <= eps_N*s^3/6+K_N*s^5/10.                         (6)

For fixed priors with positive aspect ratios bounded above,
F2,F3,F4=O(1/N), W,A,Q(1) are uniformly bounded,
eps_N=O(N^(-1/2)), and K_N is uniformly bounded.
If alpha_N->alpha>0,beta_N->beta>0, every limiting information
envelope therefore satisfies

 B(s)=alpha*beta^2*s^4/8+O(s^5), 0<=s<=1,            (7)

with the explicit remainder constants in (6). Existence or uniqueness
of the information limit is not required. The finite-N error in (6)
is additive O(N^(-1/2)*s^3), not a pure uniform Taylor remainder
after dividing by s^4 arbitrarily close to zero.

Equivalently the normalized mutual information has the explicit
finite-N polynomial

 P4_N(s)=beta*s/2-beta^2*s^2/4+beta^3*s^3/6
                              -(beta^4+A)*s^4/8,

and

 -eps_N*s^3/6-K_N*s^5/10
 <= I(X;Y)/d-P4_N(s)
 <= [beta^5+A*(D(1)-1)]*s^5/10.                     (6a)

The elementary identity log(1+x)=x-x^2/2+x^3/3-x^4/4
+integral_0^x t^4/(1+t)dt, valid for all x>=0, pays the log remainder.
Thus the limiting quartic term in I/(NP) is
-(beta^4+alpha*beta^2)*s^4/8, and no prior fourth cumulant enters
at that order within this class. The channel parameter is s=1/Delta;
I(UV^T;Y)=I(X;Y) because deterministic nonzero rescaling of the
input is invertible.

## Non-Gaussian example and whole-family scope

Both priors may independently be uniform on [-sqrt(3),sqrt(3)].
For either law take tau(x)=(3-x^2)/2, eta(x)=x-x^3/3;
for the V law take zeta(x)=-eta(x)/2. Their endpoint values vanish,
and their negative derivatives are x, x^2-1, and tau(x)-1,
respectively. Ordinary one-dimensional integration by parts proves
(1), without a Gaussian prior or a boundary contribution.
Exact constants are T=3/2, fourth moment9/5, t=6/5,
e=8/35, z=2/35, a=3/5, b=h=0.
Gaussian priors also satisfy (1) with tau=1,eta=x,zeta=0.
The result applies to every fixed law satisfying the stated kernel
conditions, not just these examples. Discrete Rademacher priors do
not satisfy (1) for arbitrary smooth tests and are not covered.
Specifically choose a compact smooth cutoff of (3*x-x^3)/2 which
equals that polynomial near {-1,1}. At a Rademacher input, h(u)=u
and h'(u)=0, so E[u*h(u)]=1 while E[tau(u)*h'(u)]=0 for every
finite function tau on its support. This is an obstruction to
applying the present derivative-transfer route to that law, not a
counterexample to quartic universality for discrete priors.

More concretely, each of U and V may have any standardized beta
law, with its own arbitrary fixed positive shape parameters p,q.
Let k=p+q, C=1/k, B=(q-p)*sqrt(k+1)/(k*sqrt(p*q)), and
x=(t-p/k)/sqrt(p*q/[k^2*(k+1)]) for t~Beta(p,q). Then

 tau(x)=1+C+B*x-C*x^2,
 eta(x)=tau(x)*(x+B)/(1+C),
 zeta(x)=B*tau(x)-C*eta(x).

The beta density times tau vanishes at both endpoints, including
when the density itself is unbounded there, because p,q>0.
Direct integration of its derivative proves E[x h]=E[tau h'].
Writing Q=x^2-1, the identity tau-1=B*x-C*Q and applying this
first identity to x*h(x) give
(1+C)E[Q*h]=E[tau*(x+B)*h']; this proves the eta identity.
The zeta identity follows by the same linear relation tau-1.
All kernels are bounded on the compact standardized support, so
every hypothesis of (1) is paid. This covers two asymmetric beta
priors as well as the symmetric subfamily. For an asymmetric exact
check, Beta(2,3) standardized as x=5*t-2 has
tau=(6+x-x^2)/5, eta=tau*(1+5*x)/6, zeta=tau*(1-x)/6.

## Derivation of the relative-score decomposition

All identities here are under the original independent U,V,Z.
For compact smooth scalar f(Y), apply scalar Stein in V and Gaussian
IBP in Z to obtain, writing tau^U_ia=tau_U(U_ia) and similarly,

 E[Y_ij*f]/v_s-E[partial_ij f]
 =s/(v_s*N) sum_(a,k)
       E[(U_ia*U_ka*tau^V_ja-delta_ik)*partial_kj f]. (8)

For k=i split U_ia^2*tau^V_ja-1 into
(U_ia^2-1)*tau^V_ja+(tau^V_ja-1).
Use eta_U on the first part, zeta_V on the second. Each derivative
of Y with respect to a factor supplies sqrt(s/N) times the other
factor. This gives degree-two noise terms Ceta,Czeta below.

For k!=i use tau_U twice in its two independent coordinates. The
result is

 s^2/(v_s*N^2) sum_(a,k!=i,l,m)
 E[tau^U_ia*tau^U_ka*tau^V_ja*V_la*V_ma
                              *partial_il partial_km partial_kj f]. (9)

Partition its column indices into three disjoint cases:

 (i) l=m!=j: write V_la^2=1+(V_la^2-1). The1 part supplies
the leading cubic and its centered coefficient error. Apply eta_V
once to the centered part, obtaining the degree-four term C4.

 (ii) l!=m with l,m!=j: apply tau_V in the two distinct coordinates
V_la,V_ma. These derivatives never hit tau^V_ja, since j,l,m
are distinct. This gives the degree-five term W5.

 (iii) l=j or m=j: leave the expression unchanged, giving Cc.
These column coincidences have a vanishing tensor norm, bounded
explicitly below. No derivative of a Stein kernel is taken.

Define Wick products in standard noise Z by the generating function
exp(<t,Z>-||t||^2/2), allowing repeated indices. Noise IBP replaces
derivatives in (8)-(9) by the corresponding Wick products. Define

 A0_ij=(beta/N) sum_(k!=i,l!=j) :Z_il Z_kl Z_kj:,
 Ce_ij=N^(-2) sum_(k!=i,l!=j)
   [sum_a tau^U_ia*tau^U_ka*tau^V_ja-M] :Z_il Z_kl Z_kj:,
 Cc_ij=N^(-2) sum_(k!=i,l,m: l=j or m=j)
   [sum_a tau^U_ia*tau^U_ka*tau^V_ja*V_la*V_ma]
                                             :Z_il Z_km Z_kj:,
 Ceta_ij=N^(-3/2) sum_l
   [sum_a eta^U_ia*tau^V_ja*V_la] :Z_il Z_ij:,
 Czeta_ij=N^(-3/2) sum_r
   [sum_a zeta^V_ja*U_ra] :Z_rj Z_ij:,
 C4_ij=N^(-5/2) sum_(k!=i,l!=j,r)
   [sum_a tau^U_ia*tau^U_ka*tau^V_ja*eta^V_la*U_ra]
                                          :Z_il Z_kl Z_kj Z_rl:,
 W5_ij=N^(-3) sum_(k!=i,l!=m,l,m!=j,r,t)
   [sum_a tau^U_ia*tau^U_ka*tau^V_ja*tau^V_la*tau^V_ma*U_ra*U_ta]
                                      :Z_il Z_km Z_kj Z_rl Z_tm:.

The exact relative-score identity is

 r(Y)=grad log p_Y(Y)+Y/v_s
 =E[(s^2*A0+s^2*(Ce+Cc)+s^(3/2)*(Ceta+Czeta)
                                +s^(5/2)*C4+s^3*W5)/v_s | Y]. (10)

## Justification and Wick norm bounds

Gaussian convolution gives a smooth positive output density and a
square-integrable score by the conditional-noise formula. Every
coefficient in (10) is independent of Z. The estimates below prove
all fields in (10) are square integrable. Scalar Stein identities
are applied only to bounded smooth compositions with bounded scalar
derivatives for each fixed other coordinate; their polynomial random
prefactors are integrable by the stated moment hypotheses. Truncation
of those prefactors, followed by dominated convergence, justifies
successive integrations. The noise IBPs use bounded derivatives
and polynomial noise moments. No density-ratio Taylor series or
conditional independence assumption enters the proof. Equality
against every compact smooth f identifies the L2 score in (10).

For a degree-h ordered coefficient tensor independent of Z, the
Wick norm is h! times the squared Hilbert-Schmidt norm of its
symmetrization, at most h! times its ordered squared norm.
For each field above, its summation indices map injectively to its
ordered noise positions. The explicit restrictions on k,l,m are
retained in counting these ordered coefficients.

The three noise positions in A0 are distinct. Between two such
triples with fixed output i,j, only the identity Wick matching
survives: every other matching would force k=i or l=j. Hence

 E A0_ij^2=beta^2*(N-1)*(P-1)/N^2=A.                (11)

Hidden-index sums are sums of M independent copies. Their second
moments equal M times the single-copy second moment plus
M*(M-1) times its squared mean. Applying this observation and the
ordered Wick inequality gives, for every i,j,

 E Ce_ij^2<=E3, E Cc_ij^2<=Ec,
 E Ceta_ij^2<=Eeta, E Czeta_ij^2<=Ezeta,
 E C4_ij^2<=E4, E W5_ij^2<=W.                       (12)

Here are all moment and index counts paying (12):

Ce: (N-1)*(P-1) ordered triples. The coefficient's single-copy
mean is1, second moment t_U^2*t_V, so its variance is
M*(t_U^2*t_V-1). The Wick factor is3!=6.

Cc: for fixed k!=i the colliding column set has 2*(P-1) off-diagonal
pairs and one (j,j) pair. Summing the single-copy squared coefficients
is at most T_U^4*T_V^2*[2*(P-1)+v4]. Its mean is zero except at
(j,j), where it is a_V. Multiply by N-1, N^(-4), and3!.

Ceta: the single-copy second moment is at most e_U*T_V^2 for
each of P choices of l. Its mean is zero unless l=j, where it is
h_U*b_V. Multiply the hidden-index second-moment expression by
N^(-3) and2!.

Czeta: independence and E U_ra=0 give zero coefficient mean and
single-copy second moment z_V for each of N choices of r.
Multiply by M, N^(-3) and2!.

C4: there are (N-1)*(P-1) choices of k,l. The sum over r of
single-copy second moments is at most T_U^4*T_V^2*e_V*N.
Its mean is zero except r=i or r=k, where it equals b_U*h_V.
The summed squared means therefore equal2*b_U^2*h_V^2.
Multiply by N^(-5) and4!=24.

W5: there are (N-1)*(P-1)*(P-2) choices of k,l,m.
The summed single-copy second moments over r,t are at most
T_U^4*T_V^6*E(sum_r U_ra^2)^2
=T_U^4*T_V^6*N*(N-1+u4).
The V kernel product has expectation1 because j,l,m are distinct.
The summed squared means over r,t consequently equal L_N:
N-2 diagonal pairs outside {i,k} contribute1 each;
(i,i),(k,k) contribute a_U^2 each;
(i,k),(k,i) contribute b_U^4 each;
every other pair contains a centered independent unweighted U.
Multiply by N^(-6) and5!=120. At P=2 this field is empty.

All counts are per output entry; summing over i,j then dividing by
NP introduces no extra factor. The moment bounds use finite fourth
moments for U,V, bounded tau kernels, and square-integrable eta,zeta,
not uncontrolled sixth moments of either prior.

## Conclude the residual and information bounds

Conditional expectation contracts L2. Group Ceta+Czeta, Ce+Cc
using ||x+y||^2<=2||x||^2+2||y||^2, and use (10)-(12) to obtain

 sqrt(E||r||^2/d)
 <=[s^2*sqrt(A)+s^3*sqrt(W)
                   +s^(3/2)*sqrt(F2)+s^2*sqrt(F3)+s^(5/2)*sqrt(F4)]/v_s.

Split the first two and last three summands. Apply
(x+y)^2<=(1+delta)x^2+(1+1/delta)y^2, and bound the square of
the three-term error by three times the sum of its squared terms.
The Gaussian-channel identity E||r||^2/d=s*(g-m_N) proves (3).

038 defines R_N=(g-m_N)-A*s^3/[v_s^2*Q(s)] exactly. Q has
nonnegative coefficients and Q(0)=1, hence for 0<=s<=1,
1-1/Q(s)<=Q(s)-1<=s*(Q(1)-1).
Subtracting038 from (3), bounding v_s^(-2)<=1 and s^3,s^4<=s^2
in the vanishing error terms, gives

 R_N<=eps_N*s^2+
  [A*(Q(1)-1)+(1+delta_N)*(2*sqrt(A*W)+W)]*s^4.

Finally 2*sqrt(A*W)<=A+W proves (4). Integrating gives (5).
038's explicit lower bound, and D>=1 in its exact integral, give
(6), with denominators6 and10 from integrating s^2 and s^4.

Every rate claimed after (6) follows directly from (2): fixed scalar
constants and bounded P/N,M/N imply E3,Ec,Eeta,Ezeta,E4=O(1/N),
W=O(1), A=O(1), Q(1)=O(1); floor(sqrt(N)) lies between
sqrt(N)/2 and sqrt(N), so eps_N=O(N^(-1/2)). No SNR derivative
is interchanged with the dimension limit to obtain (7).

For completely dimension-independent constants, if alpha<=alpha_*
and beta<=beta_*, let A_*=alpha_* beta_*^2 and put

 C3_*=6 alpha_* beta_* (t_U^2*t_V-1),
 Cc_*=6[beta_* T_U^4 T_V^2(v4/2+2 alpha_*)+beta_*^2 a_V^2],
 Ceta_*=2[alpha_* beta_* e_U T_V^2+beta_*^2 h_U^2 b_V^2],
 Czeta_*=2 beta_* z_V,
 C4_*=24 alpha_*[beta_* T_U^4 T_V^2 e_V
                                  +2 beta_*^2 b_U^2 h_V^2],
 C_*=2(Ceta_*+Czeta_*)+2(C3_*+Cc_*)+C4_*,
 W_*=120 alpha_*^2[beta_* T_U^4 T_V^6(1+u4)/2
                                  +beta_*^2(1+a_U^2+b_U^4)],
 a_*=1+max(u4-3,0)/2,
 b_*=alpha_*+max(v4-3,0)/2,
 Q_*=(1+beta_*)^3+beta_*(a_*+b_*)(1+beta_*)+beta_* a_* b_*.

Then E3<=C3_*/N, Ec<=Cc_*/N, Eeta<=Ceta_*/N,
Ezeta<=Czeta_*/N, E4<=C4_*/N and W<=W_*.
For W, use N(N-1+u4)<=N^2(1+u4)/2 and
L_N<=N(1+a_U^2+b_U^4), valid because N>=2,u4>=1.
Also Q(1)<=Q_*, and

 eps_N<=(2 A_*+6 C_*)/sqrt(N),
 K_N<=A_*(Q_*-1)+2(A_*+2 W_*).                      (13)

The lower fifth-order constant in (6) is at most
A_*[(1+beta_*)^2 Q_*-1]/10. Thus every constant in the
limiting O(s^5) assertion has an explicit dimension-independent value.

Exact validation is in scripts/check_two_stein_score.py and
logs/two_stein_score_checks.json: polynomial Gaussian-noise integration
and rational uniform/Beta(2,3) moments test the unsimplified weak
score identity. Separate exact Wick norm computations test the
coefficient bounds. These finite checks exercise diagonal, collision,
fourth-order and fifth-order fields, including asymmetric kernels;
they do not independently audit the analytic theorem for all dimensions.

The first step still unpaid for full Target1 is replacing the scalar
Stein transfer hypotheses (1) by arbitrary finite-moment iid laws,
including discrete priors, with a similarly uniform remainder.
This theorem also does not locate the first prior-dependent term
beyond the now-universal quartic coefficient in its stated class.

For the conditioned covariance mixture in the previous NEXT,
specialize V to Gaussian and impose the sub-Gaussian U hypothesis
of034. The same two-sided inequality (6) holds for its conditioned
normalized KL K_E,N after subtracting H_N(s) from the lower bound
and adding H_N(s) to the upper bound, using the exact transfer
|K_E,N-B_N|<=H_N from038(9). Standardized beta U is bounded, hence
has a finite Hoeffding sub-Gaussian proxy. This pays the requested
conditioned-mixture sharp coefficient on that family; the previously

[Lemma 13 of arXiv:2605.21424, 'A dice game, a multinomial walk, and the inverted Dirichlet distribution'] Let \((G_n)_{n\in \N}\) be a sequence of random variables, \(G_n\sim \operatorname{Gamma}(n,1)\).
Then 
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{G_n}{n}= 1 \quad\text{in probability.}
\]

[Definition 30 (Trajectorial completeness) of arXiv:2606.17452, 'Optional Stopping for Superhedging Supermartingales'] Suppose $(S^n)_{n\ge 0}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal{S}$ satisfying
	\begin{equation}
	S^n_i = S^{n+1}_i, \;\; 0 \leq i \leq n,
	\end{equation}
	for all $n\in \mathbb{N}_0$. Then, its \emph{limit} is defined as
	$$
	\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} S^n\equiv \overline{S}\equiv (\overline{S}_i)_{i \geq 0},~~\mbox{wherein}~~~\overline{S}_i \equiv S^i_i.
	$$
	Denote by $\overline{\Se}$ be the set of all such limits $\overline{S}$. Then, $\overline{\Se}$ is called the \emph{trajectorial completion} of $\Se$ and  the trajectory set $\Se$ is said to be  \emph{trajectorially complete}, (TC) for short, if $\Se=\overline{\Se}$.
title: Trajectorial completeness

body: In mathematics, a real-valued function is called convex if the line segment between any two distinct points on the graph of the function lies above or on the graph of the function between the two points. Equivalently, a function is convex if its epigraph (the set of points on or above the graph of the function) is a convex set. In simple terms, a convex function graph is shaped like a cup $\cup$ (or a straight line like a linear function), while a concave function's graph is shaped like a cap $\cap$.

Let m(t) be the renewal function of a renewal process with inter-arrival distribution F having finite mean \mu = \int_0^\infty x dF(x) > 0. If F is non-lattice, then for every fixed h > 0, \lim_{t \to \infty} [m(t + h) - m(t)] = \frac{h}{\mu}. If F is lattice with span d, then \lim_{n \to \infty} [m(n d) - m((n-1)d)] = \frac{d}{\mu}.

[Definition of arXiv:2411.04590, 'Singular stochastic delay equations driven by fractional Brownian motion: Dynamics, longti'] Let \( J \subset \mathbb{R} \) with \( 0 \in J \). The space \( \mathcal{C}_0^{0,1-\text{var}}(J, \mathbb{R}^d) \) is defined as the closure of the set of paths \( x \colon J \to \mathbb{R}^d \) that are arbitrarily often differentiable and satisfy \( x_0 = 0 \), under the \( 1 \)-variation norm.
			Let $p\geq 1$, then by \( C_{0}^{0,p-\text{var}}(J, \mathbb{R}^d) \), we denote the set of continuous maps \( \mathbf{x} \colon J \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^d \) such that \( \mathbf{x}_0 = 0 \), and there exists a sequence \( \{x_n\} \) with \( x_n \in \mathcal{C}_0^{0,1-\text{var}}(J, \mathbb{R}^d) \) satisfying
			\[
			d_{p-\text{var}}\big{(}\mathbf{x}, x_n\big{)} := \left( \sup_{\mathcal{P} \subset J} \sum_{t_k \in \mathcal{P}} \left| (\delta \mathbf{x})_{t_k, t_{k+1}} - (\delta x_n)_{t_k, t_{k+1}} \right|^{p} \right)^{\frac{1}{p}} \to 0
			\]
			as \( n \to \infty \), where \( \mathcal{P} \) denotes the set of finite partitions of \( J \). The space \( C_{0}^{0,p-\text{var}}(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R}^d) \) consists of all continuous paths \( \mathbf{x} \colon \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^d \) for which \( \mathbf{x}|_J \in C_{0}^{0,p-\text{var}}(J, \mathbb{R}^d) \) for every \( J \) as above.
			Similarly, the space \( C_{0}^{0,p-\text{var}}(J, \tilde{T}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^d)) \) consists of continuous maps \( \mathbf{x} \colon J \to \tilde{T}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^d) \) with \( \mathbf{x}_0 = \mathbf{1} \), for which there exists a sequence \( \{x_n\} \) with \( x_n \in \mathcal{C}_0^{0,1-\text{var}}(J, \mathbb{R}^d) \) such that
			\[
			d_{p-\text{var}}\big{(}\mathbf{x}, \tilde{S}_{2}(x_n)\big{)} := \sup_{i,j \in \{1,2\}} \left( \sup_{\mathcal{P} \subset J} \sum_{t_k \in \mathcal{P}} \left| \Pi_{i}^{j}\left(\mathbf{x}_{t_k, t_{k+1}} - \tilde{S}_{2}(x_n)_{t_k, t_{k+1}}\right) \right|^{\frac{p}{i}} \right)^{\frac{1}{p}} \to 0
			\]
			as \( n \to \infty \). Here, \( \mathcal{P} \) represents the set of finite partitions of \( J \), and \( \mathbf{x}_{s,t} := \mathbf{x}_s^{-1} \circledast \mathbf{x}_t \). The space \( C_{0}^{0,p-\text{var}}(\mathbb{R}, \tilde{T}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^d)) \) consists of all continuous paths \( \mathbf{x} \colon \mathbb{R} \to \tilde{T}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^d) \) such that for every interval \( J \subset \mathbb{R} \), the restriction \( \mathbf{x}|_J \) belongs to \( C_{0}^{0,p-\text{var}}(J, \tilde{T}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^d)) \).

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.02362, '\textbf{Farthest-cell triplet entropy: high-dimensional shell limits and hyperbolic...'] We introduce farthest-cell triplet entropy, the conditional Shannon entropy of the farthest-prototype label given three random prototypes. For independent queries and prototypes, its estimator records only the farthest label, not coordinates or numerical distances. The statistic is bounded by $\log 3$, is invariant under common strictly increasing transformations of the dissimilarities, and has an exact mutual-information interpretation. In high-dimensional isotropic radial models $X_d=R_dU_d$, the Euclidean ordering reduces to scores $\lambda_d\xi_{i,d}-Z_i$, where $\lambda_d=\sqrt d\,\operatorname{sd}(R_d)/\E R_d$ and the $Z_i$ are independent standard Gaussian variables. This gives angular-dominated, intermediate, and radial-dominated entropy limits $\log 3$, $\Hinf(\lambda;F)$, and $0$. In hyperbolic space of curvature $-\kappa_d^2$, the same master curve appears at $\lambda_{d,\mathbb H}=\sqrt d\,\tau_d A(s_d)$, where $\tau_d=\operatorname{sd}(R_d)/\E R_d$, $s_d=\kappa_d\E R_d$, and $A(s)=s\coth s$. With a calibrated radial law and $\tau_d$, and a monotone operating interval, entropy inversion identifies the scale-invariant target $s_d^2$; absolute curvature requires an external length unit. CPU simulations give Euclidean and hyperbolic master-curve RMSEs of $0.0164$ and $0.0209$. Inversion from observed synthetic latent coordinates has a median relative error in $\kappa$ of $6.6\%$, while angular anisotropy increases this error to $68.9\%$. Thus the entropy statistic is comparison-based, whereas curvature recovery remains model-calibrated, is not graph-only, and is not robust to anisotropy.

[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2607.08242, 'Convergence of random sums in non-commutative probability'] Let $\{N_n\}$ be non-negative integer-valued rvs

independent of iid rvs $\{Y_n\}$ with $0<\mathbb{E}[Y_n^2]<\infty$. Let $Z$ be a standard Gaussian rv. \vskip5pt

\noindent (i) Suppose $\mathbb{E}[Y_1]\neq0$, and 

as $n\rightarrow\infty$, $\sigma_n^2\rightarrow\infty$, then for $t_1,t_2\in\mathbb{R}$, we have 
\begin{equation*}
    \mathbb{E}\exp\Big[\iota t_1(\frac{S_{N_n}-\mathbb{E}[N_nY_1]}{\sigma_n})
    
    +\iota \delta_nt_2\tilde{N}_n\Big]=\mathbb{E}\exp[\iota\delta_n(t_1+t_2)\tilde{N}_n]\mathbb{E}\exp[\iota t_1\sqrt{1-\delta_n^2}Z]+o(1).
\end{equation*}
\noindent (ii) Suppose $\mathbb{E}[Y_1]=0$. 
If as $n\rightarrow\infty$, $\mathbb{E}[N_n]\rightarrow\infty$, and the probability measures of $\frac{N_n}{\mathbb{E}[N_n]}$ weakly converge to a probability measure $\mu$, then
\begin{equation*}
    \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\exp\Big[\iota t_1\frac{S_{N_n}}{\sigma_n}
    +\iota t_2\frac{N_n}{\mathbb{E}[N_n]}\Big]=\int_{0}^{\infty}\exp(-\frac{t_1^2}{2}x+\iota t_2x)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}x),\ t_1,t_2\in\mathbb{R}.
\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 4 of arXiv:2607.08242

body: [Definition d:cone-null of arXiv:2510.13659, 'On the energy image density conjecture of Bouleau and Hirsch'] If $C=C(v,\theta)$ is a cone with $v \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}, \theta \in (0,\pi/2)$ and $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact set, then $K\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is called $C$-cone null, if for every Lipschitz curve $\gamma:I\to \mathbb{R}^n$  such that $I \subset \mathbb{R}$ is a compact interval, $\gamma'(t)\in C$ for $\mathcal{L}_1$-a.e.~$t\in I$ we have $\cH^1(\operatorname{image}(\gamma) \cap K)=0$.
title: Definition d:cone-null of arXiv:2510.13659

  $\Gamma(a+\alpha)/\Gamma(a)\le{c_1}(d,\alpha)2^{\alpha(r-l)}$
  with ${c_1}$ as in Fact (fact:sabot-tarres-recurrence of the paper). Then, 
  the restriction $X^{\Lambda_l\neq}$ of errw to $\Lambda_l$ with self-loops
  removed is a mixture of

Let (Omega, F, mu) be a measure space, I a nonempty open interval of R, and f : I x Omega -> R with: (i) for every t in I the function omega -> f(t, omega) is mu-integrable; (ii) for mu-almost every omega the map t -> f(t, omega) is differentiable on I, with derivative d_t f(t, omega); (iii) there exists g in L^1(mu) with |d_t f(t, omega)| <= g(omega) for all t in I and mu-almost every omega. Then F(t) = integral f(t, omega) dmu(omega) is differentiable on I and F'(t) = integral d_t f(t, omega) dmu(omega). It suffices to have (iii) LOCALLY: for each t_0 in I a neighbourhood J of t_0 and g_{t_0} in L^1 dominating |d_t f| on J x Omega, since differentiability is local. The dominating function must dominate the DERIVATIVE and must not depend on t; a bound |f(t, omega)| <= g(omega) on the function itself is not enough. body: Chaos theory is a branch of mathematics and an interdisciplinary area of scientific study. It focuses on underlying patterns and deterministic laws of dynamical systems that are highly sensitive to initial conditions. These were once thought to have completely random states of disorder and irregularities. The theory states that within the apparent randomness of chaotic complex systems, there are underlying patterns, interconnection, constant feedback loops, repetition, self-similarity, fractals and self-organization. The butterfly effect, an underlying principle of chaos, describes how a small change in one state of a deterministic nonlinear system can result in large differences in a later state. A metaphor for this behavior is that a butterfly flapping its wings in Brazil can cause or prevent a tornado in Texas.
title: Chaos theory

[Definition of arXiv:2510.13659, 'On the energy image density conjecture of Bouleau and Hirsch'] Let  $(X,\mathcal{X},\mu,\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$ be a Dirichlet structure. The \emph{generator} $A:D(A) \to L^2(X,\mu)$ is the linear operator with domain
		\[
		D(A):= \{ f\in \mathcal{F} \vert \mbox{there exists $C>0$ such that $\abs{\mathcal{E}(f,g)} \le C \norm{g}_{L^2(\mu)}$ for all $g \in \mathcal{F}$}\}.
		\]
		For any $f \in D(A)$, the element $A(f) \in L^2(X,\mu)$ is defined by
		\[
		\mathcal{E}(f,g)= -\langle A(f), g \rangle_{L^2(\mu)}.
		\] 
		
		We define the \emph{energy measure} as $\Gamma(f,g)= \gamma(f,g)\cdot \mu$ for all $f,g \in \mathcal{F}$, where $\gamma: \mathcal{F} \times \mathcal{F} \to L^1(X,\mu)$ is the associated carr\'e du champ.

body: Two sets A and B are equinumerous (have the same cardinality, written |A| = |B|) when there exists a bijection from A onto B. One writes |A| <= |B| when there is an injection from A into B. Equinumerosity is an equivalence relation, and <= is reflexive and transitive; by the Schroder-Bernstein theorem it is antisymmetric up to bijection (|A| <= |B| and |B| <= |A| imply |A| = |B|), all without the axiom of choice. With the axiom of choice any two sets are comparable (trichotomy), and every set is equinumerous with a unique initial ordinal, its cardinal number. A set is finite if it is equinumerous with {1, ..., n} for some natural number n; countably infinite if equinumerous with the set N of natural numbers; countable if finite or countably infinite; uncountable otherwise. Strict inequality |A| < |B| means |A| <= |B| and there is no bijection between A and B.
title: Cardinality and bijections

[Theorem 18 of arXiv:2506.10856, 'The space of multifurcating ranked tree shapes: enumeration, lattice structure, and Markov'] The forwards degree of a tree $T_{N,K}$ is \[  \text{deg}^+(T_{N,K}) = 1 + \sum_{e=2}^{K} \mathds{1}(F_{e, 1:e-1} = F_{e+1, 1:e-1} ). \]
The backwards degree of $T_{N,K}$ is \[ \text{deg}^-(T_{N,K}) \coloneq \sum_{i=1}^K U(k_i, l_i) = \sum_{i=1}^K \Big ((l_i+1)2^{k_i} -k_i-3 + \mathds{1}(l_i=0) \Big ), \] where $l_i, k_i, i=1,...,K$ are the number of leaves and internal nodes that subtend from node $i$ respectively, and $U(k_i, l_i)$ denotes the number of ways a single collapse edge operation can result in an internal node with ranking $i$ that subtends $l_i$ leaves and $k_i$ internal nodes. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Let $\mathcal B$ be a field of characteristic $0$.  Let $\mathcal C$ and $\mathcal E$ be $\mathcal B[H]$-modules. For a field extension $\mathcal B\rightarrow\mathcal B'$ the following properties hold.

\medskip
{\bf (1)} The $\mathcal B[H]$-modules $\mathcal C$ and $\mathcal E$ are isomorphic if and only if the $\mathcal B'[H]$-modules $\mathcal C\otimes_\mathcal B \mathcal B'$ and $\mathcal E\otimes_\mathcal B \mathcal B'$ are isomorphic.

\smallskip
{\bf (2)} The $\mathcal B[H]$-module $\mathcal C$ is rational if and only if the $\mathcal B'[H]$-module $\mathcal C\otimes_\mathcal B \mathcal B'$ is rational.

[Proposition 31 of arXiv:2605.30030, 'Critical exponents for planar random-cluster model with cluster-weight~$q=4$'] Consider boundary conditions~$\xi\leq \xi'$ on~$G$. 
    Let~$\mathbf{T} = \left(e_1,(\psi_t)_{2\leq t\leq n}\right)$ be a decision tree and~$(U_e)_{e\in E}$ be a set of i.i.d.~uniform random variables on~$[0,1]$ under some probability measure~$\P_\mathbf{T}$. Define~$\omega,\omega'\in\{0,1\}^E$ inductively by
    \begin{align*}
        \omega_{e_{t+1}} &:=\one\big(U_{e_{t+1}}\geq \rcP_{G_t}^{\xi_t}[e_{t+1}\text{ closed}]\big),\\
        \omega'_{e_{t+1}} &:= \one\big(U_{e_{t+1}}\geq \rcP_{G_t}^{\xi'_t}[e_{t+1}\text{ closed}]\big),\quad\forall 0\leq t<n,
    \end{align*}
where~$\xi_t$ and~$\xi'_t$ are the boundary conditions on~${G_t}$ induced by~$\omega^\xi_{[t]}$ and~$\big(\omega'_{[t]}\big)^{\xi'}$ respectively. When~$t=0$, these are~$\xi$ and~$\xi'$. 

Then, $\omega$ and~$\omega'$ have laws~$\rcP^{\xi}_{G}$ and~$\rcP^{\xi'}_{G}$, respectively, and~$\omega\leq \omega'$~$\P_\mathbf{T}$-almost surely.

The same procedure may be applied to couple increasingly~$\phi_G^{\xi}$ to~$\phi_G^{\xi}[\cdot\,|\,A]$ for an increasing event~$A$. We will also use it to couple (finite restrictions of) infinite volume measures. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 31 of arXiv:2605.30030

body: In mathematics, Itô's lemma or Itô's formula is an identity used in Itô calculus to find the differential of a time-dependent function of a stochastic process. It serves as the stochastic calculus counterpart of the chain rule. It can be heuristically derived by forming the Taylor series expansion of the function up to its second derivatives and retaining terms up to first order in the time increment and second order in the Wiener process increment. The lemma is widely employed in mathematical finance, and its best known application is in the derivation of the Black–Scholes equation for option values.
title: Itô's lemma

body:
[Lemma le:close_geodesic_general of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] There exists $c>0$ (not depending on $M,a,a_1,a_0$) such that the following is true. Fix $M,a,a_1 > 0$ such that $a,a_1$ are sufficiently small (depending on $a_0$). 
Let $\widehat{G}_{M,a}$ be the event that for every $0 \le s < t \le \infty$, the domain $D \setminus \eta([0,s]\cup[t,\infty))$ is $(M,a)$-good. Let $U \subseteq D_\eta$ be the $\delta^{1+a_1}$-neighborhood of $\eta$.

Let $G_{\delta}$ denote the event that there exists a finite collection of intervals $[s_i,t_i] \subseteq [0,\infty]$ such that
\begin{itemize}
\item if $\mathrm{dist}(\eta(t),\partial D) \le \delta$, then $t \in \bigcup_i [s_i,t_i]$,
\item $\bigcap_i G^U_{s_i,t_i}(r_i)$ holds for some $(r_i)$ with
\[
\sum_i r_i \le M\delta^{-c(a+a_1)} .
\]
\end{itemize}
Then
\[ \mathbf{P}[ G_{\delta}^c \cap \widehat{G}_{M,a} ] = O(M\delta^{{\alpha_{\mathrm{apr}}}-ca-ca_1}) \quad\text{as}\quad \delta \to 0.\]

[Lem LAN of arXiv:2604.07183, 'Stopping on the last success with unknown odds: asymptotic minimax optimality of the plug-'] Fix~$h>0$ and an integer~$k\ge2$, let
$$
p_n^\pm:=\frac1k\pm\frac{h\sigma_k}{\sqrt n},
\quad
\textrm{with } 
\
\sigma_k:=
\sqrt{\frac1k\Big(1-\frac1k\Big)}
,
$$
write~$N:=n-k$, and let~$\mathbb P^\pm_N$ denote the law of~$(X_1,\ldots,X_N)$ under~$\mathbb P_{p_n^\pm}$, with likelihood ratio~$L_N:=d\mathbb P^+_N/d\mathbb P^-_N$. Then, (i) one has
$$
\log L_N
\ \stackrel{d}{\longrightarrow}\
\mathcal N(-2h^2,4h^2)
\qquad
\textrm{under }\mathbb P^-_N
,
$$
so that, as~$n$ diverges to infinity, the local experiments~$(\mathbb P^-_N,\mathbb P^+_N)$ converge to the Gaussian shift experiment~$(\mathcal N(-h,1),\mathcal N(h,1))$; (ii) if~$Q_n^\pm$ denotes the law of~$(X_1,\ldots,X_N,U)$ under~$\mathbb P_{p_n^\pm}$, where~$U$ realizes the possible internal randomization of a rule (independent of the~$X_t$'s, with a \mbox{$p$-free} distribution), then
$$
1-\mathrm{TV}(Q_n^+,Q_n^-)
\to
2\Phi(-h)
,
$$
as~$n$ diverges to infinity (recall that~$\mathrm{TV}$ denotes the total variation distance).

[Definition def-MW of arXiv:2411.19810, 'Radial conformal welding in Liouville quantum gravity'] Let $W \in (0, \frac{\gamma^2}2)$. 
	Sample a quantum disk $ \mathcal{D} \sim {\mathcal{M}}^\mathrm{disk}_{0,2}(W)$ and restrict to the event that the left boundary length of $ \mathcal{D}$ is greater than its right boundary length, and conformally weld the entire right boundary arc to the initial segment of the left boundary arc starting from the first marked point. Embed the resulting quantum surface as $(\mathbb{H}, \phi, \eta, i, \infty)$ where $i$ and $\infty$ correspond to the first and second marked point of $\tilde \mathcal{D}$ respectively, and the curve $\eta$ goes from $\infty$ to $i$. Let $M_W$ be the law of $(\phi, \eta)$.

[Cor co:exponent_iic of arXiv:2604.14122, 'The scaling limit of random walk and\\ the intrinsic metric on planar critical percolation'] Let $\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{IIC}}$ denote the law of the IIC on the entire lattice $\mathbf{T}$ and let $S_n$ be the geodesic distance (resp.\ effective resistance) between $0$ and $\partial B(0,n)$. Let $\beta \in \{\beta^{\mathrm {geo}},\beta^{\mathrm {res}}\}$ be the scaling exponent of the CLE$_6$ geodesic (resp.\ resistance) metric defined in [my2025metric,my2025diffusion]. Under $\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{IIC}}$, almost surely,
    \[
    S_n = n^{\beta+o(1)}
    \quad\text{as } n \to \infty .
    \]
    Moreover, for each $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\alpha > 0$ there exists $c(\varepsilon,\alpha)$ such that
    \[
    \mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{IIC}}[ S_n \notin [n^{\beta-\varepsilon},n^{\beta+\varepsilon}] ] \le cn^{-\alpha} .
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Cor co:exponent_iic of arXiv:2604.14122

DRAFT sufficient bridge, review pending; combines the independently audited w453 outward-face argument with w454 conditioning. Let X start at 0 in Z^d in a nearest-neighbor environment with every transition at least kappa, 0<kappa<=1/(2d). Let tau be an arbitrary nonnegative integer random time, R_tau the maximum infinity-norm of the path up to tau, and D any event with P(D)=p>0. For integers r,t>=0, P(tau>t|D)<=P(R_tau>r|D)+p^-1(1-kappa^(r+1))^floor(t/(r+1)). The deterministic-time cube survival estimate is proved in the original law by conditional iteration, then divided by p; the conditioned law is not assumed to retain ellipticity. If P(R_tau>r|D)<=C exp(-lambda r) with lambda>log(1/kappa), this bound is summable in t and gives E[tau|D]<infinity. C0041 does not supply that radius-tail rate in this derivation, and the condition is sufficient, not necessary.

[Theorem 11 of arXiv:2607.23526, 'Equivalence of Canonical and Microcanonical Ensembles for Euclidean Lattices'] Let $\lambda\in\mathcal{D}$. Assume that $\langle(F_1(x),\cdots,F_r(x)):x\in\Lambda\rangle_{\Z}=\Z^r$. For $N\geq1$, suppose there are $\lambda_N\in\mathcal{D}$ such that $\lambda_N\to\lambda$, $N\to+\infty$. Let $n_N=(n_{N,1},\cdots,n_{N,r})\in\Z^r$ be reachable such that
\[\Xi_N:=n_N-N\bm{m}(\lambda_N)=O(1),\quad N\to+\infty.\]
Consider the exact-shell microcanonical ensemble $\mu_{N,E_N}^{\sh}$ on $\Gamma_N(E_N)$, where $E_N=\sum_{j=1}^ra_jn_{N,j}$. For every $k\geq1$,
\begin{equation}
\left\|(\pi_k)_*\mu^{\sh}_{N,E_N}-\bm{p}_{\lambda}^{\otimes k}\right\|_{\TV}\to0,\quad N\to+\infty.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 11 of arXiv:2607.23526

Result: The n/log n bound is the BKS entropy method; a power improvement n^{1-eps} would follow from a chaos exponent: if the polymer measure decorrelates under a noise of size n^{-eps'} on the environment (superconcentration with a rate), Talagrand's/Chatterjee's equivalence gives Var(log Z_n) <= n^{1-eps}. body: Let (X_1, X_2, X_3) be uniform on {000, 011, 101, 110}, the three-bit words of even parity, and let A_i = {X_i = 1}. Then P(A_i) = 1/2 for each i and every pair of these events is independent, but the three are not mutually independent. The union has probability 3/4, which equals the pairwise Chung-Erdős bound S^2/(S^2 + S - Q) with S = 3/2 and Q = 3/4, whereas the mutual-independence formula 1 - prod_i (1 - P(A_i)) = 7/8 overstates it. So the pairwise bound is sharp, and the product formula needs mutual independence.

body: The Ising model, named after the physicists Ernst Ising and Wilhelm Lenz, is a mathematical model of ferromagnetism in statistical mechanics. The model consists of discrete variables that represent magnetic dipole moments of atomic "spins" that can be in one of two states. The spins are arranged in a graph, usually a lattice, allowing each spin to interact with its neighbors. Neighboring spins that agree have a lower energy than those that disagree; the system tends to the lowest energy but heat disturbs this tendency, thus creating the possibility of different structural phases. The two-dimensional square-lattice Ising model is one of the simplest statistical models to show a phase transition. Though it is a highly simplified model of a magnetic material, the Ising model can still provide qualitative and sometimes quantitative results applicable to real physical systems, and in general, it can be seen as a specialization of Stanley's n-vector model for n = 1.
title: Ising model

[Lemma 2 (The transference principle) of arXiv:2609.01460, 'On cost-induced Santal\'o-type inequalities \\ in Polish measure spaces'] For $m\in\N$, let $(X_1,\mu_{X_1}),\dots, (X_m,\mu_{X_m})$ be Polish measure spaces. Let $c \colon X_1 \times\cdots \times X_m \to (-\infty,\infty)$ be a continuous cost function. Fix $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m \in (0,1)$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1$.

Consider collections, for $i=1,\dots,m$, $\mathcal{C}_{X_i}$ of $\mu_{X_i}$-measurable subsets of $X_i$. Let $a,b\in \R\cup\{\pm\infty\}$ be such that for all non-empty $A_i\in \mathcal{C}_{X_i}$, $\sup_{\substack{x_i\in A_i \\ 1\leq i \leq m}} -c(x_1,\dots,x_m) \in [a,b]$ and consider a continuous, non-decreasing function $F \colon (a,b]\to [0,\infty)$ satisfying $F(a^+)=0$.

Then, the following are equivalent:\begin{enumerate}
    \item For every non-empty $A_1\in \mathcal{C}_{X_1},\dots,A_m\in\mathcal{C}_{X_m}$, one has
    \[
\prod_{i=1}^m\mu_{X_i}(A_i)^{\lambda_i} \leq F\left(\sup_{\substack{x_i\in A_i \\ 1\leq i \leq m}} -c(x_1,\dots,x_m) \right).
\]
\item For every $(m+1)$-tuple of measurable functions $f_1 \in \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{C}_{X_1}),\dots, f_m\in \mathcal{F}\left(\mathcal{C}_{X_m}\right)$ and $\Omega \colon (a,b]  \to [0,\infty)$, where $\Omega$ is non-increasing, that satisfy
\begin{align*}
\prod_{i=1}^mf_i(x_i)^{\lambda_i} &\leq \Omega(-c(x_1,\dots,x_m)) \text{ for all } 
\\
&(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in X_1\times\cdots\times  X_m, \text{ with } -c(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in (a,b],
\end{align*}
one has
\[
\prod_{i=1}^m\left(\int_{X_i} f_i(x) d\mu_{X_i}(x) \right)^{{\lambda_i}} \leq \int_{a}^b \Omega(r) dF(r).
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: The transference principle

body: In computability theory, the halting problem is the decision problem of, given an arbitrary computer program and an input, determining whether said program will eventually finish running and halt, or will continue to run forever. Alan Turing proved in 1937 that the halting problem is undecidable, meaning that no general algorithm exists that can correctly solve the problem for all possible program–input pairs. The problem comes up often in discussions of computability since it demonstrates that some functions are mathematically definable but not computable.
title: Halting problem

body: [Lemma 9 of arXiv:2512.02538, 'On the spectral geometry of Liouville quantum gravity'] Almost surely, $\mathbf{G}$ is a nonnegative operator on $L^2 (\mu_\ph)$. That is, almost surely, for all $f \in L^2 ( \mu_\ph)$ we have $\langle f, \mathbf{G}f \rangle_{L^2(\mu_\ph)} \ge 0$. In particular all the eigenvalues $\bmu_n $ of $\mathbf{G}$ are nonnegative. Furthermore, $\ker (\mathbf{G}) = 0$ a.s., thus $\bmu_n >0$ for all $n\ge 0$, a.s.

$$
\mathbb{E}[\log\|X_1\|]<\infty.
$$
Also, assume that $G_X$ is not compact and is strongly irreducible, i.e. there exists no $G_X$-invariant finite union of proper subspaces of~${\mathbb R}^d$. Then there exists a positive constant $\lambda_F$ (Lyapunov exponent) such that with probability one
$$
\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{1}{n}\log\|X_n\ldots X_2X_1\|=\lambda_F>0.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:arrangement of arXiv:2608.28004, 'Hausdorff Dimension of the Set of Extreme Points\\ of a Random Countable Stable Zonotope'] Let \(\mathcal D\subset\mathbb R^N\) be convex and let
\(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_m\) be affine functions on \(\mathbb R^N\). The partition of
\(\mathcal D\) into nonempty level sets of the vector-valued map
\[
    t\longmapsto\bigl(\1_{\{\ell_1(t)>0\}},\ldots,
    \1_{\{\ell_m(t)>0\}}\bigr)
\]
has at most \(C_N(m+1)^N\) members. We call these sets \emph{sign strata};
the count includes strata contained in the hyperplanes
\(\{\ell_j=0\}\) themselves. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In mathematics, an elliptic curve is a smooth, projective, algebraic curve of genus one, on which there is a specified point O. An elliptic curve is defined over a field K and describes points in K^{2}, the Cartesian product of K with itself. If the field's characteristic is different from 2 and 3, then the curve can be described as a plane algebraic curve which consists of solutions (x, y) for: $$y^{2}=x^{3}+ax+b$$

 \frac2\pi-\mathcal J(G_N,P_N)
 =\frac{\pi}{24N^2}+O(N^{-4}).
 
\end{equation}

[Lem 117 (temporal smoothing of budget constraint) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Analogously to \eqref{e:budget.constraint.Ising.plus.coarse} and the bound from Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.budget}, with high probability we have 
	\begin{align*}
	\breve{C}^N(t)
	- \frac{\bar{W}^N(t)^2}{\alpha} 
	\le
	\bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N \tep^{1/2}
	+ 3\epsilon^\circ
	\end{align*}
for all $t\in[q_*,1]$. Additionally, with $J^N\equiv J(p^N,\tep,\lambda)$ as  defined by \eqref{e:bad.times.J}, we have
	\[
	\Big|\breve{C}^N(t)
	-\bar{C}^N(t)
	\Big|
	\le \bigg(\frac{ \trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2
	\lambda^{1/2}
	\]
for all $t\in[q_*,1] \setminus J^N$.

\begin{proof}
We continue to use the abbreviations introduced above. The function $\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}$ is convex on the expanded domain $\{(b,v,u) : v \ge u^2-2\bar{\lambda}\}$. Recall $\tGam^N\equiv(\tbbb,\tvvv,\tuuu)^N$
and $\TGam^N\equiv(\Tbbb,\Tvvv,\Tuuu)^N$: we have from Lemma~\ref{l:t.smooth.domain} that
(with high probability)
 $\TGam^N(t,y)$ lies in the expanded domain for all $(t,y)\in[q_*,1]\times \R$, while
$\tGam^N(t,y)$ lies in the expanded domain for all $(t,y)\in ([q_*,1]\setminus J^N)\times \R$. Lemma~\ref{l:t.smooth.domain} implies, for $(t,y)\in ([q_*,1]\setminus J^N)\times \R$,
	\[
	\bigg|
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}
	\Big( \tGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	-\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}
	\Big( \TGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	\bigg|
	\le
	\bigg(\frac{ \trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2
	\lambda^{1/2}\,.
	\]
Integrating with respect to $\overline{\varrho_{\vY,N,t}*\sphi(y)}\,dy$ proves the second conclusion. For all $(t,y)\in[q_*,1]\times\R$, we can bound
	\begin{align*}
	& \Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}
	\Big(\TGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	=
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}\bigg( \tE \Big[\sGam(t-\sss,y)\Big]\bigg) \\
	&\qquad\le \tE\bigg[
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}\Big( \sGam(t-\sss,y)\Big)\bigg]
	= \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}( \sGam(s,y) )\,ds\,.
	\end{align*}
Integrating with respect to $\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\,dy$ gives
	\begin{align*}
	&\breve{C}^N(t)
	=
	\int_{\R} \Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}\Big(\TGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\,dy
	\le
	\int_{\R}
	\bigg[
	 \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}( \sGam(s,y) )\,ds\bigg]
	\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\,dy \\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\bigg[\int_{\R}
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}( \sGam(s,y) )
	\overline{\varrho_s*\sphi(y)} \,dy\bigg]\,ds
	+O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N
	\tep^{1/2}\bigg]\\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\tilde{C}^N(s)\,ds
	+O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N
	\tep^{1/2}\bigg]
	\,,
	\end{align*}
where the error estimate uses the bounds on $\sGam=(\sbbb,\svvv,\suuu)$ proved in Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg}, along with the regularity of the map $t\mapsto \overline{\varrho_s*\sphi}$ proved in Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.cty}. 
 Similarly, note that
	\[
	S_t(w)
	\equiv
	\bigg( \int_{\R} w(y)^{1/2} \varsigma_t*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2
	\]
is a concave function. It follows that
	\begin{align*}
	&\bar{W}^N(t)^2 
	=\bigg(\int_{\R} \twww(t,y)^{1/2} \varsigma_t*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2
	= S_t\bigg(\tE\Big[ \swww(t-\sss,\cdot)\Big]\bigg)
	\ge \tE\bigg[ S_t\Big( \swww(t-\sss,\cdot)\Big)\bigg]\\
	&\qquad= \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\bigg( \int_{\R} \swww(s,y)^{1/2} 
		\varsigma_t*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2\,ds\\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\bigg( \int_{\R} \swww(s,y)^{1/2} 
		\varsigma_s*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2
	\,ds
	+
	O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N \tep^{1/2}\bigg]
	\\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\tilde{W}^N(s)^2\,ds
	+
	O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N \tep^{1/2}\bigg]
	\end{align*}
where the error estimate again follows from Lemmas \ref{l:sp.smooth.reg} and \ref{l:sp.smooth.cty}. The claim then follows by combining with
Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.budget}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: temporal smoothing of budget constraint

body: The estimator, per output coordinate: form the error covariance of the ensemble members in the per-sample relative metric (case weights $1/\|y_i\|^2$), replace its sample eigenvalues by the Ledoit-Peche nonlinear-shrinkage values (floored at a small fraction of the bulk level), and take the long-only minimum-variance weights $\arg\min_w w^T \Xi w$ subject to $w \ge 0$, $\mathbf{1}^T w = 1$, with the intercept closing the weighted mean error. Nothing in it is cross-validated. Measured on the EMIT lookup-table pool (seed 101, 23 members, 932 calibration rows): on the two components where regularisation matters it is the best estimator found - Y2 $0.1126$ against least squares $0.1292$ ($+12.9$ percent) and against the pool's cross-validated best heuristic $0.1186$ ($+5.1$ percent), Y4 $1.7559$ against $1.8981$ / $1.8340$ ($+7.5$ / $+4.3$ percent) - and it beats the same cleaned estimator with a cross-validated shrink toward the pooled simplex weights ($0.1141$ / $1.7716$) on both; on the easy component (Y1, where shrinking had nothing to give) it is within 3 percent. It keeps 7 to 11 of the 23 members active. The reading: the residual gain that the pool's heuristic obtained by interpolating toward the pooled simplex weights was the nonnegativity constraint, which by Jagannathan-Ma is an implicit shrinkage of the covariance with a data-determined amount; combined with the objective correction (the relative metric) and the spectral cleaning (nonlinear shrinkage), every ingredient of the heuristic is now a derived step. Three cells of one seed at the time of writing; the seventy-cell population test on both corpora was running.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Compare the invasion cluster two-point function with the IIC two-point function and locate the difference. Result: The IIC two-point function P_IIC(x in cluster) is asymptotic to A' |x|^{-(d-4)} in high dimensions (from the lace expansion of the IIC, Hofstad-Jarai), and the invasion percolation cluster is expected to have the same decay exponent because the invasion cluster near infinity looks like a critical cluster with a slightly supercritical 'ponds' structure at scales below the current pond size. The source notes that the IIC and IPC have different scaling limits on the tree (Angel-Goodman-den Hollander-Slade), so the constants A and A' differ and the exponent may agree. A rigorous bound: since the invasion cluster contains the IIC-like structure... no inclusion holds in either direction. The ponds structure: invasion percolation on Z^d invades the cluster of the origin at level p_c + eps_k where eps_k decreases to 0 along the pond sequence; the probability that x at distance r is invaded is roughly the probability that x lies in the p_c + eps(r) cluster of the origin restricted to the ball of radius r, with eps(r) the level at scale r; in high dimensions eps(r) ~ r^{-2} (mean-field correlation length exponent 1/2), and P_{p_c + r^{-2}}(0 <-> x, |x| = r) is of order r^{-(d-2)} times the number of extra connections... a computation via the slightly supercritical two-point function gives P(x in IPC) ~ r^{-(d-2)} x (number of vertices at distance about r in the cluster)/... I could not make this precise; the mean-field prediction of the exponent d-4 comes from the IIC analogy. Not resolved; the reduction is to a slightly supercritical two-point function estimate at p_c + r^{-2} with matching constants, which is a Problem 11.1-type supercritical quantity. Obstruction: Requires slightly supercritical two-point asymptotics with constants (C0065-type input).

Let A be a nonempty subset of a finite set B. Then sum over X inside B with X union A = B of (-1)^|X| = 0, so a uniformly random subset X of B, conditioned on X union A = B, has E[(-1)^|X|] = 0. If instead each element of B is put in X independently with probability p in (0, 1], then P(X union A = B) = p^|B minus A| > 0 and E[(-1)^|X| | X union A = B] = (-1)^|B minus A| (1 - 2p)^|A|, which is 0 only at p = 1/2.

body: [Definition def:local-limit of arXiv:2605.01444, 'From second moments to pairwise negative correlation: \\applications to minimal and unifor'] Let $(G_n)_{n\;\geqslant\;1}$ be a sequence of locally finite, connected graphs (possibly random). Choose $\rho_n$ uniformly from $V(G_n)$, independently of each other. [Lem convolution-sup-bounds of arXiv:2601.19145, 'Stochastic Persistence in Infinite Dimensions'] Fix $2 \leq r < \infty$ and $\mathcal{B} \coloneqq L^r$. For all $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$, $\epsilon \in (0,1/2)$, $p > \epsilon^{-1}$, $T > 0$ the following hold:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item For $y \in L^p([0,T]; \mathcal{B}_{\alpha - 1 + \epsilon})$,
        $$[0,T] \ni t \mapsto (S*y)_t \in \mathcal{B}_\alpha$$
        is continuous and
        $$
        \sup_{t \leq T} \|(S * y)_t\|^p_\alpha \lesssim \int_0^T \|y_t\|^p_{\alpha - 1 + \epsilon} dt \,.$$
        \item For $Z \in L^p(\Omega \times [0,T];\gamma(\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{B}_{\alpha - 1/2 + \epsilon}))$,
        $$[0,T] \ni t \mapsto (S\diamond Z)_t \in \mathcal{B}_\alpha$$
        is continuous and
        $$\mathbb{E}\Big[\sup_{t \leq T} \|(S \diamond Z)_t\|^p_\alpha \Big] \lesssim \mathbb{E}\Big[\int_0^T \|Z_t\|^p_{\gamma(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{B}_{\alpha - 1/2 + \epsilon})} dt\Big] \,.$$
    \end{enumerate}
    In the above, the constants in $\lesssim$'s do not depend on $x,y,Z$, and the dependence on $T$ is uniform over bounded subsets of $(0,\infty)$.

Independent review pending. Let G be a countable connected locally finite graph with p_c(G)>0 and sample iid Bernoulli bond percolation at p_c(G). Almost surely every infinite open component C, regarded as a fixed graph after conditioning on the sampled field, has quenched bond threshold p_c(C)=1. For rational r<1, independent r-thinning of the sampled open bonds is unconditionally iid bond percolation at p_c(G)r<p_c(G), so its probability of any infinite component is zero. Conditioning, then intersecting over rational r and using monotonicity, proves simultaneous failure of percolation below r=1 on every C. Infinitude of C alone therefore supplies no robustness under thinning.

[Theorem eq:abstract-pressure-bridge of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:conditional-transfer}
For all sufficiently large \(N\), suppose
\(\widehat Q_{N,L}\) and
\(\widehat P_{N,L}(\varepsilon,\eta)\) are finite for every
\(\varepsilon,\eta>0\).  Suppose also that there exist \(\Phi\in\mathbb R\) and a
function \(F\) on \((0,\infty)^2\) such that
\begin{equation}
 \widehat P_{N,L}(\varepsilon,\eta)\longrightarrow F(\varepsilon,\eta)
 \quad\text{for every fixed }\varepsilon,\eta>0,
 \qquad
 F(\varepsilon,\eta)\longrightarrow\Phi
 \quad\text{as }(\varepsilon,\eta)\to(0,0).
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{align}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\widehat Q_{N,L}
 &\le\Phi+\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{up}}(V),
 \\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\widehat Q_{N,L}
 &\ge\Phi-\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{low}}(V).
 
\end{align}
Consequently,
\begin{align}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &\le
 \max\{\Phi+\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{up}}(V),
            \overline\Lambda_L^J(V)\},\\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &\ge
 \max\{\Phi-\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{low}}(V),
            \underline\Lambda_L^J(V)\}.
 
\end{align}
If both de-regularization defects vanish, then
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N
 \log\widehat{\mathscr C}_{N,L}^J(V)=\Phi
\end{equation}
and the exact identities
\begin{align}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &=\max\{\Phi,\overline\Lambda_L^J(V)\},
 \\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &=\max\{\Phi,\underline\Lambda_L^J(V)\}
 
\end{align}
hold.  In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)=\Phi
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \overline\Lambda_L^J(V)\le\Phi.
\end{equation}

A concrete sufficient condition for (equation eq:abstract-pressure-bridge of the paper)
is that, for any fixed \(L>0\), the disorder array and \(V\) satisfy the
hypotheses of (thm:bulk-universality of the paper) with \(m=2\).
Indeed, (equation eq:point-Haar-zero-cost of the paper) is automatic.  In this concrete
case,
\[
 \Phi=\Phi_p^{\rm bulk}(V)
 =\sup_{u\in\mathbb R}\{\theta_p(u)-V(u)\}.
\]
When the two de-regularization defects vanish,
(equation eq:exact-universality-iff-localized-defect of the paper) therefore gives a
criterion for the localized branch that is both necessary and sufficient. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Write rho_i = ||f(x_i) - y_i|| / m_i for the per-row ratio. Then S = mean rho_i and Q = mean rho_i^2 = (mean rho_i)^2 + var(rho_i). Two estimators f and g with the same S can differ in Q by the difference of their ratio variances, and an estimator with the smaller Q can have the larger S whenever its ratios are less dispersed but larger on average - the ordering by Q is the ordering by S only when the ratio dispersion is comparable across candidates. On a corpus whose ratios have a heavy right tail (near-floor rows, where a fixed absolute error is a ratio of hundreds), the dispersion term dominates Q and the candidates are ordered by their tails, not by their mean ratio. Computed 2026-08-30 by exhaustive enumeration on Z^2; the enumerator reproduces the published unconstrained counts 780, 5916, 44100 and 324932 at lengths 6, 8, 10 and 12.

Assumes: square lattice Z^2, nearest-neighbour steps
title: There are exactly 2125 self-avoiding walks of length 10 that start at (0,0), stay in the strip 0 <= y < 3, and avoid the sites (4,2).

body: In mathematics, especially group theory, two elements $a$ and $b$ of a group are conjugate if there is an element $g$ in the group such that $b=gag^{-1}.$ This is an equivalence relation whose equivalence classes are called conjugacy classes. In other words, each conjugacy class is closed under the maps $a\mapsto gag^{-1},$ with $g$ an element of the group.
