    E_0=0,
    E_{l+1}=(1+3H D^4 Wmax^3 K_l^2) E_l
                       +3H D^4 Wmax^2 K_l^3,
    Lambda=D Wmax E_L+D K_L > 0.

For any two parameter vectors theta,theta' in the cube at sup distance
rho, the outputs obey

    sup_W max(|mu_theta-mu_theta'|,|v_theta-v_theta'|)
        <= Lambda rho.                                  (3)

To verify this, use the sup norm across all tokens and coordinates. Each
transformed coordinate Qh has magnitude <=D Wmax K_l; each score has
magnitude <=D^3 Wmax^2 K_l^2; each Vh coordinate has magnitude
<=D Wmax K_l. The normalized sum cancels N and proves the K recurrence.

At fixed weights, changing inputs by d changes one head by at most
3D^4 Wmax^3 K_l^2 d: two terms differentiate the score and one term
the value; ReLU is 1-Lipschitz. At fixed inputs of size K_l, changing
matrix entries by rho changes a head by at most
3D^4 Wmax^2 K_l^3 rho, by the same three-term product split. Splitting
the joint change into these two changes and adding the residual proves
the E recurrence by induction. The readout change is bounded by
D Wmax E_L rho+D K_L rho. Clipping is 1-Lipschitz, proving (3).
These estimates compare actual heads directly, and require no independence
among tokens or between successive layers.

Divide [-Wmax,Wmax] into q equal intervals. There are q+1 grid values;
each parameter has a grid value within 2Wmax/q<=gamma/Lambda.
Thus the full grid has J elements and gives a gamma cover in the output
metric of (3). It is fixed before seeing the training tasks. In particular
log J <= P log(2+2Wmax Lambda/gamma) except when the max with 1 is active;
in that case q=1 and the same bound still holds since 2+2Wmax Lambda/gamma>=2.

## 3. A uniform exponential moment and finite-cover concentration

Write Z=(Y-a(W))/sqrt(b(W)). Its conditional law given W is standard
normal, hence Z is independent of W. For every theta,

    0 <= ell_theta <= C+A Z^2.

Indeed |Y-mu_theta|<=D0+sqrt(V)|Z| and (r+s)^2<=2r^2+2s^2.
Since C/K<=1/4 and A/K<=1/4, Gaussian integration yields

    E exp(ell_theta/K)
       <= exp(C/K)(1-2A/K)^(-1/2)
       <= exp(1/4)sqrt(2) < 2.                           (4)

The last inequality follows from log(2)>1/2 (integrate 1/x on [1,2]).
It follows from the nonnegative exponential series that
E ell_theta^k <= 2 k! K^k for every integer k>=1. For
X=ell_theta-E ell_theta, convexity gives

    E|X|^k <= 2^k E ell_theta^k <= 2^(k+1) k! K^k.

For |z|<1/(2K), the centered exponential series therefore gives

    log E exp(z X) <= 8K^2 z^2/(1-2K|z|).              (5)

Interchange of expectation and the series is justified by the absolute
moment series, which converges at these z. Independence across the m
tasks gives for their centered sum the same bound with 8mK^2 in
the numerator. Chernoff's inequality and (5) give each one-sided tail

    Pr(|Rhat(theta)-R(theta)| >
                  sqrt(32)K sqrt(u/m)+2K u/m) <= 2exp(-u).

For completeness, the generic bound log E exp(z S)<=v z^2/[2(1-cz)]
implies Pr(S>=sqrt(2vu)+cu)<=exp(-u): substitute
z=r/(1+cr), r=sqrt(2u/v), into the exponential Markov bound.
Here v=16mK^2, c=2K; apply it also to -S and divide by m.
No bounded-label assumption has been used.

A union bound on the J fixed grid predictors, with u=log(4J/alpha),
shows all their risk deviations are <=beta except on probability alpha/2.

## 4. From the grid to every parameter

For two clipped predictors within gamma in both output coordinates,
the elementary log derivative and a difference-of-squares split give

    |ell_theta(W,Y)-ell_theta'(W,Y)| <= gamma L(Y),
    L(Y)=1/(2v0)+(|Y|+U)/v0+(|Y|+U)^2/(2v0^2).       (6)

In detail, the log term costs gamma/(2v0). Hold v fixed and vary the
mean to get gamma(|Y|+U)/v0. Hold the new mean fixed and vary 1/v to
get gamma(|Y|+U)^2/(2v0^2). Both denominators use the common positive
floor v0. Thus E L(Y)<=Q: E|Y|<=M+sqrt(V) and
E(|Y|+U)^2<=2D0^2+2V.

The standard-normal exponential integral E exp(zZ)=exp(z^2/2), followed
by exponential Markov at z=x, gives Pr(|Z|>x)<=2exp(-x^2/2).
For t=log(4m/alpha), a union bound gives |Y_i|<=T for all i except
on probability alpha/2. On that event the empirical average of L(Y_i)
is at most L_T. Combine this event with the grid concentration event.
For each theta choose a grid point theta' satisfying (3). Insert
R(theta') and Rhat(theta') and use (6) to obtain the first line of (1).
The approximate-ERM inequality then gives the second line of (1).
The same event works for all approximate ERMs, without a union over
their potentially data-dependent choice. This proves (1) and (2).

## 5. GP comparator and scope

For the finite-rank noisy GP in C002, with supplied features bounded by R,
context length <=n and context labels bounded by B, one can use

    M=nR^2 B/s, V=s+R^2.

Take a desired comparator accuracy eps_c>0, U=M+sqrt(s eps_c),
v0=s, v1=V+s min(1/2,sqrt(eps_c)). C002's scalar error estimates
ensure its outputs lie in these intervals and its expected forward KL
is <=eps_c. Its padded encoding has K0=max(1,R,B,s), width D=7p+4,
at most H=5 heads and L=T_c+2 layers. The construction gives fixed
explicit matrices and readout. Choose Wmax at least 1 and their largest
absolute scalar entry; this is an explicitly computable maximum of the
finite matrices specified by C002 Section 4, independent of task data.
The class of Section 2 then contains that comparator, and (2) implies

    E_W KL(P_W || h_thetahat(W)) <= eps_c+2E_m+xi.        (7)

One may use the internally clipped variant with the explicit common cap

    Kcap=max(1,R,B,s,2nRB/s,2R/s,U,v1).

It preserves the C002 comparator exactly: its feature and query registers
are bounded by R; for every Chebyshev iteration j, |r_j(lambda)|<=1,
so the mean-solve iterates have norm <=2nRB/s and the variance-solve
iterates have norm <=2R/s. The previous-iterate registers have the same
bounds. Initialization, broadcast, constants, and final output registers
are covered by the other displayed terms. Thus clipping changes none
of its states. For this class the parameter Lipschitz recurrence uses a
constant Kcap, and log Lambda grows at most linearly with depth, avoiding
the very loose cubic growth of the unclipped K recurrence. The statistical
bound (7) is consequently explicit for a class containing the comparator
with either choice of internal clipping. All added clipping parameters
are fixed, so P still counts exactly the trainable entries.

For R=0 use a constant exact comparator instead of C002's formulas that
divide by R. The class can contain it by initializing a constant coordinate
and choosing a readout that outputs (0,s).

If training uses rejection to enforce bounded context labels, (7) concerns
the resulting conditioned task distribution. It is not silently a theorem
for the original unconditioned GP context law. With unconditioned contexts,
the C002 comparator guarantee and this bounded-input parameter cover do
not apply as stated. This is the precise remaining distributional scope
issue, separate from the unbounded Gaussian query labels handled above.

All constants here are explicit but loose. The parameter cube and finite
cover give a statistical ERM guarantee, not SGD convergence, efficient
enumeration of the cover, a finite-bit realization theorem for the original
solver, or a claim that Chebyshev depth beats Newton-type solvers.

## 6. Sources and status

Bai, Chen, Wang, Xiong and Mei, arXiv:2306.04637v2, Section 5.1,
PDF pages 14-15, define pretraining ERM for square loss and give Theorem 20.
That is the related parameter-entropy/ERM framework, not a citation for
the Gaussian log-loss bound above. Sections 2-4 provide its proof directly.
C002 v1 supplies the independently checked uniform-KL comparator.
This extension itself remains unaudited. [Theorem 4 (Varying environment) of arXiv:2605.04048, 'Catastrophe--dispersion models in random and varying environments across generations'] Assume $(\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ is deterministic and $0<\mu_n<+\infty$ for all $n$.
Define
\[
\underline{\Lambda}=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{S_n}{n},\qquad
\overline{\Lambda}=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{S_n}{n}.
\]
\begin{itemize}
  \item[(a)] If $\overline{\Lambda}<0$, then $\p(Z_n\to0)=1$ (extinction).
  \item[(b)] If $\underline{\Lambda}>0$, then $\p(Z_n\to\infty)>0$ (survival with positive probability).
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: For an m by n matrix A = (a_{ij}) and a p by q matrix B, the Kronecker product A tensor B is the (mp) by (nq) matrix written in m by n block form, whose (i,j) block, of size p by q, equals a_{ij} B, for i = 1,...,m and j = 1,...,n. The Kronecker product satisfies the mixed-product property (A tensor B)(C tensor D) = (AC) tensor (BD) whenever the ordinary products AC and BD are defined, and if A is n by n with eigenvalues lambda_1,...,lambda_n and B is m by m with eigenvalues mu_1,...,mu_m, then A tensor B is nm by nm with eigenvalues lambda_i mu_j for all i,j. [standard, e.g. Horn and Johnson, Topics in Matrix Analysis]
title: Kronecker Product of Two Matrices

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] The divisible sandpile on $\Z^d$ starts from i.i.d.\ masses at each site, and, in each discrete time step, a site with mass above one keeps one unit and sends the excess equally to its neighbors. \citet*{LMPU} showed that at mean one this process explodes, with every site emitting infinite mass. We show that the mass emitted from a site by time $t$ is of order $t^{(4-d)/4}$ for $d\leq3$, of order $\log t$ for $d=4$, and a tail-dependent, divergent rate for $d\geq5$. We further show that the mass emitted, after diffusive rescaling, converges to a Brownian optimal-stopping value for $d\leq3$ and to tail-dependent, weighted membrane fields for $d\geq5$, while at the critical dimension $d=4$, after superdiffusive rescaling, it converges to the membrane model. Using these estimates, we prove that, for every $d\geq2$, the set of sites that topple contains an infinite component at some mean below one, hence it has a non-trivial percolation phase transition. This answers a variant of a question of \citet*{FMR}. The proof adapts ideas from the theory of level-set percolation of strongly correlated Gaussian fields.
title: Abstract of arXiv:2609.02829: Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile

such that $|B_R|=|E|$, then
$$\operatorname{Cap}_s(E)\geq \operatorname{Cap}_s(B_R).$$
Moreover,
$$\operatorname{Cap}_s(B_R)=\frac{\Gamma(n/2)}{\gamma_{n,s}\Gamma(s/2)\Gamma((n-s+2)/2)}R^{n-s}.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Ill-conditioned Gram coordinates do not make the projection unstable.

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, Posterior cones and sharp reconstruction thresholds on finite-mean Galton-Watson trees (October 2026), proves that for symmetric ferromagnetic Potts broadcasting with three or four states on an observed Galton-Watson tree with any finite mean offspring d and 0 < lambda < 1, reconstruction holds exactly when d lambda^2 > 1; at equality the root cannot be reconstructed. No assumption on the offspring variance or tail is needed. The three-state argument uses an explicit invariant cone of posterior laws built from H = y - x^2/2, where x and y are the quadratic and cubic centred posterior invariants; its two global inequalities are certified by exact nonnegative polynomial coefficients (80,532 coefficients, produced by two independent integer programs). The four-state case combines the same argument with a posterior cone from earlier work, which the paper credits. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/posterior-cones-reconstruction (commit fc9659e64c43). Not refereed.
title: Sharp reconstruction threshold d lambda^2 > 1 for three- and four-state Potts broadcasting on finite-mean Galton-Watson trees, via posterior cones (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/posterior-cones-reconstruction)

[Thmintro rigidityspherical of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Assume $\bm{s} = (s_1, \dots, s_n) \in \mathcal{Z}(\Phi)$ is a spherical multislope or a $\mathbb{T}^2$-type planar multislope. Then either 
    $$\left((s_1, +\infty) \times \dots \times (s_n, +\infty)\right) \cap \mathcal{Z}(\Phi) = \varnothing$$
    or

    $$
    \limsup_{n \to + \infty} \frac{|Z_n|}{ \sqrt{\log(n+2)}} >0.

A topological space X is normal (meaning every pair of disjoint closed subsets has disjoint open neighbourhoods) if and only if for every pair of disjoint closed subsets A, B of X there exists a continuous function f: X -> [0, 1] with f = 0 on A and f = 1 on B (Urysohn's lemma and its converse). No T1 axiom is needed for this equivalence under this definition of normality.

Normality, in the equivalent form 'whenever C is closed, O is open, and C is contained in O, there is an open U with C contained in U and the closure of U contained in O', is applied repeatedly to build open sets U_q indexed by the rational numbers q in (0,1) (dyadic rationals suffice) such that A is contained in every U_q, every closure of U_q avoids B, and q < r implies the closure of U_q is contained in U_r. One starts with A inside the open set X minus B and interpolates one new index at a time. Define f(x) = inf of the set of q with x in U_q, with f(x) = 1 when x belongs to no U_q. Then f = 0 on A and f = 1 on B. Continuity: f(x) < a holds exactly when x lies in some U_q with q < a, an open condition; f(x) > a holds exactly when x lies outside the closure of some U_q with q > a, again an open condition; preimages of subbasic intervals [0,a) and (a,1] are therefore open, so f is continuous. Conversely, if such an f exists for disjoint closed A and B, then f^{-1}([0, 1/2)) and f^{-1}((1/2, 1]) are disjoint open sets containing A and B, so X is normal. body: [Definition DefDLE of arXiv:2410.23899, 'Tightness for interlacing geometric random walk bridges'] Let $\Sigma \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ and $\llbracket T_0, T_1 \rrbracket$ be a non-empty integer interval in $\mathbb{Z}$. Consider the set $Y$ of functions $f: \Sigma \times \llbracket T_0, T_1 \rrbracket \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that $f(i, j+1) - f(i,j) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ when $i \in \Sigma$ and $j \in\llbracket T_0, T_1 -1 \rrbracket$ and let $\mathcal{D}$ denote the discrete $\sigma$-algebra on $Y$. We call a function $g: \llbracket T_0, T_1 \rrbracket \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that $f( j+1) - f(j) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ when $j \in\llbracket T_0, T_1 -1 \rrbracket$  an {\em increasing path} and elements in $Y$ {\em collections of increasing paths}. A $\Sigma$-{\em indexed geometric line ensemble $\mathfrak{L}$ on $\llbracket T_0, T_1 \rrbracket$}  is a random variable defined on a probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{B}, \mathbb{P})$, taking values in $Y$ such that $\mathfrak{L}$ is a $(\mathcal{B}, \mathcal{D})$-measurable function. Unless otherwise specified, we will assume that $T_0 \leq T_1$ are both integers, although the above definition makes sense if $T_0 = -\infty$, or $T_1 = \infty$, or both.

[Theorem 28 (Coupling from the past) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Consider a Glauber dynamic $R$ for a measure $\mu$ on $S^V$.
    Suppose that $S$ is partially ordered and that $R$ is monotone.
    Suppose moreover $S$ has a largest element $\alpha^+$ and a smallest element $\alpha^-$.
    We also write $\alpha^\pm$ for the corresponding elements in $S^V$.
    Then for any fixed $\Pi\in\Omega$:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item For any bounded $B\subset V\times\R_{\leq 0}$, the map $R_{\Pi(B)}:S^V\to S^V$ is monotone,
        \item The element $R_{\Pi(\Lambda\times[-t,0])}(\alpha^+)$ is decreasing in $\Lambda$ and $t$,
        \item The element $R_{\Pi(\Lambda\times[-t,0])}(\alpha^-)$ is increasing in $\Lambda$ and $t$.
    \end{itemize}
    In particular, if
    \[R_{\Pi(\Lambda\times[-t,0])}(\alpha^+)_u=R_{\Pi(\Lambda\times[-t,0])}(\alpha^-)_u\]
    then this value will not change if we replace $\alpha^+$ by any other $\alpha\in S^V$,
    $\Lambda$ by any larger set, and $t$ by any larger time. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Off an event with probability at most $2^{-b R}$,  we have that,  on the event that there are exactly four crossings of $A$ made by loops in $\overline{\Gamma}$ with height in $\{-\lambda,\lambda\}$,  every crossing of $B_{1/2}(0) \setminus \overline{B_{2^{-R/3}}(0)}$ and every crossing of $B_{2^{-2R/3}}(0) \setminus \overline{B_{2^{-R}}(0)}$ made by a loop in $\overline{\Gamma}$ with height in $\{-\lambda,\lambda\}$ is part of one of these four crossings of $A$.

body:
[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2609.01114, 'Unbalanced spectral Tur\'an problem for color-critical graphs with prescribed large maximu'] Fix $p\ge2$. The following claims hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
\item If a complete multipartite graph has positive part sizes $s_1,\ldots,s_p$, then its spectral radius is the unique positive solution of
\begin{equation}
        \sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{s_i}{\lambda+s_i}=1 .
\end{equation}
\item For fixed $D$ and $p$, the graph $(n-D)K_1\vee K_{m_1,\ldots,m_p}$ with $\sum_{i=1}^{p} m_i= D$ has maximum spectral radius when $m_1,\ldots,m_p$ are as equal as possible, and equality occurs only for such a balanced choice, up to permutation of the parts.
\item For fixed $n$, define the function $f_{n,p}(D):=\rho(S_{n,D,p})$, where $\left\lceil\frac{p}{p+1}n\right\rceil\le D\le n-1$.

Then $f_{n,p}(D)$ is strictly decreasing in $D$.
\item Denote $\eta_p:=\frac{2p-1}{p(p-1)}$.

There are constants $\beta_p\in(0,(100p^2)^{-1}]$ and $C_p>0$ such that, uniformly for $(1-\beta_p)n\le D\le n$,
\begin{equation}
        \left|\rho(S_{n,D,p})-\rho(T(n,p))-\eta_p(n-D)\right|
        \le C_p\left(\frac{(n-D)^2}{n}+1\right).
\end{equation}
In particular,
\[
        \rho(S_{n,D,p})-\rho(T(n,p))
        =\eta_p(n-D)+O_p((n-D)^2/n)+O_p(1).
\]
\item For fixed $D$ and $p$, define $g_{D,p}(N):=\rho(S_{N,D,p})$, where $N\geq D+1$.

Then $g_{D,p}(N)$ is strictly increasing in $N$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Lemma 19 of arXiv:2609.01114

body: An outer measure on a set X is a function mu* from all subsets of X to [0, infinity] with mu*(empty) = 0, monotonicity (A subset B implies mu*(A) <= mu*(B)), and countable subadditivity (mu* of a countable union <= sum of mu*). Outer measures are cheap to build (e.g. by covering with a distinguished class and summing a premeasure), but are generally not additive on all sets - additivity is recovered on the Caratheodory-measurable sets.
title: Outer Measure

[Proposition prop:LehnerFormula of arXiv:2510.01021, '\Large Random Matrices, Intrinsic Freeness, and Sharp Non-Asymptotic Inequalities\relatedv'] [Lehner's formula~[LehnerFormula1999] (see also~[bandeira2023free])]

Let $A_0,A_1,\dots,A_n$ be self-adjoint matrices and $X_{\mathrm{free}}$ as in Definition~(def:Xfree of the paper):
\begin{equation}
\big\| X_{\mathrm{free}} \big\| = \max_{\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}} \inf_{Z\succeq 0} \lambda_{\max}\left(Z^{-1} + \varepsilon A_0 + \sum_{k=1}^n A_k Z A_k \right).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop:LehnerFormula of arXiv:2510.01021

[Theorem thm:simplicity_CM of arXiv:2607.16911, 'Multipartite random graphs with given degrees: local limit, revisiting the giant, distance'] Assume the pair $(i,j)$ is $\rm GOOD$, $i,j\in [k]$.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item If $i=j$, $\liminf_{n \to \infty}\Prob{CM_n^{i,i}\textrm{ is simple}}=e^{-\phi_i/2-(\phi_i)^2/4}>0$.
        \item  If $i \neq j$, $\liminf_{n \to \infty}\Prob{CM_n^{i,j}\textrm{ is simple}}=e^{-\phi_{i,j}}>0$.
        \item The law of $CM_n^{i,i}$ conditionally on the event $\{CM_n^{(i,i)}\textrm{ is simple}\}$ is uniform on the set of all simple graphs on $\mathcal N^{(i)}$ with degree sequence $\mathbf d_i(n)$.
        \item The law of $CM_n^{i,j}$ conditionally on the event $\{CM_n^{(i,j)}\textrm{ is simple}\}$ is uniform on the set of all simple bipartite graphs on $\mathcal N^{(i)}\cup \mathcal N^{(j)}$ with bi-degree sequence $(\mathbf d_{(i,j)}(n),\mathbf d_{(j,i)}(n))$.
    \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Simplicity probability of configuration models

Method: Sharp constant-one comparisons of reversible mixing and stopping parameters structural calculation Result: The stopping half follows from Dynkin optional sampling. Let Lf=-lambda*f with lambda=1/tau2, mean_pi f=0, and choose x with f(x)=M=max f>0. For any integrable randomized stopping time U from x with X_U distributed as pi, E f(X_U)-f(x)=-lambda*E integral_0^U f(X_s)ds. Thus M=lambda*E integral f<=lambda*M*E U, giving E U>=tau2. The discrete-time proof replaces the integral by sum_(s<U)f(X_s). Check: Apply the identity first at U wedge n. The bounded function and integrability of U justify dominated convergence of the integral and of f(X_(U wedge n)). This avoids the false assertion that an exponential eigenfunction martingale is automatically uniformly integrable at U. Obstruction: The bound on tau1 by tau0 remains unresolved here. Worst-start total variation cannot be bounded solely by an unweighted spectral trace without controlling eigenfunction amplitudes. The source convention uses the continuized threshold and pairwise total variation, not the usual distance-to-pi threshold.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Kernel criteria for critical inhomogeneous random-graph universality structural reduction Result: L3 integrability of the principal eigenfunction does not itself give a spectral gap. Partition[0,1] into blocks of masses p_i tending to0, choose epsilon_i>0 tending to0, and let m=sum p_i epsilon_i. On blocks i,j set kappa=(1-epsilon_i)1{i=j}/p_i+epsilon_i epsilon_j/m. This symmetric positive kernel has row integral1, so its principal eigenfunction is the constant1 in L3. For the centered indicator of block i, the Rayleigh quotient tends to1 as epsilon_i tends to0. Check: The row integral is1-epsilon_i+epsilon_i=1. The Dirichlet energy of the block indicator is at most p_i epsilon_i, while its centered L2 norm squared is p_i(1-p_i). Thus the spectral gap is at most epsilon_i/(1-p_i), tending to0. Positivity of the kernel makes the constant eigenfunction unique up to scale. Obstruction: The example is an obstruction to using an unstated spectral-gap consequence of the conjectured criterion. It is not asserted to refute random-graph universality; the component scaling for this explicit kernel remains to be analyzed.

body: Fubini's theorem gives the conditions under which a double integral can be computed as an iterated integral, i.e. by integrating in one variable at a time. Intuitively, just as the volume of a loaf of bread is the same whether one sums over standard slices or over long thin slices, the value of a double integral does not depend on the order of integration when the hypotheses of the theorem are satisfied. The theorem is named after Guido Fubini, who proved a general result in 1907; special cases were known earlier through results such as Cavalieri's principle, which was used by Leonhard Euler.
title: Fubini's theorem

    Then, there exists a constant $C(b,\sigma)>0$ such that for any $r\in\{1,2,\cdots,d\}$,

			\sup_{t\in[0,\infty)}\bb E[|X_t|^2]\le C(b,\sigma)\big(1+\bb E[|X_0|^2]\big)$.

[Lemma 31 (Rational Tori Invariance) of arXiv:2609.00974, 'On Algebraic Integrability\\ of Vector Fields \\ with Rational Function Coefficients\\ tha'] Let $D$ be a derivation of the form $D= \sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i)\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}$ where $f_i\in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}(X)$ are nonzero rational functions, let $A_1,\ldots,A_n\in \mathbb{Q}$ be nonzero rational numbers. Then $D$ defines an algebraically integrable foliation if and only if
    $E=\sum_{i=1}^n A_if_i(x_i)\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}$ does too.
title: Rational Tori Invariance

CONJECTURE, NOT PROVED HERE. For every infinite finitely generated group Gamma and every fixed finite symmetric generating set S excluding the identity, let G be its simple undirected Cayley graph. For independent Bernoulli bond percolation, p_c is the infimum of p with an infinite cluster almost surely, and p_u is the infimum of p with exactly one infinite cluster almost surely. The assertion is p_c(G)<p_u(G) if and only if Gamma is nonamenable. Existence of a favorable S does not settle the universal assertion. The amenable direction is known. [Proposition prop:almost_Linfty of arXiv:2607.15140, 'On the absence of blow-up in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations with transport noise'] Let $I\subset (-1/4,\infty)$ be an interval of length $T<\infty$.
Let $p,q\in (2,\infty)$ be such that the Sobolev index $\mathtt{Sob}=1-\frac{2}{p}-\frac{d}{q}$ satisfies  (equation eq:assumption_suboptimal_Lq_finite_time1 of the paper), and set $q_{{\rm max}}\stackrel{{\rm def}}{=}-\frac{d^2}{d-2}\frac{1}{\mathtt{Sob}}$, 
with the convention $q_{{\rm max}}=\infty$ if $d=2$.
Then, for all $p_0\in (2,\infty)$ and $q_0\in (2,q_{{\rm max}})$ for which (equation eq:suboptimal_Lq_finite_time_suboptimality_condition of the paper) holds, and $r\in (1,\infty)$, there exists a constant $C_0>0$ such that, for all $N$, and
progressively measurable processes $F,G$
satisfying (equation eq:almost_Linfty01 of the paper)-(equation eq:almost_Linfty02 of the paper), the unique energy solution $v^N$ to (equation eq:turbulent_Stokes_scaling_uniform_estimates_modified of the paper) satisfies
\begin{align}

\big({\mathbf E}\|v^N\|_{L^{p_0}(I;L^{q_0} (\mathbb{T}^d))}^{r} \big)^{1/r}
&\leq 
 C_0  \big({\mathbf E}\|F\|_{L^p(I;L^q(\mathbb{T}^d))}^r\big)^{1/r}\\
 \nonumber
& +C_0 \big({\mathbf E}\|G\|_{L^p(I;L^q(\mathbb{T}^d))}^r\big)^{1/r}.
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let (X,X_prime) be an exchangeable pair on a Polish state space, let f be measurable with E[f(X)]=0, and let F be a measurable integrable real function of two states such that F(X,X_prime)=-F(X_prime,X) almost surely and E[F(X,X_prime)|X]=f(X). For every measurable h with E|h(X)*F(X,X_prime)|<infinity, E[h(X)*f(X)]=(1/2)*E[(h(X)-h(X_prime))*F(X,X_prime)]. This identity does not require f(X_prime) to have a scalar linear regression on f(X).
Exchangeable pair; integrable antisymmetric kernel with conditional mean f(X).
Centered integrable f; E|h(X)*F(X,X_prime)|<infinity.

body:
[Theorem eq:bounded-coexistence-ratio of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:bounded-coexistence}
For every \(p\ge3\), there is a law \(\mu\) as in
(thm:bounded-block-counterexample of the paper), chosen to match Gaussian
moments through order \(2p\).  For this compactly supported law and
every fixed \(L,\varepsilon>0\), \(V\in\mathcal V_{2p}\), and either
\(f\in\mathcal F_{2p}\) or \(f=\ell_\eta\) for fixed \(\eta>0\),
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\mathbb E_\mu\mathcal Z_{N,L}^J(V,\varepsilon,f)}
 {\mathbb E\mathcal Z_{N,L}^G(V,\varepsilon,f)}
 \longrightarrow1,
\end{equation}
and likewise for the point-incoherent functional.  Nevertheless, on
the compact interval \(B\) supplied by that theorem,
\[
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathbb E_\mu\operatorname{Crt}_N^J(B)
 >
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathbb E\operatorname{Crt}_N^G(B).
\]
The analogous coexistence holds in the standard symmetric-coordinate
model for a compactly supported law supplied by
(cor:symmetric-bounded-block of the paper) with matching order \(2p\).

[Proposition properties of r of arXiv:2507.10294, 'Guessing Strategies for Shelf-Shuffling Machines'] i.) The stopped process $r_{j\wedge\tau}$ is homogeneous and Markov. The transition probabilities of $r_j$ when both cards $n-1$ and $n$ have not been shown are 
\begin{equation}
    P(r_{j+1}=i\,|\,r_j=k,\,\tau>j)=\frac{\binom{i-k-1}{0}+\binom{i-k-1}{n-k-1}}{2^{i-k}}=\frac{1_{\{k+1\leq i\leq n\}}+1_{\{i=n\}}}{2^{i-k}}
\end{equation}

ii.) $\tau-1$ has a $\text{Binomial}(n-2,\,1/2)$ distribution.

iii.) After the $n-1$st or $n$th card is shown, the cards are deterministic and their order is given uniquely by $K_{\tau}$, if $\tau=\tau^n$. If $\tau=\tau^{n-1}$, then $r_{\tau+1}=n$ a.s. and the remaining cards, in order, are given by $K_{\tau}$. That is,
\[P(r_{\tau+m}=i\,|\,\tau=\tau^{n})=1_{\{K_{\tau}^m=i\}}\]
and
\[P(r_{\tau+1}=n\,|\,\tau=\tau^{n-1})=1, \;\;\;\;P(r_{\tau+m+1}=i\,|\,\tau=\tau^{n-1})=1_{\{K_{\tau}^m=i\}}\]

\begin{proof}

    First we prove i.). Fix $j<\tau$ and $k$ such that $p_{k,j}>0$. Recall that cards go to the top and the bottom of the pile via a $\text{Bernoulli}(1/2)$ distribution. Let $N_k$ be the number of cards at the top up to and including when card $k$ is selected. Then, $N_k$ is $\text{Binomial}(k,\,1/2)$. Observe that $\{r_j=k\}=\{N_k=j\}$ as events (intersected with $\{j<\tau\}$). Also notice that the number of cards that have not gone to the top is $k-N_k$. So we are left with a shuffle of $n-(N_k+k-N_k)=n-k$ cards according to the distribution from Theorem $(positionmatrix of the paper)$, with card $k+1$ at the top of the deck. This proves i.). 

    To prove ii.), we first notice that cards $n-1$ and $n$ always appear consecutively in the deck, with both orderings having probability $1/2$. Label this block of two cards $B$ and shuffle the remaining $n-2$ cards. Then $\{\tau=k\}$ if and only if $k-1$ cards have been selected, each with probability $1/2$, to go above $B$. Hence, 
    \[P(\tau=k)=\frac{\binom{n-2}{k-1}}{2^{k-1}}\]
    so that 
    \[P(\tau-1=k)=\frac{\binom{n-2}{k}}{2^k}\]
    showing ii.). 

    As for iii.), we note that after card $n$ is shown, the cards are almost surely in strictly decreasing order. This is because cards are drawn from the bottom of the deck. There is one unique arrangement of the remaining cards in decreasing order, namely, by removing the already selected cards from $[n]$ and reversing. This is exactly as in the construction of $K_{j\wedge \tau}$, proving iii.).
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space and $T: X \to X$ a homeomorphism. $T$ is called expansive if there is a constant $\delta > 0$ (an expansive constant) such that for every pair of distinct points $x \neq y$ in $X$ there exists an integer $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ (positive, zero or negative) with $d(T^n x, T^n y) > \delta$. Equivalently: two orbits that stay within distance $\delta$ of each other for all times $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ are the same orbit, i.e. the same point. Any $\delta' < \delta$ is again an expansive constant; on a compact metric space the property (though not the constant) does not depend on the choice of a compatible metric. A map $T$ (not necessarily invertible) is positively expansive if the same holds with $n$ restricted to $n \geq 0$. Examples: the full shift on $k$ symbols and every subshift (with $\delta$ below the distance between two sequences differing in the zeroth coordinate); hyperbolic toral automorphisms; Axiom A restricted to a basic set. Non-examples: the identity, any isometry (e.g. a circle rotation), any map with a nontrivial equicontinuous factor of the same type. Warning: the definition uses two-sided time for homeomorphisms; a homeomorphism of an infinite compact metric space is never positively expansive.
X is a compact metric space
T is a homeomorphism of X (bijective, continuous, continuous inverse)
the expansive constant delta is strictly positive and depends on the metric

[Theorem 8 (Random moderately sparse separation) of arXiv:2608.16701, 'Order-Sensitive Fast-Synapse Limits in Sparse Excitatory--Inhibitory Threshold--Reset Netw'] Let $N=4m$, and let $q_N>0$ satisfy
\begin{equation}
 q_N\longrightarrow\infty,
 \qquad \frac{q_N}{N}\longrightarrow0.
 
\end{equation}
Partition the vertices into source sets $S_\E,S_\I$ and a target set $T$
with sizes $N/4,N/4,N/2$.  Independently retain every possible edge from
$S_\E$ to $T$ and from $S_\I$ to $T$ with probability
\begin{equation}
 p_N=\frac{2q_N}{N}.
 
\end{equation}
This is a valid probability for all sufficiently large $N$ by
\eqref{eq:q-sparse}.  Give vertices in $S_\E$ and $S_\I$ types $\E$ and
$\I$, respectively; target types may be arbitrary.
Give retained excitatory edges weight $2a/q_N$ and retained inhibitory
edges weight $-2b/q_N$, and add no other edges.  Initialize every source at
threshold and every target at the same $x<\theta$.  All drifts vanish.
Assume that for some $\eta>0$,
\begin{equation}
 x+a\ge\theta+3\eta,
 \qquad x+a-b\le\theta-3\eta.
 
\end{equation}
Then, for every fixed $t_*>0$ and every deterministic sequence
$\varepsilon_N\downarrow0$,
\begin{equation}
 F_N^{\varepsilon_N,\E}(t_*)
 -F_N^{\varepsilon_N,\I}(t_*)
 \xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{L^1(\Prob_G)}\frac12.
 
\end{equation}
Moreover, if $d_N(G)=|E_N|/N$, then
\begin{equation}
 \frac{d_N(G)}{q_N}\xrightarrow{\Prob_G}\frac12.
 
\end{equation}
If in addition $q_N/\log N\to\infty$, then the count difference equals
$1/2$ with probability tending to one.  The graph obeys Dale's law.

[Lem 10 of arXiv:2603.29549, 'Multitype PCR branching processes'] Define the diagonal matrix 
$$
M(n) :=\mathrm{diag}\big(b_1^{-n},\ldots, b_1^{-n}, m_{d_0+1}(n), ...,m_d(n)\big),
$$
and assume that
\[0<m_i(n)\le Cb_1^{-n},\quad i=d_0+1,\ldots, d.\]
Then, for any $i>d_0$ and $\bar x\in \Real_+^d$, 
\begin{equation}
\frac 1{m_i(n)b_i^n} \, F^{(n)}_i(M(n) \bar x)\to  x_iG_i(x_0), \quad n\to \infty,
\end{equation}
where convergence is uniform on compact subsets of $\Real_+^d$.

body:
[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] Let $(X_t)_{t\in \mathbb{N}}$ be a RWBD chain with parameters $n,d$ and let $\Phi$ be defined as in Corollary \ref{Wilson-eig}. Then,
   \[\mathbb{E}_x\left(|\Phi(X_1)-\Phi(x)|^2\right)\leq \frac{n^2}{d^2(n-1)^2},\quad \forall x\in \Omega\]
   \begin{proof}
      Let $x\in \Omega$ be arbitrary and let $c = \frac{n}{d(n-1)}$. Then,
      \begin{align*}
         \mathbb{E}_x\left[|\Phi(X_1)-\Phi(x)|^2\right] &= \sum_{y\in \Omega} |\Phi(y) - \Phi(x)|^2\cdot P(y,x)\\
         &= |\Phi(x-1) - \Phi(x)|^2\frac{x}{d(n-1)} + |\Phi(x) - \Phi(x)|^2\frac{x(n-2)}{d(n-1)}  +|\Phi(x+1) - \Phi(x)|^2\frac{d-x}{d} \\
         &= |\Phi(x-1) - \Phi(x)|^2\frac{x}{d(n-1)}  +|\Phi(x+1) - \Phi(x)|^2\frac{d-x}{d} \\
         &= |1-c(x-1) - 1+cx|^2\frac{x}{d(n-1)}  +|1-c(x+1) - 1+cx|^2\frac{d-x}{d} \\
         &= c^2\frac{x}{d(n-1)}  +(-c)^2\frac{d-x}{d} \\
         &= \left(\frac{n}{d(n-1)}\right)^2\left(\frac{x}{d(n-1)}  +\frac{d-x}{d}\right) \\ \displaybreak[2]
         &= \left(\frac{n^2}{d^2(n-1)^2}\right)\left(\frac{x+(d-x)(n-1)}{d(n-1)}  \right) \\ \displaybreak[2]
         &= \left(\frac{n^2}{d^2(n-1)^2}\right)\left(\frac{x+d(n-1)-x(n-1)}{d(n-1)}  \right) \\ \displaybreak[2]
         &= \left(\frac{n^2}{d^2(n-1)^2}\right)\left(\frac{d(n-1)+x(2-n)}{d(n-1)}  \right) \\ \displaybreak[2]
         &= \left(\frac{n^2}{d^2(n-1)^2}\right)\left(1 + \frac{x(2-n)}{d(n-1)}  \right) \\
         &= \frac{n^2}{d^2(n-1)^2} + \frac{xn^2(2-n)}{d^3(n-1)^3} \\
         &= \frac{n^2(d(n-1)+x(2-n))}{d^3(n-1)^3} 
      \end{align*}
     Now, maximizing over $x\in \Omega$ we get that for all $x\in \Omega$,
     \begin{align*}
         \mathbb{E}_x\left[|\Phi(X_1)-\Phi(x)|^2\right] &\leq \frac{n^2(d(n-1)+0(2-n))}{d^3(n-1)^3} \tag{$\because n> 2$}\\
         &= \frac{n^2}{d^2(n-1)^2} 
     \end{align*}
   \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 19 of arXiv:2604.07478

[Proposition 14 (Almost-sure convergence of the input pairs) of arXiv:2511.12623, 'The eigenvector bead process'] For each fixed $j\in\mathbb{Z}$, the random pairs \eqref{eq:mu-rescale},\eqref{eq:def-local-g} $(\mu_{j}^{(N)}, g_{j}^{(N)})$ converge almost surely, as $N\to\infty$, to a limiting pair $(\mu_{j}^{(s=0)}, g_{j}^{(s=0)})$; that is,
\[
(\mu_{j}^{(N)}, g_{j}^{(N)}) \xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}} (\mu_{j}^{(s=0)}, g_{j}^{(s=0)}) \qquad (N\to\infty).
\]
Moreover, the limiting points $(\mu_{j}^{(s=0)})_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}$ form the sine--$\beta$ point process, and $(g_{j}^{(s=0)})_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}$ are independent Gaussian random variables, independent of $(\mu_{j}^{(s=0)})_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:mom-cum of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] Let $\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ such that it's
  moments $(\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ are given by
  \begin{equation}
    \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_n = \sum_{m = 0}^{n - 1} \frac{n!}{m! (m + 1) ! (n - m) !}
    \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi' (x))^{n - m}) {\mbox{\rotatebox[origin=c]{-90}{${-\!\!-}$}}}_{x =
    0}, 
  \end{equation}
  where $\Psi$ is a smooth function in a neighborhood of $0$. Then the free
  cumulants $(\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of $\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ are
  given by
  \[ \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}_n = \frac{\Psi^{(n)} (0)}{(n - 1) !}, \text{\qquad for
     all } \ n \in \mathbb{N}, \]
  i.e., $\Psi'$ is the $R$-transform of $\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$.
title: Lemma lem:mom-cum of arXiv:2412.09290

[Corollary 62 of arXiv:2608.29585, '2608.29585'] For every zero-framed knot $K$, set
\[
 \mathsf H_0(K;A,q)=1,\qquad
 \mathsf H_k(K;A,q)
 =\frac{\{-1;A\}G_k(K;A,q)}{\{k\}!}\quad(k\ge1).
\]
Then $\mathsf H_k(K;A,q)\in\mathscr I_q^{\ge2}$ and
\[
 \mathsf H_k(K;q^n,q)=H_k^{(n)}(K;q)
 \qquad(n\ge2).
\]
For each $k\ge0$, the element $\mathsf H_k(K;A,q)$ is the unique
element of $\Bbbk[A^{\pm1}]$ with these specializations, and
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf H_k(K;-A,q)=(-1)^k\mathsf H_k(K;A,q).
\end{equation}

There exists $\zeta > 0$ such that the following is true. Let $x,y \in \eta_1 \cap \eta_2$ be the first intersection point outside $B(0,1)$ (resp.\@ $B(0,2)$), and $\eta^{x,y}_1$ (resp.\@ $\eta^{x,y}_2$) the segments of $\eta_1$ (resp.\@ $\eta_2$) from $x$ to $y$. Then
\[
\mathbf{P}\left[ \eta^{x,y}_1,\eta^{x,y}_2 \subseteq [-u,u] \times [u^{-1},u] \right] = 1-O(u^{-\zeta}) \quad \text{as } u\to\infty .

[Theorem thm: main result of arXiv:2411.07947, 'Approximation rates of entropic maps in semidiscrete optimal transport'] Fix $\alpha \in (0,1]$.

    |\langle \varphi, T^\varepsilon - T^0 \rangle_{L^2(P)}| \lesssim \| \varphi \|_{\infty}\varepsilon^2 \log^3(1/\varepsilon)   + \| \varphi \|_{\mathcal{C}^\alpha}\varepsilon^{1+\alpha}, \quad \forall \varepsilon \in (0,1),

    where the inequality $\lesssim$ holds up to a constant that depends only on $\alpha,\mathcal{X}, \rho, \mathcal{Y}$, and $c_0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 13 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] Let $(X_t)_{t\in \mathbb{N}}$ be a birth-death chain over state space $\Omega=\{0,\dots,d\}$ with transition probabilities from some $x\in \Omega$,
  \begin{align*}
   P(x+1,x) &= p_x\\
   P(x-1,x) &= q_x\\
   P(x,x) &= r_x = 1 - p_x-q_x\\
   P(x,y) &= 0, \quad \forall y \not\in\{x,x+1,x-1\}
  \end{align*}
  Additionally, assume that $p_x$ and $q_x$ are affine in $x$. That is, there exists $\alpha,\beta,\xi,\eta\in \mathbb{R}$ such that,
  \[p_x = \alpha + \beta x \quad \text{and} \quad q_x = \xi + \eta x\]
  Finally, let $(K_m)_{m=0}^d$ be a sequence of degree $m$ polynomials that are orthogonal with respect to $\langle\cdot ,\cdot \rangle_\pi$ where $\pi$ is the stationary distribution. Then, $(K_m)_{m=0}^d$ are the eigenfunctions of $P$.
  \begin{proof}
   Let $x\in \Omega$ and $j\in \{0,\dots,d\}$ and consider,
   \begin{align*}
      (PK_j)(x) &= \sum_{y\in \Omega} P(x,y)K_j(y)\\
      &= P(x,x+1)K_j(x+1) + P(x,x-1)K_j(x-1) + P(x,x)K_j(x)\\
      &= q_{x+1} K_j(x+1) + p_{x-1} K_j(x-1) + r_x K_j(x)\\
      &= (\xi + \eta (x-1))K_j(x+1) + (\alpha + \beta (x+1))K_j(x-1) +(1 -(\alpha +\xi) - (\beta + \eta)x) K_j(x)
   \end{align*}
   Now, let $c$ be the coefficient of $x^{j}$ in $K_j(x)$. That is,
   \[K_j(x) = cx^j + o(x^{j-1})\]
   At this point, we examine the coefficient of $x^{j+1}$ in $(PK_j)(x)$. Using the above form and considering only relevant terms we have
   \begin{align*}
   (PK_j)(x)&= (\xi -\eta + \eta x)K_j(x+1) + (\alpha + \beta + \beta x)K_j(x-1) +(1 -(\alpha +\xi) - (\beta + \eta)x) K_j(x)\\
   &= \eta xc(x+1)^j + \beta x c(x-1)^j - (\beta + \eta)x cx^j + o(x^j)\\
   &=  \eta  cx^{j+1}+ \beta cx^{j+1} - (\beta + \eta)cx^{j+1} +  o(x^j)\\
   &= 0\cdot x^{j+1} + o(x^j)
   \end{align*}
   Thus, the coefficient of $x^{j+1}$ in $(PK_j)(x)$ is $0$. Also, notice that $(PK_j)(x)$ has no terms of order larger than $x^{j+1}$. This implies that $PK_j \in \mathbf{P}_j$ where $\mathbf{P}_j$ is the vector space of polynomials with degree at most $j$. This means that $\mathbf{P}_j$ is an invariant subspace with respect to $P$. Now, for any fixed $m\in \{0,\dots,d\}$, we know that $\{K_0,\dots K_{m-1}\}$ are orthogonal and therefore linearly independent. Thus, $\{K_0,\dots K_{m-1}\}$ span $\mathbf{P}_{m-1}$. Hence, any polynomial in $\mathbf{P}_j$ where $j < m$ is also orthogonal to $K_m$ by linearity of the inner product. Thus, $PK_j \in \mathbf{P}_j$, is orthogonal to $K_m$. That is,
   \[\langle K_m, PK_j \rangle_\pi = 0\]
   Hence, by Lemma \ref{self_ajoint},
   \[\langle PK_m, K_j\rangle_\pi=0 \quad \text{for}\quad j<m\]
   Finally, $PK_m \in \mathbf{P}_m$ so it admits the following presentation,
   \[PK_m = a_0 K_0 + a_1 K_1 + \cdots + a_m K_m\]
   where $a_0,\dots, a_m$ are constants. Hence,
   \begin{align*}
   0&= \langle PK_m, K_j\rangle_\pi\\
   &= \langle a_0 K_0 + a_1 K_1 + \cdots + a_m K_m, K_j\rangle_\pi\\
   &= a_0\langle K_0, K_j\rangle + \cdots + a_m\langle K_m, K_j\rangle_\pi \tag{by linearity}\\
   &= a_j\langle K_j, K_j\rangle_\pi \tag{by orthogonality}
   \end{align*}
   Therefore, $a_j = 0$ for all $j<m$. Thus,
   \[PK_m = a_m K_m\]
   and therefore, $K_m$ is an eigenfunction.
   \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 13 of arXiv:2604.07478

[Dfn of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{Probability functor}]
  Given a functor $\tau$,
  we define the probability functor $\sigma = \tau_{\mathcal{P}}$ as follows.
  \begin{itemize}
    \item 
      For $(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S}) \in \mathfrak{M}$, 
      set $\sigma(S) \coloneqq \mathcal{P}(\tau(S))$ to be the collection of probability measures on $\tau(S)$
      and $d_{\sigma}^{S, \rho_{S}} \coloneqq d_{P}^{\tau(S)}$
      to be the Prohorov metric on $\mathcal{P}(\tau(S))$
      defined by the metric $d_{\tau}^{S, \rho_{S}}$ on $\tau(S)$. 
    \item 
      For each $(S_{i}, d^{S_{i}}, \rho_{S_{i}}) \in \mathfrak{M},\, i=1,2$
      and root-and-distance-preserving map $f: S_{1} \to S_{2}$, 
      set $\sigma_{f}(P) \coloneqq P \circ \tau_{f}^{-1}$,
      that is, $\sigma_{f}(P)$ is the pushforward measure of $P$ by 
      the distance-preserving map $\tau_{f} : \tau(S_{1}) \to \tau(S_{2})$.
  \end{itemize}

body: [Proposition regularity_of_Sv of arXiv:2411.17653, 'Exclusion processes with non-reversible boundary: hydrodynamics and large deviations'] For any mild solution $v: {\Omega_T} \to [0,1]$ of (equation PDE_problem_linear of the paper) that belongs to $L^2([0,T],H^1([0,1]))$, we have that $ {v} \in H^{1}([0,T], C^2([0,1]))$.  {Moreover, if $\rho: {\Omega_T} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a function satisfying $\langle M(\rho,t),G \rangle = 0$ for any $G \in C^{1,2}( {\Omega_T})$, then $F(S \rho,G,t) = 0$ for any $G \in C^{1,2}([0,T]\times[0,1])$ and every $t \geq 0$, and so $S \rho$ is a (strong) solution of (equation PDE_problem_linear of the paper).}

[Defn def:3.1 of arXiv:2606.16237, 'The Backward Stochastic Partial Differential Integral Equations: Solvability and Compariso'] A triple of processes \((u, q, r) \in \mathbb{S}^2(H^0) \cap \mathbb{H}^1 \times \mathbb{H}^0 \times \mathbb{H}^{\nu,0}\) is called a weak solution to BSPDIE (equation eq:2.1 of the paper) if, for any \(t \in [0, T]\) and test function \(\eta \in C_0^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)\),
\begin{eqnarray*}
&&\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} u(t, x) \eta(x) \, dx \nonumber\\
&=& \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \varphi(x) \eta(x) \, dx + \int_t^T \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \Bigg(
- a^{ij}(s, x) D_{j} u(s, x) D_{i} \eta(x) + b^i(s, x) D_{i} u(s, x) \eta(x)  \nonumber
\\&&+ c(s, x) u(s, x) \eta(x) \nonumber + \int_Z \Big[ u(s, x + k(s, e, x)) - u(s, x) - k^i(s, e, x) D_{i} u(s, x) \Big] \eta(x) \nu(de) \nonumber\\
&&- \sigma^i(s, x) q(s, x) D_{i} \eta(x) + v(s, x) q(s, x) \eta(x) + f_0(s, x) \eta(x) \nonumber\\
&&+ \int_Z \Big[ r(s, x + k(s, e, x)) - r(s, e, x) \Big] \eta(x) \nu(de)
\Bigg)dxds \nonumber\\
&&- \int_t^T \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} q(s, x) \eta(x)dxdW_s - \int_t^T \int_Z \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} r(s, e, x) \eta(x)dx\tilde{\mu}(de, ds).
\end{eqnarray*}
title: Defn def:3.1 of arXiv:2606.16237

[Definition def:grafting_full of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] We define, for any $\mu \in [0,1]$, a ``grafting with scale'' $\graft^{\mu}: \text{${\mcb{C}}$} \otimes \text{${\mcb{C}}$} \rightarrow \text{${\mcb{C}}$}$. 

Let $\mu \in [0,1]$. 
Given $\tau_1,\tau_2 \in \mathfrak{T}$ and $\text{$\mathfrak{z}$}^{\tau_1} \in \text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\tau_1]$, $\text{$\mathfrak{z}$}^{\tau_2} \in \text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\tau_2]$, we define $\text{$\mathfrak{z}$}^{\tau_2} \graft^{\mu} \text{$\mathfrak{z}$}^{\tau_1} \in \text{${\mcb{C}}$}$ as follows. 
We first choose $\underline{\tau}_1 \in \tau_1$, $\underline{\tau}_2 \in \tau_2$, and write  $\text{$\mathfrak{z}$}^{\underline{\tau}_1} = \iota_{\tau_1,\underline{\tau}_1} \text{$\mathfrak{z}$}^{\tau_1}$, $\text{$\mathfrak{z}$}^{\underline{\tau}_2} = \iota_{\tau_2,\underline{\tau}_2} \text{$\mathfrak{z}$}^{\tau_2}$. 
We then set
\begin{equ}
\text{$\mathfrak{z}$}^{\tau_2} \graft^{\mu} \text{$\mathfrak{z}$}^{\tau_1} 
\eqdef \sum_{n \in N(\underline{\tau}_1)} 
\pi_{\underline{\tau}_{1,2,n}} \big(
\text{$\mathfrak{z}$}^{\underline{\tau}_1}\graft^\mu_n\text{$\mathfrak{z}$}^{\underline{\tau}_2}\big)\,,
\end{equ}
where $\graft^\mu_n$ is given in Definition~(def:scaledlabeledgraft of the paper). 
where we are writing $\underline{\tau}_{1,2,n} = \underline{\tau}_{2} \graft_n \underline{\tau}_{1}$, and using, for $\underline{\sigma} \in \sigma \in \mathfrak{T}$, the shorthand $\pi_{\underline{\sigma}} =\pi_{\sigma,\underline{\sigma}}$.

body: On the open cone define Phi = Phi_F + Phi_G + Phi_V with Phi_F(u,v) = (u - v)^{-alpha_0}, Phi_G(u,v) = (lambda_N v - u)^{-beta_0}, Phi_V(u,v) = e^{gamma_0 v}, where alpha_0, beta_0 > 0 satisfy 2(2 alpha_0 + 1) max_l (lambda_l - 1)(1 + delta_l) < sum_l (lambda_l - 1)(1 + delta_l) and 2(2 beta_0 + 1) max_l (lambda_N - lambda_l)(1 + delta_l) < sum_l (lambda_N - lambda_l)(1 + delta_l), and gamma_0 = 1/(2a). Then A~ Phi_F <= c_F, A~ Phi_G <= c_G and A~ Phi_V <= c_V on the open cone, and for suitable f_0, g_0, v_0 > 0, with Gamma = {u - v >= f_0, lambda_N v - u >= g_0, v <= v_0} and c_Phi = c_F + c_G + c_V, the triple Phi, Gamma, c_Phi satisfies the Lyapunov-Foster condition A~ Phi <= -1 off Gamma and A~ Phi <= c_Phi on Gamma. With it the cone diffusion is positive Harris recurrent and has a unique stationary law (Theorem 4.1).

[Lemma lem:one-point-conditional-determinant of arXiv:2607.29330, 'Large deviations for the maximum of\\ the generalized TAP free energy'] Under the hypotheses and notation of
		Proposition~(prop:one-point-conditional-hessian of the paper), the following
		hold for \(\sigma\in\{-,+\}\):
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
			\item
			\begin{equation}
				\begin{aligned}
					\frac1N
					\log\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{m},f_N}
					\left|\det\nabla_\sigma^2F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})\right|
					={}&
					-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N
					\log\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(q,b_i)
					+\frac{\xi''(q)}2
					\left(
					\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N
					\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(q,b_i)
					\right)^2
					+o(1)\\
					\longrightarrow{}&
					-\mathbb{E}\log\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(q,X_q)
					+\frac{\xi''(q)}2\widehat\zeta(q)^2 .
				\end{aligned}
			\end{equation}
			In the \(\varepsilon\)-window above, the error in
			(equation eq:one-point-conditional-determinant of the paper) is
			\(o_\varepsilon(1)+o_N(1)\).
			
			\item
			Suppose that, for some \(\kappa_0>0\) and \(L<\infty\),
			\[
			\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N
			\exp\{(8+\kappa_0)|b_i|\}\le L.
			\]
			Set
			\[
			D_{\mathbf{m},\sigma}
			:=
			\det\nabla_\sigma^2F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}).
			\]
			There are \(c_L>0\) and a deterministic \(r_N=o(N)\) such that
			\begin{equation}
				\mathbb{P}_{\mathbf{m},f_N}\left(
				|D_{\mathbf{m},\sigma}|
				<e^{-r_N}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{m},f_N}|D_{\mathbf{m},\sigma}|
				\right)
				\le e^{-c_LN}.
			\end{equation}
			Moreover, the estimate is uniform over the same window, subject to the
			exponential-moment bound above. There is a function \(\rho_{\det}\),
			with \(\rho_{\det}(\varepsilon)\downarrow0\), and there are nonnegative
			deterministic numbers \(r_{N,\varepsilon}=o_N(N)\) such that
			\begin{equation}
				\mathbb{P}_{\mathbf{m},f_N}\left(
				|D_{\mathbf{m},\sigma}|
				<
				\exp\{-N\rho_{\det}(\varepsilon)-r_{N,\varepsilon}\}
				\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{m},f_N}|D_{\mathbf{m},\sigma}|
				\right)
				\le e^{-c_LN}.
			\end{equation}
			Here \(r_{N,\varepsilon}/N\to0\) for fixed \(\varepsilon\), and \(N\to\infty\)
			before \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
		\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 13 of arXiv:2608.19744, 'Conditioned Brownian motion and local equivalence of path ensembles'] A densely defined form $\mathfrak a$ is sectorial with vertex
$\omega\in\mathbb R$ and semi-angle $\alpha<\pi/2$ if
\[
  \mathfrak a[f]-\omega\|f\|^2\in\overline{\Sigma_\alpha},
  \qquad f\in\mathcal D(\mathfrak a).
\]
Equivalently, after a real shift, its imaginary part is controlled by its real
part: there is $C<\infty$ such that
\[
  |\Im \mathfrak a[f]|
  \leq C\bigl(\Re\mathfrak a[f]-\omega\|f\|^2\bigr),
  \qquad f\in\mathcal D(\mathfrak a).
\]
If $\omega=0$ and $\Re \mathfrak a[f]\geq0$, the form is called
accretive.

body: Let X be a Banach space and A a subset of X. Then A is relatively weakly compact (its weak closure is weakly compact) if and only if A is relatively weakly sequentially compact, meaning every sequence in A has a subsequence that converges weakly to some point of X. In particular, on a Banach space, weak compactness and weak sequential compactness of a subset coincide, even though the weak topology need not be metrizable. [standard, e.g. Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis]

Let X be a metric space, x_0 a limit point of X, and f_n : X \ {x_0} -> R (or into any complete metric space). Suppose (i) f_n -> f uniformly on X \ {x_0}, and (ii) for each n the limit A_n = lim_{x -> x_0} f_n(x) exists. Then (A_n) converges, lim_{x -> x_0} f(x) exists, and the two iterated limits agree: lim_n lim_{x -> x_0} f_n(x) = lim_{x -> x_0} lim_n f_n(x). Uniformity in (i) is not removable: with f_n(x) = x^n on (0,1) one gets lim_n lim_{x->1} f_n = 1 and lim_{x->1} lim_n f_n = 0. Uniform convergence may be replaced by uniform convergence of the OTHER family (in n, uniformly in x) - only one of the two limits needs to be uniform. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 7.11]
f_n -> f uniformly on a punctured neighbourhood of x_0 (or the analogous uniformity in the other variable)
each f_n has a limit at x_0

[Prop 4 of arXiv:2605.15501, 'Well-posedness of the obstacle problem for generalized Dean--Kawasaki equation\thanks{ The'] Let $(u,\nu)$ be a stochastic kinetic solution of the obstacle problem for \eqref{eq:main} under Definition \ref{def:def of stochastic kinetic solution}, and $\chi$ be a kinetic function of $u$.
Then, $\chi$ admits almost surely left and right limits at all points $t\in[0,T]$, which means that for all $t\in[0,T]$ there exist some kinetic functions $\tilde{\chi}_{t}^{\pm}$ on $\Omega\times\mathbb{T}^d\times\mathbb{R}$ such that $\mathbb{P}$-a.s.
\[
\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\chi(x,\xi,t\pm\epsilon)\phi(x,\xi)\mathrm{d}\xi\mathrm{d}x\to \int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\tilde{\chi}_{t}^{\pm}(x,\xi)\phi(x,\xi)\mathrm{d}\xi\mathrm{d}x,\quad \text{as }\epsilon\to 0,
\]
for all $\phi\in C_c^{1}(\mathbb{T}^d\times(0,\infty))$ and almost surely
\begin{align}
&\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\big[\tilde{\chi}_{t}^{+}(x,\xi)-\tilde{\chi}_{t}^{-}(x,\xi)\big]\phi(x,\xi)\mathrm{d}\xi\mathrm{d}x\\
&=-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\partial_{\xi}\phi(x,\xi)\mathbf{1}_{\{t\}}(s)\mathrm{d}q(x,\xi,s)
-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,\psi(x,s))\mathbf{1}_{\{t\}}(s)\mathrm{d}\nu(x,s)\nonumber.

\end{align}
In particular, almost surely, the set of $t\in[0,T]$ such that $\tilde{\chi}_{t}^{-}\neq\tilde{\chi}_{t}^+$ is countable. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop 4 of arXiv:2605.15501

[Proposition 6 of arXiv:2609.01166, 'Nonparametric inference for density-dependent McKean--Vlasov diffusions'] Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be i.i.d. from $\pi_0$, and let $\widehat\Xi_n$ be the full MLE over $\cX_m$. Then with probability at least $(1-\delta)(1-\tau_0(M))^n\geq 1-\delta-n\tau_0(M)$ it holds that
\begin{align}
 \KL(\pi_0\Vert\pi_{\widehat\Xi_n})
 &\leq \frac{C_1}{c_M}\inf_{\xi\in\cX_m}\KL(\pi_0\Vert\pi_\xi)
 +C_2\frac{B_{\gamma_M}(\mathcal H_m(\ve,M)+\log(2/\delta))}{n} \nonumber\\
 & +C_3\omega_m(\ve,M)
 +C_4\left(
 1+\frac{1}{c_M}
 \right)d_m(M)
 +C_5\left(
 1+\frac{1}{c_M}
 \right)\bar R_m(M)
\end{align}
with some constants \(C_i>0\), \(i\in\{1,...,5\}\), and \(c_M\) defined as in Lemma~\ref{lem:full-truncated-kl}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let H=diag(lambda_1,lambda_2) be fixed positive definite and f(x)=x^T H x/2. Run uncorrected full-batch Adam with beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eta>0, epsilon>0 added outside sqrt, initial v>=0, and x_t nonzero for every t. Let c=1/19, D_t=diag(sqrt(v_(t+1))+epsilon), w_i,max=c eta lambda_i/epsilon, and assume w_i,max>2 for both coordinates. Define W_t=c eta (g_t^T D_t^(-1) H D_t^(-1) g_t)/(g_t^T D_t^(-1)g_t). Fong-Yang Theorem 3.4 proves: if W_t>=2+delta eventually for some delta>0, then sum_t ||x_t||^2<infinity and w_i,t tends to w_i,max. Thus every trajectory with limsup_t ||x_t||>0 has liminf_t W_t<=2. Also limsup_t W_t>=W_diag(beta1,beta2), where the explicit cutoff satisfies W_diag(0.9,0.999)>=1.9. These are distinct subsequential bounds; they do not assert convergence W_t->2 or shrinking-band confinement. The theorem is for uncorrected Adam, not the empirically studied bias-corrected variant.

[Theorem T:dd main of arXiv:2507.01236, 'Disintegration theorem for multifunctions, \\ with applications to empirical Wasserstein d'] Let $\mathfrak{X} = [0, 1]^D$ be the unit cube in dimension~$D$, endowed with the $\ell^{\infty}$ metric $d$ and its Borel $\sigma$-field,
and let~$\mu$ be an absolutely continuous probability measure on~$\mathfrak{X}$ with density $f$ satisfying
\[
c\leq f(x)\leq C\mbox{\rm \ for every $x \in \mathfrak{X}$},
\]
where $0<c\leq C<\infty$. Given $\alpha \in (0, \infty)$, let
\begin{equation}

  r(n)\equiv r(n,D,c,\alpha) := c^{-1/D}(4 \cdot 3^{D - 1})^{1/D} (2 + \alpha)^{1/(2D)} \left( \frac{\ln n}{n} \right)^{1/(2 D)}.
\end{equation}
Then there exists $n_0\equiv n_0(D,c,C,\alpha)$ such that for every $n\geq n_0$, the space $(\mathfrak{X},d,\mu)$ is $(n^{-\alpha},r(n))$-disintegrable.
title: Theorem T:dd main of arXiv:2507.01236

[Conjecture eq:sparse-lower of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[conjecture]{conj:sparse-lower}
For smooth centered unit-variance entry laws satisfying the preceding large-deviation hypothesis and stability of the conditional critical-point exponent under an \(o(1)\) perturbation of the exposed block,
\begin{equation}
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 \ge\sup_{r\ge0}\sup_{\substack{A\in\mathbb R^{[r]^p}:\\ \mathcal J_\mu(A)<\infty}}
 \left\{\underline\Phi_{p,\mathrm{sf}}^{J,A}(V)-\mathcal J_\mu(A)\right\}.
\end{equation}
Under the additional hypothesis (equation eq:deformed-background-univ of the paper),
the right-hand side could be written with the Gaussian spike-free
pressure, but the preceding bounded example shows that this hypothesis
is not available under finite moment matching and entrywise cutoff.
The \(r=0\) term is merely the cutoff residual branch: for bounded
disorder it equals the full non-Gaussian pressure and already contains
the mesoscopic obstruction.  Thus the conjecture is informative only
when that residual branch has been controlled separately.  The
one-entry instance proved in (thm:one-spike of the paper) is a coarse form of
the bound; general \(A\) allows localized clusters and mixed
spike--bulk critical points. (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)

Let $\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$, identified with $[0,1)$ with Lebesgue measure, and $f\in L^1(\mathbb{T})$. The Fourier coefficients are $\hat f(n)=\int_0^1 f(x)e^{-2\pi i n x}\,dx$, $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, with $|\hat f(n)|\le\|f\|_1$; the Fourier series is $\sum_n\hat f(n)e^{2\pi i n x}$. Convolution on $\mathbb T$ is $(f*g)(x)=\int_0^1 f(x-y)g(y)\,dy$ and $\widehat{f*g}(n)=\hat f(n)\hat g(n)$. The symmetric partial sums are $S_Nf(x)=\sum_{|n|\le N}\hat f(n)e^{2\pi i n x}=(f*D_N)(x)$ with the Dirichlet kernel $D_N(x)=\sum_{|n|\le N}e^{2\pi i n x}=\sin((2N+1)\pi x)/\sin(\pi x)$; $D_N$ is even, $\int_0^1 D_N=1$, but it changes sign and its Lebesgue constants $\|D_N\|_{L^1(\mathbb T)}=\frac{4}{\pi^2}\log N+O(1)$ tend to infinity. The Fejer (Cesaro) means are $\sigma_Nf=\frac{1}{N+1}\sum_{k=0}^N S_kf=f*F_N$ with the Fejer kernel $F_N(x)=\frac{1}{N+1}\left(\frac{\sin((N+1)\pi x)}{\sin(\pi x)}\right)^2=\sum_{|n|\le N}\left(1-\frac{|n|}{N+1}\right)e^{2\pi i n x}$; $F_N\ge0$, $\int_0^1F_N=1$, and $F_N(x)\le\min\{N+1,\;1/((N+1)\sin^2(\pi x))\}$. Periods other than 1 are handled by rescaling (for period $2\pi$: $\hat f(n)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(t)e^{-int}dt$).
f is 1-periodic and Lebesgue integrable over one period

[Theorem discreteIPS of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let the input process for the discrete-time interacting particle system be 
$\tilde{\mathcal{P}} = \left\{(x, M(x),\mathbf{L}_x)\in\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb {M}  \times \mathbb{L}^J\right\}$,
where $J \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbf{L}_x$ are vectors of i.i.d.
elements of $\mathbb{L}$, independent of $\sum_x \delta_{(x,M(x))}$. Put
\begin{equation}

\mu_n^{\xi} := \sum_{x \in \mathcal{P} \cap W_n} \xi (\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n)  \delta_{n^{-1/d}x}.
\end{equation}
If 
$\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ and $\xi$ respectively satisfy assumptions~(i.thmIPS of the paper) and~(iii.thmIPS of the paper) in Theorem ~(thmIPS of the paper), 
$\Phi_j$ are update rules as at ~(equation e:updaterulef-discrete of the paper) with respect to a stabilizing interaction graph $\Psi$ on finite windows with respect to $\mathcal{P}$ as in (equation e:ddecay of the paper), then
 the random measures $(\mu_n^{\xi})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ satisfy the central limit theorem. That is, for every test function $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$ such that
$
{\rm Var}[\mu_n^{\xi}(f)] = \Omega(n^{\nu})$ for some $\nu > 0$,
we have
$$
({\rm Var}[\mu_n^{\xi}(f)])^{-1/2} \big(\mu_n^{\xi}(f) - \mathbb {E} [\mu_n^{\xi}(f)]\big)  \stackrel{d}{\Rightarrow} Z,$$
where $Z$ is a standard Gaussian random variable. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 5 of arXiv:2604.25336, 'Central limit theorem for slow-fast system under mixed fractional Brownian motion'] Under assumptions \textbf{A1}-\textbf{A3} and \(\bar g (x)= \int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}} g(x,y)\mu(dy)=0\). Define that 
\begin{equation}
\Psi(x,y) =\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathcal{P}_t g(x, Y_t) \dd t.
\end{equation} 
The \(\Psi(x,y)\) is the solution to the Poisson equation \eqref{Poisson_eq} where \(h\) is replaced by \(g\).
Moreover, \(\Psi(x,y)\in C^2\). For all \((x,y)\in \mathbb{R}^n\times \mathbb{R}^m\), \(D_x\Psi(x,y)\) and \(D^2_{xx}\Psi(x,y)\) is linear growth. \(D_y\Psi(x,y), D^2_{xy}\Psi(x,y), D^2_{yy}\Psi(x,y)\) is globally bounded. 
Furthermore, since \(Y\) is independent of \(x\), \(\Psi\in C^2\) is Lipshitz continuous with respect to \(y\) uniformly over all \(x\) . (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Prop 15 of arXiv:2607.03924, 'Tree Coordinates and Range Martingales for Positive Operator-Valued Measures'] Let $\left(K,P,V\right)$ be a minimal Naimark dilation
of $E$, and let $c>0$. If $F\in\mathcal{M}_{+}\left(\Omega_{m},H\right)$
satisfies $F\leq cE$, then there is a unique positive operator $T\in B\left(K\right)$
such that 
\[
0\leq T\leq cI_{K},
\]
\[
TP\left(B\right)=P\left(B\right)T,\qquad B\in\mathcal{B}\left(\Omega_{m}\right),
\]
and 
\[
F\left(B\right)=V^{*}P\left(B\right)TV,\qquad B\in\mathcal{B}\left(\Omega_{m}\right).
\]
Conversely, every such operator $T$ defines an element $F\in\mathcal{M}_{+}\left(\Omega_{m},H\right)$
satisfying $F\leq cE$ by this formula. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:cbe9e4ed6fdc483573f34c7453ada190ee174833760b9c1ecbb8ea736f12aecc","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/cb/cbe9e4ed6fdc483573f34c7453ada190ee174833760b9c1ecbb8ea736f12aecc.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:62b37a0e5b3f43f2b597c9eb36466623aae3077347358d7d6bad31f4eae5889b","bundle_entry_key":"multiple-top-parameter-escape","bundle_id":"population.t232-square-two-gaussian-second-step-chain-20261020","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"deep linear networks; asymmetric factorization; saddle-to-saddle dynamics","draft":"w704/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.deep_linear_networks:multiple-top-parameter-escape","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T232 Target 1: dominant parameter escape with a multiple top eigenvalue

Status: proof draft (unaudited). This lemma replaces an unproved extension of the published local-minimum Gram theorem; it does not assume that extension.

## General local ODE lemma
Let F be C^2 near zero in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, F(0)=0, and J=DF(0) symmetric. Let lambda>0 be its largest eigenvalue, E its full eigenspace, and P the orthogonal projection onto E. The multiplicity of lambda is arbitrary. Fix a unit u in E. Let initial data d_epsilon satisfy
  P d_epsilon=p_epsilon u, p_epsilon>0, p_epsilon->0,
  ||d_epsilon||<=C p_epsilon.
Then the solutions shifted by tau_epsilon=log(1/p_epsilon)/lambda converge uniformly on every compact interval where the canonical solution exists to a unique path h solving
  h'=F(h),
  h(t)=exp(lambda t)u+integral_-infinity^t exp(J(t-v))N(h(v))dv,
  N(x)=F(x)-Jx.
In particular h(t)=exp(lambda t)u+O(exp(2lambda t)) backwards. The canonical path is defined on a negative half-line and extended by its ODE. Forward compact convergence is asserted only up to its maximal forward lifetime unless an independent global-existence argument is available.

## Proof
On a small ball, ||N(x)||<=K||x||^2 and ||N(x)-N(y)||<=K(||x||+||y||)||x-y||. In shifted time the initial time is -tau. The free evolution obeys
  ||exp(J(t+tau))d||<=C exp(lambda t), t>=-tau,
since J is symmetric and every eigenvalue is <=lambda. In a weighted supremum ||x(t)||exp(-lambda t), Duhamel bounds the quadratic term by
  (K/ lambda) A^2 exp(lambda T)
on [-tau,T] whenever the weighted norm is <=A. Choose a fixed negative T so a continuity bootstrap from C to 2C cannot cross 2C, and so the resulting ball stays in the local domain of F. Thus ||x_epsilon(t)||<=2C exp(lambda t) there, uniformly in epsilon.

The top part of the free evolution is exactly exp(lambda t)u. For an eigenspace with eigenvalue nu<lambda its free part has norm bounded by
  C p_epsilon^(1-nu/lambda) exp(nu t),
which tends to zero uniformly on each fixed shifted compact interval. No convergence of the bounded normalized lower initial components is needed. On each such interval, the solutions and their derivatives are uniformly bounded. Diagonal Arzela-Ascoli therefore yields a locally uniform subsequential limit on (-infinity,T].

The nonlinear integrand is bounded uniformly by
  exp(lambda(t-v)) K(2C)^2 exp(2lambda v)
    =K(2C)^2 exp(lambda t)exp(lambda v),
which is integrable at minus infinity. A fixed-tail split passes Duhamel to the displayed Volterra equation. Its operator is a contraction in the exp(lambda t) weighted ball on a sufficiently negative half-line: its Lipschitz constant is bounded by a fixed multiple of exp(lambda T)/lambda. Thus its solution is unique in the class O(exp(lambda t)); for two possible bounds choose a common larger bound and a more negative T. Existence follows from the subsequential limit. Uniqueness identifies every subsequential limit, proving whole-family convergence. Integrating the same quadratic bound gives the O(exp(2lambda t)) backward remainder. Finite-interval continuous dependence extends convergence along every compact part of the canonical solution. QED, subject to independent review.

## The two essential restrictions
The normalized FULL top projection must be fixed (or converge to u with an explicit equivalent argument). A rotating top vector need not converge when the top eigenspace has dimension above one. Also ||d||=O(p) cannot be omitted: for J=diag(2,1), initial data (p,sqrt(p)) have top projection p e1 but at the shift log(1/p)/2 their lower coordinate stays of order one and changes the limit. This is an exact linear boundary, not numerical evidence.

## Application to the actual rank-one saddle
Use the full parameter space of B,A and its Euclidean factor metric, centered at theta1=[zstar,0,...,0], where zstar is a nonzero balanced rank-one critical factor. The factor flow is negative gradient of the scalar loss, so its Jacobian is symmetric. Direct differentiation at zero dormant columns makes it block diagonal:
  Jfull=diag(Jact,Lstar,...,Lstar).
C009 proves largest eigenvalue(Jact)=r<s. Each frozen dormant block has eigenvalues s,0,0,-s. Thus the full largest eigenvalue is s, with multiplicity w-1, and its full eigenspace consists of v times arbitrary dormant hidden rows. A nonminimal active saddle does not change this strict spectral separation.

At the aligned arrival supplied by C009, the active endpoint error is O(p^2), the dormant norm is O(p), and the row v^T X has norm p. Make a hidden orthogonal rotation of the DORMANT columns only, fixed for the subsequent flow, taking that row to (p,0,...,0). This leaves theta1 unchanged. The full top parameter projection is now EXACTLY p times the fixed vector u having v in the first dormant column and zero elsewhere; total parameter error is O(p). The general lemma applies with lambda=s even though its top eigenvalue is multiple. This is a parameter theorem; it does not smuggle a simple-top assumption into a multiple-top Hessian.

## The canonical path has a nonzero width-two realization
The subspace with only the active and first dormant columns nonzero is invariant under the factor ODE. It is also preserved by J and the Volterra map because every zero factor column has identically zero derivative. Uniqueness therefore makes the canonical path have exactly this width-two realization. The backward expansion gives
  z(t)=zstar+O(exp(2st)),
  x(t)=exp(st)v+O(exp(2st)).
The input part of v is a nonzero residual singular vector perpendicular to astar, and its output part is perpendicular to bstar. The input and output square factors consequently have determinants with nonzero leading terms of order exp(st); both are invertible for all sufficiently negative finite t. This proves a nonzero rank-two canonical mode; rank is not inferred from limits of finite-rank matrices alone.

The factor balance matrix is conserved and tends to its value at theta1, which is zero, so the canonical width-two factors are exactly balanced. In the oriented endpoint frames, v=(delta lperp;rperp)/sqrt(2) up to simultaneous sign, with delta=sign det M by C003's determinant identity. The graph determinant of the canonical two-column plane is therefore delta at sufficiently negative times and remains so. Its loss is strictly below the first critical loss because the path is nonconstant gradient flow, and that critical loss is strictly below C(0) by the stationary energy identity in C010. C010 therefore gives global forward existence, factor convergence and endpoint product M for this canonical path.

## Clocks and original factor rotations
The parameter shift in this lemma is log(1/p)/s. At the actual C009 arrival, z-zstar=O(p^2) and v perpendicular to zstar, so
  a=v^T Z v=p^2+(v^T z)^2=p^2+O(p^4).
Therefore log(1/a)/(2s)-log(1/p)/s=O(p^2)->0. The parameter and Gram clocks agree asymptotically. Compose the original fixed seed rotation with the arrival's dormant rotation; their product is one rotation per alpha, fixed in time, so the asserted factor convergence has the required form.

## Scope
This establishes the central local escape link IF the upstream C006/C008/C009 hypotheses and proofs hold. Those analytic arguments and this lemma all await independent review. The multiple-top extension and canonical width-two realization are written explicitly; neither is certified by an algebra-only check or by the published simple-top theorem. A separate final composition must state data and initialization assumptions and prove the first canonical orbit has a nonzero critical endpoint. K$. Then there exists a function $\chi \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ with the 
following properties.

\begin{enumerate}[1.]

$$
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma of arXiv:2607.22480, 'Distinguishability threshold for random geometric graphs'] Let $\boldsymbol{u}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{u}_m, \boldsymbol{w}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{w}_\ell$ be sampled uniformly at random from $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, and let \[L=\{x:\langle \boldsymbol{u}_i, x\rangle \geq c_{p, d}/\sqrt{d} \text{ for all } i\in [m] \text{ and } \langle \boldsymbol{w}_j, x\rangle < c_{p, d}/\sqrt{d} \text{ for all } j\in [\ell]\}.\] If $\mu=\mathbb{P}[\boldsymbol{x}\in L]$ is the probability that a uniformly sampled point $\boldsymbol{x}\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ lands in $L$, then there is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that for every $\varepsilon>0$ we have
\[\mathbb{P}\Big[\big|\frac{\mu}{p^m(1-p)^\ell}-1\big|\geq \varepsilon \Big]\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{cd\varepsilon^2}{(\log d)^2\log p^{-1}}\right)+O\bigg(p^{-2}\exp\Big(-\frac{cd}{(\log d)^2\log p^{-1}}\Big)\bigg).\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let (X_t)_{t in T} be a centered Gaussian process indexed by a set T with natural metric d(s, t) = (E[(X_s - X_t)^2])^{1/2}. Then there exist universal constants c, C > 0 such that c * gamma_2(T, d) <= E[ sup_{t in T} X_t ] <= C * gamma_2(T, d).
(X_t)_{t in T} is a centered Gaussian process
d is the L^2 distance

Let d>=2, p=d-1, S a nondegenerate centered p-simplex, A invertible, c(y)=c_0+y*c_1, and r(y)=alpha+(beta-alpha)y with alpha,beta>=0 and alpha+beta>0. The uniform law on C={(y,z):0<=y<=1, z in c(y)+A(r(y)S)} is n-CM for every n>=d+1. This includes simplex prisms and truncated simplex pyramids/frustums and invertible affine images. The height density is proportional to r(y)^(d-1), so the same monotone-height mix and radius bound as for ellipsoidal frustums apply. Given the heights, d*max_i rho_i<=sum_i rho_i, and the measurable weighted-simplex theorem couples the section laws with zero sum. Affine section centers give the full centroid sum. General nonhomothetic/nonaffine sections remain outside the argument; novelty UNKNOWN.

[Lemma lem:chirurgieloc of arXiv:2601.20502, 'Optimal matching under size priority'] Fix a rooted graph in $\Omega^{\mathrm{very\, good}}$ then fix a family of weights $w(e)_{e \in E(G_n)}$ and pick $e_1 \in B_H(G_n,o_n)$.
         Assume that $i(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_1})+i(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_1})=1$.
         Then there exists $e_2 \sim e_1$ such that $i(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_2})+i(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_2})=1$ and:
         \begin{itemize}
             \item If $e_1\in M_{\mathrm{opt}}$ then there exists $a>0$ such that setting $w'(e_2)=a$ and $w'=w$ elsewhere gives $\max(Z_-(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_2}),Z_+(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_2}))+\max(Z_-(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_2}),Z_+(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_2}))<w'(e_2)=a.$
             \item If $e_1 \notin M_{\mathrm{opt}}$, then there exists $b>0$ such that setting $w'(e_1)=b$ and $w'=w$ elsewhere gives $\max(Z_-(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_1}),Z_+(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_1}))+\max(Z_-(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_1}),Z_+(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_1}))<w'(e_1)=b$.
         \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:main of arXiv:2607.22480, 'Distinguishability threshold for random geometric graphs'] For every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a large constant $C_\varepsilon>0$  with the following property. Let $n$ be a large positive integer and $p\in (0, 1)$ a probability satisfying $1/3\geq p\geq n^{-1/5}(\log n)^A$, where $A$ is a large absolute constant. For every $d\geq C_\varepsilon n^3p^3 (\log p^{-1})^3$, we have
\[\TV(G(n, p), G(n, d, p))\leq \varepsilon.\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let (M,g) be a connected Riemannian manifold with induced distance function d. The following are equivalent: (1) (M,d) is a complete metric space; (2) M is geodesically complete, i.e. for every p in M the exponential map exp_p is defined on all of T_pM; (3) M is geodesically complete at some single point p, i.e. exp_p is defined on all of T_pM for at least one p; (4) every closed and bounded subset of M is compact. If any of these hold, then any two points of M can be joined by a minimizing geodesic, a geodesic segment whose length equals the distance between its endpoints.
M is a connected smooth Riemannian manifold

[Proposition p:mppmix_double of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Fix $p,q \in \mathbb{N}$ and $r \in (0, \infty)$. Assume that $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ satisfies condition~(ii:mppmix_double of the paper)  of Lemma~(p:mppmixcl_double of the paper). Let $\xi: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K} \times \mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}} \to \mathbb{K}'$ be a marking function such that $\xi(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mu}) =  \xi^{(r)}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mu}) =\xi(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mu}\cap B_r(x))$ for all $(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mu}) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K} \times \mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}}$. Consider the marked point process $\dbtilde\mathcal{P}=\sum_{x \in \mathcal{P}} \delta_{(x,V(x))}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d\times \mathbb{K}'$ where $V(x) := \xi(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}})$.  

Then, for  all $f \in \mathbb{B} ((\mathbb{K}')^p),$   $g \in \mathbb{B} ((\mathbb{K}')^q)$, for almost all $\bk x1{p+q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d(p+q)}$ such that $s:=d(\bk x1p,\bk x{p+1}{p+q}) >4r$, and with ${w}_0= 4(p+q)\theta_d r^d$
we have
\begin{align} \nonumber
& \Big| \mathbb {E} _{\bk x1{p+q}}[f(\bk V1{p})g(\bk V{p+1}{p+q})]\rho^{(p+q)}(\bk x1{p+q}) -
\mathbb {E} _{\bk x1p}[f(\bk V1p)] \rho^{(p)}(\bk x1{p}) \; \mathbb {E} _{\bk x{p+1}{p+q}}[g(\bk V{p+1}{p+q})]\rho^{(q)}(\bk
x{p+1}{p+q}) \Big|
\\
&\le 
\phi( \frac{s}{2})\sum_{l=1}^\infty \frac{w_0^l}{l!}  C_{l+p+q}
=:\phi( \frac{s}{2})\hat{C}_{p+q}<\infty.
\end{align}

Thus the marked point process
 $\dbtilde\mathcal{P}$ satisfies the inequality~(equation e.Bmppmixing of the paper)  in Definition~(B-omega-mixing of the paper)(Bmixing of the paper) 
for $s>4r$, with  $\omega_{p+q}(s):=\hat C_{p+q}\phi(s/2)$ where  $p,q,\phi$ are as above.

[Lemma le:replace of arXiv:2604.21142, 'Gaussian fluctuations for Internal DLA on cylinders'] Fix $y_0 > 0$ and $\n > 0$, and assume $a_N \gg \log N + \log_+ a_N$ as $N \to \infty$ and that Assumption~(a:spectral of the paper) holds for each $2 \leq k \leq K$. Let $T \coloneqq N \lfloor a_N y_0\rfloor$, $h \coloneqq T/N$, and let $(\Delta_N)_{N \geq 1}$ be positive reals satisfying $\Delta_N = O\!\left(\sqrt{a_N(\log N + \log_+ a_N)}\right)$ and
	\[ {\ensuremath{\mathbb P}} \big(R_{\lfloor h - \Delta_N\rfloor} \subseteq A(T) \subseteq R_{h + \Delta_N}\big) \geq 1 - N^{-\n} \qquad \text{for } N \text{ large enough}\,. \]
Let $\phi : V_N \times {\ensuremath{\mathbb R}}  \to {\ensuremath{\mathbb R}} $ be a test function of the form $\phi(x, y) = \sum_{k=2}^K \a_k(y)\, f_k^N(x)$, where each $\a_k : {\ensuremath{\mathbb R}}  \to {\ensuremath{\mathbb R}} $ is independent of $N$ and has bounded derivative in a neighbourhood of $y_0$; let $\varphi(x, y) \coloneqq \phi(x, y/a_N)$, and let $\psi$ be the discrete harmonic extension of $\varphi$ defined in~(equation eq:truepsi of the paper). Then
	\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt{Na_N}}\,\langle \! \langle D_T, \varphi - \psi\rangle \! \rangle \;\longrightarrow\; 0 \qquad \text{in probability as } N \to \infty\,. \]

[Lemma zygmund-marcinkiewicz of arXiv:2411.07737, 'On Asymptotic Behavior of Extinction Moment of Critical Bisexual Branching Process in Rand'] Let $\{ \xi_n \}_{n = 1}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of i.i.d. r.v. with $\ER \abs*{\xi_n}^{\alpha} < \infty$, where $1 \leq \alpha \leq 2$, and $\ER \xi_n = 0$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
    Then, there is a constant $c_{\alpha} > 0$ such that
    \[
        \left( \ER \abs*{ \sum_{i = 1}^n \xi_i } \right)^{\alpha}
        \leq \ER \abs*{ \sum_{i = 1}^n \xi_i }^{\alpha}
        \leq c_{\alpha} \sum_{i = 1}^n \ER \abs*{\xi_i}^{\alpha}.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund inequality,~\cite{Marcinkiewicz1938}

body:
[Prop P:two-point-bd of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Take $n \in \mathbb{N}$, parameter $\alpha \ge 1/2 - n^{-1/6}$, and $x, y, z_0 \in \llbracket0, n/100 \rrbracket$, $a > 0$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
	
C_0 \max \left(\frac{z_0^2}{n}, \frac{z_0 |y-x|}{n}, z_0(1/2 - \alpha)\vee 0 \right) < a < C_* z_0,
\end{equation}
where $C_0>0$ is a universal constant, and $C_*>0$ is any large enough number.
Then for a constant $c>0$ depending only on $C_*$, we have
$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{z \in\llbracket0,z_0 \rrbracket} \left|\bar X[x, 1; y + z, n]_\textsf{L} - \bar X[x, 1; y, n]_\textsf{L} \right| \ge a \right) \le 2\exp(- c a^2/z_0) + 2 \exp(-c \sqrt{n}).
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop P:two-point-bd of arXiv:2604.10020

[Cor 15 of arXiv:2604.25725, 'What is The Probability That A Random Graph With A Given Degree Sequence is Connected?'] Fix $0<\eps<10^{-6}$ and let $\cD$ be such that $m$ is large enough and $n_1,n_2 \le 10^{-6} m$.
    Let $v\in[n]$ be fixed. Then the probability that there exists an $i$  with  $1\leq i \leq m$  such that  $2|E(H_{i-1})|+|X_{i-1}| \leq \eps m$, and such that neither
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
    \item $X_i \ge 0.9\sum_{j=1}^i d_j(v_j)-\frac{m}{\log m}$, nor
    \item  $D^*\ge \epsilon m$ and 
    $H_i$ contains a vertex of degree at least $\sqrt{m}(\log m)^{-2}$
\end{enumerate}
holds, is at most $e^{-m^{1/11}}$.
title: Cor 15 of arXiv:2604.25725
