[Proposition 16 ($K_\infty$ is generically not Hilbert--Schmidt) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] Let $k_\infty(\xi,\eta)$ be the limiting boundary kernel of the operator programme of Section 1.1, so that $k_\infty(\xi,\eta)\asymp
u_h(B_{\xi\wedge\eta})^{- eta}$ for some $ eta>0$ determined by the transmission/Martin exponents, where $\xi\wedge\eta$ is the confluence depth. Then
 egin{align*}
\|K_\infty\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2&=\iint_{\partial T	imes\partial T}|k_\infty(\xi,\eta)|^2\,d
u_h(\xi)\,d
u_h(\eta)\
&\asymp\sum_{n\ge0} r(T)^{2n eta}\cdot
u_h\otimes
u_h ig(\{|\xi\wedge\eta|=n\} ig)\asymp\sum_{n\ge0} r(T)^{n(2 eta-1)}
\end{align*}
whenever $2 eta\ge1$ and $g$ is supercritical ($ r(T)>1$). For the Martin-kernel construction one has $ eta\ge1$, since $K(x,\cdot)\asymp
u_h(B_{|x|})^{-1}$ on the cylinder of $x$ (the Martin kernel is the harmonic-measure density $d
u_h^x/d
u_h$). Hence $K_\infty$ is not Hilbert--Schmidt, and the Krein--Rutman route through Hilbert--Schmidt compactness is unavailable.

body:
[Proposition 2.5 of arXiv:2512.19517v1, 'Spiking and Resetting' (Cédric Bernardin and Vsevolod Vladimirovich Tarsamaev); numbered Proposition 6 in the earlier card; corrected to the increment form]

## Proposition 2.5 (increment form)

Assume the standing hypotheses of Section 1: (f,h\in C^2([0,1])), (f(1)<0<f(0)), (h(1)=0), (h'(1)\ne0), and (h(x)>0) on ([0,1)). Let

\[
e_1^\varepsilon=\inf\{t\ge0:X_t^\varepsilon>y_*^\varepsilon\},\qquad
e_2^\varepsilon=\inf\{t\ge e_1^\varepsilon:X_t^\varepsilon=0\},
\]

and define the post-(e_1^\varepsilon) holding time

\[
d_2^\varepsilon:=e_2^\varepsilon-e_1^\varepsilon.
\]

Then, for every (t\ge0),

\[
\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathbb P(d_2^\varepsilon>t)=e^{f(1)t},
\]

so (d_2^\varepsilon\Rightarrow \operatorname{Exp}(-f(1))).

The proof in the paper restarts the deterministic flow at (e_1^\varepsilon) with local time (s=0); its displayed survival integral is therefore for (d_2^\varepsilon), not the absolute epoch (e_2^\varepsilon). The source says that after the stopping time “the process evolves deterministically until the next reset” (v1 HTML lines 252-257), which is precisely an increment statement.

## Later alternating holding-time sentence

For the recursively defined epochs (e_k^\varepsilon), the strong Markov property applies to the increments

\[
e_{2k+1}^\varepsilon-e_{2k}^\varepsilon,
\qquad
e_{2k+2}^\varepsilon-e_{2k+1}^\varepsilon,
\]

not to the increasing absolute epochs themselves. The alternating increments are the quantities that can be independent and have the two respective holding-time laws. Any downstream card should preserve this distinction.

## Why the absolute-time statement cannot hold as written

For every (\varepsilon), (e_2^\varepsilon\ge e_1^\varepsilon), hence

\[
\mathbb P(e_2^\varepsilon>t)\ge\mathbb P(e_1^\varepsilon>t).
\]

This stochastic order must persist at continuity points of any weak limits. Yet the paper permits (f(x)=1-3x) and (h(x)=1-x), for which (f(0)=1) and (f(1)=-2). Its two displayed absolute-time limits would require (e^{-2t}\ge e^{-t}) for (t>0), an immediate contradiction. No additional relation between (f(0)) and (f(1)) is present in the standing hypotheses.

body: A standard Brownian motion, or Wiener process, is a real-valued stochastic process (W_t)_{t >= 0} on a probability space such that (i) W_0 = 0 almost surely; (ii) for 0 <= s < t the increment W_t - W_s is normally distributed with mean 0 and variance t - s; (iii) increments over disjoint time intervals are independent; (iv) almost every sample path t |-> W_t is continuous. Existence is Wiener's theorem (constructed for instance by the Levy-Ciesielski series or as the Kolmogorov-extension limit with continuity from Kolmogorov's criterion, since E|W_t - W_s|^4 = 3 (t - s)^2). Consequences packaged with the definition: the covariance is E[W_s W_t] = min(s, t); paths are almost surely nowhere differentiable and have unbounded variation on every interval, with quadratic variation t; Brownian scaling c^{-1/2} W_{c t}, time inversion t W_{1/t}, and reflection are again Brownian motions; W is a continuous martingale and a Markov process with transition density the Gaussian kernel. Conditions (i)-(iii) characterise the finite-dimensional laws; (iv) selects the continuous version, which is the object meant in every theorem about paths.

In population dynamics, environmental stochasticity is modeled via multiplicative noise sigma_ext(N) = sigma * N dB_t, representing climate or exogenous fluctuations affecting all individuals identically; its diffusion variance is quadratic in population size and creates strong boundary absorption at zero. By contrast, internal demographic noise arises from independent individual events with variance sigma_int^2(N) ~ O(N), which becomes negligibly small relative to drift near the origin, preserving the invariance of the positive state space.

 \int_{\mathbb T}\phi\,dM_x^\partial=0,

 \phi^{\rm c}\in C(\mathbb T),

\[
 \|\phi^{\rm c}\|_\infty
 \le\Lambda K_G^\partial(x)^{1/2}.
\]

[Definition 165 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] We say that $(\hat A,\hat B,\hat C,\hat D, \hat{\mathfrak{h}},\hat{\mathfrak{t}})$ is \emph{non-degenerate} if there exists $\eps>0$ such that
 \[
 \hat{A},\hat{B},\hat{C} \in \big(\eps,\tfrac{1}{\eps}\big),\qquad \hat{D},\hat{\mathfrak{h}},\hat{n} > \eps,\qquad \hat{D} + \eps < \hat{\mathfrak{t}} < \hat{B} + \hat{C} - \hat{D} - \eps,
 \]
 and
 \[
 \hat{\mathfrak{h}} + \hat{D} + \eps < \left\{\begin{array}{lll}
 \hat A+\hat{\mathfrak{t}}&& \textnormal{if}\,\,0<\hat{\mathfrak{t}}\leq \min(\hat B,\hat C),\\
 \hat A+\min(\hat B,\hat C)&& \textnormal{if}\,\,\min(\hat B,\hat C)\leq \hat{\mathfrak{t}}\leq \max(\hat B,\hat C),\\
 \hat A+\hat B+\hat C-\hat{\mathfrak{t}}&& \textnormal{if}\,\,\max(\hat B,\hat C)\leq \hat{\mathfrak{t}}<\hat B+\hat C, \end{array} \right.
\]
 and the equilibrium measure of the discrete ensemble \eqref{eq_Hahn_hole_ensemble} has a band in each of the segments $[\hat a'_1+\eps,\hat b'_1-\eps]$ and $[\hat a'_2+\eps,\hat b'_2-\eps]$.

Under the forward Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model dU_s=-U_s ds+sqrt(2)dW_s, put Sigma_s=exp(-2s)*Sigma+(1-exp(-2s))*I and p_s(x,i)=w_i*N(x;exp(-s)*mu_i,Sigma_s). Let p_s(x)=sum_i p_s(x,i) and q_s(i|x)=p_s(x,i)/p_s(x). Fix a class y, finite horizon T>0 and a constant guidance increment eta>=0. In increasing sampling time t, s=T-t, define guided DDIM by dX_t/dt=b_eta(X_t,t), b_eta(x,t)=x+grad_x log p_s(x,y)+eta*grad_x log q_s(y|x). Unguided DDIM is dZ_t/dt=b_0(Z_t,t). Let Phi_t be the guided flow and J_t(a)=D_a Phi_t(a), with J_0=I. Let M_t solve M_dot=(I-Sigma_(T-t)^(-1))*M, M_0=I; the unguided flow is affine Z_t=M_t Z_0+xi_t. For all a in R^d and 0<=t<=T, 0<det J_t(a)<=det M_t. For the fixed model and finite horizon, det J_t(a) is bounded above and bounded away from zero uniformly in a and t. This is the determinant comparison used in the paper's entropy proof; its constants are not dimension-free or uniform over eta.

body: Brouwer's fixed-point theorem is a fixed-point theorem in topology, named after L. E. J. (Bertus) Brouwer. It states that for any continuous function f mapping a nonempty compact convex set to itself, there is a point x_0 such that f(x_0) = x_0. The simplest forms of Brouwer's theorem are for continuous functions f from a closed interval I in the real numbers to itself or from a closed disk D to itself. A more general form than the latter is for continuous functions from a nonempty convex compact subset K of Euclidean space to itself.

body: [Theorem thm:h00 of arXiv:2608.26564, 'Real ideal points, Conway spheres, and left-orderable Dehn fillings'] Let $B$ be a real half-branch as in Proposition (prop:branchmodel of the paper), with associated representations $\rho_u$ and meridian-normalized lifts $\widetilde\rho_u$. Suppose the homological longitude admits a four-longitude decomposition $\lambda=\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3\ell_4$ in positive parabolic normal form along $B$. Then for $u$ sufficiently small, the expanding eigenline $v_u\in\mathbb RP^1$ of $\rho_u(\mu)$ is well-defined and depends continuously on $u$. The pairs $(\widetilde\rho_u,v_u)$ form a continuous family of augmented peripherally hyperbolic representations, and $\operatorname{EV}(\widetilde\rho_u,v_u) = \bigl(x(u),y(u);0,h_1+h_2+h_3+h_4\bigr)$, where $x(u)=\log|a_\mu(u)|$ and $y(u)=\log|a_\lambda(u)|$, and $a_\mu(u),a_\lambda(u)$ are the eigenvalues of $\rho_u(\mu),\rho_u(\lambda)$ on $v_u$. Consequently, the image of this family is an augmented holonomy arc contained in $H_{0,h_1+h_2+h_3+h_4}(M)$.

\beq

body: [Theorem 2.3 (Von Neumann’s Minimax Theorem (see [Sim95]) of arXiv:2203.06168, 'Cheeger Inequalities for Vertex Expansion and Reweighted Eigenvalues'] ). Let X, Y be compact convex sets. If f is a real-valued continuous function on X × Y with f(x, ·) concave on Y for all x ∈X and f(·, y) convex on X for all y ∈Y , then min x∈X max y∈Y f(x, y) = max y∈Y min x∈X f(x, y). Several eigenvalue optimization problems can be formulated as semidefinite programs.

[Theorem thm:cc of arXiv:2605.26048, 'Classification of the eternal solutions and multiple coalescing shocks in the KPZ fixed po'] For almost-every $\omega$, the following hold. 
    \begin{enumerate} [label=(\roman*), font=\normalfont]
        \item For every $b \in \mathcal{B}_\omega$, the set $\pmb{\xi}^b$ is at most countable. 
        \item For every $\varphi \in \Phi_\omega$, $\pmb{\xi}^{W \star \varphi} = \operatorname{Dom}(\varphi)$, and this set is dense in $\operatorname{supp}(\varphi)$. 
        \item  For every $\varphi \in \Phi_\omega$, $\xi \in \pmb{\xi}^{W\star \varphi}$, and $(x,t) \in \mathfrak{C}^{W\star \varphi}(\xi)$,
        \[
        (W\star \varphi)(x,t) = \varphi(\xi) + W^\xi(0,0;x,t). 
        \]
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Defn localization of measure of arXiv:2505.16093, 'Multiple chordal SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Moser system'] Let $\Omega \subsetneq \mathbb{C}$ be a simply connected domain, and let $u$ be a marked boundary point. Let $z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n$ be distinct prime ends of $\partial \Omega$, and let $U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n$ be disjoint closed neighborhoods of $z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n$ in $\Omega$ such that $u \notin U_j$ for all $j$ and $U_i \cap U_j = \emptyset$ for $1 \leq i < j \leq n$. 

We consider probability measures
\[
\mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n\right)}
\]
on $n$-tuples of unparametrized continuous curves, where each curve starts at $z_j$, is contained in $U_j$, and exits $U_j$ almost surely. 

A family of such measures, indexed by different choices of neighborhoods $\left(U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n\right)$, is called \emph{compatible} if for all $U_j \subset U_j'$, the measure $\mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n\right)}$ is obtained from 
\[
\mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, u\right)}^{\left(U_1', U_2', \ldots, U_n'\right)}
\]
by restricting each curve to the portion before it first exits the smaller domain $U_j$.
title: Localization of measures

[Cor cor_upper_boundary_examples of arXiv:2606.23648, '\textsc{Optimal Stopping for a Diffusion with Unobserved Bernoulli Drift}'] Assume that the hypotheses of Proposition
    (prop_upper_boundary_asymptotics of the paper) hold.

    \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
        \item For power costs
        \(
            k(s)=\alpha s^\beta+\gamma,
            \, \alpha>0, \beta>1,
        \)
        one has
        \(
            b(x)\to+\infty,
        \)
        and more precisely
        \begin{equation}
            b(x)
            =
            y_0+\frac12\log\frac{2x}{\beta}+o(1), \qquad x \to \infty.
        \end{equation}

        \item For exponential costs
        \(
            k(s)=\alpha(e^{\lambda s}-\gamma),
            \, \alpha>0, 0<\lambda<2,
        \)
        one has
        \begin{equation}
            b(x)\to
            y_0+\frac12\log\frac{2-\lambda}{\lambda}.
        \end{equation}
    \end{enumerate}

[Prop eq:q(t|s) of arXiv:2604.20629, 'Rates of forgetting for the sequentially Markov coalescent'] The SMC jump chain $(X_{n})$ defined by ((eq:Xn+1 of the paper)) has
transition density
\begin{equation}
q_{\mathrm{SMC}}(t\mid s)=\frac{e^{-t}\left(e^{s\wedge t}-1\right)}{s},\quad s>0, t>0.
\end{equation}
It is irreducible and reversible with respect to 
\[
\mu(dt)=te^{-t} dt,
\]
and $\mu$ is the unique invariant probability measure.

The SMC' jump chain $(X'_{n})$ has transition density
$q_{\mathrm{SMC}'}(t\mid s)$ given above. 
It is irreducible and reversible with respect to 
\[
\mu'(dt)=\frac{3}{8} \bigl(2t+1-e^{-2t}\bigr)e^{-t} dt.
\]
and $\mu'$ is the unique invariant probability measure. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

    ,

  considered as a subset of $\XX = L^2 (\R^2)$, satisfies $\md(\SC) = 1$ and

  Moreover, there exist a suitable \emph{cone-adapted shearlet system}
  (see \cite[Definition~5.6]{VoigtlaenderPeinAnalysisVSSynthesisSparsityAlphaShearlets}),
  a suitable enumeration $\CalG = (g_n)_{n \in \N}$ of this system,

  defined in \Cref{prop:PolynomiallyBoundedNTermApproximationControlledComplexity}
  is optimal for $\SC$ in the class of families of controlled complexity in $L^2(\RR^2)$.
  In particular, a phase transition as in
  \Cref{thm:PhaseTransitionForFamiliesWithControlledComplexity} occurs. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem thm:honest-region of arXiv:2608.20295, 'Physical-Support Confidence Sets for Highly Coherent Dictionaries'] Under Assumption~(ass:frozen-shell of the paper) and the calibration coverage condition
in Equation~(equation eq:training-rectangle of the paper), the totalized correspondence
$\widehat{\mathfrak C}_{q,r,s}^{p}$ is measurable, nonempty, and
compact-valued. Uniformly over $\mathfrak P^p_{q,r}(s)$,
\begin{equation}
\mathbb P_{p_\star,\nu_\star,D_\star}^N
\left[
\mathbb P_{\mu_\star,\sigma_\star}^T
\left\{
    \vartheta_\star
    \in
    \widehat{\mathfrak C}_{q,r,s}^{p}
    \mid Y_{1:N}
\right\}
\ge1-\alpha_T
\right]
\ge1-\alpha_D.

\end{equation}
Consequently, by independence of the calibration and deployment experiments,
with
\[
    \alpha
    =
    1-(1-\alpha_D)(1-\alpha_T),
\]
\begin{equation}
\inf_{\xi\in\mathfrak P^p_{q,r}(s)}
\mathbb P_\xi^{N,T}
\left\{
    \vartheta(\xi)
    \in
    \widehat{\mathfrak C}_{q,r,s}^{p}
\right\}
\ge1-\alpha.

\end{equation}

For $N$ above the fixed block threshold of the robust calibration-moment
construction, define
\begin{equation}
\rho_N(s)
=
C\left[
    (s\wedge\epsilon_N)
    +
    \left(s\wedge\frac{\epsilon_N}{s}\right)
    +
    \left(s\wedge\frac{\epsilon_N}{s^2}\right)
\right].

\end{equation}
Any two dictionaries retained by the same nonempty calibration region have
quotient-dictionary distance at most $\rho_N(s)$.  If
$\epsilon_N\le CN^{-1/2}$, then
\begin{equation}
    \rho_N(s)
    \le
    C\left(
        s\wedge\frac{1}{\sqrt N\,s^2}
    \right).
    
\end{equation}
Below the block threshold, retaining the full compact shell yields the same
order after adjustment of fixed constants.

For every realization,
\begin{align}
\operatorname{diam}_{\mathrm{pr}}
\left(
    \widehat{\mathfrak C}_{q,r,s}^{p}
\right)
\le{}&
C\rho_N(s)
\notag\\
&+
Cs\,
\mathbf 1
\left\{
    2\tau_{T,q}\ge m_S(\rho_N(s))
\right\}
\notag\\
&+
C\,
\mathbf 1
\left\{
    2\tau_{T,q}\ge m_G(\rho_N(s))
\right\}.

\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Coverage and resolution of the cross-dictionary correspondence

Let P_X be an input probability law and P_F a law on measurable functions F:X->{-1,1}, with measurable evaluation. Draw F and F_prime independently from P_F. Draw X_1,...,X_m iid from P_X, independently of both functions, where m>=1 is an integer; each sampled function is held fixed throughout the batch. Define CP_infinity = E_{F,F_prime}[(E_X F(X)*F_prime(X))^2]. Define CP_m=E[((1/m) sum_{i=1}^m F(X_i)*F_prime(X_i))^2]. Then CP_m=1/m+(1-1/m)*CP_infinity. Equivalently, for K(x,x_prime)=E_F[F(x)*F(x_prime)], CP_infinity=E_{X,X_prime}[K(X,X_prime)^2], with X,X_prime independent under P_X. Thus0<=CP_infinity<=1, CP_m>=1/m and CP_1=1. No balanced-label assumption is needed for these identities.
Binary-valued functions; measurable evaluation and the stated probability laws.
The input batch is iid and independent of two iid function draws.
The same function pair is reused throughout the batch; it is not redrawn per input.

[Lemma 11 (Endpoint reduction and contact identities) of arXiv:2608.06523, 'On the Gardner Transition in the Ising Pure $p$-Spin Glass II'] For the measure in \eqref{eq:mu},
\begin{equation}
 \partial_x\Phi_\mu(x,q)=\tanh x,\qquad
 \partial_{xx}\Phi_\mu(x,q)=\cosh^{-2}x.
 
\end{equation}
For every smooth test function $\varphi$ such that
$\varphi,\varphi',\varphi''$ have at most exponential growth and which
does not depend on $m$ or $\xi'(q)$,
\begin{equation}
 \E[\varphi(M(q))e^{W_\mu(q)}]
 =\frac{\E\!\left[
 \varphi(\sqrt{\xi'(q)}z)\cosh^m(\sqrt{\xi'(q)}z)\right]}
 {\E[\cosh^m(\sqrt{\xi'(q)}z)]},
 \qquad \E e^{W_\mu(q)}=1.
 
\end{equation}
At a stationary marginal point,
\begin{align}
 \Gamma_\mu(q)
 &=\E[\tanh^2(M(q))e^{W_\mu(q)}]=q,
 \\
 q&=(p-1)\xi'(q)
 \E[\cosh^{-4}(M(q))e^{W_\mu(q)}],
 \\
 \E[\cosh^{-2}(M(q))e^{W_\mu(q)}]&=1-q,
 \\
 \E[\cosh^{-4}(M(q))e^{W_\mu(q)}]
 &=\frac{q}{(p-1)\xi'(q)}.
 
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def:vary of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] Let $\mathcal W$ be a white noise with respect to some filtration $\mathcal F$. Let $\overline{\delta}$ be a drift function with respect to $\mathcal F$. We call a collection of continuous processes $\mathcal S=(\mathcal S_{r,x}(a),\, x\ge r)_{r\in {\mathbb R},a\ge 0}$ a ${\rm BESQ}(\overline{\delta})$ flow driven by $\mathcal W$ if 
   
    (1) The restriction of $\mathcal S$ to each $A_i$ is a ${\rm BESQ}^{\delta_i}$ flow driven by $\mathcal W$.

    (2) The regularity conditions of Definition (def:BESQflow of the paper) hold.
 

If $E$ is a (possibly random) Borel set, we call $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow killed on $E$ the flow obtained from the $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow by absorbing the flow line $\mathcal S_{r,\cdot}(a)$ at $0$ at time $\inf\{x \in E\cap (r,\infty) \,:\, \mathcal S_{r,x}(a)=0\}$.

 If $E={\mathbb R}$, we will simply say that $\mathcal S$ is a killed  $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow. We call general  $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow a $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow or a  killed $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow.
title: Definition def:vary of arXiv:2411.04773

body:
[Theorem 11 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Let $V$ be a $k[H]$-module. Let $R$ be such that it contains $R_s$. Let $t\in\mathbb Z\setminus p\mathbb Z$. Let $o$ be the order of $[t]_{p^s}\in (\mathbb Z/p^s\mathbb Z)^{\times}$. Then the following properties hold.

\medskip
{\bf (1)} The following statements are equivalent.

\medskip\noindent
{\bf (1.a)} The $k[H]$-module $V$ is cyclic.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.b)} The $k[H]$-module $V$ is indecomposable.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.c)} The $k[H]$-module $V$ is strongly indecomposable.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.d)} We have $\imath_V\in\{0,1\}$.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.e)} Each lift $\mathcal V$ of $V$ to $R$ is cyclic.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.f)} Each lift $\mathcal V$ of $V$ to $R$ is cyclic and strongly indecomposable.

\medskip
{\bf (2)} The $k[H]$-module $V$ has a lift $\mathcal H$ to $R$ which is an end-hull of $V$ and a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules. Moreover, if $\jmath_V=0$, then we can also assume that $r_{\mathcal H}=0$.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} Suppose that $V$ is cyclic. Let $\mathcal V_1$ and $\mathcal V_2$ be two lifts of $V$. Then the $R[H]$-modules $\mathcal V_1$ and $\mathcal V_2$ are isomorphic if and only if the $B[H]$-modules $\mathcal V_1\otimes_R B$ and $\mathcal V_2\otimes_R B$ are isomorphic.

\smallskip
{\bf (4)} The $k[H]$-modules $V$ and $V^{(t)}$ are isomorphic.

\smallskip
{\bf (5)} The following statements are equivalent.

\medskip\noindent
{\bf (5.a)} There exists a lift $\mathcal V$ of $V$ to $R$ which is $t$-invariant and a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules (resp.\ which is $t$-invariant and a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules with $r_{\mathcal V^H}=0$).

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (5.b)} For each $b\in\llbracket1,p^s\rrbracket\setminus o\llbracket1,\lfloor\frac{p^s}{t}\rfloor\rrbracket$ such that $\mu_V(b)\neq 0$, $\mu_V(b)$ is a sum of cardinals of orbits of the action of $[t]_{p^s}$ on $\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s)$ (resp.\ $\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s^{\ast})$), equivalently of subsets $\Phi$ of $\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s)$ (resp.\ $\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s^{\ast})$) with $[t]_{p^s}\cdot\Phi=\Phi$.

\medskip
{\bf (6)} Suppose that $p$ is odd, $[t]_{p^s}=[p^s-1]_{p^s}$ (equivalently, $o=2$) and $\dim_k(V)$ is even. Then $V$ has a lift to $R$ which is a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules and is $t$-invariant.

\medskip
{\bf (7)} Suppose that $p$ is odd, $[t]_{p^s}=[p^s-1]_{p^s}$, $\mu_V(d)$ is even for each odd $d\in\llbracket1,p^s\rrbracket$, and $\jmath_V=0$. Then $V$ has a lift $\mathcal V$ to $R$ which is a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules and is $t$-invariant with $r_{\mathcal V}=0$.

[Lemma 18 (Ricci quadratic estimate; cf.\ Lemma A.1 of \cite{Brendle2019}, Lemma 4.7 of \cite{Chen2024}) of arXiv:2608.26598, 'Pinching cones for positive isotropic curvature in dimensions seven and eight'] Let $0\le\zeta\le1$ and $0<\varrho\le1$, and let $H$ be a symmetric two-tensor whose largest
    eigenvalue is at most $\frac12\mathrm{tr}\,H$ and whose two smallest eigenvalues have sum at
    least $\frac{2(1-\zeta)}{n}\mathrm{tr}\,H$. Then, with
    $H^0=H-\frac1n\mathrm{tr}(H)\,\mathrm{id}$, every orthonormal pair $\{e_1,e_2\}$ satisfies
    \begin{equation}
        \frac{n-2}{n}\,\mathrm{tr}(H)\,\bigl(H_{11}+H_{22}\bigr)
        -\varrho\bigl((H^0)^2_{11}+(H^0)^2_{22}\bigr)
        \ge\frac{2}{n^2}\left((n-2)(1-\zeta)-2\zeta^2\varrho\,
        \frac{n^2-2n+2}{(n-2)^2}\right)\mathrm{tr}(H)^2.
    \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let p/d->psi>0, let f_j be independent uniform vectors on the sphere of radius sqrt(d), and let g~N(0,I_d) be independent. Fix a globally Lipschitz activation rho with E rho(G)=0 and v=E rho(G)^2>0 for G~N(0,1). Define W_jk=f_j^T f_k/d and C_jk=E_g rho(f_j^T g/sqrt(d))rho(f_k^T g/sqrt(d)). With b=(E G rho(G))^2 and tau=v-b, C=tau I+bW+E where E_jj=0, |E_jk|<=tau|W_jk|^2 and E||E||_F^2<=3 tau^2 p(p-1)/[d(d+2)]. The Schur product contraction gives ||C||<=v||W||. Hence C has limiting empirical law law(tau+b MP_psi), since its resolvent trace differs from that of tau I+bW by at most ||E||_F/(sqrt(p) s^2) at every s>0. Operator-norm equivalence is not asserted. For variance-one centered ReLU rho(t)=sqrt(2 pi/(pi-1))[max(t,0)-1/sqrt(2 pi)], b=pi/[2(pi-1)], tau=(pi-2)/[2(pi-1)]. Its second Hermite coefficient square is 1/[2(pi-1)]. If e is the unit all-ones vector, E e^T E e >=(p-1)/[2(pi-1)d]; the uniformly bounded second moment makes e^T E e uniformly integrable, proving that ||E|| does not converge to zero in probability. The spectral-law comparison is sufficient for the weighted sample-covariance resolvent, even though this stronger operator approximation fails. All claims remain unaudited own-work drafts.

body: The nerve of a finite collection A of nonempty sets is the simplicial complex N(A) := {sigma : nonempty sigma subset of A with intersection over B in sigma of B nonempty}. If the sets are convex subsets of R^d (in the paper, the grains x + K of the union Z_W), the union is homotopy equivalent to the nerve (a variant of the Nerve Theorem, Edelsbrunner-Harer p. 76). For general sets contractibility of the intersections is not enough; the usual hypotheses are open sets, or closed convex sets.

The planar set C={(x,y): x>0 and |y-x^2|<1} is open, connected and unbounded, but contains no straight ray with nonzero direction. A ray with negative x direction exits x>0, a vertical ray exits the bounded vertical strip at its fixed x, and a ray with positive x direction has y-x^2 tending to minus infinity quadratically. This is a geometric counterexample to an unbounded-component implies straight-visibility inference; no permitted mirror configuration or reflected-ray trapping is asserted.
All hypotheses and scope restrictions in the statement apply.

Lemma 1. Every unbounded open convex set C in R^d contains an unbounded straight ray starting at each x in C. Therefore, if a mirror-complement component is unbounded, open and convex, an origin in it has an unobstructed escaping launch direction and cannot have every reflected ray bounded.

Proof: choose r>0 with B(x,r) contained in C and y_k in C with |y_k-x| tending to infinity. A subsequence of d_k=(y_k-x)/|y_k-x| tends to a unit direction d. For fixed t>=0 and sufficiently large k, convexity gives a ball centered at x+t*d_k with radius (1-t/|y_k-x|)*r contained in C. Eventually this radius exceeds 3r/4 and the center is within r/4 of x+t*d, so B(x+t*d,r/2) is in C. This holds for every fixed t with the same subsequential direction d, proving the entire ray stays inside C. No collision occurs along it.

Lemma 2. C={(x,y): x>0 and |y-x^2|<1} is open, connected and unbounded but contains no unbounded straight ray.

Proof: (x,u)->(x,x^2+u) is a homeomorphism from (0,infinity) times (-1,1), proving the first three properties. For a ray (a+bt,c+dt), t>=0, with nonzero direction: b<0 eventually violates x>0; b=0 and d!=0 eventually violates the strip condition; b>0 makes y-x^2 a quadratic with leading coefficient -b^2, whose magnitude diverges. Thus all possible directions leave C in finite time.

This gives an explicit algebraic version of the previous spiral-corridor obstruction: unbounded connected vacancy alone does not supply a straight ray. The corridor is not represented as a permitted mirror arrangement, and absence of straight rays does not establish trapping of reflected rays. In the p=2 coercive regime b^2<2, applying Ito to ||A^(1/2)u||^2 yields control of E integral ||Au||^2 for additive input in D(A^(1/2)), after absorbing its cross term by Young inequality. Check: The moment identity follows both from the explicit stochastic exponential and from Ito applied to |X|^p. The coercive calculation uses the weighted norm A^(1/2)u, so it controls the full domain D(A), not merely the energy domain. Obstruction: A criterion handling noncommuting A,B in Banach spaces must replace scalar coercivity and preserve the correct p-dependence. No such general criterion is proved here. [Prop lamclass of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Suppose $\Lambda$ is a minimal lamination on $M$ transverse to $\partial M$. Then at least one of the following holds:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\Lambda$ has a leaf $\lambda$ such that $\pi_1(\lambda)$ is not normally generated by boundary parallel curves.
        \item $\Lambda$ is a compact planar surface.
        \item $\Lambda$ has a leaf with a noncompact boundary component inside a Reeb, $\sharp$, or $\flat$ annulus on $\partial M$.
        \item $\Lambda$ is a $\mathbb{T}^3$-type planar lamination.
        \item $\Lambda$ is a $\mathbb{T}^2$-type planar lamination.
    \end{enumerate}

Define the elementary factors E_0(w) = 1 - w and, for p ≥ 1, E_p(w) = (1 - w) exp(w + w^2/2 + ... + w^p/p). Let m ≥ 0 be an integer and let (a_n) be a finite or infinite sequence of nonzero complex numbers, repetitions allowed, with |a_n| → ∞ if the sequence is infinite. Choose nonnegative integers p_n such that the series Σ_n (r/|a_n|)^{p_n + 1} converges for every r > 0 (the choice p_n = n - 1 always works). Then the product P(z) = z^m Π_n E_{p_n}(z/a_n) converges absolutely and uniformly on compact subsets of C and defines an entire function whose zero set is exactly {0} (with multiplicity m, omitted if m = 0) together with the points a_n, each with multiplicity equal to the number of times it is listed. Conversely, every entire function f whose zeros are exactly these (with these multiplicities) has the form f(z) = exp(g(z)) P(z) for some entire function g. Consequently every entire function admits such a factorization, and every meromorphic function on C is a quotient of two entire functions.
the prescribed zeros form a sequence with no finite accumulation point (|a_n| → ∞ if infinite)
the integers p_n satisfy Σ_n (r/|a_n|)^{p_n+1} < ∞ for every r > 0
multiplicities are encoded by repetition in the list

Let H be a complex Hilbert space. (a) If A is self-adjoint on H, then U(t) = e^{itA} (Borel functional calculus) defines a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group: U(t + s) = U(t)U(s), U(0) = I, U(t)* = U(−t), and t ↦ U(t)x is continuous on ℝ for each x. Moreover D(A) = {x ∈ H : lim_{t→0} (U(t)x − x)/t exists} and for x ∈ D(A) that limit equals iAx; D(A) is invariant under each U(t). (b) Conversely, let (U(t))_{t ∈ ℝ} be a family of unitary operators with U(t + s) = U(t)U(s), U(0) = I, and t ↦ U(t)x continuous for each x ∈ H. Then there is a unique self-adjoint operator A with U(t) = e^{itA} for all t, namely Ax = lim_{t→0} (U(t)x − x)/(it) on the set where the limit exists. (c) Weak continuity suffices in (b): if t ↦ ⟨U(t)x, y⟩ is continuous for all x, y, the group is strongly continuous, since ‖U(t)x − x‖² = 2‖x‖² − 2Re⟨U(t)x, x⟩. If H is separable, weak measurability of t ↦ ⟨U(t)x, y⟩ already implies strong continuity (von Neumann). (d) A subspace D ⊂ D(A) that is dense in H and invariant under every U(t) is a core for A (Nelson's criterion via invariant domains).
H is a complex Hilbert space
in (a): A is self-adjoint, not merely symmetric
in (b): U(t) unitary for every real t, group law on all of ℝ, and strong (or weak) continuity

body: [Lemma 1 of arXiv:2511.18562, 'Ensuring Calibration Robustness in Split Conformal Prediction Under Adversarial Attacks'] Let $f:=f_{y}(x)\in\mathbb{R}$ be a scalar score and $g:=\|\nabla f\|\geq 0$. Let $F_{f}$ and $f_{f}$ denote the CDF and PDF of $f$, respectively. For $\varepsilon\geq 0$ define $Z_{\varepsilon}:=f-\varepsilon g$ and $q(\varepsilon):=Q_{1-\alpha}(Z_{\varepsilon})$, i.e. $F_{Z_{\varepsilon}}(q(\varepsilon))=1-\alpha$. [Corollary 6 (Finite-family covariance domination) of arXiv:2608.27657, '\bfseries Stein Kernels and Normal Approximation\\ for Log-Concave Bilinear Forms'] Assume the estimates in \cref{thm:letwin}.  Let
\(A_1,\ldots,A_k\in\mathsf S_n\), and define
\[
  K_{ij}
  =
  \Cov\!\left(\Tr(A_iH),\Tr(A_jH)\right),
  \qquad
  G_{ij}
  =
  \Tr(A_iA_j).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
  0\preceq K\preceq4G.
  \tag{3.19}
\end{equation}
In particular, if \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\) are Hilbert--Schmidt orthonormal,
then \(K\preceq4I_k\).  For two arbitrary directions this also gives
\[
  \left|
  \Cov\!\left(\Tr(AH),\Tr(BH)\right)
  \right|
  \leq
  4\sqrt{\Tr(A^2)\Tr(B^2)}.
\]

[Proposition prop:KW of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $\Lambda$ be a finite cubical subcomplex of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, $\mathbb{G}$ a finite abelian group, $1\leq k\leq d$, $(J_{\mathbf{c}})_{\mathbf{c}\in \Lambda^{*,k}}$ be positive coupling constants and $h:\mathbb{G}\to \mathbb{R}$ be even. Let $\Omega:=\mathrm{Im}(\partial_{d-k+1})$  and $\Sigma:=C^{k-1}$. Define $f:\Omega\to 2^{\Sigma}$ by $f(\eta) = \{\sigma \in \Sigma \mid d^k(\sigma) = \eta^* \} = (*\circ d^k)^{-1}(\eta)$ and
     $$
     \rho[\eta]\propto \prod_{\mathbf{c}\in {\Lambda_{d-k}}}\exp(J_{\mathbf{c}} h(\eta_{\mathfrak{c}})), \;\forall \eta\in \Omega, \qquad \gamma[\sigma]\propto 1,\;\forall\sigma\in\Sigma.
     $$
     Then, under the coupling measure $\mathscr{P}$ defined in Theorem (thm:generalcoupling of the paper), 
    \begin{enumerate}
		\item[(a)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Sigma$ is the spin model $\mu^{*}_{\Lambda^{k-1}}$. 
        For each $\eta \in\Omega$,  the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \eta]$ is the uniform measure on $f(\eta)$, that is the uniform assignment of a spin configuration consistent with the domain walls $\eta$.
		\item[(b)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Omega$ is the domain wall measure $\mu_{\Lambda_{d-k}}$.  For each $\sigma \in\Sigma$, the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \sigma] = \delta_{(d^k(\sigma))^*}$, the Dirac measure on the dual of the co-boundary of $\sigma$ corresponding to taking the domain walls of the spin configuration. 
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Spin Models and Domain Walls

Let n>=1 and y_i in {-1,+1}, and let f(w;x_i) be continuously differentiable in w in R^D. Assume global constants rho>0 and beta>0 satisfy ||grad f(w;x_i)||_2<=rho and ||grad f(w;x_i)-grad f(v;x_i)||_2<=beta||w-v||_2 for every w,v and every training index i. Define L(w)=(1/n)sum_i log(1+exp(-y_i f(w;x_i))) and w_{k+1}=w_k-eta grad L(w_k), where eta>0 denotes the source paper's eta_tilde. At any iterate w with L(w)<=1/(eta rho^2), writing g=grad L(w) and w_plus=w-eta g, one has -eta(1+beta eta L(w))||g||_2^2<=L(w_plus)-L(w)<=-eta(1-(2rho^2+beta)eta L(w))||g||_2^2. In particular L(w)<=1/[eta(2rho^2+beta)] implies L(w_plus)<=L(w). The model need not be convex or twice differentiable. Near-homogeneity and linear separability are not hypotheses of this one-step result.

[Theorem thm:L of arXiv:2412.01015, 'Classical beta ensembles and related eigenvalues processes at high temperature and the Mar'] Under the moment assumption~(equation moment-assumption of the paper), it holds that 
\[
	S_n^{(N)}(t) \to m_n(t) \quad \text{as} \quad N \to \infty,
\]
in probability as random elements in $C([0, T])$. Here the limiting moment processes are recursively defined by $m_0(t) = 1,$ 
\begin{align}
	m_n(t) &= a_n + \sigma n (n+\alpha - 1)\int_0^t m_{n-1}(s)ds + \sigma {cn} \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\int_0^t m_j(u) m_{n-1-j}(u) du,  
\end{align}
for $n \ge 1$.
If, in addition, the initial limiting moments $\{a_n\}$ satisfy a condition that
\[
	a_n \le (\Lambda n)^{2n}, \quad n \ge 0,
\]
for some constant $\Lambda > 0$. Then for any $ t \ge 0$, $\{m_n(t)\}_{n \ge 0}$ are moments of a unique probability measure $\mu_t$ on $[0, \infty)$. Moreover, the probability measure-valued process $\mu_t$ is continuous and the empirical measure process $(\mu_t^{(N)})_{0 \le t \le T}$ converges to $(\mu_t)_{0 \le t \le T}$ in probability under the topology of uniform convergence. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:L of arXiv:2412.01015

[Definition 7 of arXiv:2605.13727, 'Stochastic evolution equations\\ driven by arbitrary cylindrical Lévy processes'] A predictable process $\Psi \colon \Omega \times [0,T] \rightarrow L_2(U,H)$ is $L$-integrable if there exists a sequence $(\Psi_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of processes in $\mathcal{S}_{\rm prd}^{\rm HS}$ such that
	\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
		\item[{\rm (1)}]  $(\Psi_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges $P_T$-a.e. to $\Psi$;
		\item[{\rm (2)}] $\displaystyle \lim_{m,n \rightarrow \infty}d_T^{em}(I(\Psi_m),I(\Psi_n))=0.$
	\end{enumerate}
	In this case,  the stochastic integral process $(I(\Psi)(t):\, t\in [0,T])$ of $\Psi$ is defined as the limit 
	of $(I(\Psi_n))_{n\in\N}$ in $\dem_T$. The class of all $L$-integrable $L_2(U,H)$-valued predictable processes will be denoted by $\mathcal{I}_{{\rm prd},L}^{\rm HS}:=\mathcal{I}_{{\rm prd},L}^{\rm HS}(U,H)$.

body:
Let G be a finite connected undirected multigraph on n vertices, loops discarded, with Laplacian L = D - A where D is the diagonal degree matrix and A the adjacency matrix (A_{ij} the number of edges between i and j). Then the number of spanning trees of G equals every cofactor of L: deleting any row i and any column j and taking (-1)^{i+j} times the determinant gives the same value. Equivalently, if 0 = lambda_1 < lambda_2 <= ... <= lambda_n are the eigenvalues of L, the number of spanning trees is (lambda_2 lambda_3 ... lambda_n) / n.
G finite and undirected; for a disconnected graph every cofactor is 0
loops do not affect spanning trees and are removed

[Lem 39 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any constants $C,\delta > 0$, there exists a positive constant $c(C,\delta)$ such that the following holds: let $\bA$ be any $N\times N$ diagonal matrix with $\|\bA\|_{\op} \le C$, and suppose $\bg,\acute{\bg}$ are independent standard gaussian vectors in $\R^N$. Then,
    \[
        \frac{|(\bA \bg, \bg) - \Tr(\bA)|}{N}\,,
        \frac{|(\bA \bg, \acute{\bg})|}{N}
        \le \delta
    \]
    with probability at least $1-e^{- c(C,\delta) N}$.

\begin{proof}
We rewrite the random variables of interest as
    \begin{align*}
    (\bA \bg, \bg) - \Tr(\bA)
    &=
    \sum_{i=1}^N a_{i,i}
    \Big((g_i)^2-1\Big)\,,\\
    (\bA\bg,\bg')
    &=
    \sum_{i=1}^N a_{i,i}
        g_i\acute{g}_i\,.
    \end{align*}
The claim then follows by standard Chernoff bounds.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 30 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] For \(\mu_n, \mu \in \mathcal{D}\) and their corresponding PCAFs \(A^{\mu_n}, A^{\mu}\), if \(\mu_n\) converges to \(\mu\) in \(d_\mathcal{D}\), then \(A^{\mu_n}\) converges to \(A^{\mu}\) in \(L^1(\mathbb{P}_x)\) uniformly for \(x\) with the local uniform topology for \(t\), that is, for any \(T>0\),

[Theorem 232 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Consider a solution $\boldsymbol{F}(z) = (F_h(z))_{h = 1}^H$ of the master Riemann--Hilbert problem with zero source, such that $\boldsymbol{F}(z) = O(z^d)$ as $z \rightarrow \infty$ for some $d \in \amsmathbb{Z}$. Then, for any non-zero $\boldsymbol{v} \in \amsmathbb{R}^H$, there exists a unique meromorphic function $F_{\boldsymbol{v}}$ on $\Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v}}$ such that, for any $\boldsymbol{w} \in \mathfrak{G}.\boldsymbol{v}$ and $p \in \Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{w}}$ we have
\[
F_{\boldsymbol{v}}(p) = \big \langle \boldsymbol{w} \cdot \boldsymbol{F}(z) \big \rangle = \sum_{h = 1}^H w_h F_h(z) \qquad \textnormal{with}\quad z = Z_{\boldsymbol{v}}(p).
\]
The function $F_{\boldsymbol{v}}$ can have poles only at ramification points with order at most equal to the tameness exponent of $\boldsymbol{F}$, and at $Z^{-1}_{\boldsymbol{v}}(\{\infty\})$ with order at most $d$. If the $\mathfrak{G}$-orbit of $\boldsymbol{v}$ is finite, then $\Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v}}$ is a compact Riemann surface, and
\[
\big\{\langle \boldsymbol{w} \cdot \boldsymbol{F}(z)\rangle \,\,\big|\,\,\boldsymbol{w} \in \mathfrak{G}.\boldsymbol{v}\big\}
\]
are the various branches of an algebraic function. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2609.03954, 'Galois representations ramified at one prime via relative deformation theory'] For every $m\in\Z$, the groups $H^i(G_{\{p\}},\Zp(m))$ are finitely generated $\Zp$-modules for $i=1,2$, and the canonical maps
\[
 H^i(G_{\{p\}},\Zp(m))\otimes_{\Zp}\Qp
 \longrightarrow
 H^i(G_{\{p\}},\Qp(m))
 \qquad \text{for}\quad i=1,2
\]
are isomorphisms.  In particular, the degree-two map
\[
 H^2(G_{\{p\}},\Zp(m))\otimes_{\Zp}\Qp
 \longrightarrow
 H^2(G_{\{p\}},\Qp(m))
\]

 \mathbb{P}\!\left(

     \frac{t}{\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}

Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^d)$ (equivalently, by the argument below, $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d)$). If both $\{x:f(x)\ne0\}$ and $\{\xi:\hat f(\xi)\ne0\}$ have finite Lebesgue measure, then $f=0$ almost everywhere. In particular $f$ and $\hat f$ cannot both have compact support unless $f=0$, and a nonzero bandlimited function cannot vanish outside a set of finite measure. Quantitative companion (Amrein-Berthier, Nazarov in $d=1$): for sets $S,\Sigma\subset\mathbb R^d$ of finite measure there is $C=C(S,\Sigma)>0$ with $\|f\|_2\le C(\|f\|_{L^2(S^c)}+\|\hat f\|_{L^2(\Sigma^c)})$ for all $f\in L^2$.

BOTH the support of f and the support of its transform have finite Lebesgue measure
no smoothness or decay is assumed

body: For an n by n complex matrix A, the numerical range (field of values) of A is the set W(A) = {x* A x : x in C^n, x* x = 1}, a subset of the complex plane. W(A) contains every eigenvalue of A, and if A is normal (A A* = A* A), W(A) equals the convex hull of the eigenvalues of A. [standard, e.g. Horn and Johnson, Topics in Matrix Analysis]
title: Numerical Range (Field of Values) of a Matrix

[Lemma 43 (Finite-dimensional relative entropy chain rule) of arXiv:2608.28827, 'Quantitative Target Convergence and Uniform-in-Time\\ Propagation of Chaos for Langevin-Re'] Fix \(N\geq1\).  Let \(P_t^N\) and \(Q_t^N\) be the laws of two
diffusions on \((\R^d)^N\) with common diffusion coefficient
\(\sqrt{2\varepsilon}I\) and respective drifts \(b_t^N\) and
\(\bar b_t^N\), that is, with Fokker-Planck equations given by
\begin{equation}
    \partial_tP_t^N
    =
    -\nabla\cdot(b_t^NP_t^N)+\varepsilon\Delta P_t^N,
    \qquad
    \partial_tQ_t^N
    =
    -\nabla\cdot(\bar b_t^NQ_t^N)+\varepsilon\Delta Q_t^N,
\end{equation}
where \(\varepsilon>0\).
Suppose that \(P_0^N,Q_0^N\in\mathcal P_2((\R^d)^N)\)
and that, for every \(T<\infty\), \(b_t^N\) and
\(\bar b_t^N\) are in $C_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\alpha/2,\,1+\alpha}
    \bigl((0,T]\times\mathbb R^{dN};\mathbb R^{dN}\bigr)$ for some $\alpha \in (0,1)$, and
satisfy
\[
    \|b_t^N(X)\|+\|\bar b_t^N(X)\|
    \leq C_{N,T}(1+\|X\|),
    \qquad 0\leq t\leq T.
\]
If \(\KL(P_0^N\|Q_0^N)<\infty\), then 
\(u\mapsto\KL(P_u^N\|Q_u^N)\) is locally absolutely continuous and,
for \(0\leq s\leq t\),
\begin{align}
    \KL(P_t^N\|Q_t^N)-\KL(P_s^N\|Q_s^N)
    &=
    \int_s^t\int
       \left\langle
          b_u^N-\bar b_u^N,
          \nabla\log\frac{dP_u^N}{dQ_u^N}
       \right\rangle
       dP_u^N\,du
    \notag\\
    &\quad
    -\varepsilon\int_s^t
       I(P_u^N\|Q_u^N)\,du.

\end{align}

[Prop of arXiv:2411.00663, 'Ergodicity and Mixing of invariant capacities and applications'] Let $(\Omega_1, \mathcal{F}_1, V_1, T_1)$ and $(\Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_2, V_2, T_2)$ be two capacity preserving systems, where $V_1$ and $V_2$ are upper probabilities.
	Then the upper probability $V_1\times V_2$ is $T_1\times T_2$-invariant. In particular,
	$(\Omega_1 \times \Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_1 \times \mathcal{F}_2, V_1 \times V_2,T_1\times T_2)$  is a capacity preserving system.

[Lemma 35 of arXiv:2609.03962, '$L^p$ isomorphisms for the fractional Laplacian on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their application'] Let $s\in(0,2)$ and $u\in\cL_s$. Then
    \[
      \langle\flap u,\eta\rangle:=\int_{\R^n}u\,\flap\eta\,dx,
      \qquad\eta\in\mathscr S(\R^n),
    \]
    converges absolutely and defines the unique extension of the
    distribution $\flap u$ of Definition~\ref{def_fracLap} to a tempered
    distribution. Consequently, if $F\in\mathscr S'(\R^n)$ and $\flap u=F$
    in $\mathscr D'(\R^n)$, then
    $\langle F,\eta\rangle=\int_{\R^n}u\,\flap\eta\,dx$ for all
    $\eta\in\mathscr S(\R^n)$.

body: Certificate (campaign status: proved): (S14 (10)-(20).) Put d = ceil(n/3), s = 3d-n in {0,1,2}; choose cyclically ordered U = {u_1,...,u_d} with exactly s gaps of length two and d-s of length three (lengths sum 2s+3(d-s) = n). Write a length-two gap as u_j,m_j,u_{j+1} and a length-three gap as u_j,m_j,w_j,u_{j+1}. Then B_n = {A} u {C_{u_j,m_j} : all j} u (length-three gaps) {C_{m_j,w_j}, B_{w_j}} u (length-two gaps) {B_{m_j}} has 1+d+2(d-s)+s = n+1 forms and is a coordinate basis: relative to A a length-two gap contributes B_{u_j}+B_{m_j}, B_{m_j}, a length-three gap B_{u_j}+B_{m_j}, B_{m_j}+B_{w_j}, B_{w_j}, on disjoint coordinate sets. Selectors: B_{u_j} -> -A (residual L_{u_j}); B_{m_j} -> C_{u_j,m_j} in a length-three gap (residual -L_{u_j}); with v_j = m_j or w_j, C_{v_j,u_{j+1}} -> B_{v_j} (residual L_{u_{j+1}}). Notes: All selector residuals lie in the d-dimensional R = span{L_u}, so d_cb(A_n) <= d, and with S10's lower bound this proves d_cb = d_geo = ceil(n/3).

Let g: R^n -> R be a Lipschitz continuous function and let X_1, ..., X_n belong to D^{1, 2}. Then G = g(X_1, ..., X_n) belongs to D^{1, 2}. Its Brownian Malliavin derivative satisfies D_t^{(1)} G = sum_{i=1}^n partial_i g(X_1, ..., X_n) D_t^{(1)} X_i almost everywhere, and its Poisson Malliavin difference derivative satisfies D_{t, z}^{(2)} G = g(X_1 + D_{t, z}^{(2)} X_1, ..., X_n + D_{t, z}^{(2)} X_n) - g(X_1, ..., X_n).

[Lemma 26 of arXiv:2603.24616, 'Pinning in non-critical half-space geometric last passage percolation'] Fix $T_1$, $\vec{y}$, $q$, and $c$ as in Definition \ref{Def.InterlacingInteractingPairs}, and suppose that $g: \llbracket 0, T_1 \rrbracket \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ is an increasing path with $g(T_1) \leq y_{2k}$. Let $\mathfrak{Q} = \{Q_i\}_{i = 1}^{2k}$ be a line ensemble with law $\mathbb{P}^{T_1, \vec{y}, g}_{\ice; q,c}$, and define the $\llbracket 1, 2k+1 \rrbracket$-indexed line ensemble $\mathfrak{L} = \{L_i\}_{i = 1}^{2k+1}$ on $\llbracket 0, T_1 \rrbracket$ through
$$L_i(s) = Q_i(s) \mbox{ and } L_{2k+1}(s) = g(s) \mbox{ for } i \in \llbracket 1, 2k \rrbracket \mbox{ and } s \in \llbracket 0, T_1 \rrbracket.$$
Then, $\mathfrak{L}$ satisfies the interacting pair Gibbs property of Definition \ref{Def.IPGP} with $N = 2k+1$.
title: Lemma 26 of arXiv:2603.24616

$
\dist\bigl(u,\supp(\mu)\bigr)\ge \varepsilon.
$
Suppose that
\begin{equation}
|m_{Y_n}(z)-m_{\mu}(z)|\ll \frac{1}{n\eta},\quad 
\Im m_{\mu}(z)\ll \frac{1}{n\eta},
\end{equation}
then
$
  \operatorname{spec}(Y_n)\cap[u-\eta,u+\eta]=\varnothing.
$

body:
[Lemma lem:covering of arXiv:2412.04539, 'Counting minimal cutsets and $p_c<1$'] Let $n \geq 1$. Let $P=(p_{i,j})_{i,j \in [n]}$ be a symmetric matrix of non-negative entries such that\footnote{We can think of $P$ as the transition matrix of a Markov chain which is killed at $i$ with probability $1-\sum_{j} p(i,j)$.} $\sum_{j \in [n]} p(i,j) \leq 1$ for all $i \in [n]$. Let $\Gamma$ be the set of all sequences $\gamma=(\gamma_0,\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_k)$ in $[n]$ (for any $k \geq 1$) with $\gamma_0=1$ such that the unique element $i\in [k]$ satisfying both $\gamma_i=1$ and $\{\gamma_0,\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_i\} = [n]$ is $i=k$. For every such sequence $\gamma$, define
\[
          p(\gamma) := \prod_{i=1}^k p\left(\gamma_{i-1},\gamma_i\right).
\]
For each $\varepsilon > 0$, if every non-empty proper subset $I$ of $[n]$ satisfies
\begin{equation} 
          \sum_{i \in I} \sum_{j \in [n] \backslash I} p(i,j) \geq \varepsilon,
\end{equation}
then $\delta :=\frac{\varepsilon^2}{16e^2}$ satisfies
\[
          \sum_{\gamma \in \Gamma} p(\gamma) \geq \delta^n.
\]

For f in L^1_loc(R^d) define the centred maximal function Mf(x) = sup_{r > 0} (1/|B(x,r)|) integral_{B(x,r)} |f(y)| dy. Then M is of WEAK type (1,1): for every f in L^1(R^d) and every lambda > 0, |{x : Mf(x) > lambda}| <= 3^d ||f||_1 / lambda. For 1 < p <= infinity, M is bounded on L^p: ||Mf||_p <= C(d,p) ||f||_p, with C(d,p) blowing up like p/(p-1) as p decreases to 1. M is NOT bounded on L^1: if f is not almost everywhere zero then Mf(x) >= c_d ||f||_1 / |x|^d for |x| large, which is not integrable, so Mf is in L^1 only when f = 0 a.e. The uncentred maximal function (supremum over all balls containing x) is comparable to the centred one, with constants depending only on d. [standard; e.g. Stein and Shakarchi, Real Analysis, Theorem 1.1 and Chapter 3]
f in L^1(R^d) for the weak (1,1) bound; f in L^p for the strong bound
Lebesgue measure on R^d (the doubling property of the measure is what the proof uses)

body:
Let X be a discrete random variable taking values in a finite set of size m, let Y be any random variable jointly distributed with X, and let X_hat = g(Y) be any estimator of X computed from Y alone, so that X -> Y -> X_hat forms a Markov chain. Let P_e = Pr(X_hat != X) be the error probability. Then H(X|Y) <= H_b(P_e) + P_e * log(m-1), where H_b(p) = -p*log p - (1-p)*log(1-p) is the binary entropy function. Consequently, if the conditional entropy H(X|Y) is bounded away from 0, the error probability P_e cannot be made arbitrarily small.

X_hat is a function of Y alone, so X -> Y -> X_hat is a Markov chain
P_e = Pr(X_hat != X)

Since E is a deterministic function of X and X_hat (itself determined by Y), H(E|X,Y) = 0. Conditioning cannot increase entropy, so H(E|Y) <= H(E) = H_b(P_e). For H(X|E,Y): when E=0, X = X_hat is already known, contributing 0; when E=1, X takes one of the remaining m-1 possible values, so H(X|E=1,Y) <= log(m-1); weighting by Pr(E=1)=P_e gives H(X|E,Y) <= P_e*log(m-1). [Lemma 5 of arXiv:2608.19744, 'Conditioned Brownian motion and local equivalence of path ensembles'] For every  $\tau>0 $, define
\[
 g_\tau(x)=\mathbb E^{\prob_x}[\mathrm e^{-\beta A_\tau}]
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \ell_{\tau,x}(f)=(\mathrm e^{-\tau H_\beta}f)(x)
\]
for any $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d)$.
Then  $g_\tau\in L^2(\mathbb R^d) $, and for $x\in\mathbb R^d$ we have
\begin{equation}
 |\ell_{\tau,x}(f)|\le (4\pi\tau)^{-d/4}\|f\|_2.
 
\end{equation}
Moreover, for  $T\ge 2\tau $,
\begin{equation}
 Z_T(\beta,x)=\mathbb E^{\prob_x}[\mathrm e^{-\beta A_T}]
 =\ell_{\tau,x}\!\left(\mathrm e^{-(T-2\tau)H}g_\tau\right).
 
\end{equation}

[Thm 9 of arXiv:2609.02686, 'The Bonnet-Myers theorem on Finsler manifolds with integral weighted Ricci curvature bound'] Let $(M, F, m)$ be an $n$-dimensional $(n \geq 2)$  forward complete connected Finsler metric measure manifold with $\Lambda_{F}<\infty$. Assume that $\mathbf{S}\geq -\vartheta$ for some $\vartheta \geq 0$. Let $R_{0}>\Lambda_{F}\pi$ be a constant. Given $p \in (\frac{n}{2}, n]$, $\alpha\in [\frac{1}{2},1)$. Then there exist nonnegative constant $\varepsilon =\varepsilon(n,p,\Lambda_{F},\vartheta,\alpha,R_{0})$ and positive constants $C_{3}=C_{3}(n,p,\Lambda_{F},\vartheta,\alpha,R_{0})$ and $\beta =\beta(n,p,\vartheta,\alpha,R_{0})$ such that when
$$
\overline{\left\|{\rm{Ric}}_{\infty}^{\Lambda_{F}^{2}}\right\|}_{p, R_{0}, \vartheta}\leq \varepsilon ,
$$
we have
\be
{\rm{diam}}(M) \leq \Lambda_{F}^{-1}\left(\pi+C_{3}\overline{\left\|{\rm{Ric}}_{\infty}^{\Lambda_{F}^{2}}\right\|}_{p, R_{0}, \vartheta}^{\beta}\right) \leq \frac{\Lambda_{F}^{-1}(\Lambda_{F}+1)\pi}{2}, 
\ee
where
\beqn
\varepsilon &:=&\min\Big\{\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)^{2-\frac{1}{p}}, C_{3}^{-\frac{1}{\beta}}\left(\frac{(\Lambda_{F}-1)\pi}{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{\beta}}, \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{2p-1}{p}} D_{1}(n,p,\vartheta,R_{0})^{-\frac{2p-1}{p}}\Big\},\\
C_{3} &:=&\max\Big\{\left(32 e^{\frac{\vartheta R_{0}}{2 p-1}} \Lambda_{F}^{\left(3\vartheta R_{0} b(p,\alpha)+\frac{9n-2p}{2p-1}\right)} D_{2}\right)^{\frac{2p-1}{(2p-1)\vartheta R_{0} b(p,\alpha)+4n-2p}} R_{0},\\
&&\ \ \ \ \ \ \left(2^{8p-3}C_{1}e^{2\vartheta R_{0}}\Lambda_{F}^{3(2p-1)\vartheta R_{0} b(p,\alpha)+8n-1} \right)^{\frac{1}{(2p-1)\vartheta R_{0}b(p,\alpha)+3n-1}} R_{0}^{2},\\
&&\ \ \ \ \ \ \left(2\Lambda_{F}^{-\frac{2p-n}{2p-1}}D_{2}(n,p,\Lambda_{F},\vartheta,\alpha,R_{0})\right)^{-\frac{2p-1}{2p-n}} R_{0}\Big\},\\
\beta &:=& \min\left\{\frac{p}{(2p-1)\vartheta R_{0} b(p,\alpha)+4n-2p}, \ \frac{(n-1)p}{(2p-1)\left[(2p-1)\vartheta R_{0}b(p,\alpha)+3n-1\right]}\right\}.
\eeqn
Furthermore, $M$ is in fact compact.

with $Q' := Q[E\cup F\mid G)]$.

body:
Own work, proof (unaudited); standard-form construction, novelty unestablished.
Let p be a Lebesgue density supported on a finite interval [a,b],
p(x)>=m>0 for almost every x in that interval. Assume E u=0,
E u^2=1. No continuity, differentiability, or upper bound on p is
assumed. Define, almost everywhere on its support,

 tau(x)=[integral_x^b y*p(y)dy]/p(x),
 eta(x)=[integral_x^b (y^2-1)*p(y)dy]/p(x),
 zeta(x)=[integral_x^b (tau(y)-1)*p(y)dy]/p(x).       (1)

Then, for every bounded C1 h with bounded derivative,

 E[u*h(u)]=E[tau(u)*h'(u)],
 E[(u^2-1)*h(u)]=E[eta(u)*h'(u)],
 E[(tau(u)-1)*h(u)]=E[zeta(u)*h'(u)],               (2)

and the explicit bounds are

 0<=tau<=1/m, E tau=1,
 |eta|<=2/m, |zeta|<=2/m.                           (3)


Matrix corollary: let U in R^(N by M), V in R^(P by M) be independent iid factor arrays with fixed real laws having the preceding compact-density, centering and variance hypotheses, each with its own positive density floor. Let Z be independent standard Gaussian noise, X=UV^T/sqrt(N), Y=sqrt(s)X+Z, and I be measured in nats. If P/N->alpha>0 and M/N->beta>0 are finite, every limiting upper or lower per-entry information envelope satisfies I(X;Y)/(NP)=beta*s/2-beta^2*s^2/4+beta^3*s^3/6-(beta^4+alpha*beta^2)*s^4/8+O(s^5) as s decreases to zero. The remainder constant depends on the fixed priors and aspect bounds, not the matrix dimensions. No assertion of information-limit uniqueness or discrete-prior coverage is made.
Real Lebesgue density p supported on a finite interval; p>=m>0 almost everywhere
Mean zero and variance one; no continuity, derivative or upper density bound assumed
For the matrix corollary: fixed independent iid real factor laws, Gaussian observation noise, N,P>=2,M>=1, positive finite aspect limits

Let p be a Lebesgue density supported on a finite interval [a,b],

 E[(u^2-1)*h(u)]=E[eta(u)*h'(u)],
 E[(tau(u)-1)*h(u)]=E[zeta(u)*h'(u)],               (2)

and the explicit bounds are

 |eta|<=2/m, |zeta|<=2/m.                           (3)

Consequently any two fixed independent priors of this form satisfy
every scalar hypothesis of042v2, with T_U=1/m_U,T_V=1/m_V,
e_U<=4/m_U^2,e_V<=4/m_V^2,z_V<=4/m_V^2 and finite fourth moments.

information expansion on a nonparametric class of two non-Gaussian
factor priors. This is a whole new descriptive range beyond the beta
examples; no finite list of densities is being extrapolated.

## Proof of every kernel hypothesis

Write F_g(x)=integral_x^b g(y)*p(y)dy for centered integrable g.
It is absolutely continuous, F_g'=-g*p almost everywhere, and
F_g(a)=F_g(b)=0. Ordinary integration by parts for an absolutely
continuous function and C1 h gives

 integral_a^b g(x)*p(x)*h(x)dx
 =integral_a^b F_g(x)*h'(x)dx.

All integrals here are absolutely convergent: the interval is compact,
g is integrable, and h,h' are bounded. Dividing by p defines a
measurable kernel almost everywhere; since p>=m>0 it satisfies
|F_g/p|<=E|g|/m. The zero endpoint conditions are essential.

Apply this first with g(x)=x, centered by assumption. The first
identity in (2) follows. For x>=0 the tail integral defining tau is
nonnegative. For x<=0 use mean zero to write it as
-integral_a^x y*p(y)dy, also nonnegative. Cauchy-Schwarz gives
E|u|<=1, proving 0<=tau<=1/m. Choose a bounded C1 function equal
to x on the compact support. The first identity gives E tau=E u^2=1.

E|u^2-1|<=E u^2+1=2. This proves the eta identity and its bound.

to this g proves the zeta identity and its bound. Square integrability
of eta,zeta follows from their pointwise bounds. Compact support
pays every factor moment used by042. This proves the claimed
nonparametric matrix-factor corollary without new posterior arguments.

For an exact non-Pearson example take p=1/3 on[-1,1] and p=1/6
on[-2,-1] union[1,2]. Its total mass is1, mean0, variance1,
fourth moment11/5, and density floor m=1/6.
For x>=0 its kernels in (1) are

 0<=x<=1:
 tau=5/4-x^2/2, eta=x-x^3/3, zeta=-x/4+x^3/6;
 1<=x<=2:
 tau=2-x^2/2, eta=2/3+x-x^3/3, zeta=2/3-x+x^3/6.

Extend tau evenly and eta,zeta oddly. The kernels themselves jump
at |x|=1, but the fluxes p*tau,p*eta,p*zeta are continuous there.
Their derivatives are exactly -x*p, -(x^2-1)*p, -(tau-1)*p
on every interval, and all boundary fluxes vanish at -2 and2.
These facts certify (2) for every smooth test, not merely for the
finite monomial checks. scripts/check_density_floor_flux.py verifies
the local rational polynomial identities, joins and endpoint values.

does not provide constants uniform when m goes to zero. In particular

does not prove the discrete-prior theorem: the kernel constants in

body:
[Proposition 106 of arXiv:2609.03875, 'Measure theory without infinities'] Let $\mf A$ be an HTM, $\sm{\mf A}{k\in K}{f(k)}$, and $x = \sum_{k\in K}f(k)$.
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item[(i)] Let $\sm{\mf A}{k\in K}{g(k)}$. Then $\sum_{k\in K}(f(k) + g(k)) = x + \sum_{k\in K}g(k)$.
  \item[(ii)] Let $\mf B$ be an HTM and $\varphi\colon\mf A\to\mf B$ be a continuous homomorphism. Then $\sum_{k\in K} \varphi(f(k)) = \varphi(x)$.   
  \item [(iii)] Suppose $\mf A$ is an HTG. Then $\sum_{k\in K}(-f(k)) = -x$.
  \item [(iv)] Suppose $\mf A$ is an HTG and $\sm{\mf A}{k\in K}{g(k)}$. Then $\sum_{k\in K}(f(k) - g(k)) = x - \sum_{k\in K}g(k)$.
  \end{enumerate}

\eqref{Ft_P}.  Then $(F,F_t)$ is exchangeable and

\noi
\begin{align}
 \frac1t\E[F_t-F | \eta]  &\xrightarrow{t\downarrow 0} -qF  \quad\text{in $L^4(\PP)$},  
 \notag \\
 \frac1t\E[(F_t-F)^2 | \eta]  &\xrightarrow{t\downarrow 0}    2\Gamma(F,F)  \quad \text{in $L^2(\PP)$},  
 \notag \\
 \frac1t\E[(F_t-F)^4] &\xrightarrow{t\downarrow 0}   -4q\,m_4(F)+12\E[F^2\Gamma(F,F)]  \geq0.  
 \notag
\end{align}

Moreover, the first regression is exact:
$
 \E[F_t-F | \eta]
 =-(1-e^{-qt})F.
$
Moreover, if $F, G$ live in the sum of finitely many chaoses, 
with $F_t, G_t$ defined as above, we have 
\noi
\begin{align}
 \frac1t\E[(F_t-F)(G_t-G) | \eta]
\xrightarrow{t\downarrow 0}    2\Gamma(F,G)  \quad\text{in $L^2(\PP)$}.

body:
Consider bond first-passage percolation on Z^2 with iid edge weights supported in [a,b], where 0<a<=b<infinity, and fixed distinct vertices u,v. Let X=T(u,v) and choose a measurable canonical topmost minimizing geodesic (atoms and ties are allowed). Partition the edges into deterministic blocks Lambda. For each block independently redraw its weights from the original law, independently of the environment, and write X^Lambda for the passage time with only that block replaced. Let U_Lambda be the event that the original chosen geodesic uses an edge in Lambda. Give the blocks iid Uniform[0,1] labels tau_Lambda independent of all original and redrawn weights. F_t reveals each labeled block and its original/redrawn weight pair when tau_Lambda<=t; equivalently, for the probabilities of U_Lambda one may reveal only original weights. Define A2=sum_Lambda E[1_U_Lambda (X^Lambda-X)^2], A2plus=sum_Lambda E[((X^Lambda-X)^+)^2], A4=sum_Lambda E[1_U_Lambda ((X^Lambda-X)^+)^4], and Pbar(kappa)=sum_Lambda E[P(U_Lambda|F_(1-kappa))^2]. For every 0<kappa<1, Var(X)<=kappa A2plus+sqrt(A4 Pbar(kappa))<=kappa A2+sqrt(A4 Pbar(kappa)). Positivity and boundedness localize all relevant paths to a deterministic finite edge set, so only finitely many blocks contribute. The proof needs independent blocks, off-geodesic monotonicity and conditional expectations; isotropy and FKG are not assumptions.

Fixed distinct endpoints in Z^2 and measurable canonical topmost geodesic selection
Deterministic edge partition; independent same-law block redraws and independent uniform reveal labels

Let phi be real-valued and smooth on (a,b) with |phi^{(k)}| >= 1 there, where k >= 2, or k = 1 and phi' monotone. Then |int_a^b e^{i lambda phi(x)} dx| <= c_k lambda^{-1/k} for lambda > 0, with c_k depending only on k (for k = 1 the sharp constant is 2). Since the hypotheses hold on every subinterval, one integration by parts gives, for psi of bounded variation on [a,b]: |int_a^b e^{i lambda phi} psi dx| <= c_k lambda^{-1/k} (|psi(b)| + int_a^b |psi'(x)| dx), the integral read as the total variation. For an integrable psi of bounded variation on R and |phi''| >= 1 on R: |int e^{i lambda phi} psi| <= c_2 lambda^{-1/2} TV(psi).

Assumes: real phase with a lower bound on one derivative; amplitude of bounded variation

body: Taylor's theorem: Let k >= 1 and let f be k times differentiable at the point a, and set P_k(x) = sum_{j=0}^{k} f^{(j)}(a) (x - a)^j / j!, the k-th order Taylor polynomial of f at a (the unique polynomial of degree at most k agreeing with f in value and in the first k derivatives at a). Peano form: f(x) - P_k(x) = o(|x - a|^k) as x -> a. Lagrange form: if in addition f is k+1 times differentiable on an open interval I containing a, then for each x in I there is a point xi strictly between a and x with f(x) - P_k(x) = f^{(k+1)}(xi) (x - a)^{k+1} / (k+1)!. The case k = 1 is the linear approximation and k = 2 the quadratic approximation; for a smooth f, P_k is the truncation at order k of the Taylor series of f at a.

body: An explicit s-stage Runge-Kutta method for the initial value problem y' = f(t,y), y(t_0) = y_0, advances y_n to y_{n+1} = y_n + h * sum_{i=1}^{s} b_i * k_i, where k_i = f( t_n + c_i*h, y_n + h*sum_{j<i} a_{ij}*k_j ), and the coefficients a_{ij}, b_i, c_i (the Butcher tableau) typically satisfy c_i = sum_{j<i} a_{ij}. The method has order p if, for sufficiently smooth f, its Taylor expansion in h agrees with the Taylor expansion of the exact solution through the h^p term (equivalently, the local truncation error is O(h^{p+1})). Matching these Taylor expansions imposes polynomial equations on (a_{ij}, b_i, c_i) called order conditions: for example, order 1 requires sum_i b_i = 1, and order 2 additionally requires sum_i b_i*c_i = 1/2. In Butcher's rooted-tree theory there is one order condition per rooted tree up to order p, and the number of independent conditions grows faster than the number of stages s, which is why, for instance, no explicit Runge-Kutta method can reach an order equal to its stage count once the order exceeds 4.
title: Runge-Kutta Order Conditions

[Lemma lem:poisson-difference-cc of arXiv:2608.06159, 'Majority Dynamics on Resampled Sparse Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi Graphs:\\[0.5ex] Gaussian Winner '] Let \(P_X\sim\Pois(\lambda_X)\) and
\(P_Y\sim\Pois(\lambda_Y)\) be independent, and set
\[
S\coloneqq P_X-P_Y,
\qquad
\lambda\coloneqq\lambda_X+\lambda_Y,
\qquad
m\coloneqq\lambda_X-\lambda_Y.
\]
Suppose that for some fixed \(M>0\), \(|m|\le M\sqrt{\lambda}\) as \(\lambda\to\infty\). Then uniformly over integers \(k,\ell\),
\begin{subequations}
\begin{align}
\P(S\le\ell)
&=
\Phi\left(
\frac{\ell+1/2-m}{\sqrt{\lambda}}
\right)
+O_M(\lambda^{-1}),
\\
\P(S=k)
&=
\frac1{\sqrt{\lambda}}
\varphi\left(
\frac{k-m}{\sqrt{\lambda}}
\right)
+O_M(\lambda^{-3/2}).

\end{align}
\end{subequations}

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author_checked; reduction plus asserted conditional, not a solution] Svante Janson's Problem 18.39 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510, asks whether Y_(1)/n -> 0 in probability is possible in the condensation regime 0 < nu < lambda. Janson conjectures that it is not possible for the full sequence and, more strongly, that there are always epsilon > 0 and a subsequence along which Y_(1) >= epsilon n w.h.p. (Example 18.36 gives Y_(1)/n -> 0 in probability along a subsequence.) Setting: let w_k >= 0 with w_0 > 0, let Phi(z) = sum_k w_k z^k have radius rho in (0,infinity) with Phi(rho) < infinity, and put pi_k = w_k rho^k/Phi(rho), a law with generating-function radius one and finite mean nu > 0. Let m_n/n -> lambda > nu. (Y_1,...,Y_n) is n i.i.d. pi variables conditioned on sum m_n, Y_(1) = max_i Y_i, and M = (lambda-nu)n. Heuristic rate: carrying M in r = M/a boxes of size a has class weight binomial(n,r) pi_a^r up to the bulk's fluctuation, giving log P = M Lambda(a) + o(M) with Lambda(a) = [log pi_a + log(a/(lambda-nu)) + 1]/a. For pi_k ~ c k^(-beta) and for pi_a = exp(-a^gamma), 0<gamma<1, Lambda increases on large a, so the optimum is a = M (one box), matching the known condensation picture. Since limsup_a Lambda(a) = 0 and Lambda < 0 for large a, Lambda has infinitely many upper records a_1 < a_2 < ... (Lambda(a_j) > Lambda(a) for all a < a_j) exactly when Lambda(a) < 0 for every a; if Lambda(a) >= 0 for some a the maximum is attained and there are finitely many records (Lambda(1) = log pi_1 + log(1/(lambda-nu)) + 1 is positive once lambda - nu < e pi_1). The record asserts, as author-checked and with no proof given beyond reference to an analogous step for Problem 18.40 in a companion memo, the following Proposition: if for some epsilon > 0 and every C, along infinitely many records, Lambda(a_j) - max_{a <= epsilon a_j} Lambda(a) > C a_j^(-1/2), then along n_j = a_j/(lambda-nu), P(Y_(1) >= ((lambda-nu)/2) n_j) -> 1, so the conjecture holds. Caveat: the only derivation offered is the heuristic rate with an o(M) error, which is coarser than the order sqrt(a_j) resolution this hypothesis requires, so the record does not establish the Proposition. The record poses the open Question whether, for every law pi on Z_{>=0} with radius one and finite mean, [log pi_a + log a]/a has infinitely many records with gap exceeding a_j^(-1/2) below max_{a <= epsilon a_j} for some fixed epsilon > 0. This is not a proved equivalence with the conjecture. A negative answer would only give a candidate counterexample, still requiring proof that the allocation spreads. The Question's normalisation and fixed threshold also differ from the Proposition's hypothesis. The problem remains open. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
The allocations are defined along sizes with positive conditioning probability.
0 < nu < lambda and the boundary-tilted law pi has generating-function radius one.

[Lemma 1 of arXiv:2604.01257, '2604.01257'] Let conditions $[{f_{\nu}}]$, $[{{\mathcal{L}}_{\nu}}]$ and $[{{\omega}_{\nu}}]$ be satisfied. Then
\begin{equation}                              
    \frac{1}{\Lambda(R(t;s))}-\frac{1}{\Lambda(1-s)}=\nu{t}+
    \int_{\tau(0;s)}^{\tau(t)}{\frac{\varepsilon(x)}{{x^{1-\nu}}\mathcal{L}(x)}dx}+
    \mathcal{O}\left(1/t\right)
\end{equation}
    as $t\to\infty$, where $\tau(t)={{(\nu{t})}^{1/\nu}}\big/{\mathcal{N}(t)}$ and $\mathcal{N}(t)$ is defined
    in {(\ref{IIB3.2})}. By incorporating the supplementary constraint {(\ref{IIB3.3})}, we directly derive the
    following fundamental identity:
\begin{equation}                              
    \frac{1}{\Lambda(R(t;s))}-\frac{1}{\Lambda(1-s)}=\nu{t}-\frac{1}{\nu}\ln\left[\Lambda(1-s)\nu{t}\right]+\rho(t;s),
\end{equation}
    where $\rho(t;s)=o(\ln{t})$ as $t\to\infty$ uniformly in $s\in[0,1)$.
