[Thm exponent of arXiv:2505.24821, 'Asymptotics for the harmonic descent chain and applications to critical beta-splitting tre'] We have that 
    \begin{enumerate}[ref=(\roman*)]
        \item  $x_{n+1} < x_n$ for all $n \geq k$. In particular, for any fixed $k$, the limit $x \coloneqq \lim_{n \to\infty} x_n$ exists.
        \item  For all $n \geq k$, $x_n - x = O(\frac{kx_k}{n-k})$.
        \item 
        For fixed $c \geq 2$ and $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$, and for $k$ sufficiently large, $x_{k+m} \leq \frac{c^\ell x_k}{mh_k}$ for each $m \leq k^{d_\ell}$ where $d_\ell = 1-\frac{1}{c+1} - 2^{-\ell}$.

        \item  For fixed $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $x_n - x = n^{-\gamma_*+o(1)}$, where $\gamma_*$ is the solution to 
        \begin{equation}
        \sum_{i=1}^\infty \left(\frac{1}{i} - \frac{i}{(i+1)(i+1-\gamma)}\right) = 0 
        \end{equation}
        with $1.5 < \gamma_* < 2$.
        \item  For all $\epsilon > 0$ and $k = o(n/\log^3 n)$, there exist $0 < c(k, \epsilon) < C(k, \epsilon) = O_\epsilon(x_k k^{0.01})$ such that $c(k, \epsilon)(n / k)^{-\gamma_*-\epsilon} \leq x_n - x \leq C(k, \epsilon)(n / k)^{-\gamma_*+\epsilon}$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm exponent of arXiv:2505.24821

[Dfn 3 of arXiv:2604.01748, 'Largest-loop-first loop-erased random walk on $\mathbb{Z}^{4}$'] Let $m \ge 0$ be an integer. A sequence of points 
 $$\lambda = [\lambda(0), \lambda(1), \cdots, \lambda(m)] \subset \mathbb{Z}^{d}$$ is called a path of length $m$ if $|\lambda(k) - \lambda(k+1)| = 1$ for all $0 \le k \le m-1$. We write $\text{len}\, (\lambda) = m$ for the length of $\lambda$. For $0 \le a \le b \le m$, we set $\lambda[a,b] = [\lambda(a), \lambda(a+1), \cdots, \lambda(b)]$ to denote the portion of the path $\lambda$ between times $a$ and $b$. Furthermore, $\lambda$ is said to be a simple path if $\lambda(j) \neq \lambda(k)$ for all $0 \le j < k \le m$.

     Let $\lambda_{1} = [\lambda_{1}(0), \cdots, \lambda_{1}(m_{1})]$ and $\lambda_{2} = [\lambda_{2}(0), \cdots, \lambda_{2}(m_{2})]$ be two paths in $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ of lengths $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$, respectively, and suppose that $\lambda_{1}(m_{1}) = \lambda_{2}(0)$. We define the concatenation of $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$, denoted by $\lambda_{1} \oplus \lambda_{2}$, by
$$\lambda_{1} \oplus \lambda_{2} = [ \lambda_{1} (0), \cdots , \lambda_{1} (m_{1}) , \lambda_{2} (1), \cdots , \lambda_{2} (m_{2})]. $$
    Then $\lambda_{1} \oplus \lambda_{2}$ is a path of length $m_{1}+m_{2}$.
title: Definition 3 of arXiv:2604.01748

[Corollary cor:jump of arXiv:2412.05030, 'Characterization of Subordinate Symmetric Markov Processes'] Let $(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$ be a regular non-killing Dirichlet form on $L^2(M;\mu)$ that 
  satisfies the jump type heat kernel estimates HK$(\phi_j)$.
  $X$ denotes the $\mu$-symmetric Hunt process corresponding to $(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$
  and set $\phi := \phi_j$.
  Given a scale function $\psi$, the following are equivalent. 
  \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
    \item There exists a pure jump regular Dirichlet form $(\mathcal{E}^j,\mathcal{F}^j)$  whose jump kernel satisfies ((eq:jumpKernelEstimate of the paper)).
    \item There exists a subordinator $S_t$\ such that the jump kernel of the subordinate process $X_{S_t}$ satisfies  ((eq:jumpKernelEstimate of the paper)).
    \item The scale function $\psi$ satisfies
    \begin{equation}
      \int_0^1 \frac{\phi(s)}{s\psi(s)}ds < \infty.

body: In computational complexity theory, an interactive proof system is an abstract machine that models computation as the exchange of messages between two parties: a prover and a verifier. The parties interact by exchanging messages in order to ascertain whether a given string belongs to a language or not. The prover is assumed to possess unlimited computational resources but cannot be trusted, while the verifier has bounded computation power but is assumed to be always honest. Messages are sent between the verifier and prover until the verifier has an answer to the problem and has "convinced" itself that it is correct.

For every k distinct sites x_1,...,x_k and every nonnegative measurable function F of the entire active-count field, E[F(A_t) product_i H_t(x_i)] <= [p/(1-p)]^k E[F(A_t)]. In particular E[H_t(x) A_t(z)] <= [p/(1-p)]h_t, where h_t=E H_t(0)=E A_t(0). The estimate holds at each finite t; it does not assert conditional stochastic domination. Novelty: UNCHECKED. Extension of the KNOWN unvisited-hole deletion argument in source Lemma 8.4 and own C5. No earlier explicit mixed-moment statement found in the limited source searches. This result is valid in all dimensions, but does not give the time-dependent thinning needed by C7.

Use the sparse iid critical law P(η=1)=P(η=−1)=p, P(η=0)=1−2p with 0<p<1/2, stationary capacity-one holes and synchronous nearest-neighbor dynamics on Z^d. Let q=p/(1−p). For a finite set K of k distinct sites and any nonnegative measurable function F of the entire active-particle count field at a fixed finite time t,

E[F(A_t) product_{x∈K}H_t(x)]≤q^k E[F(A_t)].

The assertion allows expectations equal to infinity, in which case the inequality is interpreted in the extended nonnegative sense. In particular, with h_t=EH_t(0)=EA_t(0),

E[H_t(x)A_t(z)]≤q h_t,
E[H_t(x)1_{A_t(z)>0}]≤q P(A_t(z)>0)≤q h_t.

No independence or negative association of surviving holes and active particles is claimed.

## Proof

On E_K={H_t(x)=1 for all x∈K}, every specified initial value equals −1 and no particle has arrived at any specified site by time t. For each subset J⊂K replace the initial −1 values at J by zero, leaving every other sign and every walk/stack/tie variable fixed. The modified dynamics agree with the original particle dynamics through t: before a first putative arrival at a modified site, nothing affecting any particle has changed, so such an arrival would also occur in the original dynamics, a contradiction. Hence the active-count field A_t is identical in every image, and F(A_t) is unchanged.

These 2^k images are disjoint, because their initial coordinate assignments on K distinguish exactly which values are zero versus −1. Let c=(1−2p)/p. For a bounded nonnegative F, the image weighted expectation is exactly c^{|J|}E[F(A_t)1_{E_K}], by conditioning on all variables except the k specified initial coordinates. The transformations are injective with the prescribed original values restored. Their union is a subset of the full probability space. Since F is unchanged on each image,

E[F(A_t)]≥sum_{J⊂K}c^{|J|}E[F(A_t)1_{E_K}]
=(1+c)^k E[F(A_t)1_{E_K}]
=q^{−k}E[F(A_t)1_{E_K}].

This proves the inequality for bounded F. Apply it to min(F,m) and use monotone convergence as m→∞ to cover every nonnegative measurable F. The change-of-coordinate argument is finite, even if F depends on infinitely many active counts; at fixed t all specified hole-survival events have finite propagation cones, and the deletion leaves the entire particle evolution unchanged through t.

For F(A)=A(z) or 1_{A(z)>0}, translation invariance and critical signed-density conservation give the displayed specializations. The same moment bound holds at x=z, where the left side is zero. Active counts have finite expectation because the initial particles that can reach a site by t lie in a finite ball and there is at most one initial particle per site.

## Application and limitation

C7's mixed sum has the upper bound q h_t|B_{2R}|. This is useful at R=O(p^−1/d). At R=O(h_t^−1/d), dividing by h_t gives an upper bound of order q/h_t, which grows without limit for fixed p as h_t→0. \lambda_{\sigma,m}=-a_0+\sum_{k=1}^{N}h_{2k}c^{2k}\sigma^{(2k-1)m-2k}+O\!\left(\sigma^{(2N+1)m-2N-2}\right),
\]
where $\cH(v)=\sum_{k\ge1}h_{2k}v^{2k}$ near $0$ and $h_2=(2D_2)^{-1}$, $h_4=-D_4/(24D_2^4)$, $h_6=(10D_4^2-D_2D_6)/(720D_2^7)$. In particular,
\[
\lambda_{\sigma,2}=\frac{c^2}{2D_2}-a_0-\frac{D_4c^4}{24D_2^4}\sigma^2+\frac{(10D_4^2-D_2D_6)c^6}{720D_2^7}\sigma^4+O(\sigma^6).
\]
If $0\le m<1$ and $J(R_+-t)=Kt^\nu(1+o(1))$ as $t\downarrow0$, with $p=\nu+1$ and $A=K\Gamma(p)$, then
\[
\lambda_{\sigma,m}=\frac{c}{R_+\sigma}\left[(1-m)|\log\sigma|+p\log|\log\sigma|+C_{m,c,J}+o(1)\right]-a_0,
\]
where $C_{m,c,J}=\log c+p\log(1-m)-p\log R_+-\log(R_+A)-1$.

body: Three hypotheses of the De Giorgi-Nash-Moser theorem are load-bearing, and each fails concretely. (1) Scalar. The theorem is false for systems: De Giorgi (1968) exhibited, for n >= 3, a linear elliptic system with bounded measurable coefficients satisfying the Legendre-Hadamard and even the strong ellipticity condition whose weak solution is u(x) = x |x|^{-gamma} for an explicit gamma with 1 < gamma < n/2 - a solution in H^1 that is unbounded, hence not even locally bounded, let alone Hoelder. So a referee must check that an application of De Giorgi-Nash-Moser or of Moser's Harnack inequality is to a single equation, not to a system, and that the maximum-principle-based truncations used in the proof are available. (2) The energy class u in H^1_loc. A distributional solution whose gradient is only in L^p for some p < 2 need not be bounded. In the plane take A(x) = I + (mu - 1) x x^T/|x|^2 with mu > 1 (uniformly elliptic, bounded, measurable, discontinuous only at the origin). In polar coordinates div(A grad u) = (1/r) d/dr ( r mu u_r ) + (1/r^2) u_{theta theta}, so u = r^s cos(theta) solves the equation away from 0 exactly when mu s^2 = 1. The choice s = -1/sqrt(mu) in (-1,0) gives u = r^{-1/sqrt(mu)} cos(theta), which is unbounded at 0, lies in W^{1,p}_loc precisely for p < 2/(1 + 1/sqrt(mu)) < 2, and is a distributional solution across the origin (the flux through small circles tends to 0 because s > -1). (3) The Hoelder exponent depends on the ellipticity ratio and cannot be improved to Lipschitz. The same coefficients with s = +alpha, i.e. mu = 1/alpha^2, give the H^1 solution u = r^alpha cos(theta) of a uniformly elliptic equation with ellipticity ratio alpha^{-2}: it is exactly C^{0,alpha} at the origin and no better. Hence the exponent alpha(n, Lambda/lambda) in the theorem must degenerate to 0 as Lambda/lambda tends to infinity, and 'bounded measurable coefficients give Lipschitz solutions' is false. Gradient bounds require continuity (or Dini/Hoelder continuity) of the coefficients.
title: Pitfall: De Giorgi-Nash-Moser Needs a Scalar Equation and an Energy-Class Solution

body: [Definition of arXiv:2605.02226, 'Finitely Dependent Processes on Subshifts'] A subshift of finite type $ X \subset A^{G}$ satisfies the $k$-extension property if there exists a finite collection $ \mathcal{F} $ of forbidden patterns for which $ X = X(\mathcal{F})$ and such that any locally allowed pattern $ w$ supported on a set $S \subset G$ which extends to a locally allowed pattern on $ S \cdot \mathbf{B}(k) $, is globally allowed.  $ X$ has finite extension property (FEP) if it satisfies $ k$-extension property for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For simple random walk on the incipient infinite cluster of critical percolation, or more generally on critical random media with anomalous volume growth, Kesten's argument establishes subdiffusive behavior, that the walk's typical displacement after n steps is of order n^{1/d_w} with walk dimension d_w > 2 rather than the diffusive n^{1/2}, by combining a volume-growth estimate showing balls of radius r typically contain of order r^{d_f} points, with d_f the fractal (volume) dimension of the cluster, and an effective-resistance estimate R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) of order r^{zeta}, reflecting the long dangling ends and low-conductance bottlenecks characteristic of the critical cluster. The expected exit time from a ball of radius r is then of order r^{d_f+zeta} (volume times resistance: the Einstein relation d_w = d_f + zeta), so the displacement is of order n^{1/(d_f+zeta)}, subdiffusive when d_f + zeta > 2; the Nash/heat-kernel machinery or a direct expected-exit-time computation turns the two estimates into bounds. In balls of the intrinsic (graph) metric with unit conductances R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) <= r, so zeta <= 1 there: for the high-dimensional incipient infinite cluster the intrinsic volume grows as r^2 and the resistance as r, giving d_w = 3. The argument does not give the exact value of the subdiffusivity exponent in most dimensions, only bounds, with the precise exponent known rigorously only in specific settings such as sufficiently high dimension or tree-like/hierarchical models, and it is specific to critical (not subcritical or supercritical) percolation geometry, where the fractal, tree-like structure with many bottlenecks is essential to the argument. Typical failure: Assuming the subdiffusivity exponent established for one setting, such as high-dimensional or tree-based incipient infinite clusters where exact computation is possible, transfers to two-dimensional critical percolation, where the exact random-walk dimension remains a major open problem; volume-growth and resistance-growth exponents are model- and dimension-specific quantities that must be independently estimated rather than imported across models with superficially similar critical geometry. Canonical reference: Kesten, 1986, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare, Probabilites et Statistiques; Barlow, Jarai, Kumagai and Slade, 2008, Communications in Mathematical Physics.
the walk is on the incipient infinite cluster or a similarly statistically self-similar critical random graph
a known or boundable volume-growth exponent d_f for balls in the cluster
a known or boundable effective-resistance-growth exponent reflecting the bottleneck/dangling-end structure
typically also requires the cluster's law to have appropriate scale-invariance, or at least comparable behavior across scales

[Cor finite-order of arXiv:2608.30847, 'An Almgren-type formula for planar $p$-harmonic functions'] Let $u$ be a nonconstant planar $p$-harmonic function and $x_0\in\Omega$.  If $u(x_0)=0$, then $u$ has finite vanishing order at $x_0$ in the following sense: either $D u(x_0)\ne0$ and the order is $1$, or $x_0$ is critical and
$$
  |u(x_0+r\theta)|\le Cr^{\lambda_N(p)},
  \qquad
  \sup_{\theta\in\mathbb S^1}|u(x_0+r\theta)|\ge c r^{\lambda_N(p)}
$$
for all sufficiently small $r>0$, with constants $c,C>0$.

[Proposition 2 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] For any subclasses \(\mathcal{T}, \mathcal{T}_n\) and \(n\in \mathbb{N}\), the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(\left(\bigcap_n \mathcal{T}_n \right)_{loc} = \bigcap_n (\mathcal{T}_n)_{loc}\) and \(\left(\bigcup_n \mathcal{T}_n \right)_{loc} \supset \bigcup_n (\mathcal{T}_n)_{loc}\).
\item \(\left(\bigcap_n \mathcal{T}_n \right)_{col} \subset \bigcap_n (\mathcal{T}_n)_{col}\) and \(\left(\bigcup_n \mathcal{T}_n \right)_{col} = \bigcup_n (\mathcal{T}_n)_{col}\).
\item If \(\mathcal{T}_1 \subset \mathcal{T}_2\), then \((\mathcal{T}_{1})_{loc} \subset (\mathcal{T}_{2})_{loc}\) and  \((\mathcal{T}_{1})_{col} \subset (\mathcal{T}_{2})_{col}\).
\item For any \(\{F_k\}_k \in \nest\), \(\mathcal{T}_{loc} \subset \mathcal{T}(\{F_k\}) \subset \mathcal{T}_{col}\).
\item \((\mathcal{T}_{loc})_{loc} = \mathcal{T}_{loc}\) and \((\mathcal{T}_{col})_{col} = \mathcal{T}_{col}\).
\item \(\mathcal{T}_{loc} \subset (\mathcal{T}_{loc})_{col} \subset \mathcal{T}_{col}\) and \(\mathcal{T}_{loc} \subset (\mathcal{T}_{col})_{loc} \subset \mathcal{T}_{col}\).
\end{enumerate}

[Proposition propmain2e of arXiv:2605.01878, '\Large Random trade timing and power-law tails in realized prices'] Let $(X_t, t\geq 0)$ be a Markov modulated L\'{e}vy process, described in Section (smain1a of the paper) and let the trade time $T$, described in Sections (smain1b of the paper)-(smain1c of the paper), satisfy (equation itm of the paper) and (equation itmadd of the paper). 
Suppose that Assumption (asshol of the paper) holds and there exists $\alpha>0$ such that $r_D(A(-\alpha)) = \lambda_{\min}$.
Then such $\alpha$ is unique, and the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=(\roman*)]
\item There exist constants \(0<C_1\le C_2<\infty\) such that
\begin{align} 
\widetilde M C_1 \le (\log y)^{-\beta} y^\alpha \mathbb{P}(P_T>y) \le \widetilde M C_2 
\end{align}
for sufficiently large $y$, where $\beta$ is determined by the following case distinction:
 \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*), ref=(\alph*)]
    \item  If $\lambda_{\min} = \lambda_1 < \mu_1$, then $\beta = 0$.
    \item  If $\lambda_{\min}  = \mu_1 < \lambda_1$, then $\beta = r_1-1$.
    \item  If $\lambda_{\min}  = \lambda_1 =  \mu_1$, then $\beta = r_1$.
\end{enumerate}
    \item    Suppose, in addition, the nonlattice condition in Proposition (propmain of the paper)\,(propmainb of the paper) holds, and $\lambda_{\min}=\lambda_1 < \mu_1$ or $\lambda_{\min}  = \mu_1 < \lambda_1$ with $r_1 = 1$. Then,  as $y\to\infty$,
\[
\lim_{y \to \infty}  y^\alpha \mathbb{P}(P_T>y) = \widetilde M/\alpha.
\]
\end{enumerate}
In (propmain2ea of the paper) and (propmain2eb of the paper), $\widetilde M \coloneqq \lim_{s \to -\alpha}(s+\alpha)^{\beta+1} M_T(s)$, which is positive.

body: Fix d >= 2 and let E(Z^d) be the set of nearest-neighbour edges of the integer lattice. Assign to each edge e an independent random weight tau_e >= 0 with common distribution F; the collection (tau_e) is the environment. The PASSAGE TIME of a finite lattice path gamma is T(gamma) = sum over the edges of gamma of tau_e, and the passage time between vertices x and y is T(x,y) = inf over finite paths from x to y of T(gamma). T is a random pseudometric on Z^d: it is symmetric, satisfies the triangle inequality, and vanishes on the diagonal, but T(x,y) = 0 is possible for x != y when F has an atom at 0. A GEODESIC from x to y is a path attaining the infimum. Geodesics need not exist for a general F, and when F(0) is at least the critical probability p_c(d) the infimum can be 0 and attained by infinitely many paths; when F(0) < p_c a geodesic exists almost surely for every pair, and it is almost surely unique for every pair when F is continuous, since ties then have probability 0. The standing notation in the literature is T(0, x) for the point-to-point time, mu or g for the time constant, chi for the fluctuation exponent and xi for the wandering exponent; the store already records that those exponents are DEFINED differently by different theorems and are not interchangeable. [standard; e.g. Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Chapters 1 and 4]

[Lemma lem:closure of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] For $2\le|S|\le3$ let
$K_S=\operatorname{conv}\{B_{ij}:i,j\in S,\ t_i\ne t_j\}$ (discard $S$ with no valid
pair). Then
\[
  \inf_{\substack{\operatorname{supp} q\subseteq S\\ |\mu(q)|<1}}C(q)
  \;=\;\operatorname{dist}^2\bigl(0,K_S\bigr),
  \qquad
  \inf_{\substack{|\operatorname{supp} q|\le3\\ |\mu(q)|<1}}C(q)
  \;=\;\min_{S}\operatorname{dist}^2(0,K_S) .
\]
For three pairwise distinct directions the interior of the edge-weight
triangle is attained by positive weights (via
$q_1{:}q_2{:}q_3=\frac{d_{23}}{\alpha_{23}}{:}\frac{d_{13}}{\alpha_{13}}

[Lemma 4 (Euclidean score reduction) of arXiv:2609.02362, '\textbf{Farthest-cell triplet entropy: high-dimensional shell limits and hyperbolic curvat'] For the independent query $(R_{0,d},U_{0,d})$ and prototypes
$(R_{i,d},U_{i,d})$, $i=1,2,3$, the farthest-distance ordering is the
ordering of
\begin{equation}
  S_{i,d}
  =
  \lambda_d\xi_{i,d}-Z_{i,d}+r_{i,d},
  \qquad
  Z_{i,d}
  =
  \sqrt d\,\langle U_{0,d},U_{i,d}\rangle.
  
\end{equation}
Conditionally on the prototypes,
\[
  (Z_{1,d},Z_{2,d},Z_{3,d})
  \Rightarrow N(0,I_3)
\]
in probability \cite{diaconisfreedman1987}.  Moreover,
\[
  \max_{1\leq i\leq3}|r_{i,d}|
  \xrightarrow{p}0
\]
when $\lambda_d=O(1)$, whereas
\[
  \frac{1}{\lambda_d}
  \max_{1\leq i\leq3}|r_{i,d}|
  \xrightarrow{p}0
\]
when $\lambda_d\to\infty$.

Let (M,g) be a Riemannian (or pseudo-Riemannian) manifold. There exists a unique affine connection nabla on M, called the Levi-Civita connection of g, that is (1) torsion-free: nabla_X Y - nabla_Y X = [X,Y] for all smooth vector fields X, Y, and (2) compatible with the metric: X(g(Y,Z)) = g(nabla_X Y, Z) + g(Y, nabla_X Z) for all smooth vector fields X, Y, Z.
(M,g) is a smooth Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold

body:
Load-bearing hypothesis: uniqueness in Kruzhkov's theorem is for ENTROPY solutions; the integral (weak) formulation alone, even with Rankine-Hugoniot satisfied at every jump, does not determine the solution. Counterexample 1 (Burgers, f(u) = u^2/2, datum u0 ≡ 0): besides u ≡ 0 the function u(x,t) = 0 for x < -t/2, u = -1 for -t/2 < x < 0, u = 1 for 0 < x < t/2, u = 0 for x > t/2 is a weak solution — every jump satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot (speeds -1/2, 0, 1/2 respectively) — yet it is not an entropy solution (the jump from -1 up to 1 is an expansion shock violating Oleinik/Lax). Counterexample 2 (Burgers with u0 = 0 for x < 0, u0 = 1 for x > 0): the stationary-in-shape expansion shock u = 0 for x < t/2, u = 1 for x > t/2 satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot, but the entropy solution is the rarefaction u = 0 for x ≤ 0, u = x/t for 0 ≤ x ≤ t, u = 1 for x ≥ t. In both cases the wrong solutions create information (characteristics emanate from the shock) instead of destroying it, and they are not vanishing-viscosity limits. Auditor's check: a proof that constructs 'a' weak solution and then calls it 'the' solution — or that computes shock speeds from Rankine-Hugoniot without verifying admissibility — is incomplete; check Oleinik's chord condition at every jump (for convex flux: the state must jump DOWN as x increases).
Burgers' equation f(u) = u^2/2 in one dimension
Weak solutions are only required to satisfy the integral identity; jumps must satisfy Rankine-Hugoniot but may still be inadmissible
Uniqueness is restored by the Kruzhkov entropy inequalities (equivalently, for piecewise smooth solutions, by Oleinik's chord condition at each jump)
title: Pitfall: Weak Solutions of a Conservation Law Are Not Unique without an Entropy Condition

body: [Proposition 4 of arXiv:2512.19063, 'Sharp Decoupling Inequalities for the Variances and Second Moments of Sums of Dependent Ra'] For any sequence of random variables $\{d_{i}\}$, one can find a decoupled sequence $\{e_{i}\}$ (on a possibly enlarged probability space) which is tangent to the original sequence and in addition conditionally independent given a master $\sigma$ -algebra $\mathcal{G}$. Frequently $\mathcal{G}=\sigma(\{d_{i}\})$.

body: PageRank (PR) is an algorithm used by Google Search to rank web pages in their search engine results. It is named after both the term "web page" and co-founder Larry Page. PageRank is a way of measuring the importance of website pages. According to Google:PageRank works by counting the number and quality of links to a page to determine a rough estimate of how important the website is. The underlying assumption is that more important websites are likely to receive more links from other websites.
title: PageRank

body: In the theory of abelian groups, the torsion subgroup of an abelian group is the subgroup of consisting of all elements that have finite order. An abelian group is called a torsion group if every element of has finite order and is called torsion-free if every element of except the identity is of infinite order.
title: Torsion subgroup

[Definition of arXiv:2608.30346, '\textbf{Classification complexity of homeomorphism group actions}'] Let \(X,Y\) be standard Borel spaces and \(E,F\) be two equivalence relations on \(X,Y\) respectively. We say that \(E\) is \textit{Borel reducible} to \(F\) denoted by \(E \leq_B F\), if there exists a Borel mapping \(f: X \to Y\) called a \textit{reduction} such that
    \[x E y \iff f(x) F f(y)\]
    for all \(x,y \in X\). We say that \(E\) is \textit{Borel bireducible} to \(F\) denoted by \(E \sim_B F\), if \(E \leq_B F\) and \(F \leq_B E\). We write \(E <_B F\) if \(E \leq_B F\) and \(F \not \leq_B E\).
title: Unnumbered Definition of arXiv:2608.30346, '\textbf{Classification complexity of homeomorphism group act'

[Proposition 1 (Functional Blaschke-Santal\'o) of arXiv:2609.01460, 'On cost-induced Santal\'o-type inequalities \\ in Polish measure spaces'] Let $f:\R^n\to\R_+$ be a measurable function such that $0<\int f <+\infty$. Then, there exists $z\in \R^n$ with the following property: 
\\
for every measurable function $g:\R^n\to\R_+$ and measurable function $\Omega:\R_{+}\to\R_{+}$ satisfying
$$f(x+z)g(y)\le \Omega^{2}(\langle x,y\rangle ) \quad \text{for every } x,y\in \R^n \text{ such that } \langle x,y\rangle >0,$$
        one has
         \begin{equation}
         
         \int_{\R^n} f(x)dx\int_{\R^n} g(y)dy\le
        \left( \int_{\R^n} \Omega({|x|^{2}})dx\right)^2.\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Functional Blaschke-Santal\'o

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] Let \(L>0\) and \(a>1\). Define
\(\mathsf A_{a,L}:L^2(B_{a,L},\mathrm dA)\to L^2(0,\infty)\) by
\[
        (\mathsf A_{a,L}f)(\xi)
        :=
        \int_{B_{a,L}}\overline{u_\xi(z)}f(z)\,\mathrm dA(z).
\]
Then \(\mathsf A_{a,L}\) is Hilbert--Schmidt,
\(K_{B_{a,L}}=\mathsf A_{a,L}^*\mathsf A_{a,L}\), and \(K_{B_{a,L}}\) is a
positive trace-class operator with \(\operatorname{tr}(K_{B_{a,L}})=L\lambda_a\).

[Lemma lem:scalar_DR_variance of arXiv:2609.02491, 'Generalised Random Parking for Trapeziums on a Strip'] Let $F:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be locally bounded and continuous for all sufficiently large arguments. Suppose that, for some $C_0\in\mathbb{R}$ and all sufficiently large $x$,
\begin{equation}
F(x+a) = \frac{1}{x} \mleft( \int_0^xF(t)\,\mathrm{d} t + \int_\delta^{x+\delta}F(t)\,\mathrm{d} t \mright) + \frac{C_0}{x} + p(x+a), 
\end{equation}
where $ |p(x)|\le C\mathcal R_2(x)$ for all sufficiently large $x$. Then, there exists a constant $\rho\ge0$ such that
\[
F(x) = \rho\cdot (x+\varsigma ) + \mathcal{O}(\mathcal R_2(x)).
\]
title: Lemma lem:scalar_DR_variance of arXiv:2609.02491

body:
Let $S = n^{-1} X^T X = \sum_{i=1}^M \lambda_i u_i u_i^T$ be the sample covariance of $n$ i.i.d. rows in $\mathbb{R}^M$ with population covariance $\Sigma$, and let $M/n \to c \in (0,1)$. Among rotation-equivariant estimators $\sum_i d_i u_i u_i^T$ the Frobenius-optimal choice is the oracle $d_i^* = u_i^T \Sigma u_i$, whose large-dimensional limit is $\lambda_i / |1 - c - c\lambda_i \breve m_F(\lambda_i)|^2$ with $\breve m_F(\lambda) = \lim_{\eta \downarrow 0} m_F(\lambda + i\eta)$, $m_F(z) = \int dF(t)/(t - z)$ the Stieltjes transform of the limiting sample spectral distribution $F$ (Ledoit-Peche 2011). Writing $\operatorname{Im} \breve m_F(\lambda) = \pi f(\lambda)$ and $\operatorname{Re} \breve m_F(\lambda) = \pi H_f(\lambda)$, $H_f(x) = \pi^{-1} \mathrm{PV}\!\int f(t)/(t - x)\,dt$, the oracle reads $\tilde d_i = \lambda_i / \big[(\pi c \lambda_i f(\lambda_i))^2 + (1 - c - \pi c \lambda_i H_f(\lambda_i))^2\big]$. Ledoit and Wolf (2020) estimate $f$ and $H_f$ from the sample eigenvalues themselves with the Epanechnikov kernel $\kappa(x) = \tfrac{3}{4\sqrt5}(1 - x^2/5)^+$ and the eigenvalue-proportional bandwidth $h_j = \lambda_j n^{-1/3}$: $\tilde f(x) = M^{-1}\sum_j \kappa((x - \lambda_j)/h_j)/h_j$ and $\tilde H_f(x) = M^{-1}\sum_j H_\kappa((x - \lambda_j)/h_j)/h_j$, where $H_\kappa(x) = -\tfrac{3x}{10\pi} + \tfrac{3}{4\sqrt5\pi}(1 - x^2/5)\log\big|\tfrac{\sqrt5 - x}{\sqrt5 + x}\big|$. The resulting estimator $\hat\Sigma = \sum_i \tilde d_i u_i u_i^T$ has no tuning constant, is positive definite when $c < 1$, and its Frobenius loss (and its minimum-variance-portfolio loss) converges to the oracle's; for $c > 1$ a separate formula handles the $M - n$ null eigenvalues.
rows i.i.d. with finite twelfth moments (the Ledoit-Wolf condition)
M/n -> c in (0,1) for the stated form; the population spectral distribution has compact support (Ledoit-Peche take it bounded away from zero)
the sample eigenvalues are distinct (they are, almost surely)

[Lemma 12 (see \cite{paper1}) of arXiv:2609.01114, 'Unbalanced spectral Tur\'an problem for color-critical graphs with prescribed large maximu'] Let $F$ be singleton-boundary with $\chi(F)=p+2\ge4$.  There is a constant
	$C_\partial=C_\partial(F)$ such that every $\partial_{c}F$-free graph $H$ on
	$n$ vertices satisfies

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is a proved mean-conditioning case of Svante Janson's Problem 20.3 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510. Let w_j >= 0, w_0 > 0, Phi(z) = sum_{j>=0} w_j z^j, and rho be its radius of convergence. Choose a fixed tau in (0,rho], with Phi(tau) < infinity, and define pi_j = w_j tau^j/Phi(tau), mu = sum j pi_j > 0, and sigma^2 = sum (j-mu)^2 pi_j in (0,infinity). Allow either tau < rho, or tau = rho with finite sigma^2. Let integers m_n satisfy m_n - n mu = O(1), and restrict to feasible sizes. Draw (Y_1,...,Y_n) with probability proportional to product_i w_{Y_i}, conditional on sum_i Y_i = m_n, and put N_d = number of i with Y_i = d. For any fixed finite set D of nonnegative integers, ((N_d-n pi_d)/sqrt(n))_{d in D} converges in distribution to a centered multivariate Gaussian vector. Its diagonal covariance is V_dd = pi_d(1-pi_d) - (d-mu)^2 pi_d^2/sigma^2; for distinct d,e its covariance is V_de = -pi_d pi_e - (d-mu)(e-mu)pi_d pi_e/sigma^2. Degenerate Gaussian coordinates are allowed. In Janson's parameters, Psi(t) = t Phi'(t)/Phi(t), lambda = mu, and nu = lim_{t upward to rho} Psi(t), so the two cases are 0 < lambda < nu and lambda = nu with finite variance. The stronger O(1) centering hypothesis is explicit here; mere convergence m_n/n -> lambda is not being asserted to justify centering by the fixed law pi. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
The tilt is fixed, mu > 0, and 0 < sigma^2 < infinity.
m_n-n mu = O(1), with positive conditioning probability.
D is finite; tau is interior or is the finite-variance boundary tilt.

body:
[Thm A. thm: convergence coupling for fused resistance spaces of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] Let $(F_{n}, R_{n}, \rho_{n}),\, n \geq 1$ and $(F, R, \rho)$ be rooted compact resistance metric spaces.
  Let $(a_{n}^{(i)}, b_{n}^{(i)})_{i=1}^{N}$ and $(a^{(i)}, b^{(i)})_{i=1}^{N}$
  be distinct elements of $F_{n}$ and $F$, respectively.
  Assume that 
  \begin{equation}
    (F_{n}, R_{n}, \rho_{n}, (a_{n}^{(i)}, b_{n}^{(i)})_{i=1}^{N})
    \to     
    (F, R, \rho, (a^{(i)}, b^{(i)})_{i=1}^{N})
  \end{equation}
  in $\mathfrak{M}_{c}(\tau^{2N \text{-}\mathrm{pts}})$.
  Write $(\tilde{F}_{n}, \tilde{R}_{n})$ and $(\tilde{F}, \tilde{R})$ 
  for the resistance metric spaces fused over $\{\{a_{n}^{(i)}, b_{n}^{(i)}\}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ and $\{\{a^{(i)}, b^{(i)}\}\}_{i=1}^{N}$, respectively.
  Let $\pi_{n}: F_{n} \to \tilde{F}_{n}$ and $\pi: F \to \tilde{F}$ be the associated canonical maps,
  and set $\tilde{\rho}_{n} \coloneqq \pi_{n}(\rho_{n})$ and $\tilde{\rho} \coloneqq \pi(\rho)$.
  Then, there exist rooted compact metric spaces $(M, d^{M}, \rho_{M})$ and $(\tilde{M}, d^{\tilde{M}}, \rho_{\tilde{M}})$ 
  satisfying the following:
  \begin{enumerate} [label = (\roman*)]
    \item $(F_{n}, R_{n}, \rho_{n})$ and $(F, R, \rho)$ are embedded isometrically into $(M, d^{M}, \rho_{M})$ 
      in such a way that $\rho_{n} = \rho = \rho_{M}$ as elements of $M$,
      $F_{n} \to F$ in the Hausdorff topology on $M$,
      and $a_{n}^{(i)} \to a^{(i)}$ and $b_{n}^{(i)} \to b^{(i)}$ in $M$;
    \item $(\tilde{F}_{n}, \tilde{R}_{n}, \tilde{\rho}_{n})$ and $(\tilde{F}, \tilde{R}, \tilde{\rho})$ are embedded isometrically into 
      $(\tilde{M}, d^{\tilde{M}}, \rho_{\tilde{M}})$ in such a way that 
      $\tilde{\rho}_{n} = \tilde{\rho} = \rho_{\tilde{M}}$ as elements of $\tilde{M}$ 
      and $\tilde{F}_{n} \to \tilde{F}$ in the Hausdorff topology on $\tilde{M}$;
    \item if we regard $\pi_{n}$ and $\pi$ as elements of $\widehat{C}(M, \tilde{M})$ by the above embeddings,
      then $\pi_{n} \to \pi$ in $\widehat{C}(M, \tilde{M})$.
  \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm A. thm: convergence coupling for fused resistance spaces of arXiv:2412.08236

DRAFT, independent review pending. The density g(E)=1/[E(log(1/E))^2] on (0,exp(-1)), zero elsewhere, integrates to one and lies in no Lp for p>1. Multiplication by E on L2(g(E)dE) is a bounded self-adjoint operator whose unit-vector spectral measure is g(E)dE. Its normalized Poisson densities converge in L1 and are uniformly integrable, but their pth energy moments diverge as eta tends to zero for every p>1 on any interval containing the support in its interior. Thus a higher-moment sufficient condition is stronger than spectral absolute continuity; failure to prove it is not a refutation of the Anderson conjecture.

[Lemma lem:differential-bound of arXiv:2504.09141, 'Bounds on the distance exponent for higher-dimensional Liouville first passage percolation'] Fix $d \geq 3$.     $$
    \max \big{\{} -\xi, \frac{1}{\xi} (\lambda - 1) \big{\}} \leq \lambda' \leq \sqrt{2(d-1)+2\lambda +\xi^2} - \xi.
    $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Independently checked proof (PASS w667 and w668): C003 v1. Let F be a probability on nonempty compact K subset R^d with mean mu and n>=1. Let Z be the n-tuples in K^n whose sum is n*mu. Then F is n-CM iff for every continuous real f on K, integral f dF <= max over Z of average_i f(x_i). Equivalently F belongs to the closed convex hull of the empirical laws n^(-1)sum_i delta_(x_i) for tuples in Z. Compactness of coupling laws preserves the fixed sum and marginals; uniform coordinate permutation makes finite barycenters have identical marginals; Hahn-Banach separation supplies a common potential when the hull excludes F. Empty Z means all formulations fail. For a convex K, the tuple (mu,...,mu) makes Z nonempty. This is a standard marginal-duality specialization, not an existence proof or novelty claim.
F Borel probability on nonempty compact K
n positive integer
Fixed sum n*mean(F)
Empty-set convention retained

[Proposition 40 (Combined uniform exponential tails) of arXiv:2605.14511, 'Clumsy and Careless:\\ Stationary-Entry Flux in Non-monotone Coupon Collectors'] For the fixed-parameter combined collector, there are constants $C,c\in(0,\infty)$, depending only on $\alpha,\beta$, such that
\[
        \sup_{A\subseteq[n]}
        \Pbb_A\left(\mu_n^{\alpha,\beta}T_n^{\alpha,\beta}>x\right)
        \le Ce^{-cx},
        \qquad x\ge0,
\]
for all sufficiently large $n$.  In particular, the bound holds for the empty initial collection.

[Dfn 69 (generalized budget constraint) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall the set $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ defined in Definition~\ref{d:incr.p}.
For $p\in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ and a generalized ``budget'' function $f \in L^1([q_0,1];[0,+\infty))$, let
$\Adm(q_0;p,f)$
denote the set of progressively measurable control processes $(b,\sigma)$, with $\sigma \ge 0$,
satisfying
    \beq
    \bbE\bigg[
    (b_t)^2 + \frac{tp'(t)}{p(t)} (\sigma_t-1)^2
    \bigg]
    \le f(t)\eeq
for all $t \in [q_0,1]$. Then let
	\[
    \cM(q_0;p,f) = \bigg\{
        \mu(q_* = q_0,b,\sigma,p,\zeta = \delta_0) : (b,\sigma)
        \in \Adm(q_0;p,f)
    \bigg\}\,,
\]
where we recall from \eqref{e:control.problems.endpoint.measures} that $\mu(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)$ denotes the law of $X(1)$ where $X$ is given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} with parameters $(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)$. (Note that in order to accommodate controls $(b,\sigma)$ where the budget constraint is only satisfied in the averaged sense of condition~\ref{it:4.1}, we allow $f$ to map into $[0,+\infty)$. On the other hand, all classes of measures that we will represent using Definition~\ref{d:X.adm} will have $q_* = q_0$ and $\zeta = \delta_0$, so we will set these parameters in the definition.)

Own-work draft; C15 v1 status SKETCH, unreviewed, no novelty claim; not a certified theorem. Proposed estimate: for d>=1, N>=1 iid centers Y_i from one law supported in the radius-B Euclidean ball (B>=0), and s>0, write p_N=N^-1 sum_i phi_{s^2}(x-Y_i), p=E phi_{s^2}(x-Y), where phi_w is the centered d-dimensional Gaussian density of covariance w I. Then E TV(p_N,p)<=one half sqrt([e(1+B^2/(d s^2))]^(d/2)/N). The proof candidate uses the public Gaussian reference of variance v=s^2+B^2/d, an exact squared-density integral, iid variance divided by N, and Cauchy-Schwarz. Written derivation and exact finite arithmetic checks are available at the source; the full statement lacks independent audit and Lean certification. At circle radius O(1), B^2=O(d), and polynomial inverse effective smoothing, the resulting sufficient codebook-size threshold has log O(d log d), independent of the circle alphabet M. This obstructs automatic amplification merely by enlarging a uniform log-codebook-size prior. It supplies no efficient sampler, no general impossibility result, and no improved T306 exponent. The cited fixed-parameter circle lower-bound proof has not been extended uniformly to dimension-dependent M.
d>=1, N>=1, s>0, B>=0
iid centers from one distribution supported in radius B
O(d log d) consequence requires polynomial inverse effective smoothing and probability/TV tolerances
No algorithmic upper bound or impossibility theorem for other priors/oracles is claimed

[Theorem 8 of arXiv:2609.02732, 'Conservation of mass for solutions of Leibenson's equation on Riemannian Manifolds'] Assume that, for some $x_0\in M$ and all large enough $r>0$, \begin{equation}V(x_0, r)\leq \exp\left(C r^{\frac{p}{p-1}}\right),\end{equation} where $C$ is a positive constant.
Let $u$ be a non-negative bounded solution to (\ref{dtv}) in $M\times [0, \infty)$ with non-negative initial function $u(\cdot, 0)=u_0\in L^{1}(M)\cap L^{\infty}(M)$. Then, for all $t>0$, \begin{equation}\int_M u(x, t)=\int_M u_0(x).\end{equation}

[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2608.27374, '\Large \bf Distribution-constrained optimal multiple stopping: the Root-type solution'] For $i=1,\ldots,n$, let $F_i\in C^{1,2}(\R_+\times\R)$.  For each $T<\infty$, suppose that
$$
    |F_i(t,x)|+|\mathcal G F_i(t,x)|
    \le
    K_{i,T}(1+|x|^{r_{i,T}}),
    \qquad
    0\le t\le T,\quad x\in\R,
$$
for some $K_{i,T}<\infty$ and $r_{i,T}\ge0$, and assume that $x\longmapsto\mathcal G F_i(t,x)$
is non-decreasing for almost every $t\ge0$. Let $\rho\in\mbox{ConsStop}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)$.  Suppose that for all
$i=1,\ldots,n$ and $\theta\in\{\rho_i,\sigma_i\}$, the family 
   $ \left\{
        F_i(t\wedge\theta,X_{t\wedge\theta})
        :t\ge0
    \right\}$
is uniformly integrable, then
$$
    \E[F_i(\sigma_i,X_{\sigma_i})]
    \ge
    \E[F_i(\rho_i,X_{\rho_i})],
    \qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
$$
If the uniform-integrability condition holds for every
$\rho\in\mbox{ConsStop}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)$, then $\sigma$ maximizes
$$
    \rho
    \longmapsto
    \E\!\left[
        \sum_{i=1}^n F_i(\rho_i,X_{\rho_i})
    \right]
$$
over $\mbox{ConsStop}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 5 of arXiv:2608.27374

[Proposition 15 (Exponent lattices with prescribed integral coordinates) of arXiv:2609.02449, 'Finite Directional Coefficient Modules over Euler Fibers of $A$-Hypergeometric Systems'] Assume that $\rank_{\Q}(B_{E})=r$.
Then $\Gamma_E$ is a full-rank lattice in $\R^{r}$ containing $\Z^{r}$, and 
\[
\Gamma_{E}/\Z^{r}
\cong
\operatorname{Sat}(B_{E}\Z^{r})/B_{E}\Z^{r}.
\]
If $\mathfrak{L}_{\bm{\beta}}^{\supset E}$ is nonempty and $\Lambda_{0}$ is one of its elements, then any $\bm{\lambda}_{0}\in\Lambda_{0}$ induces a bijection
\[
\Gamma_{E}/\Z^{r}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathfrak{L}_{\bm{\beta}}^{\supset E},\quad\bm{z}+\Z^{r}\longmapsto\Lambda(\bm{\lambda}_{0}+B\bm{z}).
\]
Consequently,
\[
|\mathfrak{L}_{\bm{\beta}}^{\supset E}|=[\operatorname{Sat}(B_{E}\Z^{r}):B_{E}\Z^{r}]<\infty,
\]
and the subfamily $\mathfrak{L}_{\bm{\beta}}^{E}$ is finite.

body: Publication record. Open Problem 4.49(ii) of D. Aldous and J. A. Fill, Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, attributed to Sinclair, asks whether log n can be replaced by the diameter of the transition graph in the multicommodity flow bound on the relaxation time. For general chains the answer is negative for a simple reason (add transitions of small probability between all pairs of states of the random walk on an expander). Y. Shmalo, Multicommodity flow, the relaxation time and the diameter (2026) shows that the answer is negative also for simple random walks on graphs, for every constant and already on graphs of diameter two. Paper: https://github.com/yspennstate/flow-parameter-diameter (commit 243299cc4eda); ResearchGate record 414372242. Not refereed.
title: Aldous-Fill Open Problem 4.49(ii) (Sinclair) answered negatively: the multicommodity flow parameter, the relaxation time and the diameter (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/flow-parameter-diameter)

[Definition def:controlled-rp of arXiv:2601.21762, 'Navier-Stokes with a fractional transport noise as a limit of multi-scale dynamics'] Let $X\in C^\alpha([0,T];V)$. A pair $(Y,Y')$ with
$Y\in C^\alpha([0,T];W)$ and
$Y'\in C^\alpha([0,T];\mathcal{L}(V,W))$
is said to be \emph{controlled by $X$} if the remainder
$$
R^Y_{s,t}:=Y_{s,t}-Y'_sX_{s,t}
$$
belongs to $C^{2\alpha}(\Delta_T;W)$.
We write $(Y,Y')\in\mathcal{D}_X^{2\alpha}([0,T];W)$ and set
$$
\left\| Y,Y' \right\|_{X,2\alpha}
:=
\left\| Y' \right\|_\alpha+\left\| R^Y \right\|_{2\alpha}.
$$
title: Definition def:controlled-rp of arXiv:2601.21762

[Proposition 2 of arXiv:2608.29713, '\textbf{A Cartan geometry from a correspondence space in Riemannian geometry}'] A Cartan geometry $(q:\mathcal{P}\to M,\omega)$ of type $(\operatorname{Euc}(n),O(n))$ canonically determines a Riemannian metric $g$ on $M$ by
$$
g_{x}(v,w):=\left\langle \phi_{u}(v),\phi_{u}(w)\right\rangle,
\qquad v,w\in T_{x}M,
$$
where $u\in\mathcal{P}$ is any point with $q(u)=x$. Moreover, after fixing the canonical orthonormal basis $(E_{1},\ldots,E_{n})$ of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, the map
\[
\mathcal{P}\longrightarrow \mathcal{F}_{g}(M),
\qquad
u\mapsto\big(\phi_{u}^{-1}(E_{1}),\ldots,\phi_{u}^{-1}(E_{n})\big),
\]
is an isomorphism of $O(n)$-principal fiber bundles over $M$.
Here the right action on $\mathcal F_g(M)$ is the usual one:
\[
(e_1,\ldots,e_n)\cdot A
=
\left(
\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i A_{i1},
\ldots,
\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_i A_{in}
\right),
\qquad A=(A_{ij})\in O(n).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 2 of arXiv:2608.29713

[Lemma 1 (Gaussian fourth-moment identities) of arXiv:2609.02728, 'Momentum in large-batch training: Polyak enlarges the critical batch size, Nesterov improv'] Let \(\bx\sim\mathcal N(\bm0,\bH)\) in a separable Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), where \(\bH\) is a positive trace-class covariance operator. For any \(\bu,\bv\in\mathcal H\),
\begin{equation}

\EE\!\left[\langle\bx,\bu\rangle^2\langle\bx,\bv\rangle^2\right]
=
\langle\bu,\bH\bu\rangle\langle\bv,\bH\bv\rangle
+
2\langle\bu,\bH\bv\rangle^2.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, for any self-adjoint trace-class operator \(\bA\),
\begin{equation}

\EE\!\left[(\bx\otimes\bx)\bA(\bx\otimes\bx)\right]
=
2\bH\bA\bH+\bH\Tr(\bH\bA).
\end{equation}

b_j\cdot\left(\frac{1}{N_1} + \cdots + \frac{1}{N_j}\right) \in \ZZ, \quad \textrm{for each }j = 1, \ldots, n+1.

[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2604.04100, '\LARGE Learning Equilibrium Fluctuation Expansions from Overdamped Langevin Dynamics'] Let $n\in\mathbb N_+$. {Then for every $F\in C^{n+1}(\mathbb R)$ satisfying \eqref{assump-F}, there exists $\varepsilon_0\in (0,1]$ and a sequence of coefficients $(B_m(F))_{0\le m\le n}$ such that, for every $\varepsilon\in (0,\varepsilon_0)$,
	\begin{equation}
		\int_{\mathbb R}F(x)\mu_\varepsilon(\mathrm d x)
		=\sum_{m=0}^n \varepsilon^{m/2}B_m(F)+R_{n}(F,\varepsilon),
	\end{equation}
	where
	$$
	|R_{n}(F,\varepsilon)|\le C_n(F)\varepsilon^{(n+1)/2}.
	$$
	Moreover, for each $m\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}$,
		\begin{equation}
			B_m(F)
			=\frac12\sum_{i=0}^m \frac{d_{m,i}}{i!}F^{(i)}(1)
			+\frac12\sum_{i=0}^m \frac{\bar d_{m,i}}{i!}F^{(i)}(-1).
		\end{equation}
	Here the coefficients $d_{m,i}$ and $\bar d_{m,i}$ are uniquely determined by}
		\begin{equation}
			d_{m,i}
			=\frac{i-1}{2}d_{m-2,i-2}-\frac32 d_{m,i+1}-\frac12 d_{m,i+2},
			\quad
			\bar d_{m,i}
			=\frac{i-1}{2}\bar d_{m-2,i-2}+\frac32 \bar d_{m,i+1}-\frac12 \bar d_{m,i+2},
		\end{equation}
		for $m\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ and $i\in\{1,\dots,m\}$, with
$$
d_{0,0}=\bar d_{0,0}=1,\quad d_{m,0}=\bar d_{m,0}=0,\quad m\ge1,
$$
and the convention that
$$
d_{k,j}=\bar d_{k,j}=0
\quad\text{whenever }k<0,\text{ or } k\geq1 \text{ and }j\notin\{0,1,\dots,k\}.
$$
In particular, the recursion gives
$$
d_{1,1}=\bar d_{1,1}=0,\quad d_{2,2}=\bar d_{2,2}=\frac12.
$$

body: In applied mathematics, Arnold diffusion is the phenomenon of instability of nearly-integrable Hamiltonian systems. The phenomenon is named after Vladimir Arnold who was the first to publish a result in the field in 1964. More precisely, Arnold diffusion refers to results asserting the existence of solutions to nearly-integrable Hamiltonian systems that exhibit a significant change in the action variables.
title: Arnold diffusion

[Lemma lemxplus of arXiv:2605.01878, '\Large Random trade timing and power-law tails in realized prices'] Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable, and define $X^+ \coloneqq \max\{X,0\}$. Let $\varphi_X(s) \coloneqq E[e^{-sX}]$ and $\varphi_+(s) \coloneqq E[e^{-sX^+}]$ wherever finite. Suppose that $\varphi_X$ satisfies the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=(\roman*)]
    \item  The abscissa of convergence of $\varphi_X$ is $-\alpha$, with $0 < \alpha < \infty$.
    \item  $s = -\alpha$ is a pole of order $\ell$, and $A_\ell$ denotes the coefficient of $(s+\alpha)^{-\ell}$ in the Laurent expansion of $\varphi_X$ at $s=-\alpha$.
    \item  $\varphi_X$ is holomorphic on an open neighborhood of the segment
    \[
    \{s=-\alpha+\mathrm{i}\tau : -2\alpha\delta<\tau<2\alpha\delta\}\setminus\{-\alpha\}
    \]
    for some $\delta>0$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $\varphi_+$ also satisfies (lemxpluda of the paper)--(lemxpludc of the paper) with the same constants $\alpha$, $\ell$, $A_\ell$, and $\delta$. If, in addition, $-\alpha$ is the unique singularity of $\varphi_X$ on the axis $\mathrm{Re}(s)=-\alpha$, then the same holds for $\varphi_+$.

[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2607.17192, 'Geometric Regime--Switching Diffusions on Stratified Riemannian Spaces with an Application'] The class \(\cl D_0\) is measure determining
		on \(E\). More precisely, if \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) are finite Borel measures on \(E\) and
		\begin{equation}
			
			\int_E f\,d\mu=\int_E f\,d\nu,
			\qquad \text{for all }f\in\cl D_0,
		\end{equation}
		then \(\mu=\nu\).

body:
[Thm Loewner coordinate change in angular coordinate of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] In angular (trigonometric) coordinates, suppose $\gamma(0) = \theta \in \mathbb{R}$ and let the marked points be $\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_n \in \mathbb{C}$. Let $\gamma(t)$ be the curve generated by the deterministic Loewner chain:
\begin{equation}
\partial_t h_t(z) = \cot\left( \frac{h_t(z) - \theta_t}{2} \right), \qquad \dot{\theta}_t = b\left( \theta_t ; h_t(\theta_1), \ldots, h_t(\theta_n) \right),
\end{equation}
with initial condition $h_0(z) = z$ and $\theta_0 = \theta$, where $b : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is a smooth vector field.

Let $\tau : \mathcal{N} \to \mathbb{H}$ be a conformal map defined on a neighborhood $\mathcal{N}$ of $\theta$ such that $\gamma[0,T] \subset \mathcal{N}$ and $\tau(\partial \mathcal{N} \cap \mathbb{R}) \subset \mathbb{R}$. Define the image curve $\widetilde{\gamma}(t) := \tau(\gamma(t))$ for $t \in [0, T]$, and let $\widetilde{h}_t$ denote the conformal map associated with $\widetilde{\gamma}[0, t]$.

Define the conformal coordinate change
\[
\Psi_t := \widetilde{h}_t \circ \tau \circ h_t^{-1}.
\]

Then the image conformal map $\widetilde{h}_t(z)$ satisfies the evolution equation:
\begin{equation}
\partial_t \widetilde{h}_t(z) = \cot\left( \frac{\widetilde{h}_t(z) - \widetilde{\theta}_t}{2} \right) \cdot \left[ \Psi_t'(\theta_t) \right]^2, \qquad \widetilde{h}_0(z) = z,
\end{equation}
where the new driving function is
\[
\widetilde{\theta}_t := \widetilde{h}_t \circ \tau \circ h_t^{-1}(\theta_t) = \Psi_t(\theta_t), \quad \widetilde{\theta}_0 = \tau(\theta).
\]

Moreover, the curve $\widetilde{\gamma}(t)$ is parameterized so that its unit disk capacity satisfies
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{hcap}(\widetilde{\gamma}[0, t]) = 2 \sigma(t), \qquad \text{where} \quad \sigma(t) := \int_0^t \left| \Psi_s'(\theta_s) \right|^2 \, ds.
\end{equation}
title: Deterministic Loewner chain under coordinate change

[Corollary cor:r=2 of arXiv:2412.09145, 'Asymptotic expansions for normal deviations of random walks conditioned to stay positive'] Assume that the conditions of Theorem~(thm:lattice of the paper) hold with $r=2$. Then
\begin{align*}
&P_2(t)=\frac{2\theta_0}{\sigma}t\\
&P_3(t)=\frac{\theta_0m_3}{3\sigma^3}(t^4-5t^2+2)
+\frac{2\theta_1}{\sigma}(t^2-1),
\end{align*}
where $m_3:=\mathbf E X^3$ and 
\begin{align*}
&\theta_0=\sum_{u=1}^\infty U_1(u)\mathbf P(X<-u),\\
&\theta_1:=\sum_{u=1}^\infty U_1(u)\mathbf E[(-X-u);X<-u].
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary cor:r=2 of arXiv:2412.09145

$D_j=a\sqrt\tau+I_j/I_{j-1}$,
\[
 I_0=D_1^{-1},\qquad D_j=a\sqrt\tau+\frac{j}{D_{j+1}}.
\]
The finite fraction replaces the exact terminal value
$D_L>a\sqrt\tau$ by $a\sqrt\tau$.  Every map
$u\mapsto a\sqrt\tau+j/u$ reverses order.  Propagating to $D_1$ and

body:
[Lemma 11 of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $k,d\in\mathbb N$, and let $\varrho\in C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^k)$ be a
nonnegative function. Let
$f\in \mathcal P_d(\mathbb R^k;\mathbb R^k)$,
and let $A_f:=\operatorname{adj}(J_f)$ denote the adjugate matrix of the Jacobian $J_f$.
Then, for every $\varepsilon>0$, every unit vector $\theta\in\mathbb R^k$,
every $t>0$, and every $\varphi\in C_b^\infty(\mathbb R^k)$ satisfying
\[
\|\varphi\|_\infty\le t,
\quad
\|\partial_\theta\varphi\|_\infty\le 1,
\]
one has
\begin{align*}
\biggl|
\int_{\mathbb R^k}(\partial_\theta\varphi)(f)\varrho\,dx
\biggr|
&\le
\int_{\mathbb R^k} I_{\{(\det J_f)^2\le 2\varepsilon^2\}}\varrho\,dx
\\
&\quad
+
t\varepsilon^{-1}
\int_{\mathbb R^k}
\bigl|\langle \nabla\varrho,A_f\theta\rangle\bigr|\,dx
+
18t
\int_{\mathbb R^k}
\frac{\bigl|\langle \nabla\det J_f,A_f\theta\rangle\bigr|}
{(\det J_f)^2+\varepsilon^2}
\varrho\,dx.
\end{align*}

body:
[Theorem th:split of arXiv:2608.19358, 'An optimal Poincaré inequality\\for the complex Ginibre log-gas'] Consider the complex line $L=\mathbb{C}(1,\ldots,1)\subset\mathbb{C}^n$, and
  its orthogonal complex hyperplane $L^\perp\subset\mathbb{C}^n$. Let
  $\varphi_n(z)=c_n^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{-n|z|^2}|V_n(z)|^2$, $z\in\mathbb{C}^n$,
  be the density of the complex Ginibre log-gas $\mu_n$. Then
  $z=\operatorname{proj}_L(z)+\operatorname{proj}_{L^\perp}(z)=S(z)v+W$ where
  $S(z)=z_1+\cdots+z_n$, $v=(1/n,\ldots,1/n)$ and $W=z-S(z)v$, for all
  $z\in\mathbb{C}^n$, and
  \begin{equation}
    \varphi_n(z)=\mathrm{e}^{-|S(z)|^2}\varphi_n(W).
  \end{equation}
  In probabilistic terms, if $\mathbf{Z}\sim\mu_n$ then
  $\mathbf{S}=\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbf{Z}_k$ and
  $\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{Z}-(\mathbf{S},\ldots,\mathbf{S})/n$ are independent
  with $\mathbf{S}\sim\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{C}}(0,1)$ while $\mathbf{W}$ has
  density proportional to $\varphi_n$ for the Lebesgue measure on $L^\perp$.
  Furthermore
  \[
    \mathbf{R}=n|\mathbf{W}|^2\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\kappa,1)
    \quad\text{where}\quad
    \kappa=\frac{(n-1)(n+2)}{2}
  \]
  when $n\geq2$, while $\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{Z}$, $\mathbf{W}=0$, and
  $\mathbf{R}=0$ when $n=1$.

[Proposition 11 (Insenstivity of certain conditional laws to the choice of base vertex) of arXiv:2510.22533, 'Marginal dynamics of probabilistic cellular automata on trees'] Suppose Condition \ref{cond:GW} holds.
Then the following hold for each $k \in \N_0$:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item 
For each  $v \in \V^0$, $Y_{\V_{v+}}[k]$ is conditionally independent of $Y_{\V_{v-}}[k]$ given $Y_{\{v,\mom_v\}}[k]$.
\item The conditional law of $(Y_{vu}[k])_{u \in \V^0}$ given $(Y_v[k],Y_{\mom_v}[k])$ does not depend on the choice of $v \in \V^0$. 
More precisely, there exists a measurable map $\Theta_k \colon (\{0,1\} \times \PolishX^{k+1})^2 \rightarrow \P((\{0,1\} \times \PolishX^{k+1})^{\V^0})$ such that, for every $v \in \V^0$ and every Borel set $B \subset (\{0,1\} \times \PolishX^{k+1})^{\V^0}$, we have 
\[
\Theta_k(Y_v[k], Y_{\mom_v}[k])(B) = \Pmb\left(  (Y_{vu}[k])_{u \in \V^0} \in B \, | \, Y_v[k], Y_{\mom_v}[k] \right) \ \ a.s.
\]
\end{enumerate}

DRAFT, proof (unaudited), T411-w740-C002/C003 v1. Let d>=2 and R>=72, T_R(z)=z+(z-R)_+, and let Z,W,Z2,...,Zd be independent standard Gaussians. Set P0=Law(Z+W,Z2,...,Zd) and P1=Law(T_R(Z)+W,Z2,...,Zd). Both priors have positive smooth densities and log-Sobolev constant at most 5 in the convention Ent(f^2)<=2 C_LS E||grad f||^2. The exact OU forward score of P0 has squared L2 error at most exp(-R^2/2)/4 under the forward law of P1 at every time. Under additive Gaussian smoothing with standard deviation u, the squared error is at most Pr(Z>R)/[(1+u^2)(2+u^2)]. For the normalized observation A=e1^T, noise variance 2/5, and fixed y=2R, the posteriors of P0 and P1 differ in TV by more than 3/8. The posterior of P1 has C_P and C_LS at least exp(R^2/960)/8, although the prior ratio ||A||^2 C_LS/sigma^2 is at most 25/2. A common approximate-score oracle therefore cannot guarantee posterior TV error 1/8 for every fixed observation; adding n independent exact prior samples requires n Pr(Z>R)>1/8. These are rare-observation obstructions only: they do not establish exact-score computational hardness, do not refute high-probability-over-observations posterior sampling, and do not claim that these explicitly described posteriors are hard to sample. No novelty or independent-check claim is made.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:de3310a71477ab01682964c4e277ad250513d544cd8c6c6670c8e76427a9b90c","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/de/de3310a71477ab01682964c4e277ad250513d544cd8c6c6670c8e76427a9b90c.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:26ccb33825d24af37e9af2397e7ef37d8df43febc52d49dcaff4d7102a2d2205","bundle_entry_key":"draft-constant-lsi-rare-observation-posterior-instability","bundle_id":"population.w740-t411-constant-lsi-rare-observation-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"posterior sampling and functional inequalities","draft":"w740/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.sampling:draft-constant-lsi-rare-observation-posterior-instability","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# A constant-LSI prior does not make posterior sampling robust to unconditional score error

Status: proof draft, unaudited. Target: T411 Target 1. This is an oracle-model obstruction, not an exact-score hardness theorem and not a claim that a particular posterior is hard to sample from an explicit prior description.

## Statement

Use the convention Ent_mu(f^2) <= 2 C_LS E_mu ||grad f||^2. Fix R >= 40 and d >= 2. There are two everywhere positive smooth priors P_0,P_1 on R^d, both with C_LS <= 5 and polynomially bounded moments, and a single explicit forward score oracle s(t,x), such that:

1. s is the exact Ornstein--Uhlenbeck forward score for P_0.
2. At every t >= 0, its squared L2 error under the forward law of P_1 is at most Pr{Z>R}/2 <= exp(-R^2/2)/4, where Z is standard Gaussian.
3. For A = (sqrt(5/2),0,...,0), sigma=1 and y=sqrt(10)R, the two posterior laws have TV distance greater than 3/8.
4. Both instances satisfy ||A||^2 C_LS / sigma^2 <= 25/2. Thus they satisfy the target's proposed bound for every c>0 once log d >= 25/(2c), independently of R.

Equivalently, normalize the observation operator to A=(1,0,...,0), take sigma^2=2/5 and y=2R. This is exactly the same conditioning problem after rescaling Y by sqrt(5/2); the dimensionless ratio is unchanged and ||A||=1 as in the primary paper.

Consequently a sampler whose only prior information is this approximate score oracle, common bounds on the priors, and (d,A,sigma,y), cannot be within TV 1/8 of both posteriors. This remains true even with unlimited computation: the inputs are identical. If at most n independent exact prior samples are also supplied, TV 1/8 for both requires n Pr{Z>R} > 1/8. For R=d this excludes a polynomial number of prior samples.

This disproves the worst-observation, inverse-polynomial-unconditional-score-error interpretation of Target 1. It does not decide a high-probability-over-observations interpretation, an exact-score oracle model, or an accuracy requirement calibrated to the observation's likelihood.

## Construction and regularity

Let T_R(z)=z+(z-R)_+. Let Z,W,Z_2,...,Z_d be independent standard Gaussians. Define

P_0 = Law(Z+W,Z_2,...,Z_d),
P_1 = Law(T_R(Z)+W,Z_2,...,Z_d).

T_R is increasing and 2-Lipschitz. The map from (Z,W,Z_2,...,Z_d) to the P_1 vector is sqrt(5)-Lipschitz: the first row of its almost-everywhere derivative is (T_R'(Z),1), of squared norm at most 5, and the remaining rows are disjoint unit rows. Applying the Gaussian LSI to f composed with this map proves C_LS(P_1)<=5 directly by the chain rule. P_0 has C_LS<=2. Gaussian convolution makes the first-coordinate densities positive and C-infinity. The transform's kink is not a kink of either prior density. Since |T_R(z)|<=2|z| for R>=0, the first second moment is at most 5; all moments have Gaussian-size bounds uniformly in R. The product coordinates add no difficulty.

## Uniform score error along the entire forward process

Write beta=exp(-t), v=1+beta^2, delta(Z)=(Z-R)_+ and J(Z)=1_{Z>R}. The first-coordinate forward law for P_1 is that of

X=beta T_R(Z)+W.

Indeed the original smoothed noise and the OU noise combine into an independent standard W. The corresponding P_0 forward law is N(0,v). Set s_0(t,x)=-x/v on coordinate one and -x_j on all other coordinates.

For a smooth compactly supported scalar test function f, Gaussian integration by parts first in Z and then in W gives

E[X f(X)] = v E[f'(X)] + E[(beta delta(Z)+beta^2 J(Z)W) f(X)].

If s_1 is the true score of X, E[s_1(X)f(X)]=-E[f'(X)]. Therefore

s_1(X)+X/v = E[beta delta(Z)+beta^2 J(Z)W | X]/v

almost surely. The identity first holds distributionally; the smooth positive density identifies its score. Conditional Jensen and independence of W,Z yield

E |s_1(X)+X/v|^2 <= (beta^2 E delta^2 + beta^4 p)/(1+beta^2)^2,

where p=Pr(Z>R). There is no cross term because E W=0. Integration of Gaussian tails gives

E delta^2=(1+R^2)p-R phi(R)<=p,

using R p<=phi(R), obtained by integrating R phi(z)<=z phi(z) on z>=R. Hence the error is <= p beta^2/(1+beta^2)<=p/2. The elementary Gaussian tail bound p<=exp(-R^2/2)/2 for R>=0 follows by differentiating exp(R^2/2)Pr(Z>R) and the same Mills inequality (with the endpoint R=0 handled directly). All other coordinate scores coincide. This proves the uniform, unnormalized d-dimensional squared L2 bound.

The same conclusion holds for the additive Gaussian smoothing used in the primary paper. If the extra smoothing standard deviation is u>=0, put eta^2=1+u^2. The first coordinate has law X=T_R(Z)+eta W, and its common approximate score is -x/(2+u^2). Repeating the integration by parts gives

E |s_1(X)+X/(2+u^2)|^2 <= [E delta^2+p/eta^2]/(1+eta^2)^2 <= p/[(1+u^2)(2+u^2)].

Indeed the residual is delta+J W/eta. In particular u^2 times this squared score error is at most p. The other coordinate scores are -x_j/(1+u^2). For R=d and each fixed C, p<d^(-C) for all sufficiently large d. Thus the same explicit linear networks witness the polynomial-precision score requirement in Definition 1.1 at every d^(-C)<=u<=d^C, for either prior. Their coefficients are bounded and the covariance operator is bounded by 5. This observation does not alter the exceptional-observation limitation.

## Exact posterior calculation

Observe Y=aX_1+epsilon with a=sqrt(5/2), epsilon independent N(0,1), at y=sqrt(10)R. In particular ay=5R. Under P_0,

X_1 | Y=y ~ N(5R/3,1/3).

Under P_1, integrating W out of Y gives the conditional latent density

p(z|y) proportional to phi(z) exp((10R/7)T_R(z)-(5/14)T_R(z)^2).

On z<=R its exponent is

-(6/7)(z-5R/6)^2 + 25R^2/42.

On z>R its exponent is

-(27/14)(z-10R/9)^2 + 25R^2/42.

The two normalizing tail factors are both Phi(R/sqrt(21)). The standard deviations are sqrt(7/12) and sqrt(7/27). Thus the posterior latent law is exactly the mixture

weight 3/5: N(5R/6,7/12) restricted to z<=R;
weight 2/5: N(10R/9,7/27) restricted to z>R.

Conditionally on z and y, X_1 is Gaussian with mean (2/7)T_R(z)+10R/7 and variance 2/7. If the upper branch's truncation is temporarily removed, its X_1 marginal is N(16R/9,10/27). This marginal is only used to bound a probability; the actual posterior remains truncated.

Let B={x_1>31R/18}. Under P_0, the Gaussian tail bound gives

P_0(B|y)<=exp(-R^2/216).

The untruncated upper-branch marginal satisfies Pr(B^c)<=exp(-R^2/240). Its latent truncation event has probability Phi(R/sqrt(21))>=1/2. Dividing the bad-event probability by that probability gives

P_1(B|y)>=(2/5)(1-2 exp(-R^2/240)).

Therefore

TV(P_1(.|y),P_0(.|y)) >= 2/5-(4/5) exp(-R^2/240)-exp(-R^2/216).

For R>=40 each exponential is less than 1/100: R^2/240>=20/3, and the fourth-degree Taylor lower bound for exp(20/3) exceeds 100. The displayed TV lower bound is then greater than 191/500>3/8. Extra coordinates remain independent standard Gaussians under both posteriors, so the same bound holds in dimension d.

## Oracle consequence and exact scope

The same s_0, same observation, and common upper bounds C_LS<=5 and E||X||^2<=d+4 are valid inputs for both priors. Any algorithm with only these inputs has the same output law Q in the two cases. The triangle inequality rules out TV(Q,P_i(.|y))<=1/8 for both i, since their mutual distance exceeds 3/8.

If n independent exact prior samples are available, couple them by using the same Gaussian variables. Each P_0/P_1 sample pair is identical unless Z>R. Their n-sample transcript laws differ in TV by at most np, and data processing gives the same bound for algorithm output laws Q_0,Q_1, even if score queries are adaptive. Then

3/8 < TV(P_0(.|y),P_1(.|y)) <= 1/8 + np + 1/8,

which forces np>1/8. This is an information limitation of this approximate-oracle interface. Exact prior scores, a prior's full description, or a conditional sampler are different interfaces and are not covered.

The observation is rare as R grows. The construction deliberately does not refute a theorem averaged over Y, a high-probability observation guarantee, or a theorem requesting exponentially fine unconditional score accuracy. Neither prior nor its explicit posterior is asserted computationally difficult when its complete construction is disclosed.

This distinction is load-bearing: Gupta, Jalal, Parulekar, Price and Xun, arXiv:2402.12727v2, Definition 1.5 (PDF p.4, printed p.2), require correctness with probability 1-delta over the observation. Their error notion is coupling closeness (Definition 1.2), not TV. Their Definition 1.1 requests polynomial-precision forward scores. C002 therefore does not contradict their theorem or settle their high-probability setting after adding an LSI assumption.

Indeed TV(P_0,P_1)<=p by the explicit coupling. For any common observation channel K, write M_i=P_i K and let m_i be its Y marginal. The triangle inequality, applied after adding and subtracting m_0(y)P_1(dx|y), gives

E_{Y~m_0} TV(P_0(.|Y),P_1(.|Y)) <= TV(M_0,M_1)+TV(m_0,m_1) <= 2p.

Here TV(M_0,M_1)=TV(P_0,P_1) because the joint law retains X, and marginalization contracts TV. Hence Markov's inequality bounds the m_0 probability of posterior TV exceeding eta by 2p/eta. This explicitly confirms why a rare observation cannot refute a high-probability target.

## Checks and source obligations

Checks that could fail: LSI convention and the Lipschitz-map dimension; integration-by-parts coefficients; the OU noise variance; equal branch free energies; exact truncation probabilities and mixture weights; the posterior variances; the sign of the tail-event separation; use of conditioning in the upper branch; and the distinction between approximate and exact score access.

The finite algebraic identities and exponential lower bound are checked in scripts/check_C002.py using exact rational arithmetic. Numerical tail probabilities, if reported, are explicitly supplementary. Lean certification is attempted only for the algebraic coefficient identity; it cannot certify this analytic theorem. The Gaussian LSI input is supplied by brain card claim_4bdeb13cc86ab526b0013e02b6024d3dede00f91d34eca4a10273fa64375e52c (Gross). Primary-paper comparison and a novelty check remain obligations before describing this construction as new.


# Constant prior LSI and constant observation ratio do not bound posterior LSI

Status: proof (unaudited). This is a failure of the proposed functional-inequality transfer for arbitrary observations, not a computational sampling lower bound. Use the exact smooth P_1 prior and observation from C002. The normalized observation is A=e_1^T, sigma^2=2/5, y=2R. For R>=72,

C_P(P_1(.|y)) >= (1/8) exp(R^2/960),

and therefore the same lower bound holds for C_LS in the convention Ent(f^2)<=2 C_LS E|grad f|^2. Yet C_LS(P_1)<=5 and ||A||^2 C_LS(P_1)/sigma^2<=25/2.

The single hardest step inherited from C002 is its exact posterior branch calculation. Everything below is a direct test-function argument using those branches.

## Density domination

C002 proves that the conditional latent branches have weights 3/5 and 2/5, and each latent truncation event has probability Phi(R/sqrt(21))>=1/2. Dropping each truncation and dividing by its probability bounds the corresponding X_1 marginal density from above. Consequently its full posterior density rho satisfies

rho(x) <= (6/5) phi_{1/3}(x-5R/3) + (4/5) phi_{10/27}(x-16R/9),

where phi_v is the centered Gaussian density of variance v.

Put t=31R/18, the midpoint between the two untruncated means. For x in [t-1,t+1] and R>=36, its distance from either mean is at least R/18-1>=R/36. Both variances are at most 10/27 and both Gaussian normalizing prefactors are less than 1 (since both variances are at least 1/3). Therefore

rho(x) <= 2 exp(-R^2/960)  on [t-1,t+1].

No normalization constants of the actual posterior have been dropped: the factors 6/5 and 4/5 include the worst-case truncation probabilities.

## A test function with separated mass

Let f(x) be 0 for x<=t-1, (x-t+1)/2 for t-1<x<t+1, and 1 for x>=t+1. It is an admissible Lipschitz Sobolev test function. Its gradient energy is bounded by

E_rho |f'|^2 <= (1/4) * 2 * 2 exp(-R^2/960) = exp(-R^2/960).

On the lower latent branch, the probability X_1>t-1 is at most 2 exp(-R^2/960): first use the untruncated N(5R/3,1/3) tail, then divide by the latent truncation probability >=1/2. The exponent uses the weaker variance upper bound 10/27. Similarly, on the upper branch, Pr(X_1<t+1) <= 2 exp(-R^2/960).

For R>=72, exp(R^2/960)>=exp(27/5)>10; the quadratic Taylor lower bound 1+27/5+(27/5)^2/2 already exceeds 10. It follows that

rho(X_1<=t-1) >= (3/5)(4/5)=12/25,
rho(X_1>=t+1) >= (2/5)(4/5)=8/25.

For two independent copies X,X', Var(f(X))=(1/2)E(f(X)-f(X'))^2. The pairs from the two displayed events alone contribute at least

Var(f(X)) >= (12/25)(8/25)=96/625>1/8.

The Poincare variational inequality, applied to f, now gives the claimed lower bound. The same one-coordinate test applies to the d-dimensional posterior. Finally C_P<=C_LS follows by linearizing LSI at a constant function, so the LSI lower bound follows without an additional mixing argument.

## Consequence and limitations

Fix any c>0 and any dimension with c log d>=25/2. Letting R grow shows that the target ratio and the dimension cannot, by themselves, bound a worst-observation posterior LSI constant. Setting R=d makes the lower bound exponential in d^2 while keeping the observation polynomial in d. Thus the proposed route that replaces a bounded support radius by the prior LSI constant cannot be valid uniformly over observations.

This does not exclude another polynomial sampling algorithm: the explicit posterior here is a two-branch truncated-Gaussian construction and can be sampled efficiently when its description is provided. It does not refute a high-probability-over-observations theorem. Let $T\in(0,\infty]$ and let $u\ge0$ be continuous on $\mathbb R^n\times[0,T)$, of class $C^2_1$ on $\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$, and satisfy $u_t-\Delta u=0$ in $\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$. Then, with $\Phi(x,t)=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/(4t)}$, $u(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y,t)u(y,0)\,dy$ for all $x\in\mathbb R^n$ and $0<t<T$; in particular $\int e^{-|y|^2/(4t)}u(y,0)dy<\infty$ for every $t<T$. Consequently a nonnegative solution in this class with $u(\cdot,0)\equiv0$ vanishes identically, and two nonnegative solutions with the same initial values coincide -- no growth hypothesis is needed, one-sided boundedness replaces it. (Widder 1944 for $n=1$; the general statement, with arbitrary nonnegative initial traces given by Borel measures when continuity at $t=0$ is dropped, is due to Widder and Aronson; the divergence-form analogue is Aronson's.)

[Lemma 14 (Special case of the result in \cite{halko2011finding}) of arXiv:2609.02790, 'Full-Model Optimality for Tunable Linear Generative Priors in Compressed Sensing'] Let
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n),    \sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_n>0,$
and fix \(1\le k\le m-2\). Partition
\[
    \Sigma=
    \begin{pmatrix}
    \Sigma_1 & 0\\
    0 & \Sigma_2
    \end{pmatrix},
    \qquad
    \Sigma_1\in\mathbb R^{k\times k},
    \qquad
    \Sigma_2\in\mathbb R^{(n-k)\times(n-k)}.
\]
Let \(\Omega\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\) be a standard Gaussian matrix and
partition it as
\[
    \Omega=
    \begin{pmatrix}
    \Omega_1\\
    \Omega_2
    \end{pmatrix},
    \qquad
    \Omega_1\in\mathbb R^{k\times m},
    \qquad
    \Omega_2\in\mathbb R^{(n-k)\times m}.
\]
Let \(Y=\Sigma\Omega\), and let \(P_Y\) denote the orthogonal projector
onto \(\operatorname{range}(Y)\). Then
\[
   \mathrm E_{\Omega}
    \bigl\|(I-P_Y)\Sigma\bigr\|_F^2
    \le
    \left(1+\frac{k}{m-k-1}\right)
    \|\Sigma_2\|_F^2 .

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Homogenisation of the Green function at all scales plus the DGFF argument. Result: The quenched Green function of the random conductance model in d=2 is g_eff log|x-y| + O(1) up to the scale where homogenisation holds; the concentric decomposition needs the O(1) error to be controlled uniformly over all dyadic scales near a point, which is a quenched local limit theorem at every scale. This is available for uniformly elliptic ergodic conductances by Andres-Deuschel-Slowik type estimates for the heat kernel, so the intermediate level sets (which only need two-point covariances) follow the DGFF proof with g replaced by g_eff. The extremal-process cluster law, however, depends on the local geometry of the conductances around the maximiser and is therefore itself random (not a constant law), which changes the STATEMENT of the Theorem 9.3 analogue: the cluster law becomes a random law indexed by the environment at the maximiser. This suggests the problem as posed needs reformulation for the extremal process. Obstruction: The analogue of the cluster law is environment-dependent; the statement of Theorem 9.3 must be modified before it can be proved.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0010-dgff-over-an-ergodic-uniformly-elliptic-random-conductance-model-level
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved
title: Attempt on DGFF over an ergodic uniformly elliptic random conductance model: level sets and extremal process

[Lem magee of arXiv:2412.00593, 'A new approach to strong convergence II.\\The classical ensembles'] Fix $L,M\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ with $L+M\ge 1$, let $\lambda\vdash L$ and 
$\mu\vdash M$, and let $w(U^N_1,\ldots,U^N_r)$ be any word
in i.i.d.\ Haar-distributed elements of $\mathrm{U}(N)$. 
Then there exists a rational function $\Psi$ such that
\begin{alignat*}{2}
	&\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}} \pi_{\lambda,\mu}(w(U^N_1,\ldots,U^N_r))]
	&&= \Psi(\tfrac{1}{N}),\\
	&\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}} \pi_{\bar\lambda,\bar\mu}(w(U^N_1,\ldots,U^N_r))]
	&&= (-1)^{L+M}\Psi(-\tfrac{1}{N})
\end{alignat*}
for all $N\ge L+M$, where $\bar\lambda,\bar\mu$ denote the conjugate 
partitions of $\lambda,\mu$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In computational complexity theory, the space hierarchy theorems are separation results that show that both deterministic and nondeterministic machines can solve more problems in (asymptotically) more space, subject to certain conditions. For example, a deterministic Turing machine can solve more decision problems in space n log n than in space n. The somewhat weaker analogous theorems for time are the time hierarchy theorems.

Here a spherical t-design averages every polynomial of degree<=t exactly as normalized uniform surface measure does. Then every other set Cprime of N distinct points on the same sphere satisfies sum_(x,y in Cprime,x!=y)f(||x-y||^2)>=sum_(x,y in C,x!=y)f(||x-y||^2). This is the energy inequality of Theorem1.2, printedp104/PDFp6, of Cohn-Kumar math/0607446v2. In particular it applies to f(r)=exp(-beta*r/2) for beta>0. Existence of the comparator C at the specified dimension and cardinality is a hypothesis; the inequality does not supply such a configuration at arbitrary N. The statement records the optimal-energy comparison, rather than the additional strict-potential equality and uniqueness conclusions of the source theorem.

[Proposition prop:9 of arXiv:2512.09219, 'Strong confluence of geodesics in Liouville quantum gravity'] Fix a bounded open set $U$. Set $\varepsilon_n=2^{-n}$ for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$. Then almost surely, the following holds for all $n$ large enough. First, with $\mathcal{H}_n=((\frac{\varepsilon_n}{2})^{1/\chi}\mathbb{Z}^2)\cap U$, for all $u\in U$, there exists a $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z}\in \mathcal{H}_n$ such that $D_h(u,\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})\leq \varepsilon_n / 2$.

  Further, for any fixed $\alpha>0$, there exist random $0<\boldsymbol{\varphi}<\boldsymbol{\psi}<\alpha/20$ depending only on $U$ and $\alpha$ such that the following almost surely holds for all $n$ large enough. For all $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z}\in \mathcal{H}_n$, all $w\in U$ satisfying $D_h(w,\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})\geq \alpha$, and every $D_h$-geodesic $\Gamma_{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},w}$, there exists a $(z,r)\in \mathbb{C}\times [\varepsilon_n^{1/(2\chi')},\varepsilon_n^{1/ (4\chi')}]$ 
  satisfying the following properties.
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item  There exists a $z'\in z+\mathcal{Z}$ such that for the points $u_+,u_-,v_+,v_-$ corresponding to $z'$ and the radius $\rho r/A^2$, the event $\mathscr{X}^{u^+,v^+}_{u_-,v_-}$ occurs.
  \item 
    With $P_+=\Gamma_{u_+,v_+}, P_-=\Gamma_{u_-,v_-}$ being the unique $D_h$-geodesics corresponding to the points $u_-,u_+,v_-,v_+$ associated to the $z'$ above and with $\tau^-<\tau^+$ being such that $P_-\cap P_+=\Gamma_{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},w}\lvert_{[\tau^-,\tau^+]}$, we have $[\tau^-,\tau^+]\subseteq [\boldsymbol{\varphi},\boldsymbol{\psi}]$. 
  \item  $P_+$ (resp.\ $P_-$) intersects $\Gamma_{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},w}$ on its left (resp.\ right) side.
  \item We have $P_+\cup P_- \subseteq B_{\varepsilon_n^{1/(4\chi')}}(P_+\cap P_-)$.
  \item  
    The set $B_{16(2048\varepsilon_{n})^{1/\chi'}}(\Gamma_{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},w}\lvert_{[\tau^--2(25\times 2048\varepsilon_{n})^{\chi/(4\chi')},\tau^+ + 2(25\times 2048\varepsilon_{n})^{\chi/(4\chi')}]})$ does not intersect any of $u_-,u_+,v_-,v_+$.
 \end{enumerate}
