Version 1, 20 October 2026. Target 1, kind moved. Proofs (unaudited).
All claims below depend on the preceding unaudited C032-C041 calculations
as specified. They require the reviewer's independent check. This is a
bounded-observable result, not an expansion of the infinite raw exact
reciprocal mean. Literature novelty is not asserted.

Let a=1/(3pi), b=1/(6pi^2), and

    A=(2u+a)D+u^2 D^2,
    B=(10u+6a/5+b/u)D+(11u^2+12au/5+a^2/2)D^2
                                +(4u^3+au^2)D^3+(u^4/2)D^4,
    C=B-A^2/2=(8u+a/5+b/u)D+(4u^2-3au/5)D^2.

Let P_s be the semigroup of dV=(2V+a)ds+sqrt(2)V dW, and f(u)=1-exp(-u).
Use C039's global hybrid Gaussian/ReLU kernel Q_n for the reciprocal
U=1/(n theta). Fix theta0 in (0,pi], T<infinity.

## C042: accumulated local weak defect, with no reciprocal upper cutoff

For any deterministic v_k in [0,T], put g_k=P_(v_k)f. Uniformly in
N<=Tn, with U_k the hybrid chain started at U0=1/(n theta0),

    sum_(k=0)^(N-1) E| (Q_n-P_(1/n))g_k(U_k)
                                          -Cg_k(U_k)/n^2 |
                                             <=C_(theta0,T)/n. (1)

The v_k need not be monotone. This is a local-defect estimate along the
chain, sufficient for telescoping bounded tests. It contains no stopping
boundary correction and uses no finite raw reciprocal moment of the exact
network.

### Weighted semigroup derivative bounds

The affine solution V_v^u=V_v^0+uJ_v, J_v=exp(v+sqrt(2)W_v), gives

    D^j g_v(u)=(-1)^(j+1) E[J_v^j exp(-V_v^0-uJ_v)], j>=1.

For every nonnegative integer r and positive integer j,

    sup_(0<=v<=T,u>=0) u^r |D^j g_v(u)| < infinity.             (2)

For r=0 use E J_v^j. For r>0 use (uJ_v)^r exp(-uJ_v)<=r^r exp(-r)
and the finite lognormal moment E J_v^(j-r), uniform for v in [0,T].
Also 0<=g_v<=1. These are uniform all-state bounds, stronger than merely
bounded unweighted derivatives on fixed reciprocal compacts.

### The small-angle expansion with constants uniform in u

Fix the small-angle threshold epsilon of the hybrid kernel and set
theta=1/(nu)<=epsilon, allowing arbitrarily large u. In C032's normalized
concentration box, T_theta(z)=theta/output_angle is between fixed positive
constants, with uniformly bounded coordinate derivatives of every fixed
order needed below. By the chain rule and (2),

    |D_z^ell [g_v(uT_theta(z))]|<=C_T min(u,1), 1<=ell<=5.     (3)

For u<=1 every term contains u^j with j>=1 and a bounded derivative.
For u>=1 use (2) with r=j and the positive lower bound on T_theta.
The same bounds apply to the further finitely many weighted derivatives
needed for the theta-expansion coefficients and their mean-coordinate
variation. No derivative of g_v of order zero is asserted to decay.

Repeat C032's fourth-order centered sample-average expansion, retaining
(3). Its scaled Taylor remainder is C_T min(u,1)n^(-3/2). Freezing the
third- and fourth-moment coefficient at theta=0 costs at most
C_T min(u,1)sqrt(theta)/n. The covariance and coordinate multiplier
second-order theta remainders cost C_T min(u,1)theta^2. Deleted bounded
test terms cost C_T n exp(-cn), uniformly in u. Their polynomial Taylor
terms have the same exponential control by uniform row moments and (3).

The baseline zero-angle coefficients remain precisely C030's terms,
uniformly in u, by the same Taylor expansion and (3). The deterministic
map has displacement

    u theta/F(theta)-u=a/n+b/(n^2 u)+O(1/(n^3 u^2)),

which is O(1/n) uniformly for theta<=epsilon. Its scalar test Taylor
remainder after scaling is bounded by C_T(1+1/u+1/u^2)/n^2, exactly as
in C036. Thus the identical explicit operators A,B satisfy

    | n(Q_n-I)g_v(u)-Ag_v(u)-Bg_v(u)/n |
      <=C_T[n^(-3/2)+(1+1/u+1/u^2)/n^2+n exp(-cn)],
                                      theta=1/(nu)<=epsilon.  (4)

In simplifying, min(u,1)/sqrt(u)<=1 and
min(u,1)theta^2<=C(1+1/u+1/u^2)/n^2 were used. The constants in (4)
are independent of any upper cutoff on u. This uniformity is the new
step beyond C036; it is justified by the derivative decay in (2).

### The diffusion step and the large-angle step

The functions Ag_v,A^2g_v,A^3g_v are uniformly bounded by (2), since
their coefficients are polynomials multiplying positive-order derivatives.
Their Ito martingale coefficients are bounded as well, using the bounds
on u times their first derivatives. Iterated Dynkin identities therefore
give, with h=1/n,

    P_h g_v=g_v+hAg_v+h^2 A^2g_v/2+O_T(h^3),                 (5)

uniformly for all u>=0. One can first localize the nonexplosive linear SDE
and then remove the localization by boundedness; no assertion of a
globally analytic semigroup is needed. Combining (4)-(5) proves the
pointwise small-angle defect bound

    |(Q_n-P_h)g_v-Cg_v/n^2|
       <=C_T[n^(-5/2)+(1+1/u+1/u^2)/n^3+exp(-cn)].           (6)

If theta>epsilon, then u<=1/(n epsilon). The hybrid ratio U_next/u is
bounded, so |Q_n g_v-g_v|<=C_T u<=C_T/n by the bounded first derivative.
Also |P_hg_v-g_v|<=h||Ag_v||_infinity<=C_T/n. From the displayed formula
for C and 1/u=n theta<=n pi, |Cg_v(u)|/n^2<=C_T/n on this range.
Consequently the defect is at most C_T/n for large angles.              (7)

### Sum the defects

C039 gives E theta_k^p<=C_(p,T)/(k+1)^p, and on every hybrid state
1/U_k=n theta_k. Sum (6) at the small-angle states, using the full
positive moment bounds as upper bounds. The resulting terms are

    C_T n^(-3/2), C_T/n^2,
    (C_T/n^2)sum_(k<N)1/(k+1)<=C_T log(n+1)/n^2,
    (C_T/n)sum_(k<N)1/(k+1)^2<=C_T/n,
    C_T n exp(-cn).

For (7), C039 at p=2 bounds the expected number of large-angle visits
by epsilon^(-2)sum E theta_k^2<=C_T. Its total contribution is C_T/n.
All displayed smaller terms are O(1/n), proving (1).

## C043: the terminal bounded-observable rate

For fixed t>0, N=floor(nt), let theta_N be the exact width-n Gaussian
zero-bias ReLU angle with fixed theta0 in (0,pi]. Define its observable
to be f(1/(n theta_N)) on nondegenerate paths and zero after killing.
Then, as n tends to infinity,

    E[f(1/(n theta_N));alive]
       =E[f(V_t^0)] + (D_t/(2pi))log(n)/n+O_(theta0,t)(1/n),   (8)

where

    D_t=D P_t f(0)=E[exp(t+sqrt(2)W_t-V_t^0)]>0.

Any other fixed bounded cemetery value changes (8) only exponentially
through time N, by the same hybrid coupling. In particular the leading
bounded-observable bias is positive and is of order log(n)/n, rather
than a pure c(t)/n expansion. The O(1/n) coefficient is not identified.

Proof. Set t_n=N/n and G_k=P_((N-k)/n)f. The exact semigroup relation
G_k=P_(1/n)G_(k+1) and the Markov property of the hybrid chain give

    E f(U_N)-P_(t_n)f(U0)
      =sum_(k=0)^(N-1) E[(Q_n-P_(1/n))G_(k+1)(U_k)].          (9)

All tests are bounded. Apply (1) to conclude that (9) equals

    (1/n^2)sum_(k=0)^(N-1) E[(C G_(k+1))(U_k)]+O(1/n).      (10)

The k=0 term is O_(theta0,t)(1/n): its singular part is bounded by
C/(n^2 U0)=C theta0/n, and the other terms are smaller. For k>=1,
C041's proof applies also to the one-step shifted test G_(k+1).
Explicitly, its first derivative differs from D_t by at most
C_t[(k+1)/n+u], because |t_n-t|<=1/n. Multiplying by theta_k and
using theta_k U_k=1/n and E theta_k<=C/(k+1) shows a bounded total
weighted error after summation. C040 gives

    sum_(k=1)^(N-1) E theta_k=(1/a)log(n)+O_(theta0,t)(1).

Thus the singular part of (10) is
(b/a)D_t log(n)/n+O(1/n). The remaining parts of C contribute O(1/n),
by bounded first and second test derivatives and the hybrid reciprocal
moment bounds (4) in C040. Since b/a=1/(2pi), this identifies (10).

Finally U0=1/(n theta0). Bounded D P_s f and bounded Af imply

    |P_(t_n)f(U0)-P_t f(0)|<=C_(theta0,t)/n.

This includes the initial-angle and fractional-layer effects at the
remainder order. The global hybrid coupling through N steps fails with
probability at most C_t n exp(-cn). Since f and its cemetery value are
bounded, transfer to the exact chain changes the expectation by that
order, which is smaller than 1/n. This proves (8).

## Scope and review priority

No exact-chain raw reciprocal moment is claimed or used. The proof
performs its martingale estimates on a finite-moment regularization,
then transfers bounded observables. The estimate is for the specified
smooth bounded test, not a total-variation, Wasserstein, joint-output or
full-path quantitative rate. Independent review should check (4)'s
uniformity in unbounded u, the hybrid coupling, and the covariance
calculation underlying B before accepting (8).","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:48d5412d05f2566420246d906fe5e2cb5ea63da0a7aee9e2d7460ec5d88ae3f3","revision_digest":"sha256:a5743e2223b4ebc3751fde05957ac8fc241d52a9e0e7d13e0723bf1478d3eb00","source_id":"own-work:T244-w691-C043:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body: PROVED (separable case of the bounded-density quadratic-form conjecture, 2026-09-22). If Q(X)=sum_j lambda_j X_j^2 is diagonal in the independent coordinates X_j (densities <=1) and has at least three eigenvalues with |lambda_j|>=1, then Q(X) has a density bounded by pi, and pi is attained within this class (X1^2+X2^2+X3^2 with X_j uniform on [-1/2,1/2] has density 2 pi sqrt(y) on (0,1/4], equal to pi at y = 1/4; X1^2+X2^2 alone has density pi on (0,1/4] but only two coefficients). Proof: among three eigenvalues of modulus >=1, two share a sign (pigeonhole); each squared term lambda X^2 has density <= y^{-1/2}; two same-sign terms convolve to a density <= B(1/2,1/2)=pi (Beta integral); convolving the remaining independent terms cannot increase the sup (Young). Sharpness: one large eigenvalue gives density y^{-1/2} (unbounded); two opposite-sign give a logarithmic singularity (unbounded). The GENERAL non-separable case remains OPEN: it reduces to a uniform L1 bound on the characteristic function, but the per-direction oscillatory decay integral e^{isx^2}f dx = O(|s|^{-1/2}) is NOT uniform over densities <=1 (for each s there is an admissible f with |integral|>=1/2), so the coupled case needs the joint oscillatory-integral analysis (resolution of singularities). Paper: Downloads/Quadratic_Form_Bounded_Density_paper.pdf.

body:
PRIVATE CONDITIONAL RESOLUTION, author-recorded, sources not re-fetched. Aldous-Steele (2004) ask whether the minimal spanning forest of a homogeneous Poisson process in R^d is connected for d >= 3 and suspect it is not in high dimension. Lyons-Peres-Schramm's criterion (Ann. Probab. 2006) makes the free MSF a single tree when there is no percolation at criticality and the infinite cluster is unique above criticality; for the Poisson-Boolean (Gilbert) model uniqueness above criticality is classical and absence of percolation at the critical radius in high dimensions follows from the lace expansion for the random connection model (Heydenreich-van der Hofstad-Last-Matzke 2019). If the LPS criterion transfers verbatim to Poisson point processes, the MSF IS a single tree for d large, the reverse of the source's suspicion. Two verifications remain: the exact hypotheses of the LPS criterion in the continuum, and the exact statement of the high-dimensional continuum result. Treat as a lead with sign, not a theorem.
Homogeneous Poisson process in R^d, d large
LPS tree criterion; continuum lace expansion (both to be verified against the papers)
title: The minimal spanning forest of a Poisson process in high dimension should be a single tree (conditional, opposite to the source's guess)

body: [Defn 4 of arXiv:2506.21829, 'Some notes on Lamperti's recurrence of stochastic sequences'] The states of Markov chain $\mathscr{P}$ are said to form connected domain if for any $i\geq1$ there are $j_1(i)$ and $j_2(i)$, $0\leq j_1(i)<i<j_2(i)\leq\infty$ such that $p_{i,k}>0$ for all $j_1(i)\leq k\leq i-1$ and $i+1\leq k\leq j_2(i)$, and $\sum_{k=j_1(i)}^{j_2(i)}p_{i,k}=1.$
title: Definition 4 of arXiv:2506.21829

has the same law as a GPU process starting from $R_0$ red balls and $B_0$ blue balls. In particular, almost surely $N_{T_n}^R + N_{T_n}^B = \sigma_1+ \dots + \sigma_n$, for all $n\ge 1$.

[Lem inv_sigma of arXiv:2604.23751, 'Large deviation principles for pattern-avoiding permutations, and limit shapes for constra'] Let $\sigma$ be a $321$-avoiding permutation, and $((a_1,b_1),\dots,(a_k,b_k))$ be its list of strict RL minima. 
    Let also $\pi_1^\sigma$ and $\pi_2^\sigma$ be the associated measures on $[0,1]$,
    and $\rho_1^\sigma$ and $\rho_2^\sigma$ be their densities.
    We have:
    \[\inv(\sigma)=\sum_{i=1}^k (a_i-b_i) = n^2 \int_0^1 x \left( \rho^\sigma_1(x)-\rho^\sigma_2(x) \right) \mathrm{d}x \,.\]

[Lem 5 of arXiv:2512.05687, '$L^p$-Boltzmann-Gibbs principle \\ via Littlewood-Paley-Stein inequality'] Let $p\ge 2$.
For a function $F=F(t,\eta)$ on $[0,T]\times \mathcal{X}_{N,m}$, we have
\begin{align}  
E_{\mu_{N,m}}\Big[ \sup_{t\in [0,T]} \Big| \int_0^t L_0F(s,\eta_s) ds\Big|^p \Big]
\le C_p T^{(p-2)/2} \int_0^T E^{\mu_{N,m}}\Big[ \{\Ga(F(t,\cdot))\}^{p/2} \Big]dt,
\end{align}
where $C_p>0$ is uniform in $N$, $m\in \R$ and $\ga\in\R$.
In particular, if we take $F$ such that $-L_0F(s,\eta)=V(s,\eta)$ from a given $V$ 
on $[0,T]\times \mathcal{X}_{N,m}$ satisfying $E^{\mu_{N,m}}[V(s,\cdot)]=0$
for each $s\in [0,T]$, then we have
\begin{align}   
E_{\mu_{N,m}} & \Big[ \sup_{t\in [0,T]} \Big| \int_0^t V(s,\eta_s) ds\Big|^p \Big] \\
& \le C_p T^{(p-2)/2} \int_0^TE^{\mu_{N,m}}
\Big[ \{\Ga((-L_0)^{-1}V(t,\cdot))\}^{p/2} \Big] dt.
\notag
\end{align}
See Section \ref{sec:3.1} below \eqref{eq:1.IT} for the existence of $(-L_0)^{-1}$
noting the condition (SG) in Section \ref{sec:1.20.4}.

body:
[Lemma 24 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] If $p = \omega(1/m)$ then
  $p\,(1-p)^m\,(T_{m,p} - T_{m,0})$ converges
  in law to an exponential distribution
  with rate $1$.
  \begin{proof}
    Fix $t < 0$ and recall definition \eqref{eq:extra term}.
    The reciprocal of the
    moment-generating function of
    $p\,(1-p)^m\,(T_{m,p} - T_{m,0})$ is
    \begin{align*}
      \frac{1}{I_{m,p}(p\,(1-p)^m\,t)}
      &=
      (1-p)^{-m} - (1-p)^{-m} \int_0^1 p\,m
      \left(1-x\right)^{m\exp(p\,(1-p)^m\,(-t))-m}
      \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1} dx \\
      &=
        (1-p)^{-m} - (1-p)^{-m} \int_0^1 p\,m
      \left(1 + x\,t\,p\,m\,(1-p)^m\right)
      \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1} dx + o(1)
    \intertext{where we have used the binomial approximation
      $(1-x)^\alpha = 1 - \alpha \, x + O(\alpha^2)$, uniform in $x$,
      and a first-order expansion
      $m\exp(p\,(1-p)^m \, (-t)) - m = p\,m\,(1-p)^m\,(-t)
      + O(p^2\,m\,(1-p)^{2m})$.
      Together these give
      $(1-x)^{m\exp(p\,(1-p)^m\,(-t)) - m}
      = 1 + x\,t\,p\,m\,(1-p)^m + O(p^2\,m^2\,(1-p)^{2m})$.
      This error suffices because, upon distribution to form another integral,
      we are left with a trivial term
      $O(p^3\,m^3\,(1-p)^m) \int_0^1 \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1} dx =
      O((p\,m)^3 \, e^{-2pm}) = o(1)$, which we have written above.
      The remaining steps involve the dominated convergence theorem:
      }
      &=
        (1-p)^{-m} - (1-p)^{-m} \int_0^{pm}
      \left(1 + x\,t\,(1-p)^m\right)
      (1-x/m)^{m-1}\, dx + o(1)\\
      &= (1-p)^{-m} - (1-p)^{-m} \underbrace{\int_0^{pm} 
          \left(1-x/m\right)^{m-1} dx}_{1-(1-p)^m}\\
      &\quad\, -
        {\underbrace{\int_0^{pm}
          x\,t
          \left(1-x/m\right)^{m-1} dx}_{t+o(1)}} + o(1) \\
      &= 1 - t + o(1).
    \end{align*}
    The \textsc{mgf} of a rate $1$ exponential is
    $(1-t)^{-1}$, so we are done by Theorem \ref{thm:convergence}.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 24 of arXiv:2605.14206

[Corollary 14 of arXiv:2604.07207, 'Mixing times of step-reinforced random walks'] Let $J \subset \NN_+$ be a non-empty subset. For $n\geq 1$, write $N_J(n):=\sum_{k\in J} N_k(n)$. For any $\alpha \in (0,1)$, any $n\geq 1$ and $\varepsilon>0$, one has
$$
\PP\left(\left|\frac{N_J(n)}{n}-\sum_{k\in J} \theta_k\right| \geq \varepsilon \right) \leq C_0 e^{-C n},
$$
where $(\theta_k)_{k\geq 1}$ are defined in (\ref{limNkn}), and $C_0=C_0(\alpha,\varepsilon,J)$ and $C=C(\alpha,\varepsilon,J)$ are positive constants. In particular, for any $\alpha \in (0,1)$, any $n\geq 1$ and $\varepsilon>0$, one has
$$
\PP\left( \left|\frac{\sum_{\ell\geq 0}N_{2\ell+1}(n)}{n} - \frac{1-\alpha}{2 } \ _2F_1(1,\alpha^{-1};\alpha^{-1}+1; \frac{1}{2})\right| \geq \varepsilon \right) \leq C_1 e^{-C_2 n},
$$
where $C_1=C_1(\alpha,\varepsilon)$ and $C_2=C_2(\alpha,\varepsilon)$ are positive constants.

body:
[Prop weighted of arXiv:2607.00311, 'Thermal Concentration and Poisson--Dirichlet Edge Statistics for Random-Lattice Gibbs Ense'] Assume $n\ge3$.
Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to[0,\infty)$ be an even Borel function such that $f$ and $f^2$ are integrable.
For $L\in\mathbb X_n$, define
$$
S_f(L)=\sum_{\bm u\in L_{\operatorname{prim}}^\sharp} f(\bm u),
$$
where $f(\bm u)$ means $f(\bm v)$ for either representative of $\bm u$.
Then, with respect to the random choice of $L$ according to $\mu_n$, the
mean and variance of $S_f(L)$ are given by 
$$
\mathbb E_{\mu_n}S_f(L)=
\frac{1}{2\zeta(n)}\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(\bm x)\,d\bm x
$$
and
$$
\operatorname{Var}_{\mu_n}(S_f(L))=
\frac{1}{2\zeta(n)}\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(\bm x)^2\,d\bm x.
$$

body:
PROOF OF THE STATED SCOPED RESULT; independent audit pending. For a nearest-neighbour walk on Z^d with iid increments and mean e1 drift u>0, starting at zero, stop at longitudinal +/-L or transverse distance L^3. For some theta>0 and all sufficiently large integer L, the chance of exiting anywhere but the +L face is at most exp(-theta L)+exp(-u^2(L^3-1)/8), and hence below L^(-M) for every fixed M at large L. An exponential supermartingale handles backward exit; bounded iid increments and Hoeffding handle the delayed forward hit. The proof requires iid increments and does not infer the analogous bound from annealed velocity in a general random environment.
Homogeneous nearest-neighbour iid increments
Strictly positive e1 drift
Start at zero; boxes and stopping rule as stated

[Theorem 1 (Matrix Bernstein) of arXiv:2604.27119, '\Large Applied Random Matrix Theory\relatedversion'] Consider a statistically independent family $(\mtx{X}_1, \dots, \mtx{X}_n)$
of $d_1 \times d_2$ random matrices, real or complex, 
that are centered and uniformly bounded: $\Expect[ \mtx{X}_k ] = \mtx{0}$ and $\norm{ \mtx{X}_k } \leq B$ for each index $k$.
Form the sum, and calculate its matrix variance statistic:
\begin{equation} 
\mtx{S} \coloneqq \sum_{k=1}^n \mtx{X}_k
\quad\text{and}\quad
v(\mtx{S}) \coloneqq \norm{ \Expect[ \mtx{SS}^* ] } \vee \norm{ \Expect[ \mtx{S}^*\mtx{S} ] }.
\end{equation}
Then the spectral norm of the sum satisfies the probability inequalities
\begin{gather} 
\Expect \norm{\mtx{S}} \leq \sqrt{2 v(\mtx{S}) \log(d_1 + d_2)} + \frac{1}{3} B \log(d_1 + d_2); \\

\Prob{ \norm{\mtx{S}} \geq t} \leq (d_1 + d_2) \exp\left( \frac{-t^2/2}{v(\mtx{S}) + Bt/3} \right)
\quad\text{for $t \geq 0$.}

\end{gather} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Matrix Bernstein

body:
[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:cost}, problem~\eqref{eq:WOT}
admits a unique minimizer $\pi^*\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)$, and there exists a pair of
potentials $(\phi,\psi)\in L^1(\mu)\times L^1(\nu)$ such that
\begin{align*}
c(x,\rho)+\varepsilon H(\rho\,\|\,\nu)
&\;\geq\;\phi(x)+\rho(\psi),
&&\forall\,(x,\rho)\in\Xc\times\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d),
\\
c(x,\pi^*_x)+\varepsilon H(\pi^*_x\,\|\,\nu)
&\;=\;\phi(x)+\pi^*_x(\psi),
&&\mu\text{-a.e.\ }x.
\end{align*}
In particular, $\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)} J(\pi) = \mu(\phi)+\nu(\psi)$.

Moreover, the optimal coupling is given explicitly in
terms of the dual potential $\psi$ and the cost gradient $\hat{c}$
of~\eqref{eq:def-chat} by
\begin{equation}
\frac{d\pi^*}{d(\mu\otimes \nu)}(x,y)
\;=\;
\exp\!\left(\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\big(\phi(x)+\psi(y)
-\delta_m c(x,\pi^*_x)(y)\big)\right).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the disintegration of the optimal coupling is 
\begin{equation}
\pi^*_x(dy)
\;=\;
\frac{1}{Z(x)}\,
\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\,\delta_m c(x,\pi^*_x)(y)
\;+\;\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\,\psi(y)\right)\nu(dy),
\qquad \mu\text{-a.e.\ }x,
\end{equation}
where $Z(x)$ is the normalizing constant
\[
Z(x)\;=\;\int\exp\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\delta_m c(x,\pi^*_x)(y)
+\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\psi(y)\right)\nu(dy)
\;=\;\exp\!\big(-\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\phi(x)\big).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 6 of arXiv:2605.30560

Let $\mathcal{K}^d$ be the space of non-empty compact convex subsets of $\mathbb{R}^d$ equipped with the Hausdorff metric and Borel $\sigma$-algebra. The Boolean model with grain distribution $\Theta$ on $\mathcal{K}^d$ and intensity $\gamma > 0$ is the random closed set $Z := \bigcup_{(x, K) \in \Phi} (x + K)$, where $\Phi$ is a Poisson point process on $\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathcal{K}^d$ with intensity measure $\gamma \lambda_d \otimes \Theta$. For a bounded window $W \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, $Z^W := \bigcup_{(x, K) \in \Phi_W} (x + K)$ is the union of grains whose reference points fall in $W$.

Furthermore, we the set $R_{\operatorname{rel}}:=\{S_{k} \ \vert \  2 \dim(f^{-1}(r))+\dim(S_{k}) = n \ \forall \ r \in f^{-1}(S_{k})\}$ is referred to as the set of relevant strata.

Let X be a random variable with finite mean mu = E X and finite variance sigma^2 = Var X. Then for every t > 0, P(|X - mu| >= t) <= sigma^2 / t^2; when sigma > 0 this is equivalent to P(|X - mu| >= k sigma) <= 1/k^2 for every k > 0 (for sigma = 0 the standardized form fails: X = mu almost surely and the left side is 1). The inequality is sharp: for t >= sigma the variable taking the values mu - t and mu + t with probability sigma^2 / (2 t^2) each and the value mu otherwise has mean mu, variance sigma^2 and P(|X - mu| >= t) = sigma^2 / t^2 exactly. It gives no information for t <= sigma, and it is the classical route to the weak law of large numbers: for i.i.d. X_i with finite variance, P(|(X_1 + ... + X_n)/n - mu| >= eps) <= sigma^2 / (n eps^2) -> 0.
E X^2 < infinity (finite variance); with only a finite mean use Markov on |X - mu|

body:
[Lemma lem:primitive-lattice-shell of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix integers $D\geq3$ and $1\leq s<D$.  A sublattice
$\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^D$ is called primitive when
$\Lambda=(\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Lambda)\cap\mathbb Z^D$, and we
write
\[
 \Lambda^\perp=
 (\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Lambda)^\perp\cap\mathbb Z^D.
\]
An orientation of $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Lambda$, together with
the standard orientation of $\mathbb R^D$, induces the orientation on
$\Lambda^\perp$ used below.
Write
\[
 \mathcal X_j=\operatorname{SO}_j(\mathbb R)\backslash
 \operatorname{SL}_j(\mathbb R)/\operatorname{SL}_j(\mathbb Z)
\]
for Horesh--Karasik's shape space of oriented rank-$j$ lattices, equipped
with the invariant quotient Radon measure induced from Haar measure, with any
fixed normalization.  Write $\operatorname{Gr}^+(s,D)$ for the oriented
Grassmannian of $s$-planes in $\mathbb R^D$, equipped with its invariant
measure.  Let $\Phi\subset\operatorname{Gr}^+(s,D)$ and
$E\times F\subset\mathcal X_s\times\mathcal X_{D-s}$ be positive-measure
boundary-controllable sets (BCSs) in the sense of
[HoreshKarasik2023], with $E$ and $F$ relatively
compact.  Relatively compact domains with piecewise $C^1$ boundary suffice.
Let $N(T)$ be the number of oriented primitive rank-$s$ lattices
$\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^D$ such that
\[
 \begin{gathered}
  \dfrac{T}{2}<\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda)\leq T,\qquad
  \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Lambda\in\Phi,\\
  \operatorname{shape}(\Lambda)\in E,\qquad
  \operatorname{shape}(\Lambda^\perp)\in F.
 \end{gathered}
\]
Then, as $T\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 N(T)=\Theta_{D,s,\Phi,E,F}(T^D).

[Definition 17 of arXiv:2608.25785, 'Proper Actions on Homogeneous Spaces of the Upper Triangular Matrix Group via Coarse Geome'] Let $S$ be a set.
    A family $\mathcal{E}\subset \mathcal{P}(S\times S)$ is called a \emph{coarse structure} on $S$ if it satisfies the following five conditions (see Section \ref{subsection:notation} for notation):
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\diag(S) \in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item $E \in \mathcal{E}$ implies $E^\dagger \in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item $E_1, E_2 \in \mathcal{E}$ implies $E_1 \cup E_2 \in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item $E_1, E_2 \in \mathcal{E}$ implies $E_1\circ E_2\in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item $E \in \mathcal{E}$ implies $E' \in \mathcal{E}$ for each $E' \subset E$.
    \end{enumerate}
    The pair $(S, \mathcal{E})$ is called a \emph{coarse space} and 
    each element of $\mathcal{E}$ is referred to as an \emph{coarse entourage} or simply an \emph{entourage}.
    An entourage $E\in \mathcal{E}$ is called \emph{symmetric} if the equality $E=E^\dagger$ holds.

The auxiliary covariance flow is not claimed as new matrix-factorization theory. Novelty of the DDPM transfer relative to the broader literature has not been established.

## Statement and metric

Let d>=2, E^T E=I_2, P=EE^T, and U be the 2-by-3 matrix of unit equilateral vertices. Then U1=0 and UU^T=(3/2)I_2. The teacher is q_a=(1/3)sum_j N(a E u_j,I_d). Put V=sqrt(2/3)U^T, so V^T V=I_2 and V^T1=0. Parameterize student means as

    M=a sqrt(3/2) Z V^T,      Z in R^(d by 2).

This is a scaled isometry onto the centered mean space H={M:M1=0}. Run population Euclidean GD on H, physical step h=1, for the canonical covariance-I equal-weight mixture score. Its DDPM excess loss is

    F_a(M)=E_{X~q_a}||s_M(X)-s_teacher(X)||^2.

The architecture and DDPM identity are from Shah--Chen--Klivans, arXiv:2307.01178v1, Eqs. (5),(9). Initial Z_0 has independent N(0,1/d) entries. For 0<rho<=1/100 set

    sigma=1/(80 sqrt(d)),
    S=10 log(100/(sigma rho)).

There is an absolute c>0 such that, whenever

    0<a^2<=c rho exp(-76(S+1)),                         (1)

at N=ceil(3S/(2a^2)), with probability at least 2/5,

    min_{O in O(2)} ||Z_N-E O||_F<=rho/2.              (2)

Choosing a^2 to be a constant times rho*(sigma*rho/100)^760 makes N polynomial in d and 1/rho, with a very large fixed exponent. This is an existence complexity bound, not a useful sharp rate. For a well-separated original equilateral teacher of known radius R, choose OU time exp(-t)=a/R. The initialization and GD do not require E. Zero-centroid parameters are imposed throughout; independently initialized unrestricted means are not covered.

Each EO represents an equilateral triple, possibly after a label transposition. Thus (2) enters a small tube of one of the two cyclic equilateral subspaces used in C05, with projected radius 1+O(rho). This is not yet angular convergence or empirical learning.

## 1. Uniform high-noise vector field

On ||Z||_F<=5, the centered score expansion gives

    F_a(Z)=(a^4/4)||ZZ^T-P||_F^2+O_{C^2(Z)}(a^6).     (3)

The student and teacher center covariances are a^2 ZZ^T/2 and a^2 P/2. Their score corrections start at covariance times X, giving the leading term by Gaussian integration. The integrated loss is even in a: replace a and X by their negatives. Hence its next term is order six.

The remainder bounds in (3) are independent of d. A first or second directional derivative depends only on the columns of Z,E and its differentiation directions, a subspace of dimension at most twelve. Projected data are a mixture of unit-covariance Gaussians with bounded means. Derivatives of the three-logit softmax posterior, at each fixed order, are bounded by polynomials in those projected coordinates, uniformly for bounded Z and small a: probabilities lie in [0,1], and their derivatives introduce only bounded center factors and linear coordinates. Taylor's integral remainder, including two Z derivatives, is therefore integrable with a dimension-independent bound. This is the C05 expansion with explicit normalization.

The metric of the parameterization is (3a^2/2) times the Frobenius metric. Consequently exact physical-step GD is

    Z_{n+1}=Z_n+gamma[f(Z_n)+R_a(Z_n)],
    gamma=2a^2/3,
    f(Z)=(P-ZZ^T)Z,     ||R_a(Z)||_F<=C a^2,          (4)

on that ball. Indeed grad_Z F=a^4(ZZ^T-P)Z+O(a^6), and the inverse metric is 2/(3a^2). No empirical gradient is substituted here.

## 2. Covariance flow and quantitative entry

Let Z(s) solve Z'=f(Z) with Z(0)=Z_0. For y=||Z||_F^2,

    y'=2tr(Z^T P Z)-2tr((Z^T Z)^2)<=2y-y^2.

Thus ||Z(s)||_F<=max(||Z_0||_F,sqrt(2)) for s>=0. Its covariance Q=ZZ^T satisfies

    Q'=PQ+QP-2Q^2.                                    (5)

Write A=E^T Z_0, D=(I-P)Z_0 and

    W=e^s E A+D,
    H=I+(e^(2s)-1)A^T A+2s D^T D.

Then

    Q=W H^(-1) W^T.                                   (6)

Indeed H is positive definite for s>=0, W'=PW, and H'=2W^T W. Differentiation verifies (5) and the correct initial condition, so uniqueness proves (6). We do not claim W H^(-1/2) solves the factor ODE; matrix square roots and derivatives need not commute. Only its covariance is used.

Assume ||Z_0||_F<=4 and s_min(A)>=sigma. Put

    G=I-A^T A+2s D^T D,
    K=e^(-2s) A^(-T) G A^(-1).

Then ||G||<=17+32s and H=e^(2s)A^T(I+K)A. Formula (6) gives

    E^T Q E=(I+K)^(-1),
    tr((I-P)Q)<=2 e^(-2s)||D A^(-1)||_F^2
                 <=32 e^(-2s)/sigma^2,                 (7)

when ||K||<=1/2. Also ||K||<=e^(-2s)(17+32s)/sigma^2. Positivity of G is not assumed.

Set x=100/(sigma rho)>=1. The function (17+32s)e^(-2s) decreases for s>=0. At s=S=10log x, using log x<=x, and hence also at every s>=S,

    ||K|| <=(337/10000)rho^2 x^(-17)<=rho^2/16,
    tr((I-P)Q)<=(32/10000)rho^2 x^(-18)<=rho^2/256.   (8)

The planar singular values of Z are square roots of the eigenvalues of (I+K)^(-1). Since |(1+k)^(-1/2)-1|<=2|k| for |k|<=1/2, the planar orthogonal Procrustes error is at most 8||K||^2. Adding the perpendicular norm squared yields

    min_O ||Z(s)-EO||_F^2
      <=8rho^4/256+rho^2/256<=9rho^2/256<rho^2/16.    (9)

Thus flow entry occurs by S and persists for all later flow times.

## 3. A constant-probability initialization event

B=sqrt(d)A is a 2-by-2 standard Gaussian matrix, with columns b_1,b_2. Consider the simultaneous event

    ||Z_0||_F<=4, ||B||_F<=4, ||b_1||>=1/2, |g|>=1/10,

where g is the component of b_2 along a unit vector perpendicular to b_1. Conditional on b_1, g is standard normal. The failure probabilities of these four conditions are at most 1/8,1/4,1/8,1/10. The first two use Markov and E||Z_0||_F^2=2, E||B||_F^2=4. The third uses P(||b_1||<1/2)=1-exp(-1/8)<1/8. The fourth uses the Gaussian density bound P(|g|<1/10)<=1/(5sqrt(2pi))<1/10.

Their union bound is 3/5; no independence between the events is needed. On their complement,

    |det B|=||b_1|| |g|>=1/20,
    s_min(B)=|det B|/s_max(B)>=1/80.

Thus the hypotheses of Section 2 hold simultaneously with probability at least 2/5, uniformly in d>=2.

## 4. Exact DDPM GD perturbation on the entry interval

On the radius-5 ball f has derivative norm L=1+3*25=76 and norm at most B_0=5+125=130. On the event above the flow stays in radius 4. Its one-step Euler defect is at most (L B_0/2)gamma^2, by integrating the Lipschitz difference of f along its flow.

Until a DDPM iterate exits radius 5, comparison of (4) with the exact flow at s_n=n gamma gives

    e_{n+1}<=(1+L gamma)e_n+C a^2 gamma
                                  +(L B_0/2)gamma^2,
    e_0=0.

The geometric series and gamma=2a^2/3 imply, for an absolute C_1,

    e_n<=C_1 a^2 exp(L n gamma).                       (10)

Take a below an absolute cutoff so gamma<=1. For n<=N, n gamma<=S+1. Choosing c in (1) small enough makes (10)<=rho/4. This also prevents exit: the stopped recursion bounds the next iterate within rho/4 of a flow point of norm at most 4, hence inside radius 5. Induction establishes the recursion throughout n<=N, without circularly assuming confinement. At s_N>=S, (9) and (10) prove (2).

Since exp(76S)=(100/(sigma rho))^760, the Gronwall factor is polynomial in d and 1/rho. Gronwall is used only over this logarithmic rescaled entry interval. Applying the same comparison over the much longer angular interval would not supply a polynomial bound; that gap is not hidden here.

## Scope and checks

Remaining steps are quantitative angular anti-concentration for the perturbed entry map, accumulated angular forcing from decaying normal error, and empirical gradient stability through the slow angular phase. Unrestricted centroid dynamics require a separate argument. C06 blocks an automatic extension to arbitrary triangles. Full Target 2 remains open.

Independent review should focus on the metric in (4), noncommuting covariance formula (6), block estimates, and uniform remainder in (3). Exact symbolic checks validate algebra, not the analytic remainder or independent correctness. Source paper Eqs. body: The three-large-eigenvalue threshold is sharp. With X_i iid Uniform[-1/2,1/2] (density 1) and diagonal Q=sum lambda_j X_j^2: one eigenvalue (X^2) gives density 1/sqrt(y), UNBOUNDED (measured peak grows 52->206 as histogram bins double); two opposite-sign eigenvalues (X1^2-X2^2) give a logarithmic singularity, UNBOUNDED (peak grows 7.5->10.3); two same-sign eigenvalues (X1^2+X2^2) give density exactly pi, BOUNDED; three eigenvalues of any signs give a bounded density (measured plateau near 3.1-3.2). So >=3 large eigenvalues is the exact threshold for a bounded density, and the constant is O(pi) for this family.
title: The three-large-eigenvalue threshold is sharp. With X_i iid Uniform[-1/2,1/2] (density 1) and diagonal Q=sum lambda_j X_j^2: one eigenvalue

[Prop hook of arXiv:2510.23430, 'On the Martin boundary for discrete TASEP'] Let $\mathcal A=(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k), \mathcal B=(\beta_1, \dots, \beta_l)$ be sequences satisfying (equation ineq of the paper), $s$ denote the number of $i$ such that $\beta_i=1$ and $\tilde{\Phi}^{\mathcal A,\mathcal B}(z)=z^{-s}\Phi^{\mathcal A,\mathcal B}(z)$. We have $M_n^{\mathcal A,\mathcal B}(\lambda)=0$ unless $\lambda_n\geq s$ and
$$
\frac{M_n^\Phi(\lambda+s^n)}{\tilde\Phi^{\mathcal A,\mathcal B}(0)^{n}G_{\lambda+s^n}^{(0,-p)}(1^n)}=\sum_{\mu} g_{\mu}^{(p,0)}(x_1, \dots, x_k)g_{\lambda'/\mu'}^{(p,0)}(y_{s+1}, \dots, y_l)=\sum_{\mu} g_{\lambda/\mu}^{(p,0)}(x_1, \dots, x_k)g_{\mu'}^{(p,0)}(y_{s+1}, \dots, y_l),
$$
where $x_i=\frac{\alpha_i-p(1+\alpha_i)}{1+\alpha_i}$, and $y_i=\frac{\beta_i-p}{1-\beta_i}$.

 In particular, $M_n^\Phi(\lambda)=0$ unless $\lambda_i\leq l$ for every $i>k$, that is, $M_n^\Phi$ is supported by partitions inside the infinite "hook" with $k$ infinite rows and $l$ infinite columns.

body: [Proposition of arXiv:2609.02213, 'Invariant subspaces for free linearizations of Lipschitz maps'] Let $M$ be a bounded metric space, let $f:M\to M$ be Lipschitz, and let $e\in M$. Then $T_{f,e}$ is hypercyclic if and only if it is weakly mixing.

[Thm Hall's matching theorem of arXiv:2506.12171, 'The multinomial dimer model'] Suppose that $G$ is a finite bipartite graph with bipartition $(B,W)$ such that $|B| = |W|$. There exists a dimer cover of $G$ if and only if there is no set $C\subset W$ such that 
    $$N(C) = \{v\in B : \exists\, c\in C, (v,c)\in E\}$$
    satisfies $|N(C)| < |C|$. We call $U:=C \cup N(C)$ satisfying these conditions a \textit{counterexample} in $G$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Hall's matching theorem

body: Let (F_n)_{n >= 0} be a discrete-time filtration. A process (C_n)_{n >= 0} is predictable (previsible) with respect to (F_n) if C_n is F_{n-1}-measurable for every n >= 1, and C_0 is F_0-measurable (deterministic if F_0 is trivial). Predictable processes are exactly the integrands for which the discrete stochastic integral (martingale transform) (C . M)_n = sum_{k=1}^n C_k (M_k - M_{k-1}) is again a martingale whenever M is a martingale and each C_k is bounded. [standard, e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales]
title: Predictable (Previsible) Process

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Let $\alpha \in (1/2,1)$. Suppose $U:\T^d \to\R^d$ is a $C^{\alpha-}(\T^d)$ multiscale finite range random velocity field; that is, $U$ satisfies Assumption~\ref{asmp:main for autonomous}, and \eqref{eq:main theorem hypothesis} holds for some $p > \frac{d}{\alpha-1/2}$.
    
    Then almost surely, the ODE~\eqref{eq:main ODE autonomous data} admits a unique Lipschitz flow away from the random zero level set of $U$.
    More precisely, for all $\ep>0$, there exists an almost surely finite random constant $M_\ep>0$ such that for any $\tau \in [0,1]$ and any two integral curves of $U$ avoiding $Z_\ep$ on $[0,\tau]$---$X^i: [0,\tau] \to \T^d\backslash Z_\ep$ with $\dot X^i = U(X^i)$---we have the bi-Lipschitz stability estimate
    \begin{equation}
    
    M_\ep^{-1} d_{\T^d}(X^1_0, X^2_0) \leq d_{\T^d}(X^1_t ,X^2_t) \leq M_\ep d_{\T^d}(X^1_0, X^2_0)\qquad \mbox{for all $t \in [0,\tau]$}.
    \end{equation}
    In particular, the solution to~\eqref{eq:main ODE autonomous data} is uniquely determined up until hitting $Z$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.05931

[Lemma 24 (Stability of absorption) of arXiv:2608.16752, 'Absorption Probabilities for Random Convex Hulls: Distribution-Freeness via the Wall-Cross'] Let $q_1, \dots, q_N \in \R^d$ be such that
$0 \notin \partial \Conv(q_1, \dots, q_N)$. Then there is $\delta > 0$
such that every tuple $q'_1, \dots, q'_N \in \R^d$ with
$|q'_m - q_m| < \delta$ for all $m$ satisfies
$$
0 \in \Conv(q'_1, \dots, q'_N)
\iff
0 \in \Conv(q_1, \dots, q_N).
$$

[Definition Discrete-discrete coupling of arXiv:2411.13964, 'Long-time analysis of a pair of on-lattice and continuous run-and-tumble particles with ja'] \label
 {def:discrete_discrete_coupling}

  Let $Y^L_0 = (y^L_0, (\sigma^1_0, \sigma^2_0))$ and
  $\tilde Y^L_0 = (\tilde y^L_0, (\tilde \sigma^1_0, \tilde
  \sigma^2_0))$ in $\{1, \ldots, L\} \times \Sigma$ be given. Now turn to
  constructing a coupling between two discrete processes $Y^L$ and
  $\tilde Y^L$ with respective initial states $Y^L_0$ and
  $\tilde Y^L_0$. Let $s^1, s^2, \tilde s^1, \tilde s^2$ be four
  independent Markov jump processes with the transition rates of
  figure (fig:single_speed_transition_rates_slowman_2016 of the paper)
  (resp. (fig:single_speed_transition_rates_slowman_2017 of the paper)) and
  respective initial states
  $\sigma^1_0, \sigma^2_0, \tilde \sigma^1_0, \tilde
  \sigma^2_0$. Define
  $\tau_i = \inf \{t \ge 0 : \sigma^i(t) = \tilde \sigma^i(t)\}$ and
  set
\begin{align*}
  \sigma^i(t) = s^i(t) \text{ for all } t \ge 0, \quad \quad \tilde \sigma^i(t) = \tilde s^i(t) \text{ for } t < \tau_i \text{ and } \tilde \sigma^i(t) = s^i(t) \text{ for } t \ge \tau_i.
\end{align*}

Let $N_1^L$ and $N_2^L$ be two independent Poisson clocks with
parameter $\gamma_L = (L-1) / \ell$ independent of
the~$\sigma^i$. Finally, set
$Y^L = \mathcal Y (\sigma^1, \sigma^2, N_1^L, N_2^L, y^L_0, L)$ and
$\tilde Y^L = \mathcal Y (\tilde \sigma^1, \tilde \sigma^2, N_1^L, N_2^L,
\tilde y^L_0, L)$.
title: Discrete-discrete coupling

[Theorem 5 (Identification of coefficients, Proposition \ref{prop-invariant-exp}, Theorem \ref{thm-consistency}) of arXiv:2604.04100, '\LARGE Learning Equilibrium Fluctuation Expansions from Overdamped Langevin Dynamics'] Assume $d=1$. Let $\mu_\varepsilon$ denote the invariant measure of \eqref{SDE-0} and let $(b_m(F))_{0\le m\le n}$ be defined as in Theorem \ref{thm-longtime-intro}. Then for every $F\in C^{n+1}(\mathbb R)$ satisfying \eqref{assump-F}: 
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] There exists $\varepsilon_0\in (0,1]$ and $ (B_m(F))_{0\leq m\leq n} $ such that for every $\varepsilon\in (0,\varepsilon_0)$,
\begin{equation*}
\int_{\mathbb R} F(x)\mu_\varepsilon(\mathrm{d}x)
= \sum_{m=0}^n \varepsilon^{m/2} B_m(F) + R_{n}(F,\varepsilon),
\end{equation*}
where the remainder satisfies
$$
\bigl|R_{n}(F,\varepsilon)\bigr|\le C(n,F)\varepsilon^{(n+1)/2},
$$
for some constant $C(n,F)>0$ independent of $\varepsilon$.
\item[(ii)]  If the initial law of $\xi_0$ satisfies
$$
\mathbb P(\xi_0>0)=\mathbb P(\xi_0<0)=\frac12,
$$
then for every $m\in\{0,\dots,n\}$, we have
$$
B_m(F)=b_m(F).
$$
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Identification of coefficients, Proposition \ref{prop-invariant-exp}, Theorem \ref{thm-consistency}

[Lemma lem:Hilbert-moment-reduction of arXiv:2608.11084, 'Sharp Frobenius-Norm Concentration for Sample Moment Tensors'] Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_N\) be independent centered random vectors in a real
Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), let \(q\ge2\), and assume that
\[
\|Z_i\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)}
:=
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\mathbbm{E}\|Z_i\|_{\mathcal H}^q
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{1/q}
<\infty,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,N.
\]
Then
\[
\bigg\|
\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i
\bigg\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)}
\asymp
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\|
\bigg(
\sum_{i=1}^N \|Z_i\|_{\mathcal H}^2
\bigg)^{1/2}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\|_{L_q}
+
\sup_{\|h\|_{\mathcal H}=1}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\|
\sum_{i=1}^N
\langle h,Z_i\rangle_{\mathcal H}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\|_{L_{q/2}}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 51 (Counterexample to simultaneous mixed-degree extraction) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Let $Q=2,d=1$, and let $e,h$ be orthonormal in $\cK_1$.  Consider
\begin{equation}
 x_1=\alpha e+h,\qquad x_2=e^{\odot2},\qquad 0<\alpha\ll1.
 
\end{equation}
Then $\cN_1(F)=\mathbb Re$, so $h$ belongs to the canonical Gaussian
factor.  Nevertheless the first reduced
promotion is made at weight two and its range contains a nonzero $e\odot h$ component.
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb U_2^{-1}M_{2,\mathcal U}^{[J]}
 \not\subset\cW_2(\cN(F))
 
\end{equation}
already after the first promotion.  Moreover the defect is not confined to
the module: for this packet the simultaneous reduced trajectory promotes
$h$ itself after finitely many further steps, so that its terminal residual
at weight one is zero, whereas
$G^{\can}=I_1(h)\ne0$.

[Prop Bertini prop of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] Consider the situation of Theorem (scheme case of the paper) where we assume $r:= \dim Y > 0.$
Then, there exists a Zariski-open subset $\Omega \subseteq \mathfrak{d}^r$ of ordered $r$-tuples $([s_1], \ldots, [s_r])$ for which
\[
Z_i := V_Z(s_1, \ldots, s_i), \ \ \ X_i = V_X(f^*s_1, \ldots, f^*s_i) = X \times_{Z} Z_i,
\]
\[
Y_i := V_Y(s_1|_Y, \ldots, s_i|_Y), \ \ \ E_i := V_E(f^*s_1|_E, \ldots, f^*s_i|_E) = E\times_Z Z_i \subseteq X_i,
\]
satisfies the following, for all $1 \le i \le r$
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] $X_i, Z_i, Y_i$, and $E_i$ are smooth of dimension $n-i, n-i, r-i, n-1-i$, respectively.
\item[(ii)] $Y_r$ is a finite non-empty collection of reduced points
\item[(iii)] If $f_i := f|_{X_i} : X_i \to Z_i$ is the restriction of $f$, then $f_i(E_i) = Y_i$.
\item[(iv)] $E_i$ is a smooth Cartier divisor on $X_i$ where $\mathcal{O}_{X_i}(-E_i) \simeq \mathcal{O}_X(-E)|_{X_i}$.
\item[(v)] The morphism $f_i : X_i \to Z_i$ is projective, birational, and has connected fibers, i.e., $f_i$ is a contraction morphism with exceptional divisor $\mathrm{Exc}(f_i)= E_i$ where $f_i : X_i \setminus E_i \xrightarrow{\sim} Z_i \setminus Y_i$
\end{itemize}

body: [Theorem 3.1 of arXiv:2603.27659, 'Operator Norm Bounds for Multi-leg Matrix Tensors and Applications to Random Matrix Theory'] Let $m,N\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\in\mathcal{P}([m])$. Let $M(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2})$ and $C(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2})$ be the quantities given in Definition 2.1. Then $\displaystyle N^{M(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2})}\leq\max_{A_{1},\ldots,A_{m}}\left|\left(\mathrm{Tr}_{\sigma_{1}}\otimes\mathrm{Tr}_{\sigma_{2}}\right)\left(A_{1},\ldots,A_{m}\right)\right|\leq N^{C(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2})},$ where the maximum is taken among all unitary matrices $A_{1},\ldots,A_{m}\in M_{N}(\mathbb{C})\otimes M_{N}(\mathbb{C})$. Here, for the graph $G_{\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{k}}$ of the permutations, $M(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{k})$ is the maximum over blue-edge configurations of the number of directed cycles, and $C(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{k})=\min_{G^{\prime}}R_{G^{\prime}}$, the minimum over full simple partial graphs $G^{\prime}$ (partial graphs keeping every rectangle and containing no directed cycle for any blue-edge configuration) of the number $R_{G^{\prime}}$ of colored edges removed to obtain $G^{\prime}$ (Definition 2.1).

body: In the mathematical field of graph theory, the Erdős–Rényi models are two closely related models for generating random graphs and the evolution of a random network. These models are named after Hungarian mathematicians Paul Erdős and Alfréd Rényi, who introduced one of the models in 1959. Edgar Gilbert introduced the other model contemporaneously with and independently of Erdős and Rényi. In the model of Erdős and Rényi, all graphs on a fixed vertex set with a fixed number of edges are equally likely. In the model introduced by Gilbert, also called the Erdős–Rényi–Gilbert model, each edge has a fixed probability of being present or absent, independently of the other edges. These models can be used in the probabilistic method to prove the existence of graphs satisfying various properties, or to provide a rigorous definition of what it means for a property to hold for almost all graphs.
title: Erdős–Rényi model

body: [Theorem thm: main left of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] The process $(U(r)-r,\, r\ge 0)$ is a homogeneous Feller process starting from $0$. For any $r>0$, $\frac{U(r)}{r}$ has distribution ${\mathcal B}(\frac{2-\widehat{\delta}+\delta}{2},\frac{\widehat{\delta}}{2})$. Conditionally on $U(0)=z>0$, the process $U$ stays constant then jumps at time $\mathrm{x}$ where  $\frac{{\mathrm x}}{z}$ has distribution ${\mathcal B}(1,\frac{\delta}{2})$. Conditionally on ${\mathrm x}=x$, $\frac{z-x}{U(x)-x}\sim {\mathcal B}(\frac{2-\widehat{\delta}+\delta}{2},1)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm: main left of arXiv:2411.04773

$$\underbrace{\mathfrak{S}_l\times\cdots\times \mathfrak{S}_l}_{m\text{ times}}:=\{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_n:\sigma(i)\equiv i\pmod m\quad\forall1\le i\le n\}$$
is a subgroup of $\mathfrak{S}_n$. 
Denote by $\sim_l\backslash U_{\mathfrak{S}_n}$ the uniform distribution over $\sim_l\backslash\mathfrak{S}_n$.

[Lemma 8 (Fourth moments for the cross-polytope) of arXiv:2605.11451, '2605.11451'] Let $X\sim \nu_{1,n}$ be uniform on $B_1^n$ and let $i\neq j$. Then
\begin{align}
 \E X_i^4
 &=\frac{24}{(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)(n+4)},\notag\\
 \E X_i^2X_j^2
 &=\frac{4}{(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)(n+4)}.
\end{align}
Consequently, for every $\theta\in\sphere$,
\begin{equation}
 \E\langle\theta,X\rangle^4
 =
 3\,\E X_1^2X_2^2+\bigl(\E X_1^4-3\,\E X_1^2X_2^2\bigr)\sum_{i=1}^n\theta_i^4,
\end{equation}
and the coefficient $\E X_1^4-3\,\E X_1^2X_2^2$ is strictly positive.

Let U be a connected open subset of C and f : U → C holomorphic and not constant. Then f(V) is open for every open V ⊂ U. More precisely, if z0 is in U and f - f(z0) has a zero of order m ≥ 1 at z0, then for every sufficiently small r > 0 there is δ > 0 such that every w with 0 < |w - f(z0)| < δ has exactly m preimages (counted with multiplicity, in fact m distinct simple preimages when r is small enough) in the disk |z - z0| < r. Consequences: a nonconstant holomorphic function on a connected open set cannot have locally constant modulus, real part, or argument, and an injective holomorphic map has nonvanishing derivative and holomorphic inverse. Connectedness can be replaced by: f is nonconstant on every connected component of U.

[Defn 11 (Compound laws) of arXiv:2605.18751, '\mytitle'] Let $Q$ and $F$ be probability measures on $\N_0$ and $\N$, respectively.
  
  Define
\begin{equation}
  
X=\sum_{i=1}^N J_i
\end{equation}
	where $N$ has law $Q$, and $(J_i)_{i\ge 1}$ is a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with law $F$, each independent of $N$. 
  
  Let $q_n \coloneqq Q(\{n\})$.  Conditioning on $N$ gives
	\[
	\prob(X=k)=\sum_{n\ge0} q_n\,F^{*n}(\{k\}), \quad k\in\N_0, 
	\]
where \(F^{*0}\coloneqq \delta_0\) and \(F^{*n}\coloneqq F^{*(n-1)}*F\) for \(n\ge1\).
title: Compound laws

\mathbb E(B_k^{(e)})\sim 
\phi'   \frac{(1+\varepsilon)^{(r-2)k}}{k^{(3/2)
\left(\binom r2 -1\right)}}p,
\]
where
\[
\phi'=\beta_{{r\choose2}-2} \phi.
\]

[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2511.14740, 'Marking and re-marking'] Let $\mathbf X$ be a random variable taking values in $\mathbb N^c$, $\mathsf A \in [0,1]^{c\times d}$ with columns $|\mathbf a_i| \leq 1$, and let $\mathbf Y = \mathsf A \circ X$ be the multinomial re-marking of $\mathbf X$ with parameters $\mathsf A$. Then we have the following.
\begin{enumerate}
\item  $\mathbb E \mathbf Y = \mathsf A \,\mathbb E \mathbf X$.
\item $\DispM( \mathbf Y) = \mathsf A \DispM(\mathbf X)\, \mathsf A^\top$.
\item $\Phi_{\mathbf Y}(\mathbf t) = \Phi_{\mathbf X}(\mathsf A^\top \mathbf t)$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let H be a real or complex Hilbert space and a: H × H → K (K = ℝ or ℂ) a sesquilinear form (bilinear in the real case, linear in the first and conjugate linear in the second argument in the complex case) such that: (boundedness) |a(u, v)| ≤ C‖u‖‖v‖ for all u, v ∈ H with C < ∞; (coercivity) Re a(u, u) ≥ α‖u‖² for all u ∈ H with α > 0. Then for every continuous conjugate-linear functional F on H (equivalently every f ∈ H via F(v) = ⟨f, v⟩) there is a unique u ∈ H with a(u, v) = F(v) for all v ∈ H, and ‖u‖ ≤ ‖F‖/α. The solution map F ↦ u is bounded with norm at most 1/α. No symmetry of a is assumed; if a is Hermitian and coercive, the statement is exactly the Riesz representation theorem for the equivalent inner product a. The weaker hypothesis |a(u, u)| ≥ α‖u‖² also suffices. Standard use: for a bounded Lipschitz domain Ω, the form a(u, v) = ∫_Ω (A∇u·∇v̄ + b·∇u v̄ + c u v̄) on H = H_0^1(Ω) is bounded and coercive under uniform ellipticity of A, bounded b, c, and a smallness or sign condition making Re a(u,u) ≥ α‖u‖_{H^1}²; then the weak Dirichlet problem has a unique solution.
H is a Hilbert space (complete)
a is sesquilinear and bounded on all of H × H
a is coercive: Re a(u,u) ≥ α‖u‖² with α > 0, on the whole space H
F is a continuous (conjugate-)linear functional on H

[Definition 20 (joint typical subspace) of arXiv:2609.03736, '2609.03736'] For the operators associated with $(K,L)$, put
$z_n=z_{n,a_n}$ and $q_n=q_{n,a_n}$.
Since $q_n$ is $\mathfrak S_n$-equivariant, it defines the pointwise
multiplier
\begin{equation}
 (\widehat q_nf)(b\mathfrak S_n)
 =bq_nb^{-1}f(b\mathfrak S_n).
 
\end{equation}
Put $E_n=q_n(\CC^m)^{\otimes n}$ and
\begin{equation}
 p_n=z_n\widehat q_n.
 
\end{equation}
The range of $p_n$ is the \emph{joint typical subspace}.  Equivalently,
it is the $z_n$-isotypic summand of
$\Ind_{\mathfrak S_n}^{\mathsf B_n}E_n$, represented inside the full Fourier
model.  Let $\Omega_n$ denote its set of $\mathsf B_n$-types and let
$\Theta_n$ be the map induced by $\mathsf S_{t_n}$ on this summand.
title: joint typical subspace

[Dfn 20 of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] A \textbf{partial positive semidefinite} matrix with \textbf{block sizes} $k$, $\ell$ and $m$ is a $5$-tuple
	\[(Q_{11},Q_{12},Q_{22},Q_{23},Q_{33}) \in \rmM_{k+} \times \rmM_{k,\ell}\times \rmM_{\ell+} \times \rmM_{\ell,m}\times \rmM_{m+}\]
	with the property that both of the two-by-two-block matrices
	\[\left[\begin{array}{cc} Q_{11} & Q_{12}\\ Q_{12}^\ast & Q_{22}\end{array}\right] \qquad \hbox{and} \qquad \left[\begin{array}{cc} Q_{22} & Q_{23}\\ Q_{23}^\ast & Q_{33}\end{array}\right]\]
	are positive semidefinite.
	
	A partial positive semidefinite matrix is \textbf{partially nonsingular} if both of those two-by-two-block matrices are nonsingular; otherwise it is \textbf{partially singular}.
	
	We write $\PPSD_{k,\ell,m}$ for the space of partial positive semidefinite matrices with block sizes $k$, $\ell$ and $m$, and $\PPSD^\circ_{k,\ell,m}$ for the further subset of its partially nonsingular members.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For the product measure mu_p on {0,1}^E with each coordinate independently open with probability p and an increasing event A depending on finitely many edges, Russo's formula states d/dp mu_p(A) = sum_{e in E} mu_p(e is pivotal for A), where e is pivotal for A at a configuration omega if flipping the state of e changes the indicator of A. When different edges carry different parameters p_e, the analogous statement is d/dp_e mu(A) = mu(e is pivotal for A). This identity converts questions about how quickly an event's probability crosses a threshold into questions about counting or bounding pivotal edges, which is the basic engine behind sharp-threshold theorems when combined with the Margulis-Russo framework and tools such as hypercontractivity, the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm influence bound, or the OSSS inequality. Russo's formula does not by itself give sharp thresholds; it requires monotonicity of A, since non-monotone events need a more complex signed-pivotal generalization; and it is stated for independent-coordinate measures, so applying it to dependent measures such as the random-cluster model requires a separate Glauber-dynamics-based generalization rather than the naive product-measure formula. Typical failure: Using Russo's formula on a non-monotone event without its signed-pivotal generalization, or applying the plain product-measure version of the formula to a dependent measure such as a random-cluster or Ising Gibbs measure, where the correct analogue requires the generator of an associated Glauber dynamics rather than a simple coordinatewise derivative; both errors produce a derivative formula that looks structurally similar but is simply wrong. Canonical reference: Russo, 1981, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Margulis, 1974, Problemy Peredachi Informatsii; Grimmett, Percolation, second edition, 1999, Springer, Chapter 2.
independent (product) Bernoulli measure, possibly with coordinate-dependent parameters
A is a monotone (increasing) event depending on finitely many coordinates
differentiability in p, automatic for finite-dimensional product measures

[Theorem thm:dir_E[multi-edges] of arXiv:2604.05921, 'Simplicity of random hypergraphs'] Let $\forall e \in E: \delta_e^{\textnormal{tail}} \leq \frac{1}{2}n \mathds{E}[d_U^{\textnormal{out}}]$ and $\delta_e^{\textnormal{head}} \leq \frac{1}{2}n \mathds{E}[d_U^{\textnormal{in}}]$ and let $R(\cdot)$ be as in (equation def:B of the paper). Then, for a uniformly random directed hypergraph with degree sequence $\vb*{d}$,
    \begin{align*}
        &\mathds{E}[M_n] = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{e \in E} \sum_{\substack{e' \in E\backslash\{e\}:\\\delta_{e'}=\delta_e}} \frac{(n\mathds{E}[d_U^{\textnormal{out}}]-2\delta_e^{\textnormal{tail}})!(n\mathds{E}[d_U^{\textnormal{in}}]-2\delta_e^{\textnormal{head}})!}{(n\mathds{E}[d_U^{\textnormal{out}}])!(n\mathds{E}[d_U^{\textnormal{in}}])!}\\
        &\hspace{1cm}\times \sum_{\substack{\vb*{a} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{tail}}}:\\\sum_{i=1}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{tail}}}ia_i = \delta_e^{\textnormal{tail}}}}  \frac{\delta_e^{\textnormal{tail}}!^2}{\prod_{k=1}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{tail}}} k!^{2a_k} }
        \sum_{\alpha(\cdot) \in R(\vb*{a})} (-1)^{\sum_{\vb*{x} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{tail}}}} (\sum_{i=1}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{tail}}} x_i - 1)\alpha(\vb*{x})} \\
     &\hspace{1cm}\times 
    \prod_{\vb*{y} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{tail}}}} \Bigg( \frac{1}{\alpha(\vb*{y})!} \Big(\frac{n\mathds{E}\big[\prod_{i=1}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{tail}}} (\mathds{1}_{\{d_U^{\textnormal{out}} \geq 2i\}}\frac{d_U^{\textnormal{out}}!}{(d_U^{\textnormal{out}}-2i)!})^{y_i} \big]\big(\sum_{i=1}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{tail}}} y_i-1 \big)!}{\prod_{i=1}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{tail}}} y_i!} \Big)^{\alpha(\vb*{y})} \Bigg)\\
    &\hspace{1cm}\times \sum_{\substack{\vb*{b} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{head}}}:\\\sum_{i=1}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{head}}}ib_i = \delta_e^{\textnormal{head}}}}  \frac{\delta_e^{\textnormal{head}}!^2}{\prod_{k=1}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{head}}} k!^{2b_k} }\sum_{\beta(\cdot) \in R(\vb*{b})} (-1)^{\sum_{\vb*{x} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{head}}}} (\sum_{i=1}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{head}}} x_i - 1)\beta(\vb*{x})}\\
     &\hspace{1cm}\times
    \prod_{\vb*{z} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{head}}}} \Bigg( \frac{1}{\beta(\vb*{z})!} \Big(\frac{n\mathds{E}\big[\prod_{i=1}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{head}}} (\mathds{1}_{\{d_U^{\textnormal{in}} \geq 2i\}}\frac{d_U^{\textnormal{in}}!}{(d_U^{\textnormal{in}}-2i)!})^{z_i} \big]\big(\sum_{i=1}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{head}}} z_i-1 \big)!}{\prod_{i=1}^{\delta_e^{\textnormal{head}}} z_i!} \Big)^{\beta(\vb*{z})} \Bigg).
    \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 39 (Identification of the Hilbert--Stein and primitive--Fock splittings) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Let
\[
 X_{n,a}=I_q(f_{n,a}),
 \qquad
 \sup_n\sum_{a=1}^{d}q!\norm{f_{n,a}}^2<\infty,
\]
choose $R>0$ with
$R^2\ge\sup_n\sum_aq!\norm{f_{n,a}}^2$, and run the spectrally reduced
feedback on $x_{n,a,q}=\sqrt{q!}\,f_{n,a}$ from the zero module.  Along every
subsequence on which the covariance and all the finitely many proper
self-contraction norms converge, one may extract a further subsequence
and choose a sufficiently slow diagonal $J(n)\to\infty$ such that, with
the corresponding active and
residual Wiener polynomials $A_n^{[J(n)]},B_n^{[J(n)]}$,
\[
 (A_n^{[J(n)]},B_n^{[J(n)]})
 \Longrightarrow(A_{\mathrm{FF}},G_{\mathrm{prim}}),
 \qquad X_n\Longrightarrow A_{\mathrm{FF}}+G_{\mathrm{prim}},
 \qquad
 G_{\mathrm{prim}}\indep A_{\mathrm{FF}}.
\]
If $\xi_a=[f_{n,a}]_{\mathcal U}\in\cH_q$, then, in the terminal
primitive--Fock representation,
\begin{align}
 A_{\mathrm{FF},a}
 &=\mathbb U_q^{-1}P_{\cD_q}\xi_a,
 \\
 G_{\mathrm{prim},a}
 &=\mathbb U_q^{-1}P_{\cK_q}\xi_a.
 
\end{align}
The second term belongs to the first Gaussian chaos over $\cK_q$; the
first is the orthogonal sum of all weighted sectors containing at least
two primitive particles.  In particular the split is intrinsic relative
to the represented packet and ultrafilter, and
\begin{equation}
 \Cov(G_{\mathrm{prim}})_{ab}
 =\ip{P_{\cK_q}\xi_a}{P_{\cK_q}\xi_b}_{\cH_q}
 =q!\,\Ulim\ip{p_{n,a}}{p_{n,b}},
 
\end{equation}
where $(p_{n,a})$ is any bounded representative of
$P_{\cK_q}\xi_a$.

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$'] Let $\rho>0$, $\zeta\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|\zeta|\leq \rho$, and let $B = B_{\rho,\zeta}$ denote a Brownian motion on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$, see \eqref{eq.B.SDE.rho.zeta}.  Let $B_0$ be a random matrix in $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ independent from the process $B$ and suppose that $B_0$ converges a.s.\ in $\ast$-distribution (see Definition \ref{def.*-dist}) to an operator $b_0$ as $N\to\infty$.

Then for fixed $t>0$, a.s.\ as $N\to\infty$, the empirical law $\mu_{B_0 B(t)}$ of eigenvalues of the Brownian motion $B_0 B(t)$ converges weakly to a deterministic measure $\mu_{b_0,t}$ (see Definition \ref{def:mub0t} and Section \ref{sect.Brown(ian).meas} below). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

In a finite resistor network whose contracted intermediate interfaces yield a series chain of independently wired layer networks, the sum of those wired layer resistances is at most the original effective resistance. Rayleigh monotonicity alone cannot justify the opposite upper bound. On s-a-t and s-b-t with resistances (1,M) and (M,1), respectively, the original resistance is (M+1)/2 and the wired layer sum is 2M/(M+1). Their ratio (M+1)^2/(4M) is unbounded. To upper-bound the original resistance using layer flows, the interface current distributions must match. This does not identify a DGFF limiting law or refute an upper bound constructed using matched flows.
Finite positive-resistance network
Wired layer terminal minima
Contracted quotient is a series chain

body: In mathematics, the well-ordering theorem, also known as Zermelo's theorem, states that every set can be well-ordered. A set X is well-ordered by a strict total order if every non-empty subset of X has a least element under the ordering. The well-ordering theorem together with Zorn's lemma are the most important mathematical statements that are equivalent to the axiom of choice. Ernst Zermelo introduced the axiom of choice as an "unobjectionable logical principle" to prove the well-ordering theorem. One can conclude from the well-ordering theorem that every set is susceptible to transfinite induction, which is considered by mathematicians to be a powerful technique.
title: Well-ordering theorem

Then there exists an irreducible algebraic curve $\mathcal X \subset X(M)$ and an ideal point of its smooth projective model such that the limiting characters on $\pi_1(M_i)$ are $\chi_i$. Let n >= 2, Omega in R^n open, and let A be a measurable matrix field with lambda|xi|^2 <= A(x)xi.xi and |A(x)xi.eta| <= Lambda|xi||eta| for a.e. x in Omega and all xi, eta (0 < lambda <= Lambda; A need not be symmetric or continuous). Let u in H^1_loc(Omega) be a weak solution of div(A grad u) = 0 in Omega. Then u has a representative that is locally Hoelder continuous: there exist alpha in (0,1) and C, depending only on n and the ellipticity ratio Lambda/lambda, such that for every ball B_R(x0) contained in Omega, (a) ess sup over B_{R/2}(x0) of |u| <= C (average over B_R(x0) of u^2)^{1/2}, and (b) |u(x) - u(y)| <= C (|x-y|/R)^alpha (average over B_R(x0) of u^2)^{1/2} for all x, y in B_{R/2}(x0). Part (a) also holds for subsolutions with u replaced by u^+. In general alpha cannot be taken close to 1, and u need not be Lipschitz; the statement is for scalar equations and fails for systems.

body: [Theorem 10 of arXiv:2609.03793, 'Typical martingale diverges on a co-$\sigma$-porous set'] Let $(S, \zeta)$ be a metric space, $\mathcal B(S)$ its Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and $\mu$ a probability measure on $\mathcal B(S)$. Assume that every non-empty open set in $(S, \zeta)$ has non-zero measure. body: A differential k-form on a smooth manifold M is a smooth section of the k-th exterior power of the cotangent bundle, Lambda^k T*M; at each point it is an alternating k-linear function on tangent vectors. In local coordinates omega = sum over increasing multi-indices I of f_I dx^I, where dx^I = dx^{i_1} wedge ... wedge dx^{i_k} and f_I are smooth. 0-forms are smooth functions; k-forms are the objects integrated over k-dimensional submanifolds.
title: Differential Form

[Definition of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] An infinitesimal non-commutative probability space of order $\nu$ is a $(\nu
  + 1)$-tuple $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi^{(0)}, \ldots, \varphi^{(\nu)})$, where
  $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi^{(0)})$ is a non-commutative probability space and
  $\varphi^{(i)} : \mathcal{A} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ are linear functionals
  such that $\varphi^{(i)} (1_{\mathcal{A}}) = 0$, for every $i = 1, \ldots,
  \nu$. The infinitesimal non-commutative distribution of order $n$ of $a \in
  \mathcal{A}$ is the $(n + 1)$-tuple $(\mu_a^{(i)} : \mathbb{C} \langle
  \mathbf{x} \rangle \rightarrow \mathbb{C})_{i = 0}^n$ of linear functionals,
  defined by
  \[ \mu_a^{(i)} (P) = \varphi^{(i)} (P (a)) \text{, \quad for every } P \in
     \mathbb{C} \langle \mathbf{x} \rangle \text{ and } i = 0, \ldots, \nu .
  \]

body: [Lemma lem-lf-resample-i-infty of arXiv:2411.19810, 'Radial conformal welding in Liouville quantum gravity'] Let $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}$. Suppose $\psi \sim \mathrm{LF}_\mathbb{H}^{(\alpha, i), (\beta, \infty)}$. If $U$ is a deterministic bounded neighborhood of $i$ disjoint from $\mathbb{R}$, then conditioned on $\psi|_{\mathbb{H} \backslash U}$, we have $\psi|_U \stackrel d= h + \mathfrak h + \alpha G_U(\cdot , i)$ where $h$ is a GFF on $U$ with zero boundary conditions, $\mathfrak h$ is the harmonic extension of $\psi|_{\mathbb{H} \backslash U}$ to $U$, and $G_U$ is the Green function of $h$. If instead $U$ is a deterministic neighborhood of $\infty$ bounded away from $i$, then conditioned on $\psi|_{\mathbb{H} \backslash U}$, we have $\psi|_U \stackrel d= h + \mathfrak h + (\frac\beta2 - Q) G_U(\cdot, \infty)$ where $h$ is a GFF on $U$ with zero (resp.\ free) boundary conditions on $\partial U \cap \mathbb{H}$ (resp.\ $\partial U \cap \mathbb{R}$), $\mathfrak h$ is the harmonic extension of $\psi|_{\mathbb{H} \backslash U}$ to $U$ with zero normal derivative on $\partial U \cap \mathbb{R}$, and $G_U$ is the Green function for $h$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem-lf-resample-i-infty of arXiv:2411.19810

Own-work draft; STATUS: proof (unaudited). Independent review pending. No novelty or target-completion claim. For f(x)=a ReLU(w x1+M x2), one observed training input e1 with label y>0, initialization a=0,w=1,M>0, and both layers trained by gradient flow, the equations are a'=(y-aw)w, w'=(y-aw)a, M'=0. The entire training prediction aw and training Gram K=a^2+w^2 are independent of M, while f(e2)=M a(t). The invariant w^2-a^2=1 and positive residual ensure a(t)>0 for every t>0. Against test law uniform on {e1,e2} and single-index teacher g(x)=x1, R(t)=[(aw-1)^2+M^2 a^2]/2 diverges with M at every fixed t>0. Frozen versus nonlinear unseen predictions also differ by M[(y^3/6)t^3+O(t^4)] near zero. This rules out a deterministic population control from training-only quantities without off-sample assumptions. It does not refute standard-Gaussian-initialization bounds and is not a double-descent example.
Unrestricted deterministic initialization, not standard initialization
M>0, y>0
Gradient flow with active gates on e1 and e2
title: Draft: T267 ReLU training Gram control leaves unseen predictions unbounded

[Proposition pro:Dacorogna of arXiv:2606.21391, 'Extreme points and faces in the moment problem'] Let $\mathbf{p}\colon X\to\mathbb{R}^d$ and $f\colon X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be arbitrary maps. The optimal 
value function $g_\mathrm{fin}\colon\mathbb{R}^d\to[-\infty,+\infty]$ is convex and satisfies $g_\mathrm{a.i.}=g_\mathrm{fin}$. 
If $f$ is bounded below by a $\mathbf{p}$-convex function, then $g_\mathrm{fin}>-\infty$ pointwise and 
$\env_\mathbf{p} f=g_\mathrm{fin}\circ\mathbf{p}$.

[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2606.26619, 'Ergodicity of stochastic reaction-diffusion equations on unbounded domains driven by space'] Suppose that (H2), (H4) and (H5) hold. 
If $\alpha > \frac{L_{\sigma}^4}{8}$, 
then for any $\lambda>0$ satisfying $\frac{\lambda^2}{8}<\alpha - \frac{L_{\sigma}^4}{8}$ and $\frac{\lambda^2}{4}<\alpha$, we have
\begin{align}
  \sup_{t\geq 0}\mathbb{E} [\Vert u(t)\Vert^2_{L^2_{\lambda}}] <\infty ,
\end{align}
for every bounded continuous initial value $f$ on $\mathbb{R}$. 
In particular, there exists a unique invariant measure in $L^2_{\lambda}$. Moreover, the solution is exponentially mixing with respect to the Wasserstein metric  $W_2$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

For finite Gaussian networks indexed by n, let X_n~N(0,C_n), P_n be a finite nonempty family of nonempty positively weighted paths, K_n=|P_n|, D_xi,n=min_p sum_v a_npv exp(xi X_nv), and F_n,beta(y)=-(1/beta)log sum_p exp[-beta log(sum_v a_npv exp(y_v))]. Suppose L_n->infinity, max_i(C_n)_ii=O(L_n), and medians of log D_xi,n divided by L_n converge to -lambda(xi) at fixed 0<=a<b. If beta_n>0 and log K_n/(beta_n L_n)->0, then lambda(b)-lambda(a)=-lim_n L_n^(-1) integral_a^b xi E tr[C_n Hess F_n,beta_n(xi X_n)] dxi. This conditional reduction does not evaluate the planar limit or assert pointwise derivative convergence.
Every covariance C_n is PSD and the Gaussian is centered
All path families finite and nonempty; weights deterministic and positive on supports
L_n->infinity; maximum variance O(L_n)
Fixed 0<=a<b; median exponent convergence at both endpoints

[Lemma lem6.2 of arXiv:2508.12951, '\textbf{On the central limit question for strictly stationary, reversible Markov chains}'] Suppose that for every ordered pair
$(a,p) \in (0,1)^2$, $J(a,p)$ is a positive integer; 
and suppose that 
\begin{equation}

\lim_{a \to 0+,\thinspace p \to 0+} a \cdot J(a,p)\ =\ 1\ .
\end{equation}
Suppose that for every ordered pair $(a,p) \in (0,1)^2$,
$\zeta^{(a,p)}_1, \zeta^{(a,p)}_2, \dots,
\zeta^{(a,p)}_{J(a,p)}$ are independent, identically distributed
integer-valued random variables, each with the probability function 
${\bf g}_{a,p}$ in eq.\ ((eq6.11 of the paper)) (with the same parameters $a$ and $p$).
Then 
\begin{equation}

p \cdot \sum_{k=1}^{J(a,p)} \zeta^{(a,p)}_k\
\to\ \mu_{P1sL}\ \ {\rm in\ distribution\ as}\ \  
a \to 0+,\  p \to 0 +.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem6.2 of arXiv:2508.12951

body:
[Lemma Wg of arXiv:2607.05418, 'On the Group Randomness of 0-1 Real Sequences from Binary Linear Codes'] Assume $d^\bot \geq 5.$ Then there exists a subset $\Gamma \subset \Gamma_{\ell,p}^2/\Sigma_p$ with
    $$\sharp\Gamma=\begin{cases}
        0 &(\ell \text{ odd})\\
        (\ell-1)!!(4^{\ell/2}) &(\ell \text{ even})
    \end{cases}$$
    such that
    $$p^{v_\gamma} W_\gamma=\begin{cases}
    \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^\ell p^{3\ell/2}n^{\ell/2} &(\gamma \in \Gamma)\\
    O_\ell(n^{2\ell-1}) &(\text{otherwise})
\end{cases}.$$
title: Lemma Wg of arXiv:2607.05418

[Lemma 24 (Estimates for the standard replacement) of arXiv:2608.25971, 'Positive \texorpdfstring{$\tau$}{tau}-bi-Ricci curvature and Mean curvature flow with surg'] Fix $0<\eta<1$ and an integer $m_0\geq2$.  After fixing
  $\alpha_0^*$ and the surgery parameters in
  Lemma~\ref{lem:surgery-taubiric-preservation}, the neck quality may be
  improved and the surgery radius decreased, without changing
  $\alpha_0^*$, so that there exist
  \begin{equation*}
  \eps_s>0,\qquad
  k_s\geq m_0+2,\qquad
  L_s\geq L_b,\qquad
  r_s>0,
  \end{equation*}
  and constants $c_s>0$, $C_m<\infty$, $0\leq m\leq m_0$, with the
  following property.

  If surgery is performed on an $(\eps,k,L)$-neck of radius $r$ satisfying
  \begin{equation*}
  \eps\leq\eps_s,\qquad
  k\geq k_s,\qquad
  L\geq L_s,\qquad
  r\leq r_s,
  \end{equation*}
  and if \eqref{eq:incoming-surgery-taubiric} holds on the incoming neck,
  then every changed point satisfies
  \begin{align}
    \widetilde P_{ij}^{(\tau)}
    &\geq
    \alpha_0^*\widetilde H
    |\widetilde\lambda_p-\widetilde\lambda_q|,
    \\
    \widetilde P_{ij}^{(\tau)}
    &\geq c_sr^{-2},
    \qquad
    \widetilde H\geq c_sr^{-1},
    \\
    |\widetilde A|^2-
    \left(\frac1{n-1}+\eta\right)\widetilde H^2
    &\leq
    -c_s\widetilde H^2,
    \\
    r^{m+1}|\widetilde\nabla^m\widetilde A|
    &\leq C_m,
    \qquad
    0\leq m\leq m_0.
    
  \end{align}
  The area removed from each changed neck is at least $c_sr^n$, and the
  replacement may be chosen so that
  \begin{equation}
    \min_{\widetilde M}\widetilde H
    \geq
    \min_MH.
  \end{equation}

  If $0<R\leq1$ and
  \begin{equation}
    r\leq\frac{c_sR}{n+\alpha_2},
  \end{equation}
  then the replacement preserves
  $\CC_\tau(R,(\alpha_0^*,\alpha_1,\alpha_2))$.

body: Let X be the passage time between fixed endpoints and X^L its value after resampling a block L, and let U_L be the event that the geodesic uses an edge of L. If the geodesic avoids L then the original path survives unchanged in the resampled field, so X^L <= X on the complement of U_L. Hence the positive part (X^L - X)^+ vanishes off U_L, and any functional of the form E[1(U_L) f((X^L - X)^+)] with f(0) = 0 equals E[f((X^L - X)^+)] - the indicator carries no information. Combined with exchangeability this gives E[((X^L - X)^+)^k] = (1/2) E[|X^L - X|^k] for every k >= 1.

[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2608.13631, 'The classical discrete laws near the mode:\\ complete local expansions for the negative bi'] Let $t_c$ be the vertex of the quadratic part of $A_1(\,\cdot\,;p)$.  Then
	\begin{equation}
		t_c=-\frac{1+q}{2p}=-\frac qp-\frac12,
		\qquad\text{so}\qquad
		\mu+t_c+\tfrac12=\frac{(r-1)q}{p} ,
	\end{equation}
	and the unit window $\bigl(\mu+t_c-\tfrac12,\ \mu+t_c+\tfrac12\bigr]$ contains exactly one
	integer, $\lfloor(r-1)q/p\rfloor$.  This integer is the upper mode of $\NB(r,p)$; two modes
	occur exactly when the endpoint $(r-1)q/p$ is an integer.

[Proposition 19 of arXiv:2605.30030, 'Critical exponents for planar random-cluster model with cluster-weight~$q=4$'] There exist constants~$C,c>0$ such that for every~$x,y\in \mathbb R^2$ satisfying~$\dst:=\min\{|x|,|y|,|x-y|, |x+y|\}>0$ and~$0<\delta<\eps<\dst/2$, we have 
\begin{align}\qquad
\Ll|\bc^\delta(\eps)^4\Ll(\widetilde\pi_2^\delta(x,y,\eps)+\widetilde\Delta^\delta(x,y,\eps)\Rr)
-a_\eps(x,y)\eps^{1/2}\left(\tfrac{ |y|^2}{|x|^2|x-y|\,|x+y|}\right)^{1/4}\Rr|&\le   C\pi_1^\delta(\eps,\dst)^4\left(\tfrac{\eps}{\dst}\right)^c + o_\delta(1),
\end{align}
where~$a_{\eps}(x,y)>0$ is a quantity that converges to an absolute constant~$a_0>0$ independent of~$x,y$ as~$\eps$ tends to $0$
and~$o_\delta(1)$ is a quantity converging to~$0$ as~$\delta$ tends to $0$.

[Proposition 9 (Lopatto--Otto Poisson approximation) of arXiv:2608.20101, '\bfseries Largest bulk gap of the complex Ginibre ensemble'] Fix \(\kappa>0\), \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/16)\), and a Borel set
\(A\subset\{z:|z|<1\}\) with \(\sup_{z\in A}|z|<1\). For all large \(n\), let
\(R_{n,\kappa}(a)\) be the unique radius satisfying
\begin{equation}
 K_n(a,a)\,\Pp\{\xi_n^{a,!}(D_{R_{n,\kappa}(a)}(a))=0\}
 =\kappa.
\end{equation}
Let \(\Xi_{n,\kappa}\) be the point process of the retained unit-disk
anchors \(a\), where \(a\in\xi_n\cap D_1\) is retained when
\(d_n(a)>R_{n,\kappa}(a)\). If \(\zeta_\kappa\) is a Poisson process of
intensity \(\kappa\,\mathrm d^2z\), then, for a constant depending on
\(A,\kappa,\varepsilon\),
\begin{equation}
 d_{\mathrm{KR}}(\Xi_{n,\kappa}\cap A,
                  \zeta_\kappa\cap A)
 \le C n^{-1/16+\varepsilon}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, if \(N_{n,\kappa}(A)=\Xi_{n,\kappa}(A)\), then
\[
 N_{n,\kappa}(A)\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pois(\kappa|A|).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let X be a compact metric space, T : X -> X continuous, and let M(X,T) be the set of T-invariant Borel probability measures with the weak-star topology, a nonempty compact convex metrisable set. Suppose T is ASYMPTOTICALLY h-EXPANSIVE, i.e. its tail entropy h*(T) = lim as eps -> 0 of sup over x of h(T, Gamma_eps(x)) vanishes; this holds in particular when T is h-expansive, and a fortiori when T is expansive. THEN the entropy map mu -> h_mu(T) is upper semicontinuous on M(X,T): whenever mu_k -> mu weak-star inside M(X,T), limsup_k h_{mu_k}(T) <= h_mu(T). CONSEQUENCES: an upper semicontinuous function on a nonempty compact set attains its supremum, so by the variational principle a measure of maximal entropy exists and h_top(T) = max over mu in M(X,T) of h_mu(T); the entropy function is then a bounded, affine, upper semicontinuous function on a Choquet simplex, which is what makes the theory of maximal measures and of symbolic extensions run. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) some hypothesis of this kind is necessary. For a general continuous map the entropy map need not be upper semicontinuous and a measure of maximal entropy need not exist; this is why smoothness matters - Newhouse proved that C^infinity diffeomorphisms of compact manifolds are asymptotically h-expansive and therefore always carry maximal measures, while for finite smoothness there are counterexamples. (ii) The conclusion is strictly one-sided and cannot be improved to continuity even for expansive systems: in a mixing shift of finite type the periodic-orbit measures, all of entropy 0, are weak-star dense, so they converge to the measure of maximal entropy and the entropy map is not lower semicontinuous. (iii) Compactness of X (hence of M(X,T)) is what converts upper semicontinuity into existence of a maximiser; on a noncompact space the existence conclusion fails even when the map is upper semicontinuous. (iv) The implication is stated in one direction only: upper semicontinuity of the entropy map is a strictly weaker property than asymptotic h-expansiveness, so do not run the criterion backwards.
X is a compact metric space and T : X -> X is continuous
M(X,T) carries the weak-star topology and is nonempty (guaranteed by Krylov-Bogolyubov)
h*(T) = 0 (asymptotic h-expansiveness); h-expansiveness and expansiveness are sufficient special cases
h_mu(T) is the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy of the measure-preserving system (X, mu, T)
the existence corollary uses the variational principle, which itself needs only compactness and continuity

FIRST, a Bowen-Misiurewicz estimate: for every T-invariant mu and every finite Borel partition alpha of diameter at most eps, h_mu(T) <= h_mu(T, alpha) + sup over x of h(T, Gamma_eps(x)). One obtains it by comparing an arbitrary finite partition beta with alpha through the comparison inequality h_mu(T, beta) <= h_mu(T, alpha) + (a conditional entropy term) and bounding the residual conditional entropy by the entropy of T on the shadowing sets Gamma_eps(x), which is exactly what the tail entropy measures; taking the supremum over beta gives the stated bound. SECOND, upper semicontinuity at a fixed measure of the single-partition entropy. Given mu, choose the partition alpha with diameter less than eps AND with mu(boundary of alpha) = 0 - possible by covering X with finitely many balls whose radii are chosen so that the boundaries are mu-null, then disjointifying. For each fixed n the map nu -> H_nu(alpha join T^{-1}alpha join ... join T^{-(n-1)}alpha) is continuous AT mu, because every cell of that join has mu-null boundary and so its nu-measure converges as nu -> mu weak-star. Since for invariant nu one has h_nu(T, alpha) = inf over n of (1/n) H_nu(join), and an infimum of functions each continuous at mu is upper semicontinuous at mu, we get limsup as nu -> mu of h_nu(T, alpha) <= inf over n of (1/n) H_mu(join) = h_mu(T, alpha). [Thm 9 of arXiv:2609.03054, 'The classes of bivariate Schur and Herglotz matrix-valued rational functions: realizations'] Let $G\in \mathbb C^{m \times n}(s,p)$ be a rational matrix valued  function. Then the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[\rm (i)]
\item $G$ has no singularities in $\mathbb{GH}$ and the matrix $G(s,p)$ has norm less than or equal to one
for any $(s,p)\in \mathbb{GH}$;
\item $G$ admits a realization of the form 
    $$G(s,p)=  D+  \frac12 {C} \left(s I+ 2A -
    (s^2-4p) P(s I+ 2A)^{-1} P\right)^{-1}B. $$
    with 
    \begin{equation}
\matr{
A+A^*- C^*C  & C^*D+ B\\ D^* C+ B^*  & 
I - D^* D} \geq 0,
\end{equation}
   and $-I\le P \le I$.
   \end{enumerate}
Additionally, if $G\in {\mathbb R}^{m\times n}(s,p)$, then the matrices $A,B,C,D$ and $P$
can be chosen as real.
