AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. Let U in R^(N by M) and V in R^(P by M) be independent arrays with fixed centered symmetric iid real entry laws, variance one and finite absolute fourteenth moments. Put X=UV^T/sqrt(N), d=NP,b=M/N, and let C_j be the ordered joint cumulant tensor of vec(X). Write T4=sum_(a,b,c,d,e,f) C4(a,b,c,d) C4(a,b,e,f) C4(c,d,e,f). For standard independent Gaussian G and all s>=0, I(X;sqrt(s)X+G)=dbs/2-db^2s^2/4+db^3s^3/6+(-db^4/8-||C4||_F^2/48)s^4+(db^5/10+b||C4||_F^2/12)s^5+(-db^6/12-5b^2||C4||_F^2/24-||C6||_F^2/1440+T4/48)s^6+R(s), with |R(s)|<=3041280 E||vec(X)||^14 s^7. If P/N->alpha>0 and M/N->beta>0 finitely, the coefficients of s^j in I/d tend for j=1,...,6 to beta/2,-beta^2/4,beta^3/6,-(beta^4+alpha beta^2)/8,beta^5/10+alpha beta^3/2, and -beta^6/12-5alpha beta^4/4-alpha^2 beta^2/12+alpha(1+alpha)beta^3/12, respectively. These limits are independent of the symmetric factor laws. The proof includes complete exact enumeration of 2197 fourth-cumulant triangle terms. The remainder is finite-dimensional and grows with dimension: this does not identify Taylor coefficients of the thermodynamic MI or justify exchanging limits.
Independent fixed real symmetric iid factor laws
Centered unit variance and finite absolute fourteenth moments
Positive finite limiting aspect ratios only for the coefficient-limit conclusion

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:7f62f0f5d229c4d4fab7cc3df9b0697a63db7d47b0312fb44c0aed13c14c9b55","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/7f/7f62f0f5d229c4d4fab7cc3df9b0697a63db7d47b0312fb44c0aed13c14c9b55.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:4b63b4d5e0e27fb5fc35472ff5eb469e6c139a18443923de29d17fa9cb3919ee","bundle_entry_key":"iid-product-mi-sixth-coefficient-limits-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-all-aspect-mi-and-sixth-coefficients-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:iid-product-mi-sixth-coefficient-limits-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Prior independence of the first six finite-size MI coefficient limits

Target 1. Computer-assisted proof draft, unaudited. The finite diagram
enumeration is scripts/check_sixth_order.py; its run artifact must say
PASS before this draft is entered as a proved claim. Novelty is
unestablished. This is a theorem about limits of finite-size Taylor
coefficients. It does not interchange the Taylor expansion and the
large-matrix limit.

## Statement and explicit finite-size remainder

Let U in R^(N by M) and V in R^(P by M) have independent iid entries,
with fixed symmetric real laws, mean zero, variance one and finite
absolute fourteenth moments. The laws of U and V need not coincide.
Let X=UV^T/sqrt(N), d=NP and b=M/N. For independent standard Gaussian
noise G define I_N(s)=I(X;sqrt(s)X+G), in nats. Let C_j be the ordered
joint cumulant tensor of order j of vec(X), and put

 T_4 = sum_(a,b,c,d,e,f) C_4(a,b,c,d) C_4(a,b,e,f) C_4(c,d,e,f).

The vector input is centrally symmetric, Cov(vec X)=b I_d. Its exact
finite-dimensional Taylor polynomial through order six is

 I_N(s) = db s/2 -db^2 s^2/4 +db^3 s^3/6
   +(-db^4/8-||C_4||_F^2/48)s^4
   +(db^5/10+b||C_4||_F^2/12)s^5
   +(-db^6/12-5b^2||C_4||_F^2/24
       -||C_6||_F^2/1440+T_4/48)s^6 + R_N(s),        (1)

with the explicit bound, for all s>=0,

 |R_N(s)| <= 3041280 E||vec X||^14 s^7.              (2)

One completely factorized bound in (2) is

 E||vec X||^14 <= d^7 M^14 N^(-7)
                         E|U_11|^14 E|V_11|^14.    (3)

Let P/N->alpha in (0,infinity), M/N->beta in (0,infinity).
The coefficient of s^j in I_N(s)/d tends, for j=1,...,6, to

 c_1=beta/2,
 c_2=-beta^2/4,
 c_3=beta^3/6,
 c_4=-(beta^4+alpha beta^2)/8,
 c_5=beta^5/10+alpha beta^3/2,
 c_6=-beta^6/12-5alpha beta^4/4-alpha^2 beta^2/12
                         +alpha(1+alpha)beta^3/12. (4)

In particular none of these coefficient limits depends on the fourth
cumulant, or any higher moment, of either symmetric factor law.

## 1. Finite-dimensional Gaussian-channel coefficient extraction

First let the centrally symmetric vector X be bounded and isotropic.
Standardize the output by its covariance (1+bs)I. Relative to standard
Gaussian measure its density is 1+q_s. The Hermite generating identity is

 E exp(t.W_s-||t||^2/2)
   = exp[sum_(j>=3) C_j:t^j (s/(1+bs))^(j/2)/j!],

interpreted for coefficient extraction at zero; odd tensors vanish.
Consequently the Hermite chaos components of degrees four and six are

 q_[4] = (s/(1+bs))^2 (C_4:H_4)/4!,
 q_[6] = (s/(1+bs))^3 (C_6:H_6)/6!.

There is no degree-two component. Higher components begin at s^4.
Hermite orthogonality kills their cross terms with degrees four and six
in integral q_s^2. The entropy expansion is

 D((1+q_s)gamma || gamma)
        = (1/2) integral q_s^2 -(1/6) integral q_s^3 +O(s^7).

These local expansions are justified for bounded X in any fixed
dimension: the Mehler-density bound and Gaussian hypercontractivity
used in bounded_prior_expansion.md bound the chaos tails in L^4 for
s in a sufficiently small interval. In particular ||q_s||_4=O(s^2),
and the entropy Taylor error after the cubic term is O(||q_s||_4^4).
The scalar remainder divided by |q|^4 is bounded on [-1,infinity),
with its continuous value at q=0, so the possible endpoint q=-1
does not invalidate this argument. All constants here are allowed
to depend on the fixed bounded input and dimension.

The quadratic terms are

 ||C_4||^2 s^4/[48(1+bs)^4]
       +||C_6||^2 s^6/[1440(1+bs)^6].

For the cubic degree-four contribution, Wick pairing connects the
three Hermite factors by two edges between each pair of factors.
There are choose(4,2)^3 (2!)^3=1728 such pairings. After division by
(4!)^3 and by the entropy coefficient 6, its contribution to D is

                      -T_4 s^6/48+O(s^7).

Use I_N(s)=d log(1+bs)/2-D, and expand the displayed denominators.
This gives exactly the polynomial (1).

For its explicit remainder use the already derived posterior-replica
streaming identity in finite_moment_expansion.md. For
F(s)=E||E[X|sqrt(s)X+G]||^2, that identity bounds the k-th derivative by

 |F^(k)(s)| <= 2^k (2k)! E||X||^(2k+2).

At k=6, I_N^(7)=-F^(6)/2 gives the Taylor remainder constant
2^6 (12)!/[2(7)!]=3041280. This uses the combinatorial coefficient
bound, not an enumeration of a growing replica polynomial. It holds
on every finite SNR interval for bounded X. Symmetric norm truncation
followed by covariance whitening preserves central symmetry and
converges in L^14 to X. The finite-moment approximation argument in
finite_moment_expansion.md therefore extends (1)-(2) to finite
fourteenth moments: the polynomial tensors and remainder bounds
converge, and Gaussian-smoothed output entropy is continuous.

Finally (3) follows by Jensen first over the d coordinates and then
over the M summands in each product entry. Independence of the U and
V entry in one summand factors the fourteenth absolute moment.

## 2. Sixth-cumulant norm: its only leading terms are simple cycles

Write W_ij=u_i v_j for a single rank-one summand. Additivity and
scaling of cumulants give C_6(X)=(M/N^3) C_6(W).
Expand each U- and V-moment by its set partitions. Since the laws
are symmetric, all blocks have even size at least two. For six
positions the possible block sizes are (2,2,2), (4,2), (6).
Their coefficients are products of factor cumulants.

Each row partition imposes equality of the row indices in its blocks;
each column partition imposes the corresponding column equalities.
Non-Gaussian factor cumulants require a block of size four or six,
so there are at most two free row indices, or at most two free column
indices, in every such term. In the squared norm a second copy can
only merge index classes. Hence any term involving a higher factor
cumulant has at most five free indices and total degree at most five
in N,P. This argument applies after the moment-cumulant subtraction,
which changes coefficients but never releases an index constraint.

Terms with six free indices must have three row pairs and three
column pairs in both copies, identical respectively across copies.
For a row pairing p and column pairing q, the coefficient in C_6(W)
is one precisely when their union is a connected six-cycle. One can
see this without a limiting argument: if p,q have one shared pair,
the (4,2) subtraction cancels the moment; if p=q, the coefficient is
1-3+2=0; if their union is connected, no proper moment partition can
be factored off, so its coefficient is one.

There are 15 row pairings and eight connected column pairings for
each, giving 120. The exact script checks every one of the 225 pairs.
Consequently, with constants depending only on the fixed moments,

 ||C_6(W)||^2 =120 N^3 P^3 +polynomial of total degree <=5,
 ||C_6(X)||^2/(NP) ->120 beta^2 alpha^2.              (5)

## 3. Three fourth cumulants: complete exact index enumeration

Let k_U=E u^4-3 and k_V=E v^4-3. For the three pairings p of four
positions write delta_p(i) for its row equalities, and delta_all(i)
for equality of all four rows. The exact identity is

 C_4(W) = sum_(p!=q) delta_p(i)delta_q(j)
       +k_U delta_all(i) sum_q delta_q(j)
       +k_V delta_all(j) sum_p delta_p(i)
       +k_U k_V delta_all(i)delta_all(j).             (6)

There are 6+3+3+1=13 terms. This is just the fourth moment of u times
the fourth moment of v, minus the three covariance pairings.

In T_4(W) the three tensors use the six entry positions
(0,1,2,3), (0,1,4,5), (2,3,4,5). The script expands all 13^3 choices
in (6). Union-find separately counts the free row and column indices.
Each choice contributes exactly
N^(row classes) P^(column classes) k_U^u k_V^v.
These are integer symbolic monomials; negative numerical values of
k_U or k_V do not affect the identity.

The full polynomial is saved in logs/sixth_order_checks.json. Its
only terms of total degree at least five are

                      4 N^3 P^2+4 N^2 P^3.         (7)

Every term containing k_U or k_V has degree at most four. This is
the only computer-assisted enumeration in the proof; it is complete,
uses exact integers, has no numerical tolerance, and fits in a few
kilobytes. Its script and complete output permit every case to be
checked from (6), with no downloaded code or stochastic step.

As C_4(X)=(M/N^2)C_4(W), equation (7) implies

                T_4(X)/(NP)->4 beta^3 alpha(1+alpha). (8)

## 4. Conclusion and limitation

The fourth-cumulant norm already computed in the dossier's settled
ground, and explicitly in finite_moment_expansion.md, gives
||C_4(X)||^2/(NP)->6 beta^2 alpha. Combine this with (5),(8) and
the exact finite-size polynomial (1) to obtain all coefficients (4).

No step above asserts a size-independent bound on (2) or (3). Their
constants grow with dimension. We have not proved that the limiting
MI is six times differentiable at zero, or that its coefficients are
the limits in (4). The hardest unpaid piece of Target 1 remains a
uniform small-SNR remainder or another argument justifying the
exchange of limits. It is also open here whether all fixed-order
coefficient limits are prior independent. These findings do not
establish the conjectured universal low-SNR phase.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:1799c3714831f68ac6b63c1958639d4969ff2adb0a37bb467a220be02f1ba043","revision_digest":"sha256:ac60b259c3cb9a46e43edf02cfecb06d5cf753cb873eeff53a96bbfc3a7ad50b","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:iid-product-mi-sixth-coefficient-limits-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Theorem 5 ({\cite[Theorem 1) of arXiv:2609.03171, 'Factorization patterns and fields of definition of $\ell$-torsion points on the Jacobians '] {Xing}}]
The possible characteristic polynomials of abelian varieties of dimension three over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ (where $q=p^k$) are all $f(t) \in \mathbb{Z}[t]$ of degree six satisfying one of the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item $f(t)=t^{6}+a_{1}t^{5}+a_{2}t^{4}+a_{3}t^{3}+a_{2}qt^{2}+a_{1}q^{2}t+q^{3}$ whose roots are Weil numbers, $v_p(d(0))/k \in \mathbb{Z}$ for any irreducible factor $d(t)$ of $f(t)$ in $\mathbb{Q}_{p}[t]$, and the polynomial $t^{3}+a_{1}t^{2}+(a_{2}-3q)t+a_{3}-2qa_{1}$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.
    
    \item $f(t)=(t^{2}+\beta t+q)^{3}$, where $\beta$ is equal to either:
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
        \item $\beta=aq^{1/3}$ with $3 \mid k$, $p \nmid a$, and $|a| < 2q^{1/6}$.
        \item $\beta=\pm q^{2/3}$ with $q=8$ or $27$.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    \item $f(t)=f_{1}(t)f_{2}(t)$, where $f_{1}(t)$ and $f_{2}(t)$ are the characteristic polynomials of abelian varieties of dimensions one and two, respectively.
\end{enumerate}
The abelian varieties in case (i) and case (ii) are simple, and not simple in case (iii). The abelian varieties in case (ii) are supersingular. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

For a finite star with at least one leaf and positive edge lengths, and a nearest-unvisited walk that stops after all vertices are visited, every random start distribution satisfies sd(L)/E L<=1/(2*sqrt(6)). For at least two leaves, write S for the sum of all edge lengths and w_1>=w_2 for the largest two. All lengths lie in [2S-w_1-w_2,2S-w_1], whose endpoint ratio is at most 3/2. A one-leaf star has constant positive length and coefficient zero. The constant is sharp over arbitrary start distributions; the uniform-start case is included but no optimality claim for that subclass is made. This does not prove an absolute bound for arbitrary graphs.

For integer d>=3, in Biskup-Chayes Main Theorem (1.12) with q=3 and its rescaled Potts inner product, n=2 and kappa=2/3. At J0=4 log 2 its supplied approximation allowance is E_d=(2J0/3)I_d, where I_d=int_{[-pi,pi]^d} a(k)^2/(1-a(k)) dk/(2pi)^d and a(k)=d^{-1}sum_j cos k_j. One has I_d>=1/(2d), hence E_d>=4 log 2/(3d). For d<=818 this lower bound is at least the exact q=3 mean-field barrier Delta=log 3-(19/12)log 2, so the unmodified allowance alone cannot establish a strict below-barrier criterion in those dimensions. The actual Gibbs approximation error may be smaller; this says nothing about the true lattice transition.

body: [Lemma le:reflected_fl_law of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] Let $\kappa \in (2,4)$.  Suppose $h$ is a GFF on $\mathbf{H}$ with boundary values $-\lambda(1+\rho_L)$  on $\mathbf{R}_-$ and $\lambda-\pi\chi = \lambda(\kappa/2-1)$ on $\mathbf{R}_+$ where $\rho_L > -2$. Given $\eta_1$, let $\overline{\eta}_2$ be the angle $0$ flow line from $\infty$ to $0$ of the restriction of $h$ to the components of $\mathbf{H}\setminus\eta_1$ to the right of $\eta_1$ (i.e.\ $\overline{\eta}_2$ is reflected off $\eta_1$). Then the pair $(\eta_1,\eta_2)$ has the same law as $(\eta_1,\overline{\eta}_2)$ (modulo time reversal).

[Lemma lem:reversal of arXiv:2411.13707, 'High-degree cubature on Wiener space \\ through unshuffle expansions'] The reversal operator $*$ (equation eq:reversal of the paper) is a coalgebra morphism w.r.t.\ $\Delta_\shuffle$.
\begin{proof}
Let $v_1,\ldots,v_n \in V$, $x = v_1\ldots v_n$, $r(i) \coloneqq n - i + 1$. Then, recalling the notation (equation eq:coproduct of the paper) 
\begin{align*}
    (* \otimes *) \circ \Delta_\shuffle x 
    ={}& \sum_{I \sqcup J = [n]} (v_I)^* \otimes (v_J)^* \\
    ={}& \sum_{I \sqcup J = [n]} (v^*)_{r(I)} \otimes (v^*)_{r(J)} \\
    ={}& \sum_{I' \sqcup J' = [n]} (v^*)_{I'} \otimes (v^*)_{J'} \\
    ={}&\Delta_\shuffle(v^*) . \qedhere
\end{align*}
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

$j\colon \cal{A} \to \cal{C}$ is a left-special inclusion and $i\colon \cal{B} \to \cal{C}$ is a right-special inclusion.

body: A function f: [a, b] -> R has bounded variation if its total variation V(f; [a, b]) = sup over all partitions a = x_0 < x_1 < ... < x_n = b of sum_{i=1}^{n} |f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1})| is finite; the space of such functions is BV[a, b]. Facts (Jordan, Lebesgue): (1) f is of bounded variation if and only if f = g - h with g and h nondecreasing on [a, b] (Jordan decomposition; one may take g(x) = V(f; [a, x]), the variation function, and h = g - f, both nondecreasing); (2) a BV function is bounded, has one-sided limits at every point, has at most countably many discontinuities, all of them jumps, and is differentiable Lebesgue-almost everywhere with f' integrable and integral_a^b |f'(x)| dx <= V(f; [a, b]), with equality if and only if f is absolutely continuous; (3) monotone functions and Lipschitz functions are BV (a Lipschitz function with constant L has V <= L (b - a)), while a continuous function need not be: x sin(1/x) on (0, 1] (extended by 0) has infinite variation, and the Cantor function is continuous, nondecreasing, BV, yet has f' = 0 almost everywhere with total variation 1 (so it is not absolutely continuous); (4) BV[a, b] is a Banach space under ||f|| = |f(a)| + V(f; [a, b]); (5) f is BV exactly when the Riemann-Stieltjes integral integral_a^b g df exists for every continuous g, and then g -> integral g df is a bounded linear functional on C[a, b] of norm V(f; [a, b]) - the Riesz representation of the dual of C[a, b] (normalised BV functions correspond to finite signed Borel measures). In higher dimensions BV functions are those whose distributional gradient is a finite vector measure.

body: Load-bearing hypothesis: in the Calderon-Zygmund theory for Lu = sum a^{ij}D_{ij}u + b.Du + cu the leading coefficients must be continuous (uniform continuity on the relevant compact set), or at least of vanishing mean oscillation; only then does the freezing-and-absorption step work for every 1 < p < infinity. Mere measurable uniform ellipticity is not enough, and the failure is not a technicality: both the estimate and uniqueness fail. Counterexample (Gilbarg-Serrin type): on the unit ball B_1 in R^n, n >= 2, fix lambda in (0,1) and set a^{ij}(x) = delta^{ij} + beta x_i x_j/|x|^2 with 1 + beta = (n-1)/(1 - lambda) > 0. These coefficients are bounded, symmetric, uniformly elliptic (eigenvalues 1 with multiplicity n-1 and (n-1)/(1-lambda)) and continuous except at the origin. For radial u, D_{ij}u = u''(r) x_i x_j/r^2 + (u'(r)/r)(delta_{ij} - x_i x_j/r^2), hence Lu = (1 + beta) u'' + (n-1) u'/r, and u(x) = |x|^lambda gives Lu = r^{lambda - 2} [ (1 + beta) lambda(lambda - 1) + (n-1) lambda ] = 0. Now w = |x|^lambda - 1 lies in W^{2,p}(B_1) for every p < n/(2 - lambda), lies in W^{1,p}_0(B_1) for those p, satisfies Lw = 0 almost everywhere, and is not identically zero (w(0) = -1). Consequences: the Dirichlet problem is not uniquely solvable in W^{2,p} intersect W^{1,p}_0 for p < n/(2 - lambda), so no global estimate ||w||_{W^{2,p}} <= C ||Lw||_{L^p} can hold there; the maximum principle also fails for such strong solutions (w attains its minimum -1 at an interior point while Lw = 0 and w = 0 on the boundary). Note n/(2 - lambda) < n and lambda may be taken as close to 1 as desired, so the failure reaches every exponent below n. What survives with only measurable coefficients: the Aleksandrov-Bakelman-Pucci estimate and Krylov-Safonov theory, both of which require the solution to be in W^{2,n}_loc - which is exactly the class this example escapes.
title: Pitfall: W^{2,p} Estimates Need Continuous (or VMO) Leading Coefficients

body:
[Lem 242 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix any $\phi \in C_b(\R,\R)$ and define the domain
	\[
		\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha) = \Big\{
			\mu \in \cP_2(\R,C'(\alpha)) : \bbW_1(\mu, \ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)) \le 1
		\Big\}\,.
	\]
	Then the function
	\[
		f_\phi(\mu) \equiv \int \phi\,d\mu
	\]
	is uniformly continuous on $\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha)$ equipped with the $\bbW_1$ metric.

\begin{proof}
The set $\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha)$ is clearly closed with respect to the $\bbW_1$ metric. By Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq}, the space $\cP_2(\R,C'(\alpha))$ endowed with the $\bbW_1$ metric is compact, so $\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha)$ is also compact. It thus suffices to show that $f_\phi$ is continuous. In fact, since we are on a metric space, it suffices to show that $f_\phi$ is sequentially continuous. To this end,  consider any sequence $\mu_n$ in $\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha)$ converging to $\mu$ in $\bbW_1$. Then $\mu_n$ also converges weakly to $\mu$. Since $\phi$ was assumed to be a bounded continuous function, we obtain 
	 \[\lim_{n\to\infty} f_\phi(\mu_n) = f(\mu)\,.\]
Therefore $f_\phi$ is indeed continuous, which concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 242 of arXiv:2608.29416

body:
[Cor 3 of arXiv:2604.11489, '2604.11489'] Assume that the function $g$ is differentiable on $[0,1]$ and its derivative $g'$ is $\beta$-H\"{o}lder
continuous for some $\beta \in (0,1]$. Let
\beq
\sigma^2=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}p_{i}\left(g'\left( p_{i}\right)\right)^2-\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}p_{i}g'\left( p_{i}\right)\right)^2
\deq
and assume that
\beq
\gamma=
\begin{cases}
\beta/2 \ \ &\text{if}\ \ \beta\in (0,0.5]\\
\beta-0.5 \ \ &\text{if}\ \ \beta\in (0.5,1]
\end{cases}.
\deq
If
\begin{enumerate}[$(1)$]
\item $\beta\in (0.5,1]$ or
\item $\beta\in (0,0.5]$ and
$$
\sum_{i=1}^\infty p_{i}^{(\beta+1)/2}<\infty,
$$
\end{enumerate}
then we have
\beq
\sup_x\left|\pp\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}(\hat\theta_n-\theta)\le x\right)-\Phi(x)\right|\le
\frac{C}{n^{\gamma/2}},
\deq
where $\Phi$ denotes the standard normal distribution function. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Cor 3 of arXiv:2604.11489

[campaign status: settled_inertial_balls - author-checked, verification unreviewed; the two-ball instance was not separately simulated - the ball-and-point instance of E0105 is its validation] Let K_1 and K_2 be two compact targets in a moving Boolean model, with detection times S_1 and S_2. GENERAL EXACT REDUCTION, valid for any grain motion: writing A_i(t) for the set of grain initial conditions that detect K_i by time t, the Poisson void probability gives P(S_1 > s, S_2 > t) = exp(-lambda |A_1(s) union A_2(t)|), so P(S_1 < S_2) is an explicit integral of |A_1(s) union A_2(s)| against the intensity. The whole content of the problem is the volume of the union of two swept regions. CLAIM: for two BALLS of radii r_1 and r_2 in the homogeneous INERTIAL model, P(S_{K_1} < S_{K_2}) = P(S_{K_1} = 0 < S_{K_2}) + integral_0^infinity (d/dt Lambda)(u,u) exp(-Lambda(u,u)) du, with Lambda the void exponent of the union of two parallel capsules of radii R_i = r_i + r about the two centres, h being the perpendicular offset of b_2 - b_1 from the track - the same formula as E0105 with the point replaced by the second ball. NESTED CASE, worth stating because the naive answer is wrong: if K_1 contains K_2 then S_{K_1} <= S_{K_2} almost surely, but ties have POSITIVE probability, so the honest statement is P(S_{K_1} < S_{K_2}) = P(the first grain to touch K_1 does not simultaneously touch K_2), computable from the Palm calculus of the grain field. DISJOINT TARGETS ARE NOT INDEPENDENT: one grain path can detect both, and the dependence is exactly the Poisson two-set inclusion-exclusion above.

K_1 and K_2 are balls; the general reduction holds for arbitrary compact targets and arbitrary motion

body: In graph theory, the Robertson–Seymour theorem states that the undirected graphs, partially ordered by the graph minor relationship, form a well-quasi-ordering. Equivalently, every family of graphs that is closed under taking minors can be defined by a finite set of forbidden minors, in the same way that Wagner's theorem characterizes the planar graphs as being the graphs that do not have the complete graph or the complete bipartite graph as minors.
title: Robertson–Seymour theorem

Let k>=1 and let u_n satisfy u_(n+k)+a_1,n*u_(n+k-1)+...+a_k,n*u_n=0 for all sufficiently large integers n, with complex coefficients a_j,n tending to a_j. Assume a_k,n is nonzero on that tail, all characteristic roots of z^k+a_1*z^(k-1)+...+a_k are nonzero and have pairwise distinct absolute values, and the scalar solution is not eventually zero. Then u_n is eventually nonzero and u_(n+1)/u_n converges to one of those characteristic roots. This is the classical Poincare-Perron theorem, stated as Theorem3, printedp4, in Borcea-Friedland-Shapiro0909.1216v1. No generic initial coefficient or summability of coefficient convergence is assumed.

metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:e33092841a9618c381b33d3d207c1b28830023a19aa7ae7b85b7c24cf414c541","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/e3/e33092841a9618c381b33d3d207c1b28830023a19aa7ae7b85b7c24cf414c541.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:f4944fe474638fe387f2da0315eb803ff2b409f785a1e42129d2212014e13c93","bundle_entry_key":"equal-energy-gaussian-entropy-transport-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-finite-high-moment-cubic-expansion-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels, high-noise expansions and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_014.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:equal-energy-gaussian-entropy-transport-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Equal-energy Gaussian entropy transport

Claim w718-T287-036 v1, supporting Target1 bound, proof (unaudited).
This is an elementary consequence of the standard Gaussian score
identity; no novelty is claimed for the transport inequality.

Let A,B be random vectors in R^d with finite equal second moments
E||A||^2=E||B||^2=e. For any coupling of A,B, independent standard
Gaussian G, and s>=0,

 |I(A;sqrt(s)A+G)-I(B;sqrt(s)B+G)|
 <=s sqrt(e) sqrt(E||A-B||^2).                         (1)

Taking the infimum over couplings replaces the last square root by
W_2(Law(A),Law(B)). No equality of covariance matrices or means is
needed; the equal quantities are the full second moments. If e=0
or s=0, the assertion is immediate.

For bounded coupled vectors put D=B-A, A_t=A+tD, and
Y_t=sqrt(s)A_t+G. The standard score identity, obtained by
differentiating the Gaussian mixture density, is

 score_(Y_t)(y)=-y+sqrt(s)E[A_t|Y_t=y].

Gaussian integration and differentiation of output entropy give

 d h(Y_t)/dt
 =-sqrt(s)E[D dot score_(Y_t)(Y_t)]
 =s E[D dot A_t]-s E[D dot E[A_t|Y_t]].                (2)

In the last equality E[D dot G]=0 because G is independent of the
coupling. The sign in (2) is fixed by testing a deterministic input
shift: its two terms cancel, as the output entropy must stay fixed.

Integrating its first term gives

 s integral_0^1 E[D dot A_t]dt
 =(s/2)(E||B||^2-E||A||^2)=0.

Conditional Jensen, Cauchy-Schwarz and Minkowski imply

 |E[D dot E[A_t|Y_t]]|
 <=sqrt(E||D||^2) sqrt(E||E[A_t|Y_t]||^2)
 <=sqrt(E||D||^2) sqrt(E||A_t||^2)
 <=sqrt(E||D||^2) sqrt(e).

Integrate the remaining term in (2). Since Gaussian-channel mutual
information equals output entropy minus h(G), this proves (1) for
bounded vectors.

For general finite-second-moment coupled vectors, clip each vector
radially to a ball of radius n, then multiply each clipped vector
by a deterministic scalar to restore its own second moment to e.
For all sufficiently large n these scalars are defined, tend to one,
and the resulting bounded pair converges to (A,B) jointly in L^2.
The two second moments remain exactly equal at every n. Apply the
bounded-vector inequality and pass to the limit. The Gaussian
entropy/Wasserstein continuity inequality006 justifies convergence
of the two smoothed entropies; the coupling costs converge in L^2.
This proves the finite-moment statement without assuming a derivative
formula for an unbounded input directly.

For the product signals X=UV^T/sqrt(N) and X_R=U_R V^T/sqrt(N),
couple each unit-variance centered entry u,u_R, and keep the same
independent centered variance-one V. With beta_N=M/N and d=NP,

 E||X||^2=E||X_R||^2=beta_N d,
 E||X-X_R||^2/d=beta_N E|u-u_R|^2.

Thus their normalized mutual informations satisfy

 |i_N(s)-i_(R,N)(s)|<=s beta_N sqrt(E|u-u_R|^2).       (3)

Unlike the generic entropy transport bound with coefficient sqrt(s),
this has coefficient s because the energy term cancels exactly.
Keeping variance one after truncation is essential for this use.
Independent audit remains pending; this is not a claimed solution

[Lemme 18 of arXiv:2604.00635, 'Large deviations of the periodic Toda chain'] Let $\op{D} = \mathrm{diag}(\La_1, \dots, \La_N)$ be a diagonal matrix with positive eigenvalues $\La_k > 0$ for all $k \in \intn{1}{N}$ and let $\mc{V}^{(0)}_N$ be as in \eqref{definition sous espace V0}
and $\big(\mc{V}^{(0)}_N\big)^{\perp}$ be its orthogonal complement, so that $\R^N \, = \, \mc{V}^{(0)}_N  \overset{\perp}{\oplus} \big(\mc{V}^{(0)}_N\big)^{\perp} $.
The matrix $\op{D}$ admits the block decomposition with respect to this direct sum decomposition

\beq

\op{D} \, = \, \left( \ba{cc}  \op{D}_{\mid  \mc{V}^{(0)}_N}  & \op{D}_{12} \\

                                        \op{D}_{21}         &    \op{D}_{\mid \big(\mc{V}^{(0)}_N\big)^{\perp} } \ea \right) \;.

\enq

Then, it holds

$$\det_{N-1}\big[ \op{D}_{\mid  \mc{V}^{(0)}_N} \big] \, \geq \,  (\La_1 \dots \La_N)^{1 - \frac{1}{N}} \, .$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem l46 of arXiv:2412.04015, 'Linear fluctuation of interfaces in Glauber-Kawasaki dynamics'] Fix $T>0$ and $0<\alpha<1$. A sequence of probability measures
${\mathbb M}_n$ on $C^\alpha([0,T], {\mathbb R})$ is tight if
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] There exist a constant $a>0$ such that
$\sup_{n\ge 1} {\mathbb M}_{n} \big[ \, |\, Y_0 \,|^a \,\big] \;<\, \infty$;
\item[(ii)] There exist a finite constant $C_0$ and positive constants
$b>0$, $c>0$ such that $c/b > \alpha$ and 
$\sup_{n\ge 1} {\mathbb M}_n \big[ \, | \, Y_t \,-\,
Y_s \, |^b\,\big] \;\le\, C_0 \, |t-s|^{1+c}$ for
all $0\le s, t\le T$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem l46 of arXiv:2412.04015

[Theorem eq:mesoscopic-cap-condition of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:mesoscopic-block-lower}
Suppose the ordered entries are i.i.d., centered, and
\(K\)-sub-Gaussian with common law \(\mu\).  Let \(b,w,c>0\), put
\[
 \pi=\mu([b,b+w]),\qquad
 A=bc^{p/2},\qquad D=wc^{p/2},
\]
and assume \(\pi>0\).  There is \(M=M(p,K)<\infty\) with the following
property.  If some \(t\in(0,1)\) satisfies
\begin{equation}
 A(1-t^p)>2(M+D),
\end{equation}
then, for
\begin{equation}
 B=[A-(M+D+1),A+(M+D+1)],
\end{equation}
one has
\begin{equation}
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E_\mu\operatorname{Crt}_{N,\max}^J(B)
 \ge c^p\log\pi.
\end{equation}
The same lower bound therefore holds for the total critical-point
count.

[Theorem 5 (Quantum tomography) of arXiv:2604.27119, '\Large Applied Random Matrix Theory\relatedversion'] Let $\mtx{\rho} \in \coll{D}_d$ be a density matrix with dimension $d$.
Using a complex projective 2-design~\eqref{eqn:complex-2-design},
perform a quantum measurement on each of $n$ independent quantum systems with common state $\mtx{\rho}$.
Form the sample-average estimator $\mtx{S}_n$, as in~\eqref{eqn:state-avg-estimator}.

For $\eps \in (0,1)$,
\[
\Prob{ \norm{ \mtx{S}_n - \mtx{\rho} } \geq \eps } \leq
2d \cdot \exp \left( \frac{-3n\eps^2}{14d} \right).
$$
In particular, the sample complexity $n \geq 5 \eps^{-2} d \log(2d/\delta)$
yields a failure probability no greater than $\delta \in (0,1)$.

[Proposition 17 of arXiv:2608.19744, 'Conditioned Brownian motion and local equivalence of path ensembles'] Let $Q\in\mathcal Q$ and $\beta>0$. Then the following statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(a)] $H_\beta$ is self-adjoint, bounded below, and has compact
    resolvent.
    \item[(b)] Its lowest eigenvalue $\lambda(\beta)$ is simple, and the
    associated normalized eigenfunction $\phi_\beta$ can be chosen strictly
    positive.
    \item[(c)] There exists $a=a(\beta,Q)>0$ such that
    \[
        \exp\bigl(a\langle x\rangle^{1+p/2}\bigr)\phi_\beta
        \in H^1(\mathbb R^d),
        \qquad \langle x\rangle=(1+|x|^2)^{1/2},
    \]
    where $p$ is as in assumption \eqref{bp:ass_2}. In particular,
    $\phi_\beta\in L^1(\mathbb R^d)\cap L^2(\mathbb R^d)$.
    \item[(d)] The map $\beta\mapsto\lambda(\beta)$ and the positive,
    $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$-normalized branch $\beta\mapsto\phi_\beta$ are real analytic on
    $(0,\infty)$.

[Propo g of arXiv:2412.01673, 'Spatial SIR epidemic model with varying infectivity without movement of individuals'] For all $\varphi \in C_b(D)$, $\left\{ \overline{\mu}_t^{S,N},\overline{\mu}_t^{\mathfrak{F},N},\overline{\mu}_t^{I,N}, \overline{\mu}_t^{R,N},\ t\ge0\right\}$ satisfies
	\begin{equation}
	
	\left\lbrace
	\begin{aligned}
	(\overline{\mu}_t^{S,N},\varphi)&= (\overline{\mu}_0^{S,N},\varphi)
	-\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_N}\varphi(X^{i})A^N_i(t),\\
	(\overline{\mu}_t^{\mathfrak{F},N},\varphi) &= \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i\in\mathfrak{I}_N} \lambda_{-i}(t)\varphi({X^{i}}) +\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_N} \lambda_{i}(t- \tau_i^N)\varphi({X^{i}}),\\
	(\overline{\mu}_t^{I,N},\varphi)&= (\overline{\mu}_0^{I,N},\varphi)+\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_N}\varphi(X^{i})A^N_i(t)- \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{I}_N}\varphi(X^{-i})\mathbf{1}_{\eta_{-i}\leq t}\\
	&- \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_N}\varphi(X^{i})\int_0^t\mathbf{1}_{\eta_i\leq t-s}dA^N_i(s),\\
	(\overline{\mu}_t^{R,N},\varphi)&= (\overline{\mu}_0^{R,N},\varphi)+ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{I}_N}\varphi(X^{-i})\mathbf{1}_{\eta_{-i}\leq t}+\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_N}\varphi(X^{i})\int_0^t\mathbf{1}_{\eta_i\leq t-s}dA^N_i(s)\,.
	\end{aligned}
	\right.
	\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2607.21392, 'Gaussian Convexity Principles for Sharp Moderate Deviations of Gaussian Maxima and Critica'] Fix $\alpha\in(0,\sqrt2)$ and $\kappa>0$.
For each $N\ge2$, let $(X_1,\dots,X_N)$ be a centered Gaussian vector satisfying $\operatorname{Var}(X_i)\le 1$.

Assume that, for all sufficiently large $N$, $\E \max_{1\le i\le N}X_i \ge \alpha\sqrt{\log N},$ and $\E \max_{1\le i\le N}X_i + \kappa\sqrt{\log N} \le \sqrt{2\log N}.$ Then, as $N\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb P\!\left(\max_{1\le i\le N}X_i\ge \E \max_{1\le i\le N} X_i+\kappa\sqrt{\log N}\right)
\le
N^{-\frac{\kappa^2}{2-\alpha^2}+o(1)}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:2607.21392

Let X be a normed vector space over R or C. The closed unit ball B of the dual space X^* is COMPACT in the weak-* topology, that is the topology of pointwise convergence on X. Two refinements matter. (a) If X is SEPARABLE then the weak-* topology restricted to B is metrizable and B is weak-* SEQUENTIALLY compact, so bounded sequences of functionals have weak-* convergent subsequences; without separability compactness need not give sequential compactness. (b) The general theorem uses Tychonoff's theorem for a product of compact scalar discs and therefore, in ZF, is not provable without some choice; the separable case needs only a diagonal argument. The theorem does NOT say the ball is norm-compact: by Riesz's lemma the closed unit ball of a normed space is norm-compact if and only if the space is finite-dimensional. Nor does it say the ball of X itself is weakly compact - that characterises reflexivity (Kakutani). [standard; e.g. Rudin, Functional Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 3.15]
X a normed space; no completeness of X is needed
for metrizability and sequential compactness of the ball: X separable
Tychonoff (hence a form of the axiom of choice) in the general case

[Proposition propositionunbounded of arXiv:2412.06246, 'The smallest singular value for rectangular random matrices with Lévy entries'] (Upper bound, diverging $N/n$)  Fix $\alpha\in(0,2)$, $\delta>1$ and let integers $N,n$ satisfy $N\geq \delta n$. Consider an $N\times n$ random matrix $X=(x_{ij})$ with i.i.d. symmetric entries satisfying (equation stablelaw of the paper).
Then for any $D>0$ and $\mathbf{b}\in(0,1)$ we can find $C_4>0$ such that 
$$
\mathbb{P}(\sigma_{min}(X)\geq C_4N^\frac{1}{\alpha}(\log n)^\frac{\alpha-2}{2\alpha})\leq N^{-D}+\exp(-n^\mathbf{b}),
$$ where $C_4$ depends only on $D,\delta,\alpha,C_\ell,C_u,\mathbf{b}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 18 of arXiv:2606.11271, '\LARGE The $K$-th nearest neighbor random walk on a Poisson point process gets trapped'] There exists a constant $\kappa_7 = \kappa_7 (d) > 0$ such that, for any $\varepsilon > 0$ and $R \in \N^*$, the following inequality holds:
$$
| \V_p (\varepsilon, \sqrt{d} R) | \geq  \kappa_7 \, \big| \big\{ u \in \fE_{\infty} \,:\,  \cY^{(\varepsilon, R)}_u = 1 \big\} \big|  \,,
$$
where $\V_p (\varepsilon, \sqrt{d} R) = \big\{ x \in \chi \,:\, \exists n \geq 0 , \, X_n = x \mbox{ and $X_n$ is $(\varepsilon, \sqrt{d} R)$-pioneer} \big\}$.

[Lemma lem:read-k of arXiv:2608.06159, 'Majority Dynamics on Resampled Sparse Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi Graphs:\\[0.5ex] Gaussian Winner '] {gavinsky2015tail}}]
    
     Let \(\{\rY_j\}_{j\in[r]}\) be a read-\(k\) family of indicator random variables with \(p_j \coloneqq\P(\rY_j=1)\), and denote their average by \(\bar p \coloneqq r^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^r p_j\).
    If \(0<\bar p<1\), then
    \begin{subequations}
    \begin{align}
    \P\bigg(
    \sum_{j=1}^r \rY_j\ge (\bar p+\varepsilon)r
    \bigg)
    &\le
    \exp\bigg(
    -\frac{r}{k}\D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bar p+\varepsilon\|\bar p)
    \bigg),
    &&0<\varepsilon\le1-\bar p,
    \\
    \P\bigg(
    \sum_{j=1}^r \rY_j\le (\bar p-\varepsilon)r
    \bigg)
    &\le
    \exp\bigg(
    -\frac{r}{k}\D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bar p-\varepsilon\|\bar p)
    \bigg),
    &&0<\varepsilon\le\bar p.
    \end{align}
    \end{subequations}
    where the Kullback-Leibler divergence is defined as
    \[
    \D_{\mathrm{KL}}(u\|v)\coloneqq
    u\log(u/v)+(1-u)\log((1-u)/(1-v)).
    \]
    We use the standard convention \(0\log0=0\) at \(u\in\{0,1\}\).
    If \(\bar p\in\{0,1\}\), all the indicators are almost surely constant and
    the corresponding tail statements are trivial. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\]

\]

\[
\prod_{i\in I}B_i
\times
\prod_{i\notin I}E_i

[Defn of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a $C^0$-foliation on $M$ with a $\mathbb{T}^3$-type planar minimal set $\Lambda$, and $\varepsilon > 0$. A \textbf{maypole green} of size $\leq \varepsilon$ for $\Lambda$ is a triple $\mathfrak{G} = (N, \gamma, P)$ where
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $N$ is an open neighborhood of $\Lambda$ of size $\leq \varepsilon$,
        \item $\gamma \subset N$ is a closed loop transverse to $\mathcal{F}$,
        \item $P \subset N$ is a closed tubular neighborhood of $\gamma$ equipped with a \emph{smooth} coordinate system with respect to which $\mathcal{F}$ is the product foliation by disks.
    \end{itemize}
    We call $P$ the \textbf{maypole} with core $\gamma$.
title: Unnumbered defn of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'

body: Let (Omega, mu) be a measure space, p a real number with 2 <= p < infinity, and f, g in L^p(mu). Then ||(f+g)/2||_p^p + ||(f-g)/2||_p^p <= (||f||_p^p + ||g||_p^p) / 2. This inequality implies, via the definition of uniform convexity, that L^p(mu) is uniformly convex for every 2 <= p < infinity. [Clarkson (1936); see Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and PDEs]

Let f ∈ C^2(R) and let u0 ∈ C^1(R) with u0 and u0' bounded. Set a(x) := f'(u0(x)) (so a ∈ C^1 with bounded derivative a' = f''(u0)u0') and κ := sup_{x ∈ R} ( -a'(x) ), T* := 1/κ if κ > 0 and T* := +∞ if κ ≤ 0. Then: (i) there is a C^1 solution u of u_t + f(u)_x = 0, u(·,0) = u0, on R × [0,T*), given implicitly by u(x,t) = u0(ξ) where x = ξ + t f'(u0(ξ)); (ii) if κ > 0 then sup_x |u_x(x,t)| ≥ κ / ( M (1 - κ t) ) → ∞ as t ↑ T*, where M := max{ |f''(s)| : |s| ≤ ||u0||_∞ } > 0; (iii) if κ > 0 there is NO C^1 solution on R × [0,T) for any T > T*. Hence, unless f'∘u0 is nondecreasing, classical solutions cease to exist in finite time and one must pass to weak (entropy) solutions.
f ∈ C^2 (the flux must be twice differentiable for a to be C^1)
u0 ∈ C^1 with u0 and u0' bounded

κ > 0, i.e. x ↦ f'(u0(x)) is somewhere strictly decreasing, for the breakdown statements (ii),(iii)

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2608.23462, '2608.23462'] Let $p\geq 2$ and $\beta >0$. Suppose that Assumptions~\ref{assu:frozenLipschitz} is satisfied and the frozen variable is $p$-dissipative with constant $\beta$.
    Then, for every $x\in\R^{d_1}$, the frozen process $(\hat{Y}^{x,y}_t)_{t\geq 0}$ admits a unique invariant distribution $\mu_x\in\mathcal{P}_p(\R^{d_2})$ such that
$$
\sup_{x\in\R^{d_1}}
\int |z|^p \, \mu_x(dz)
< \infty
$$
and 
$$
W_p(\mathcal{L} (\hat{Y}^{x,y}_t),\mu_x) \leq e^{-\beta t} \Big(\int|y-z|^p \,\mu_x(dz)\Big)^{1/p}
$$
for all $x\in\R^{d_1}$, $y\in\R^{d_2}$, and $t\geq 0$.

body: [Proposition 2 ($\gamma$-folding) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] For a norm with gain $\gamma$ feeding a linear map $W$, $\;\big(x_{\mathrm{norm}}\odot\gamma\big)W^\top=x_{\mathrm{norm}}\big(W\diag(\gamma)\big)^\top$. Hence setting $W\leftarrow W\diag(\gamma)$, $\gamma\leftarrow \mathbf 1$ preserves the function exactly and moves a per-channel scale entirely onto the weights. Where a norm feeds several projections, as both norms of \Cref{sec:anatomy} do, the substitution is applied to each of them before $\gamma$ is reset. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

DRAFT; proof (unaudited), no claim of novelty or a solved spectral gap. Let d>=2, beta>0, let A,B be positive even C2 functions on S^(d-1), and let B0 be constant. Write L(ru)=A(u)r^4-2B(u)r^2+B0, r_*=sqrt(B/A), F=B0-B^2/A and Z(u)=integral_0^infinity r^(d-1)exp[-beta(A(u)r^4-2B(u)r^2)]dr. E_u denotes its normalized radial conditional. Then grad log Z=-beta(A/B)E_u[r^2]grad F-(d/4)grad log A. If K=4r_*^3 grad A-4r_* grad B, then Hess F=r_*^4 Hess A-2r_*^2 Hess B-K tensor K/(8B); nonzero critical points of L correspond to critical points of F and have Hessian inertia equal to the positive radial block 8B plus Hess F. For empirical real phase retrieval with fixed unit teacher v, A(u)=mean_i(a_i.u)^4, B(u)=mean_i(a_i.v)^2(a_i.u)^2, B0=mean_i(a_i.v)^4, iid standard Gaussian measurements a_i and m>=d, almost surely the angular marginal is not stationary at v, simultaneously for all beta>0: grad log Z(v)=-d grad A(v)/(4A(v)) is nonzero. Conditioning on z_i=a_i.v, grad A(v) is centered Gaussian on v-perp with covariance (16/m^2)sum_i z_i^6 times the identity, which is positive almost surely. For any deterministic empirical sample with A>0 and M4=mean_i|a_i|^4, |grad log A|<=4(M4/A)^(1/4). Thus the entropy force is at most d(M4/a0)^(1/4) if A>=a0>0. Neither a polynomial Poincare constant nor a quantitative displacement of angular critical points is supplied.
d>=2, beta>0
A,B positive, even and C2 on the sphere; B0 constant
M4=mean|a_i|^4 for the empirical quartic derivative bound

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:6f1d4919c789f453820e66d3e087321134100f003343dfa9ff8a4af03d3d5f07","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/6f/6f1d4919c789f453820e66d3e087321134100f003343dfa9ff8a4af03d3d5f07.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:9d0b1896cd0a966d531f1fb9da25f164c57179e2592f3e177154676bde7804d7","bundle_entry_key":"profile-entropy","bundle_id":"population.t321-angular-profile-entropy-score-unaudited","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability and statistical learning","draft":"w724/bundle_003.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.functional.inequalities:empirical-phase-retrieval-angular-profile-entropy-score-w724-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Radial optimization versus the actual angular Gibbs marginal

T321 Target 2. Kind: reduction. Status: proof (unaudited).
No polynomial spectral gap, empirical landscape theorem, or novelty is claimed.

Assume d>=2, beta>0 and even C2 functions A,B on the unit sphere with A>0
and B>0. Compactness gives uniform positive lower bounds. Let B0 be constant,
L(ru)=A(u)r^4-2B(u)r^2+B0, r>0. Set

 r_*(u)=sqrt(B/A), F(u)=B0-B(u)^2/A(u), q(u)=B(u)/sqrt(A(u)).

1. The unique positive radial minimum is r_*. Its radial second derivative
is 8B>0. The profile gradient is grad F=r_*^4 grad A-2r_*^2 grad B.
Writing K=4r_*^3 grad A-4r_* grad B, differentiation of the radial stationary
equation gives grad r_*=-K/(8B). A second differentiation of F=L(r_*,u)
therefore gives the spherical Hessian identity

 Hess F=r_*^4 Hess A-2r_*^2 Hess B-K tensor K/(8B).       (1)

This is the Schur complement of the positive radial Hessian block. At a
critical point of F, the point r_*u is a critical point of L, and conversely
every nonzero critical point of L has this form. The Hessian quadratic form
of L in polar coordinates is congruent to diag(8B,Hess F), by completing
the square in the radial displacement. At a critical point this coordinate
Hessian also represents the ambient Hessian under an invertible change of
coordinates; hence their inertia is the same. In particular a negative
profile Hessian direction corresponds to a negative ambient Hessian
direction, and conversely. Local minima correspond as well because

 L(ru)=F(u)+A(u)(r^2-B(u)/A(u))^2.                      (2)

The origin is excluded from these statements. Passing to the antipodal
quotient preserves them locally because A,B,F,r_* are even.

2. The true angular marginal is proportional to

 Z(u)=integral_0^infinity r^(d-1)exp[-beta(A r^4-2B r^2)]dr.

The constant B0 cancels. Substitute s=A(u)^(1/4)r to get the exact identity

 Z(u)=A(u)^(-d/4) J_beta(q(u)),
 J_beta(q)=integral_0^infinity s^(d-1) exp[-beta(s^4-2q s^2)]ds. (3)

In particular this is an integral, not merely exp(-beta F). Let E_u denote
expectation under the radial conditional at u. Differentiating the
normalized integral gives

 grad log Z=-beta E_u r^4 grad A+2beta E_u r^2 grad B.

Integration of the derivative of r^d exp[-beta(A r^4-2B r^2)] gives
4beta A E_u r^4=d+4beta B E_u r^2. Its two boundary values are zero:
d>0 controls zero and beta A>0 controls infinity. Substitution yields

 grad log Z=-beta (A/B) E_u r^2 grad F-(d/4) grad log A. (4)

Every normalization and derivative is justified by a uniform quartic tail
dominator on the compact sphere; its polynomial factors are integrable.
Formula (4) is also obtained by differentiating (3), using F=B0-q^2.
It retains both radial-angular dependence and the dimension d.

At a critical point of F, grad log Z=-(d/4)grad log A. Thus a profile critical
point is a marginal critical point if and only if grad A vanishes there.
Consequently (1) alone does not transfer the strict-saddle decomposition
of the empirical loss to the angular marginal. A quantitative displacement
and Hessian control, or a decomposition that directly handles the entropy
term in (4), is still required. No assertion that empirical critical points
actually move by any particular amount is made.

For clarity, critical-point coincidence can fail in this general coefficient
class: on S^1 take theta modulo 2pi, A(theta)=exp(eta sin(2theta)),
q(theta)=q0+delta cos^2(theta), B(theta)=sqrt(A(theta))q(theta), with eta>0,
q0>0 and delta>0. All coefficients are even under the antipodal map theta
->theta+pi. F has its minima at theta=0 modulo pi, where F'=0 but
(log Z)'=-d eta/2 !=0, by (4) with d=2. This is a deterministic coefficient
example, NOT an empirical phase-retrieval sample and NOT a counterexample
to Target 2.

More directly, the mismatch occurs at the empirical teacher itself. For
the empirical coefficients, at u=v one has A(v)=B(v)=B0 and
grad B(v)=grad A(v)/2. Provided A(v)>0, F(v)=0 and grad F(v)=0, while (4)
gives, for every beta>0,

 grad log Z(v)=-(d/(4A(v)))grad A(v).                    (4a)

For iid standard Gaussian measurements and fixed unit v in dimension
d>=2, grad A(v) is nonzero almost surely. To see this, write a_i=z_i v+w_i
where z_i are iid N(0,1) and w_i are independent standard Gaussian vectors
on v-perp, independent of all z_i. Then grad A(v)=(4/m)sum_i z_i^3 w_i.
Conditional on the z_i, this is a centered Gaussian on v-perp with covariance
(16/m^2)sum_i z_i^6 times the identity. That scalar is positive almost surely,
so this Gaussian has no atom at zero. Thus whenever the full sample spans
R^d and A,B are positive everywhere, the actual angular marginal almost
surely is not stationary at the exact teacher direction, simultaneously
for every beta>0. For m>=d these positivity assumptions hold almost surely:
all z_i are nonzero and the measurements span, making both quartic A and
weighted quadratic B positive on the sphere. This is an exact finite-sample
fact, not an approximation or a claim of a large shift. The marginal's
critical point can still approach the teacher as beta grows.

3. The entropy gradient has a useful deterministic sample bound. If
A(u)=mean_i(a_i.u)^4 and M4=mean_i|a_i|^4, then Holder with exponents
4/3 and 4 and projection onto the tangent space give

 |grad_S A|<=4 A^(3/4) M4^(1/4),
 |grad_S log A|<=4 (M4/A)^(1/4).                       (5)

Indeed, the ambient derivative is 4 mean_i(a_i.u)^3 a_i; take its norm,
then apply Holder to mean_i |a_i.u|^3 |a_i|. Orthogonal projection cannot
increase a vector norm. If A>=a0>0, the entropy term in (4) is thus at most
d(M4/a0)^(1/4). On the already-used sample event A>=1/4 and
M4<=2d(d+2), this is at most d[8d(d+2)]^(1/4).

This polynomial bound does not make the entropy term small relative to
the profile force: the latter vanishes at profile critical points. No
implicit-function displacement estimate follows without quantitative
Hessian, derivative and neighborhood controls. Equations (1)-(5) specify
the next missing premise of the angular decomposition route rather than
proving a gap. All statements remain unaudited; no numerical or formal

[Lemma 9 (Weighted Schur test) of arXiv:2604.00642, 'Quantitative central limit theorem for an integrated periodogram via the fourth moment the'] Let $K$ be an integral operator on $L^2$ with kernel $k(\lambda,\mu)$.
If there exists a positive weight $p$ and $M<\infty$ such that
\[
\sup_{\lambda}\frac1{p(\lambda)}\int |k(\lambda,\mu)|p(\mu)\dd\mu\le M,
\qquad
\sup_{\mu}\frac1{p(\mu)}\int |k(\lambda,\mu)|p(\lambda)\dd\lambda\le M,
\]
then $\norm{K}_{\op}\le M$.

PROOF (UNAUDITED). For normalized tanh features u_q, extended by u_0(z)=z, define delta(q,r,c)=1-E[u_q(X)u_r(Y)] for standard Gaussians of correlation c. Uniformly for q,r,s in [0,1] and c in [-1,1], |delta(q,r,c)-delta(s,s,c)| <= (121/2)(q-r)^2+20(1-c)(|q-s|+|r-s|). For c<1 its relative version has coefficients 242 and 80, dividing the contrast term by 1-c. For n independent fresh paired rows, E[(Qnew-Rnew)^2 | past] <= [(1-(q+r)/12)^2+3/n](q-r)^2+8qr(1-c)/n. These remove the absolute-Lipschitz loss in the deterministic gap comparison and expose the weighted radial-contrast term still needed for a multi-layer recursion.
q,r,s in [0,1]; c in [-1,1]; relative comparison only for c<1

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:7076d4393689293319a7309eaf3c96e6c5b82dcaf126753efdf511edf8798e81","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/70/7076d4393689293319a7309eaf3c96e6c5b82dcaf126753efdf511edf8798e81.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:945ca18bb0a98db18e19c44e0797808647334210146f2f927f040de71041804d","bundle_entry_key":"tanh_gap_radial_comparison","bundle_id":"population.w712-t250-c011-gap-radial-comparison","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Quantitative Gaussian-process limits and empirical Gram matrices","draft":"w712/bundle_007.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.neural_networks:tanh-population-gap-angular-factor-and-radial-contrast-recursion","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C011 v1: angular-factor comparison and radial-contrast recursion

Kind: moved. Target: 1, the reviewer's two-input relative-gap rung.
Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty unverified. This is a component lemma,
not the claimed multi-layer relative rate.

## Statement

Let F(q)=E tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2 for a standard Gaussian Z. On [0,1] define
h_q(z)=tanh(sqrt(q)z)/sqrt(q), h_0(z)=z, a(q)=||h_q||_2,
u_q=h_q/a(q). For a standard Gaussian pair (X,Y) with correlation c set
H(q,r,c)=E[u_q(X)u_r(Y)] and delta(q,r,c)=1-H(q,r,c).
For all q,r,s in [0,1] and c in [-1,1],

    |delta(q,r,c)-delta(s,s,c)|
      <= (121/2)(q-r)^2 + 20(1-c)(|q-s|+|r-s|).       (1)

For c<1 this gives the scale-free comparison

    |delta(q,r,c)/delta(s,s,c)-1|
      <= 242 (q-r)^2/(1-c) + 80(|q-s|+|r-s|).         (2)

For c=1 the reference gap is zero and (2) is NOT asserted; (1) still holds.

For a fresh independent collection of n standard Gaussian pairs of
correlation c, let

    Q'=mean tanh(sqrt(q)X_i)^2,
    R'=mean tanh(sqrt(r)Y_i)^2, e=q-r.

For every integer n>=1,

    E[(Q'-R')^2]
      <= [(1-(q+r)/12)^2+3/n] e^2
           + 8qr(1-c)/n.                             (3)

If q,r,c are measurable with respect to the completed network past and
the paired rows are fresh conditional on that past, (3) holds conditionally.
No future state, gradient, or sensitivity is conditioned on. In particular
at a state with equal q=r, the new contrast has zero conditional mean and
second moment at most 8q^2(1-c)/n. Equal marginal variances are not preserved
pathwise.

## 1. Uniform feature estimates

Audited C002 v2, steps 1-2, gives q/4<=F(q)<=q for 0<=q<=1,
and increasing concave F with F(0)=0 and F(q)<=q-q^2/6.
Hence 1/2<=a(q)<=1, including q=0, and |h_q(z)|<=|z|.
For t>=0,

    tanh(t)-t sech(t)^2
      = integral_0^t 2v sech(v)^2 tanh(v) dv <= 2t^3/3.

Differentiation yields |partial_q h_q(z)|<=|z|^3/3 for q>0;
at zero its continuous extension is -z^3/3. This polynomial envelope
justifies differentiation and continuity in Gaussian L2 by dominated
convergence. Thus |a'(q)|<=sqrt(15)/3<2 and

    |partial_q u_q(z)| <= (2/3)|z|^3+8|z|,
    ||partial_q u_q||_2 <= (2/3)sqrt(15)+8 <= 11.      (4)

Here E Z^6=15 and E Z^2=1. The last inequality follows from
sqrt(15)<=9/2. These are uniform bounds; endpoint derivatives are
one-sided and all parameter integrals are over [0,1]. In particular

    ||u_q-u_r||_2 <= 11|q-r|.                        (5)

The derivative in the input variable is

    w_q(z):=partial_z u_q(z)=sech(sqrt(q)z)^2/a(q),
    w_0(z)=1, 0<w_q(z)<=2.

For q>0, the derivative of the numerator in q has absolute value
|z tanh(sqrt(q)z) sech(sqrt(q)z)^2/sqrt(q)|<=z^2.
Its limit at zero is -z^2. Using a>=1/2 and |a'|<2 gives

    |partial_q w_q(z)| <= 2z^2+8,
    ||w_q-w_s||_1 <= 10|q-s|.                       (6)

The L1 norms refer to a standard Gaussian marginal, independent of the
joint correlation used below.

## 2. The gap separates into shape and angular parts

Price's identity, as in Voigtlaender, arXiv:1710.03576, Theorem 1 and
Corollary 2, gives for -1<c<1

    partial_c H(q,r,c)=J(q,r,c):=E[w_q(X)w_r(Y)].

The features have at most linear growth; their input derivatives are
bounded. Thus the identity applies at interior correlations. Coupling
Y=cX+sqrt(1-c^2)Z with independent X,Z, polynomial domination gives
continuity of H and J at both endpoints. Since |J|<=4, integration and
passage to either endpoint are justified. In particular

    delta(q,r,c)
      = (1/2)||u_q-u_r||_2^2 + integral_c^1 J(q,r,t)dt. (7)

No centered sample covariance is involved in this population identity.
At q=r=s the shape term is zero. For the same correlation t, subtract
the products w_q(X)w_r(Y) and w_s(X)w_s(Y). The triangle inequality,
the bound |w|<=2, and (6), without any independence of X,Y, give

    |J(q,r,t)-J(s,s,t)|
      <=20(|q-s|+|r-s|).                             (8)

Subtract (7) for the two states, integrate (8) over an interval of length
1-c, and use (5). This proves (1), including c=-1 and c=1.

## 3. A nonzero reference gap and relative comparison

Let b=E[Zu_s(Z)] and v(z)=u_s(z)-bz. Then E[Zv(Z)]=0 and
||v||_2^2=1-b^2. Gaussian conditional expectation E[X|Y]=cY gives
E[Xv(Y)]=E[Yv(X)]=0, including both degenerate endpoint pairs.
Cauchy-Schwarz therefore implies

    H(s,s,c)=b^2 c+E[v(X)v(Y)] <= b^2 c+1-b^2,
    delta(s,s,c)>=b^2(1-c).                          (9)

For s>0, the elementary inequality tanh(t)>=t/sqrt(1+t^2) for t>=0,
oddness, and F(s)<=s yield

    b >= E[Z^2/sqrt(1+sZ^2)]
      >= 1/sqrt(1+3s) >= 1/2.

The middle step is Jensen for the convex function x->(1+sx)^(-1/2)
under the probability measure with density Z^2, whose Z^2 mean is 3.
For s=0, b=1 directly. Consequently delta(s,s,c)>0 for c<1 and
delta(s,s,c)>=(1-c)/4. Dividing (1) by this lower bound proves (2):
(121/2)*4=242 and 20*4=80. No division by a zero endpoint gap is made.

## 4. Conditional contrast recursion

The scalar function f(t)=tanh(sqrt(t))^2 is 1-Lipschitz on [0,infinity):
for t>0 its derivative is [tanh(sqrt(t))/sqrt(t)]sech(sqrt(t))^2 in [0,1],
and its continuous derivative at zero is 1. Hence for A=sqrt(q)X,
B=sqrt(r)Y,

    |tanh(A)^2-tanh(B)^2| <= |A^2-B^2|.

Gaussian fourth moments give

    E[(A^2-B^2)^2]
      =3q^2+3r^2-2qr(1+2c^2)
      =3(q-r)^2+4qr(1-c^2)
      <=3(q-r)^2+8qr(1-c).                          (10)

The last step uses 1+c<=2 and 1-c>=0; it holds also for c=-1.
For independent paired rows, the variance of their mean difference is
the single-row variance divided by n. Bounding that variance by its
second moment and using (10) gives

    Var(Q'-R') <= [3e^2+8qr(1-c)]/n.               (11)

The mean is F(q)-F(r). For t>0, concavity and F(0)=0 imply
0<=F'(t)<=F(t)/t<=1-t/6. Differentiation is justified, for example,
by the derivative bound Z^2 for tanh(sqrt(t)Z)^2. At zero the derivative
is 1 by dominated convergence. Integrating this derivative bound between
q and r, in either order, gives

    |F(q)-F(r)| <= |q-r|[1-(q+r)/12].             (12)

The bracket is at least 5/6 because q+r<=2, so squaring preserves (12).
Add the square of this mean to (11) to obtain (3). The conditional
version uses precisely the same calculation after fixing the past;
only the fresh paired rows are independent.

## What remains open

C010 controls empirical gap noise relative to delta(Q_l,R_l,c_l).
Equation (1) removes the inappropriate absolute-Lipschitz comparison
with the GP state: its common-variance error carries the angular gap.
Equation (3) exhibits how fresh sampling creates radial contrast.
Neither is a closed relative multi-layer recursion. To iterate (2), one
must control the weighted term (Q_l-R_l)^2/(1-c_l) jointly with the
angle and the marginal errors, and compare the angle to the deterministic
angle. Replacing random denominators by their expectations or multiplying
unconditional moment bounds is not justified. No such step is asserted.

## Source and verification scope

Prior inputs: reviewer-PASS C002 v2 scalar facts; Voigtlaender's primary
Price identity at the locator above. C010 motivated this lemma but its
inverse-Lipschitz constant and unaudited moment theorem are not needed
in this proof. The new comparison and recursion await independent audit;
literature novelty has not been established. Any finite arithmetic checks
verify only their stated polynomial or rational identities, not the

body: For the l^p norm on R^2 and the axis direction e_2, the dogleg excess of a midpoint-displaced point v = (d, r/2) is exactly asymptotic to (2^p/p) d^p / r^{p-1} as d/r -> 0 (second-order Taylor of (1 + x^p)^{1/p}). Consequently the enclosing-ball (quadratic lower) curvature condition excess >= c d^2/r holds at the axis if and only if p <= 2: for p < 2 the excess is of larger order than quadratic (the condition holds with room), at p = 2 it is exactly quadratic with constant 2, and for every p > 2 the contact is quartic or flatter and the enclosing-ball constant is ZERO. The curvature hypothesis consumed by localization arguments is therefore genuinely restrictive - entire familiar norm families fail it at their axis directions - and cannot be discharged by convexity or symmetry alone. Numerically verified: measured excess/predicted ratios 0.9995-1.0000 across p in {1.5, 2, 3, 4} at two offsets, and the quadratic test excess/(d^2/r) converges to a constant for p <= 2 and to zero for p > 2.

[Definition 3 of arXiv:2605.02002, 'Glauber dynamics for random field Ising models on bounded degree graphs and MLSI'] Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph and $\mu_G$ be the RFIM measure on $G$. We say that $\mu_G$ satisfies $\operatorname{WSM}(C)$ for some $C>0$ if for all vertices $v\in V$ and $r\geq 1$, we have 
    $$
\mathbb{E}_h[d_{TV}(\mu_G(\sigma_v\in\cdot\mid \sigma_{\partial B_r(v)}=+),\mu_G(\sigma_v\in\cdot\mid \sigma_{\partial B_r(v)}=-))]\leq Ce^{-r/C}.
    $$Here $\partial B_r(v)$ is the boundary of $B_r(v)$ in $V$ and $B_r(v)$ is the ball of radius $r$ around $v$ with respect to the graph distance on $G$. We use $\sigma_{\partial B_r(v)}=+$ (resp. $\sigma_{\partial B_r(v)}=-$) to denote the all plus (resp. all minus) boundary condition.
title: Definition 3 of arXiv:2605.02002

body: Ergodic theory is a branch of mathematics that studies statistical properties of deterministic dynamical systems; it is the study of ergodicity. In this context, "statistical properties" refers to properties which are expressed through the behavior of time averages of various functions along trajectories of dynamical systems. The notion of deterministic dynamical systems assumes that the equations determining the dynamics do not contain any random perturbations, noise, etc. Thus, the statistics with which we are concerned are properties of the dynamics.
title: Ergodic theory

[Lemma lem:second_moment_recurrences of arXiv:2609.02491, 'Generalised Random Parking for Trapeziums on a Strip'] Let $B_\mathcal{P}$ and $B_\mathcal{T}$ be defined as in~(equation eq:defn_B_s of the paper). For all $x>(3a-b)/2$, it follows that
\begin{align}
B_{\mathcal{P}}(x)
&=
\frac{1}{x-a} \mleft( \int_0^{x-a}B_{\mathcal{P}}(t)\,\mathrm{d} t + \int_\delta^{x-\varsigma }B_{\mathcal{T}}(t)\,\mathrm{d} t \mright) + q_{\mathcal{P}}(x), \quad \text{ and } \\
B_{\mathcal{T}}(x)
&=
\frac{1}{x-a} \mleft( \int_\delta^{x-a}B_{\mathcal{T}}(t)\,\mathrm{d} t + \int_0^{x-\varsigma }B_{\mathcal{P}}(t)\,\mathrm{d} t \mright) + q_{\mathcal{T}}(x), 
\end{align}
where
\begin{align}
q_{\mathcal{P}}(x) 
&=
\frac{1}{x-a} \mleft( \int_0^{x-a} e_{\mathcal{P}}(t)e_{\mathcal{T}}(x-\varsigma -t)\,\mathrm{d} t + \int_\delta^{x-\varsigma } e_{\mathcal{T}}(t)e_{\mathcal{P}}(x-\varsigma -t)\,\mathrm{d} t \mright),\quad \text{ and } \\
q_{\mathcal{T}}(x)
&=
\frac{1}{x-a} \mleft( \int_0^{x-a-\delta} e_{\mathcal{T}}(t+\delta)e_{\mathcal{T}}(x-a-t)\,\mathrm{d} t + \int_0^{x-\varsigma }  e_{\mathcal{P}}(t)e_{\mathcal{P}}(x-\varsigma -t)\,\mathrm{d} t \mright). 
\end{align}

[Theorem Main 1 of arXiv:2609.02871, 'Estimating the number of real zeros of linear combinations of radicals of polynomials'] Let $a_k, b_k, c_k$ for $k=1, \dots, n$ be real. Then the function
\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}c_{k}\sqrt{(x-a_{k})^{2}+b_{k}^{2}}
\]
either has no more than $2n$ distinct real roots or is identically zero. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 17 of arXiv:2606.29512, '2606.29512'] Let Assumptions \ref{assumption1}, 
\ref{assumption2}, \ref{assumption3}  and \ref{assumption2c} hold.  
Then every admissible solution admits an $\cH$-valued c\`adl\`ag modification. 
Moreover,  there exists a constant 
$N=N(d,r)>0$
such that if $u$ is an admissible solution 
to \eqref{SNS5}--\eqref{div5}--\eqref{bin5} satisfying 
$\hat u\leq \delta/N$, then 
$$
\E e^{-\psi_{t}}|u_t-v_t|^2_{\cH}
\leq \E |u_0-v_0|_{\cH}^2\quad\text{for $t\in[0,T]$} 
$$
for any admissible solution $v$ of \eqref{SNS5}--\eqref{div5}--\eqref{bin5} 
on $[0,T]$ with $\cH$-valued initial condition 
$v_t|_{t=0}=v_0$, where 
$$
\psi_t=N\int_0^t\beta_s\,ds,
\quad 
\beta_s
=\hat u^2+\bar u_s^2+\lambda^2_s+\tilde\lambda^2_s+\vartheta^2+\chi^2_s+\kappa_s
$$
with a constant  $N=N(d,r,\delta)$. In particular, if $u_0=v_0$ 
then the $\cH$-valued c\`adl\`ag modifications 
of $u$ and $v$ coincide almost surely on  $[0,T]$.

	$I = I(x): \mathbb{R} \rightarrow [0,\infty]$ and normalizing function

	$$

Let (X, Sigma, mu) be a measure space and 1 <= p < infinity with conjugate exponent p'. For g in L^{p'}(mu) define Lambda_g(f) = int_X f g dmu. (a) If 1 < p < infinity, then g -> Lambda_g is an isometric isomorphism of L^{p'}(mu) onto the dual space (L^p(mu))*, for an arbitrary measure space. (b) If p = 1 and mu is sigma-finite (more generally, localizable), then g -> Lambda_g is an isometric isomorphism of L^infinity(mu) onto (L^1(mu))*. In particular L^p is reflexive for 1 < p < infinity. For 1 < p < infinity the map is isometric over every measure space; for p = 1 it is isometric as soon as mu is semifinite, and without sigma-finiteness (or localizability) it need not be surjective. The case p = infinity is genuinely different and is NOT covered: the analogous map L^1(mu) -> (L^infinity(mu))* is isometric when mu is semifinite but in general not surjective, so (L^infinity)* is in general strictly larger than L^1 (see the pitfall).

1 <= p < infinity (the statement is false for p = infinity)

body: A Riemannian metric g on a smooth manifold M is a smooth assignment to each point p in M of a positive-definite symmetric bilinear form g_p on the tangent space T_pM: g_p: T_pM x T_pM -> R is bilinear and symmetric, satisfies g_p(v,v) > 0 for every nonzero v in T_pM, and p |-> g_p(X(p),Y(p)) is a smooth function of p for any pair of smooth vector fields X, Y. The pair (M,g) is called a Riemannian manifold. The metric g determines lengths of tangent vectors, angles between them, and, by integration along curves, the length of any piecewise smooth curve and the induced distance function between points of M.

\[
u^N \xrightarrow{\text{law}} u \quad \text{in } C([0,T];\dot{H}^\nu),

Let (Omega, T) be a MINIMAL topological dynamical system, Omega a compact metric space and T a homeomorphism, and let V: Omega -> R be continuous. For each omega in Omega let H_omega be the discrete Schrodinger operator on l^2(Z) given by (H_omega u)(n) = u(n+1) + u(n-1) + V(T^n omega) u(n). By minimality the spectrum sigma(H_omega) is one and the same compact set Sigma contained in R for every omega. For an energy E in R define the Schrodinger cocycle (T, A^E) over (Omega,T), where A^E(omega) is the SL(2,R) matrix with rows (E - V(omega), -1) and (1, 0); its iterates are A^E_n(omega) = A^E(T^{n-1}omega) ... A^E(omega), and they transfer solutions of the difference equation u(n+1) + u(n-1) + V(T^n omega)u(n) = E u(n). The cocycle is UNIFORMLY HYPERBOLIC if there is a continuous T-invariant splitting R^2 = E^s(omega) + E^u(omega) and constants C > 0, lambda > 1 with ||A^E_n(omega)v|| <= C lambda^{-n}||v|| for v in E^s(omega) and ||A^E_{-n}(omega)v|| <= C lambda^{-n}||v|| for v in E^u(omega), for all n >= 0 and all omega; equivalently (for SL(2,R) cocycles over a compact base) ||A^E_n(omega)|| >= C lambda^n for all omega and all n >= 0. THEOREM (R. Johnson): E belongs to R \ Sigma if and only if the cocycle (T, A^E) is uniformly hyperbolic. Equivalently, Sigma is exactly the set of real energies at which the Schrodinger cocycle fails to be uniformly hyperbolic. The same statement holds in the continuum setting for Schrodinger operators -u'' + V(T_t omega)u on the line with a minimal flow, which is Johnson's original formulation, and it is the standard dictionary between spectral theory and the dynamics of the transfer-matrix cocycle. SHARP EDGES. (a) UNIFORM hyperbolicity is far stronger than a positive Lyapunov exponent, and this is the single most often misused point. In the supercritical almost Mathieu operator, and more generally in the localisation regime, the Lyapunov exponent L(E) is positive at EVERY energy of the spectrum; those energies are in Sigma, so the cocycle there is non-uniformly hyperbolic. 'Positive exponent' therefore does NOT imply 'in the resolvent set'; only uniformity does. (b) Minimality of the base is used twice: to make sigma(H_omega) independent of omega, and to propagate the exponential dichotomy from one orbit to all of Omega. For a non-minimal base the spectrum can genuinely depend on omega and the statement must be reformulated (typically with the union of the spectra over the support of an ergodic measure, or over the whole base), so do not apply the equivalence verbatim outside minimality. (c) The theorem characterises the RESOLVENT set, which is open; correspondingly uniform hyperbolicity is an open condition in E and in the cocycle, whereas positivity of the Lyapunov exponent is not open. (d) The statement is for real E; for non-real E the operator is invertible anyway and the associated cocycle is not an SL(2,R) cocycle.

(Omega, T) is minimal

H_omega is the discrete Schrodinger operator with potential n -> V(T^n omega) on l^2(Z) (equivalently, the continuum Schrodinger operator over a minimal flow)
E is a real energy
uniform hyperbolicity is understood with constants uniform over all of Omega

body:
Let X be a topological space and f: X -> (-infinity, +infinity] an extended-real function. f is lower semicontinuous (lsc) at a point x0 if for every real a < f(x0) there is a neighbourhood U of x0 with f(x) > a for all x in U. f is lsc on X iff any one of the following equivalent conditions holds: (i) the superlevel set {x : f(x) > a} is open for every real a; (ii) the sublevel set {x : f(x) <= a} is closed for every real a; (iii) the epigraph {(x,t) in X x R : t >= f(x)} is closed in X x R. If X is first countable (in particular metric), lower semicontinuity at x0 is equivalent to liminf_{x -> x0} f(x) >= f(x0). f is upper semicontinuous iff -f is lsc, and f is continuous iff it is both. Standard facts, each of which is the reason lsc is worth naming: (1) the pointwise SUPREMUM of an arbitrary family of lsc functions is lsc; (2) a sum of finitely many lsc functions is lsc provided no (+infinity) + (-infinity) occurs, and a nonnegative multiple of an lsc function is lsc; (3) a nondecreasing pointwise limit of continuous functions is lsc, and conversely on a METRIC space every lsc function bounded below is the pointwise nondecreasing limit of a sequence of Lipschitz functions (Baire); (4) the indicator 1_A is lsc iff A is open; (5) WEIERSTRASS FORM: if X is compact and f is lsc then f attains its infimum on X, because the sublevel sets {f <= a} are closed and have the finite intersection property. This is the form in which lsc is used in the direct method of the calculus of variations: coercivity plus lsc on a compact (or weakly compact) set yields a minimiser. SHARP EDGES, i.e. what is NOT true. (a) lsc buys you MINIMA only, never maxima: on the compact space [0,1] the function f(x) = x for x < 1, f(1) = 0 is lsc (every superlevel set {f > a} is (a,1) or [0,1] or empty), its supremum is 1 and it is not attained. (b) The supremum of lsc functions is lsc but the INFIMUM of infinitely many lsc functions need not be: on R the continuous functions f_n(x) = max(0, 1 - n|x|) have pointwise infimum the indicator of {0}, whose superlevel set {f > 1/2} = {0} is not open. (c) 'lsc at every point' is genuinely weaker than continuity; an lsc function may be discontinuous on a dense set. (d) Statement (3) uses metrizability of X; on a general topological space an lsc function need not be a pointwise limit of continuous functions (it is a supremum of continuous functions on compact Hausdorff or, more generally, normal spaces, by Urysohn/Katetov-Tong, but for arbitrary X no such representation is available). (e) In integration theory the useful instance is Fatou's lemma, which says exactly that f -> integral f is lsc along pointwise convergence of nonnegative measurable functions; no upper semicontinuity holds there without a domination hypothesis.
X is a topological space
f takes values in the extended reals (-infinity, +infinity]
for the liminf characterisation, X is first countable (e.g. metric)
for the attainment-of-the-infimum statement, X is compact
for the approximation by Lipschitz functions, X is metric and f is bounded below
title: Lower semicontinuity

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2607.08242, 'Convergence of random sums in non-commutative probability'] Suppose $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi)$ is an NCP. 

Let $\{a_i\}$ be self-adjoint variables such that, $\varphi(a_i)=0, \varphi(a_i^2)=1$, and  $\sup_i|\varphi(a_i^m)| < \infty$ for every positive integer $m$. 
Then the following hold for $S_n:=a_1+\cdots +a_n$.\vskip5pt

\noindent (i) If $\{a_i\}$ are free, then $S_n/\sqrt{n}\stackrel{*}{\to} s$.

\vskip5pt

\noindent (ii) If $\{a_i\}$ are independent, then $S_n/\sqrt{n}\stackrel{*}{\to} z$.

\vskip5pt

\noindent (iii) If $\{a_i\}$ are half-independent, then $S_n/\sqrt{n}
\stackrel{*}{\to} r_S$.

\vskip3pt

\noindent In other words, $\varphi(S_n/\sqrt{n})^m$ in (i), (ii) and (iii) respectively, equal $\varphi(s^m)+o(1)$, $\varphi(z^m)+o(1)$, $\varphi(r_S^m)+o(1)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 2 of arXiv:2607.08242

[Dfn 148 (centered IAMP) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\prxpsi$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:even-manual-init}, where $\eta$ is sufficiently small depending on $(\delta,L,\epsilon)$, and define
  \[
    \psi(z)=\frac{(q_0)^{1/2} \prxpsi(z)}{\bbE[\prxpsi(Z)^2]^{1/2}}\,,
  \]
  with $\psi(z) = (q_0)^{1/2} z$ if $\prxpsi(Z) = 0$ almost surely.
  In either case, $\bbE[\psi(Z)^2] = q_0$. 
  We now initialize the iteration with the vectors
  \beq
  
  \begin{aligned}
  \by^{\dagger,0}
  &\equiv \psi(\bg^{\init})\in\R^N\,,\\
  \prxby^{\dagger,0}
  &\equiv\prxpsi(\bg^{\init})\in\R^N\,,
  \end{aligned}
  \eeq
  and $\bx^{\dagger,0}=\bx^0\in\R^M$, $\prxbx^{\dagger,0}=\prxbx^0\in\R^M$ exactly as before. We then follow 
  \textbf{exactly the same} IAMP iteration, as specified in \eqref{eq:proxy-y-amp-def}--\eqref{eq:x-amp-def}.
  These modified iterates are denoted $\by^{\dagger,k}$, $\prxby^{\dagger,k}$, etc., with state evolution limits $Y^\dagger(t)$, $\prxY^\dagger(t)$, etc.
  Finally, let $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger(\bG,\bg^\aux)\equiv \by^{\dagger,\ubl}$.
title: centered IAMP

[Proposition 12 of arXiv:2511.00764, 'Further Developments on Stochastic Dominance for Convex\\ Combinations of Infinite-Mean Ra'] \

\begin{itemize}
  \item[{\rm (vi)}] Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent.
    \begin{itemize}
    \item If $X, Y\in\mathcal{G}$, then $\max\{X, Y\}\in \mathcal{G}$ \citep[][Proposition 2]{CS25}.

    \item if $X, Y\in\mathcal{H}$, then $\max\{X, Y\}\in \mathcal{H}$ \citep[][Proposition 3]{CHSZ25}.

    \item If $X, Y\in\mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}^\ast$], then $\max\{X, Y\}\in \mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}^\ast$].
    \end{itemize}

  \item[{\rm (vii)}] If $X\in \mathcal{H}$, then $(X-c)_+\in\mathcal{H}$ for any $c\in\R_{++}$ \citep[][Proposition 5]{CHSZ25}. \\
       If $X\in \mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$], then $(X-c)_+\in\mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$] for any $c\in\R_{++}$.

  \item[{\rm (viii)}] Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent such that $X\in\mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}$, $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$]. If $Y$ is non-negative, then $(X-Y)_+\in \mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}$, $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$].

  \item[{\rm (ix)}]  If $X\in \mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$], then $[X|X>c] \in \mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$] for any $c\in\R_{++}$. However, $[X|X>c]\notin \mathcal{G}$ for any $c\in\R_{++}$.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 12 of arXiv:2511.00764

body: In graph theory, the Robertson–Seymour theorem (also called the graph minors theorem) states that the undirected graphs, partially ordered by the graph minor relationship, form a well-quasi-ordering. Equivalently, every family of graphs that is closed under taking minors can be defined by a finite set of forbidden minors, in the same way that Wagner's theorem characterizes the planar graphs as being the graphs that do not have the complete graph $K_{5}$ or the complete bipartite graph $K_{3,3}$ as minors.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Bound the coefficients' growth from the lace expansion's structure and compare with the Borel condition. Result: Borel summability (Watson/Nevanlinna) needs the remainder after N terms to be bounded by C K^N N! (2d)^{-N} uniformly in a sector, and the coefficients to grow at most like K^N N!. The known coefficients a_1 = 1, a_2 = 1, a_3 = 7/2 and the computed higher ones (Mertens-Moore numerics) grow rapidly, consistent with factorial growth. The lace expansion gives the coefficient a_i as a sum over lace diagrams with i-th order random-walk contributions; the number of lace diagrams at order N grows like N! (the laces are essentially permutations of intervals), and each contributes O(1) after the 1/(2d) powers are extracted, so the factorial growth of a_N is plausible, and the remainder estimate of the same form would follow from a bound on the contribution of all diagrams of order >= N by K^N N! (2d)^{-N}. The lace expansion's remainder term is controlled in the existing proofs of the expansion only as O((2d)^{-N}) with an N-dependent constant not tracked; tracking it gives, at best, the factorial bound if the number of order-N diagrams is bounded by K^N N!, which I believe is correct for the diagrams counted with their symmetry factors. The uniform-in-sector (complex d) statement needed for Borel summability is meaningless for the lattice; one would need an analytic continuation in a parameter playing the role of 1/(2d), e.g. the spread-out range or a long-range exponent, and then the Nevanlinna condition in that parameter. So the honest reduction: Borel summability requires (i) K^N N! bounds on the lace-expansion remainder, plausible and unproved, and (ii) an analytic interpolation in the expansion parameter, for which no natural candidate is known. This mirrors the situation for the self-avoiding walk connective constant expansion (Graham's Borel-type bounds) mentioned in the source. Obstruction: No analytic interpolation in 1/(2d); remainder constants not tracked.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0080-borel-summability-of-the-1-d-expansion-of-the-percolation-threshold
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved
title: Attempt on Borel summability of the 1/d expansion of the percolation threshold
