[Proposition pr:ghf_compactness of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] Suppose $\mathcal {K}$ is a collection of non-empty compact metric spaces $(X,d)$ each equipped with a continuous function $f\colon K \to Y$. Suppose that
 \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
  \item $\{ (X,d) : (X,d,f) \in \mathcal {K}\}$ is relatively compact with respect to the GH topology.
  \item There exist $0_Y \in Y$ and $M \in (0,\infty)$ such that $\sup_{x \in K} d_Y(f(x),0_Y) \leq M$ for all $(X,d,f) \in \mathcal {K}$.
  \item For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ so that $d(x,y) < \delta$ implies $d_Y(f(x),f(y)) < \varepsilon$ for all $(X,d,f) \in \mathcal {K}$.
 \end{enumerate}
 Then $\mathcal {K}$ is relatively compact with respect to the GHf topology.

[Def of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] {{[QR]}}
   A {\em weighted embedding} $Y_\bullet \hookrightarrow X$ is defined by a sequence of closed embeddings $\{Y_n = V(I_n) \hookrightarrow X\}_{n \ge 0}$ such that $\bigoplus_{i \ge 0} I_n t^n$ defines a \textit{Rees algebra} that is, a quasicoherent, finitely-generated, graded $\mathcal{O}_X$-subalgebra of $\mathcal{O}_X[t]$, satisfying
   \begin{enumerate}
      \item[(i)] $I_0 \supset I_1 \supset I_2 \supset \cdots$
      \item[(ii)] $I_nI_m \subset I_{n+m}$
      \item[(iii)] Locally in the smooth topology on $X$, there exists a sufficiently large positive integer $d$ such that for each $n \ge 1$,
      \[
       I_n = \left ( I_1^{l_1} I_2^{l_2} \cdots I_d^{l_d} \ : \ l_i \in \mathbb{N}, \ \sum_{i=1}^d il_i = n \right )
      \]
      in which case we say $I_\bullet$ is generated in degrees $\le d.$ 
   \end{enumerate}

Let dH denote the Hamming distance on Σd.

body: [Cor hyperunif_preserved of arXiv:2509.08659, 'Gap metrics for stationary point processes and quantitative convexity of the free energy'] Let $\mathsf{P}_i\in \mathcal P_{s,1}(\Gamma)$, $i=0,1$, be hyperuniform and $ \mathsf{Q}\in  \mathsf{Cpl}_{s,m}(\mathsf{P}_0,\mathsf{P}_1)$. Set $\mathsf U:=\iota( \mathsf{Q})$ and  $\mathsf{P}_t:= \mathsf{gap}^{-1}\left((T_t)_{\#}\mathsf U\right)$. Then $\mathsf{P}_t$ is hyperuniform for every $t\in [0,1]$. Moreover, if $\mathsf{P}_0$ and $\mathsf{P}_1$ are class-1-hyperuniform, then also $\mathsf{P}_t$ is class-1-hyperuniform.

Then for every $N\ge1$, every atom $A\in\mathcal A_N$, and every $t>0$,
\begin{equation}

 \mathbb P\bigl(\{\omega\in A:\ |f(\omega)-f_A|>t\}\bigr)
 \le c_1\exp\!\left(-c_2\frac{t}{\|f\|_{\mathrm{BMO}}}\right)\mathbb P(A).
\end{equation}

body:
[Prop wnorm of arXiv:2609.00672, 'Deciding superellipticity and computing the Weierstrass normal form'] Let $q$ be a place of $k_0(\pi_0)$, let $e_q=\ord_q\bigl(N(W)\bigr)$, and let $D_q$ be the degree of the part of $\Div(d\pi_0)$ above $q$. Then

\[
e_q = \sum_{P\mid q}f(P\mid q)\,v_P(W),
\]

and 

\[
\sum_{P\mid q}\deg P\cdot w(P) = e_q\deg q+\tfrac{g(g+1)}{2}D_q.
\]

If
\[
e_q\deg q+\tfrac{g(g+1)}{2}D_q<w_{\min}\deg q,
\]
 then no point of $E$ above $q$ has weight $w(s_{n,m})$ for a pair $(n,m)$ with $n\le g+2$ satisfying (eq:genus of the paper).

[Lemma metzlerthm of arXiv:2605.01878, '\Large Random trade timing and power-law tails in realized prices'] Let $\mathbb{A}$ be a Metzler matrix. Then
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=(\roman*), series=metzler]
    \item  $r_D(\mathbb{A})$ exists.
    \item  $r_D(\mathbb{A}) \le \tau(\mathbb{A}+\mathbb{B})$ for any nonnegative matrix $\mathbb{B}$.
    \item  $(sI-\mathbb{A})^{-1}$ exists and is nonnegative if and only if $s > r_D(\mathbb{A})$.
\end{enumerate}
If, in addition, $\mathbb{A}$ is irreducible, then
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=(\roman*), resume=metzler]
    \item  the left and right eigenvectors associated with $r_D(\mathbb{A})$ may be chosen with strictly positive components.
\end{enumerate}

[Theorem thm:hardnessunknown of arXiv:2602.11129, 'Information-Theoretic Thresholds for Bipartite Latent-Space Graphs Under Noisy Observation'] Consider any fixed $p \in (0,1)$. Then with probability $1- o(1)$ over the choice of $\ \mathbf{M} \sim \mathbb{M}(n,m,q)$
    $$
        \dtv{  \mathbb{W}_{\textbf{M}}(n, m, q, p, d)}{ \ \mathbb{M}(n, m, p)} = o(1)
    $$ under one of the following conditions 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(i)] $d \gg nmq^2\log(n)$ and $d \gg m\sqrt{n}q \log(n)$.

    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 2.2 of arXiv:2110.05374, 'When Janson meets McDiarmid: Bounded difference inequalities under graph-dependence'] Let f : Ω → R be c-Lipschitz and let the Ω-valued random vector X be G-dependent. If G is a disjoint union of trees T_1, ..., T_k (a forest with k components), then for t > 0, P(f(X) − E[f(X)] ≥ t) ≤ exp(−2t² / (Σ_{i=1}^k c_{min,i}² + Σ_{{i,j}∈E(G)} (c_i + c_j)²)), where c_{min,i} := min{c_j : j ∈ V(T_i)}. When the coordinates are independent the edgeless graph is a dependency graph, every vertex is its own tree, and the bound is McDiarmid's exp(−2t²/‖c‖₂²) (Remark 2.3 of the paper).
c-Lipschitz (Definition 1.1 of the paper): Ω = Ω_1 × ... × Ω_n is a product of Polish spaces, c = (c_1, ..., c_n) ∈ R_+^n, and f : Ω → R is c-Lipschitz when |f(x) − f(x')| ≤ Σ_{i=1}^n c_i 1{x_i ≠ x'_i} for all x, x' ∈ Ω (Lipschitz for the c-weighted Hamming distance).
G-dependent (Definition 1.3 of the paper): X = (X_i)_{i∈V(G)} is G-dependent when for all disjoint S, T ⊂ V(G) with no edge of G between S and T, the families (X_i)_{i∈S} and (X_j)_{j∈T} are independent; this is stronger than pairwise independence of non-adjacent coordinates.

Let A be an n by n real symmetric (or Hermitian) matrix with eigenvalues lambda_1 >= lambda_2 >= ... >= lambda_n. Load-bearing hypothesis: in u(x,t) = min_y ( t L((x-y)/t) + g(y) ) with L = H*, the Hamiltonian H must be CONVEX (and superlinear). For a nonconvex H the formula does not solve u_t + H(Du) = 0: since H* = (H**)*, the formula reproduces the equation with H replaced by its convex envelope H**. Counterexample (n = 1): H(p) = (p^2 - 1)^2 is continuous and superlinear but not convex, and H**(p) = 0 for |p| ≤ 1, H**(p) = H(p) for |p| ≥ 1. Take the Lipschitz datum g(x) = x/2. The true solution is the classical (hence viscosity) solution u(x,t) = x/2 - t H(1/2) = x/2 - (9/16) t. The Hopf-Lax expression gives min_y ( tL((x-y)/t) + y/2 ) = x/2 - t L*(1/2) = x/2 - t H**(1/2) = x/2, which satisfies u_t + H(u_x) = 0 + (1/4 - 1)^2 = 9/16 ≠ 0 at EVERY point — it is not even an almost-everywhere solution. The correct nonconvex counterpart is the Hopf formula u(x,t) = sup_p ( x·p - t H(p) - g*(p) ), valid for continuous H when the DATUM g is convex; for nonconvex H and general Lipschitz g there is no closed formula and one works with viscosity solutions directly. Auditor's check: whenever a proof writes a value function / Hopf-Lax representation, confirm convexity (of H for Hopf-Lax, of g for Hopf) before trusting it; the corresponding control interpretation (L as a running cost) also fails without convexity.
H must be convex and superlinear for the Hopf-Lax (Lax-Oleinik) representation with L = H*
The Hopf formula requires convex initial datum g instead, with H merely continuous
Counterexample: H(p) = (p^2-1)^2, g(x) = x/2, where Hopf-Lax returns the solution for H** and misses the flux by H(1/2) - H**(1/2) = 9/16
title: Pitfall: The Hopf-Lax Formula Requires a Convex Hamiltonian

[Prop 5 of arXiv:2607.28238, 'Well-posedness and large deviations for the obstacle problem of first-order stochastic con'] Let $(u,\nu)$ be a kinetic solution in the sense of Definition
\ref{def:dfn-1}.
Let
\[
f(x,t,\xi)=\one_{u(x,t)>\xi}.
\]
Then, almost surely, $f$ admits a right weak limit $f^{+,t}$ for every
$t\in[0,T)$ and a left weak limit $f^{-,t}$ for every $t\in(0,T]$.
These limits are kinetic functions and, for every
$\varphi\in C_c^1(\mathbb T^N\times\mathbb R)$,
\[
\langle f(t+\tau),\varphi\rangle\rightarrow\langle f^{+,t},\varphi\rangle,\qquad\langle f(t-\tau),\varphi\rangle\rightarrow\langle f^{-,t},\varphi\rangle
\]
as $\tau\downarrow0$, whenever the corresponding one-sided limit is defined. 
With the convention $f^{-,0}:=f^0$, for every $t\in[0,T)$, we have
\begin{align}
\langle f^{+,t}-f^{-,t},\varphi\rangle
&=-\int_{\mathbb{T}^N\times\{t\}\times\mathbb{R}}\partial_\xi\varphi(x,\xi)\,\dd q(x,s,\xi)  \notag\\
&\quad+\int_{\mathbb{T}^N\times\{t\}}\varphi(x,\psi(x,s))\,\dd\nu(x,s).
\end{align}
In particular, the set of $t\in[0,T)$ at which $f^{+,t}\neq f^{-,t}$ is almost surely at most countable.
We denote the corresponding predictable representatives by $f^+$ and $f^-$.
title: Prop 5 of arXiv:2607.28238

[Defn 37 (SRI chain) of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Fix some integers $k,d\ge 1$, and let $I$ as always be an additive locally compact subgroup of $\mathbb R^d$. Consider a Markov kernel $\br(\x,\mathrm d \mathbf y)$ on $I^k$. We say that the $q^{th}$ moments of $\br$ are bounded by $M$ if\begin{align}\sup_{\mathbf x \in I^k} \int_{I^k}|   y_i-   x_i|^q \br(\x,\mathrm d \mathbf y)&\leq M,\text{ for all } 1\le i \le k,

\end{align} Let $F: [0,\infty) \to [0,\infty)$ be a decreasing function. Let $\nu$ be some probability measure on $I$, and let $M>0$.  
A $k\times d$ \textbf{SRI chain with base measure $\nu$ and decay function $F$} is defined as a Markov kernel $\br$ on $I^k$, satisfying 
\begin{align}\| \br(\x,\bullet) - \nu^{\otimes k} (\mathbf x-\bullet)\|_{TV} &\leq F\big(\min_{1\le i<j\le k} |    x_i-   x_j|\big)\;\;\text{ for all } \x\in I^k .
\end{align} Here $\mathbf x = (   x_1,...,   x_k) \in I^k \subset \mathbb R^{kd}$. 
We denote by $\mathcal E^{\mathrm{SRI}}_{k\times d}(q,M,F)$ the set of all SRI chains on $I^k$ whose $q^{th}$ moments are bounded by $M$, and such that \eqref{tvb2} holds with $F$ on the right side, though we allow the base measure $\nu$ to vary between different elements of $\mathcal E^{\mathrm{SRI}}_{k\times d}(q,M,F)$. 

We furthermore say that the SRI chain is \textbf{centered} if $$\int_{I^k} (y_j-x_j) \br (\x,\dr\y) = \int_I    u \;\nu(\dr    u),\;\; \x\in I^k, 1\le j \le k.$$

We will say that an SRI chain is $\delta$-\textbf{repulsive} 
$$\int_{I^k} |   y_i-   y_j-(   x_i-   x_j)| \br(\x ,\dr \y) 
> \delta
\text{ for all $\x\in I^k$ and all $1\le i <j \le k$.}$$

Ren-Nichani-Wu-Lee source model for emergence and scaling. Let X~N(0,I_d), 1<=P<=d, and let v_star,1,...,v_star,P be orthonormal unit teacher vectors. Let a_1>=...>=a_P>=0 with sum_p a_p^2=1, and f_star(x)=sum_p a_p sigma(v_star,p dot x). Here h_j=He_j/sqrt(j!) is the orthonormal probabilists' Hermite basis. The shared real link is even, with L2(N(0,1)) expansion sigma=sum_{i>=I} sigma_hat,2i h_2i for an integer I>1; sigma_hat,2I>=c_sigma>0, ||sigma||_L2=1, and ||sigma_prime||_L2,||sigma_doubleprime||_L2<=C_sigma for fixed positive constants. The link has the derivatives used here and satisfies |sigma(z)| or |sigma_prime(z)|<=C*(1+z^2)^(Q/2) for all z and fixed C,Q>0, where or means the maximum of the two magnitudes. Its information exponent is 2I>=4. For nonzero student vectors v_1,...,v_m in R^d set f_v(x)=sum_k b_k sigma(u_k dot x), u_k=v_k/||v_k||_2, b_k=||v_k||_2^2. The per-example loss is one half of (f_star(x)-f_v(x))^2. The source online-SGD algorithm takes independent fresh Gaussian X_t, uses noiseless label f_star(X_t), and updates every v_k by minus eta times the gradient of that per-example loss. Initialization is iid uniform on the sphere of radius sigma_0, with the source choosing sigma_0=d^(-C0) for a fixed positive exponent C0. Student output coefficients are coupled to first-layer norms; independently trainable output coefficients describe a different parameterization. These definitions are not the quantitative hypothesis list of the online-SGD convergence theorem, and no convergence assertion for arbitrary d,P,m,eta follows from the model alone. The source model is Gaussian single-index, rather than multitask Boolean sparse parity.
Gaussian input and noiseless orthogonal single-index teachers; normalized nonnegative teacher coefficients.
Shared even link with source Assumption2.1; student output coefficients equal squared first-layer norms.
Online fresh-sample SGD; initialization and step size do not themselves assert convergence.

[Lem 10 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\mu,\mu'$ satisfying condition~\eqref{e:def-Lambda},
if we have $\vwww'\ge0$ with $(\mu',\vwww')=1$,
then we can find $\vwww\ge0$ with $(\mu,\vwww)=1$ 
such that
	\[
	\|\vwww-\vwww'\|_1
	\le \frac{\|\mu-\mu'\|_\infty}{\iota^2}
	\,.\]
Note if $\YY' \equiv (\vBBb,\vvvv,\vUUu,\vwww)'\in\cD_{\mu'}$, and we find $\vwww$ as above, then
    $\YY=(\vBBb',\vvvv',
    \vUUu',\vwww)\in\cD_\mu$.

\begin{proof}
We start with $\vwww'\ge0$ satisfying $(\mu',\vwww')=1$, which by condition~\eqref{e:def-Lambda} implies that
	\[\|\vwww'\|_1
	\le \frac{(\mu',\vwww')}{\iota}
	=\frac{1}{\iota}\,.
	\]
Abbreviating $\delta\equiv \|\mu-\mu'\|_\infty$, it follows that
	\[
	\Big|(\mu,\vwww')-1\Big|
	=  \Big|(\mu-\mu',\vwww')\Big|
	\le \|\mu-\mu'\|_\infty \|\vwww'\|_1
	\le \frac{\delta}{\iota}\,.
	\]
We then choose $\vwww$ to satisfy $(\mu,\vwww)=1$, which we can do with a similar construction as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:random-YY-in-cD}: if $(\mu,\vwww')\ge1$
(resp.\ $(\mu,\vwww')<1$), let $\vwww$ be any vector with $\vwww\le\vwww'$ (resp.\ $\vwww\ge\vwww'$) such that $(\mu,\vwww)=1$. Then, similarly as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:random-YY-in-cD}, we can use the above to bound
	\[\frac{\delta}{\iota}
	\ge
	\Big|(\mu,\vwww')-1\Big|
	=
	\Big|(\mu,\vwww'-\vwww)\Big|
	\ge \iota\|\vwww'-\vwww\|_1\,,
	\]
which concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

For every finite irreducible Markov generator Q with stationary probability pi and nonzero nonnegative diagonal killing-rate matrix D, f(x)=pi(D-xQ)^(-1)1 is nonincreasing for x>0, strictly decreasing unless D is a positive constant times identity. The event-stationary MMPP interarrival SCV is 2*(pi D1)*f(x)-1 and has the same monotonicity. Reversibility is not required. This does not imply convexity and fails for arbitrary initial distributions. Author derivation with exact arithmetic checks; originality and independent referee verification remain unverified.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:e18ef2c7f6b8a2e64627a5623e1a642469029f2a8c8c18c3ab7a9900a91e4748","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/e1/e18ef2c7f6b8a2e64627a5623e1a642469029f2a8c8c18c3ab7a9900a91e4748.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:b8fee8c6e38e5255d080c4b4ffa097f27364855f2e364b2ad8553937a7f0b0cf","bundle_entry_key":"speed-monotonicity","bundle_id":"population.mmpp-speed-monotonicity-20260909","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory and finite Markov chains","draft":"codex-overnight-corrections-20260908/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.markov:stationary-mmpp-mean-decreases-with-modulation-speed","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Modulation speed decreases the stationary MMPP mean

Author derivation, 9 September 2026. The algebra has been checked by three exact-arithmetic routes on 144 finite examples. That check is not an independent referee certificate. Originality is unverified.

This answers the monotonicity component of the question in Qi-Ming He, *Bounds on the mean and squared coefficient of variation of phase-type distributions*, Journal of Applied Probability 58 (2021), 880?889, section 4.3, DOI [10.1017/jpr.2021.18](https://doi.org/10.1017/jpr.2021.18). Convexity is a separate property and fails in the six-state example recorded alongside this proof.

## Statement

Let Q be an irreducible generator on a finite state space, pi its stationary probability row, and D a nonzero diagonal matrix with nonnegative entries d_i. For x>0, let

    f(x) = pi (D-xQ)^(-1) 1.

Then f is nonincreasing. In fact, f'(x)<0 for every x>0 unless all d_i equal the same positive constant; in that constant-rate case f(x)=1/d for every x.

Consequently, the event-stationary squared coefficient of variation is nonincreasing in modulation speed as well, since

    SCV_event(x) = 2 lambda f(x)-1,     lambda = pi D 1 > 0.

If D is strictly positive, the conclusion includes x=0 by continuity, and the same derivative argument applies there. If a killing rate is zero, no finite value at x=0 is asserted. The initial law pi is essential: this theorem does not assert monotonicity for an arbitrary initial state or initial distribution.

## Weighted symmetric and antisymmetric parts

Work in the real inner product <u,v>_pi = sum_i pi_i u_i v_i. For an operator B its adjoint is B*=Pi^(-1) B^T Pi, where Pi=diag(pi). Define

    S = -(Q+Q*)/2,       K = -(Q-Q*)/2.

Then S*=S, K*=-K, -Q=S+K, and S1=K1=0. Moreover,

    <v,Sv>_pi = (1/2) sum_(i,j) pi_i q_ij (v_i-v_j)^2 >= 0.

Irreducibility implies ker(S)=span{1}. Indeed, zero energy forces equal values along every directed edge of positive rate, and the directed graph is strongly connected.

For x>0 put L=D+xS. This is positive definite. If its quadratic form vanished, both the D and S forms would vanish. The latter forces v=c1; the former then gives c^2 pi D1=0, hence v=0. This also proves that L+xK=D-xQ is invertible: its quadratic form has positive real part on every nonzero real vector.

## Symmetrizing the inverse

Set R=(L+xK)^(-1) and

    G = L + x^2 K* L^(-1) K.

G is self-adjoint and positive definite. The symmetric part of R is exactly

    (R+R*)/2 = G^(-1).

One derivation is

    (R+R*)/2 = R* L R,
    (R* L R)^(-1) = (L+xK)L^(-1)(L-xK)
                       = L-x^2 K L^(-1)K = G.

An independent elimination check avoids inverse-product ordering: solve (L+xK)u=b and (L-xK)u*=b. Their average v and half-difference w satisfy

    Lv+xKw=b,       Lw+xKv=0.

Eliminating w gives Gv=b. Thus the two derivations give the same symmetric inverse. Since a real scalar quadratic form depends only on the symmetric part,

    f(x) = <1,G^(-1)1>_pi.

## Sign of the derivative

Differentiate L^(-1) using L'=S. Direct calculation gives

    G' = S + K* L^(-1)(2xD+x^2 S)L^(-1)K.

For clarity, the rearrangement is

    (x^2 L^(-1))' = 2xL^(-1)-x^2 L^(-1)SL^(-1)
                  = L^(-1)(2xD+x^2 S)L^(-1).

Every operator on the right contributing a quadratic form is positive semidefinite. Hence G'>=0, so G^(-1) is nonincreasing in the Loewner order and f is nonincreasing.

More explicitly, with v=G^(-1)1 and z=L^(-1)Kv,

    -f'(x) = <v,Sv>_pi + 2x<z,Dz>_pi + x^2<z,Sz>_pi >= 0.

This is also a sum of two Markov-chain edge energies and one nonnegative diagonal term. It exposes the sign without a spectral decomposition or any reversibility assumption.

For equality, f'(x)=0 implies <v,Sv>_pi=0 and therefore v=c1. As G1=D1, the equation Gv=1 then becomes c d_i=1 for every i. Thus all rates must be equal and positive. Conversely, constant killing gives f=1/d. This establishes the asserted strictness.

## Transfer to the event-stationary SCV

Write A=D-xQ and alpha=pi D/lambda. Since pi A=pi D,

    E_alpha T = alpha A^(-1)1 = 1/lambda,
    E_alpha T^2 = 2 alpha A^(-2)1 = 2f(x)/lambda.

The displayed SCV identity follows, and its derivative has the same sign as f'. This concerns event-stationary interarrival variability, not the SCV of the time-stationary residual waiting time.

## Verification and strongest scope check

`certify_monotonicity.py` uses rational arithmetic throughout. It covers nonsymmetric generators in dimensions 2, 3, 4 and 6, nonuniform stationary laws, strictly positive rates, a zero rate, constant-rate equality controls, and x=1/100,1,20. All 144 examples agree between (i) pi R Q R1, (ii) differentiation of the symmetric inverse, and (iii) the edge-energy expression. Whole matrix identities are checked, not only one scalar entry.

The most likely scope mistake would be dropping the stationary initial law. The proof uses the same vector 1 on both sides in the pi inner product. An arbitrary initial law produces a mixed bilinear form and does not inherit the sign from a positive semidefinite derivative. No such extension is claimed. Another possible overreach would be inferring convexity from monotonicity; the exact six-state negative-curvature example disproves that inference.

The original source and later related literature still require a complete prior-art review before this may be called a new result.

A sharp initial-law control is Q=[[-1,1],[1,-1]], D=diag(2,1). Starting in state 1 gives E_1 T=(1+2x)/(2+3x), whose derivative is 1/(2+3x)^2>0. The stationary mean is (3+4x)/(4+6x), with negative derivative. [Proposition 21 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] Let $\Xc$ and $\Yc$ be complete metric spaces, let $\gamma\in\Pc(\Xc)$ and
$\lambda\in\Pc(\Yc)$, and let $(\pi_n)_n\subset\Pi(\gamma,\lambda)$.
Assume that the following conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item For every $n\ge1$, the measure $\pi_n$ is absolutely continuous with
    respect to $\gamma\otimes\lambda$, with density
    \(
    f_n:=\frac{d\pi_n}{d(\gamma\otimes\lambda)}.
    \)

    \item There exists $\alpha_1>1$ such that, for every compact set
    $K\subset\Xc\times\Yc$, there exists a constant $C_K>0$ satisfying
    \(
    \|f_n\mathbf{1}_K\|_{\L^{\alpha_1}(\gamma\otimes\lambda)} \le C_K,
    \
    \text{for all }n\ge1.
    \)

    \item We have $\pi_n\to\pi$ weakly for some $\pi\in\Pi(\gamma,\lambda)$.

    \item There exist $\alpha_2>1$ such that
    \[
    \E^{\pi_n}[g(X)\mid Y]
    \longrightarrow
    \E^\pi[g(X)\mid Y]
    \qquad
    \text{in } \ \L^{\alpha_2}(\lambda),
    \qquad
    \text{for every }g\in\L^\infty(\gamma).
    \]

    \item The function $w:\Xc\times\Yc\to\R$ is Borel-measurable and satisfies, with some $\alpha_3 >\alpha_2$
    \begin{equation}
    \sup_n \E^{\pi_n}[|w(X,Y)|^{\alpha_3}]
    + \E^\pi[|w(X,Y)|^{\alpha_3}] < \infty.
    \end{equation}

    \item The exponents satisfy
    \(
    \frac{\alpha_2}{\alpha_3}+\frac{1}{\alpha_1}<1 \), equivalently, \(
    \alpha_2\,\alpha_1' < \alpha_3.\)
\end{enumerate}
Then it holds that 
\[
\E^{\pi_n}[w(X,Y)\mid Y]
\longrightarrow
\E^\pi[w(X,Y)\mid Y]
\qquad
\text{in } \ \ \L^{\alpha_2}(\lambda).
\]

body:
[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2607.13273, 'Asymptotics of transition densities for L\'evy processes with stochastic resetting'] Let $\alpha\in(0,2)$ and $Y_t$ be a cylindrical $\alpha$-- stable process in $\Rd,$ i.e.,
    \[
       \mE e^{i\langle \xi, Y_t \rangle } = \prod_{k=1}^d e^{-t|\xi_k|^\alpha} = e^{-t\sum_{k=1}^d|\xi_k|^\alpha},\quad \xi\in\Rd, t>0.
    \]
    Let $\theta\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1} = \{y\in\Rd:\: |y|=1\} $ and let $m$ denote a number of non--zero coordinates of $\theta.$
    If $m>\frac{d-\alpha}{\alpha+1}$
    then for all $x\in\Rd, \lambda>0$ we have
    \begin{equation}
		p_\lambda(t,x,r\theta)\sim_{t,r}\, \lambda^{\frac{d-m}{\alpha}-m} C_{\alpha,d}\Big(\prod\limits_{\substack{i=1,...,d\\\theta_i\neq0}}|\theta_i|^{-(1+\alpha)}\Big) r^{-m(1+\alpha)},
    \end{equation}
    where \footnote{$A(t,r)\sim_{t,r} B(t,r)$ means, that $\lim\limits_{\substack{r\to\infty\\t\to\infty}}\frac{A(t,r)}{B(t,r)}=1,$ and $A(t,r)\sim_r B(t,r)$ means, that $\lim\limits_{r\to\infty}\frac{A(t,r)}{B(t,r)}=1.$}
    \[
       C_{\alpha,d} = \mathcal{A}_{1,\alpha}^m \Gamma\left(\frac{m-d}{\alpha}+m+1\right)\left(\frac{\Gamma(\frac{1}{\alpha})}{\alpha\pi}\right)^{d-m}.
    \]

body: Lemma (campaign status: proved): Let $n\ge3$, let $u_1,\dots,u_n$ be the standard basis of $\mathbb F_2^n$, and take indices cyclically ($u_{n+1}=u_1$). Put $\mathcal S_n=\{0\}\cup\{u_i:1\le i\le n\}\cup\{u_i+u_{i+1}:1\le i\le n\}\subseteq\mathbb F_2^n$, a set of $2n+1$ vectors. For every subspace $W\le\mathbb F_2^n$ of dimension $w$, the number of cosets of $W$ that meet $\mathcal S_n$ satisfies $\boxed{|\mathcal S_n/W|\ge2n+1-3w}$ (tag 36). Neither hypothesis can be dropped: for $n=2$ the two cycle edges give the same vector $u_1+u_2$ and $|\mathcal S_2|=4<5$, for $n=1$ one has $u_1+u_1=0$ and $|\mathcal S_1|=2<3$ (both at $W=0$), and with path indices ($1\le i\le n-1$) $|\mathcal S_n|=2n<2n+1$ at $W=0$ for every $n$. Transfer to real residuals (tag 37): let $e_0,\dots,e_n$ be the standard basis of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ and $D_n=\{A,B_i,C_i:i\in\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z\}$ with $A=e_0$, $B_i=e_i$, $C_i=e_0+e_i+e_{i+1}$. For a real residual subspace $R\le\mathbb R^{n+1}$ of dimension $d$ (in the source, a signed-difference residual), let $k_{D_n}(R)$ be the number of signed projective classes that $R$ induces on $D_n$: two members $f,g$ lie in one class when $f\equiv\pm g\pmod R$, and the members lying in $R$ form one zero class, counted once if it occurs. Replace $R$ by the rational span $R_0\subseteq R$ of its actual class witnesses (the members of $D_n$ in the zero class and the differences $f-\sigma g\in R$, $\sigma=\pm1$, that witness a class equality), so that $d_0=\dim R_0\le d$ and $R_0$ induces the same classes, and reduce the saturated lattice $\Lambda=R_0\cap\mathbb Z^{n+1}$ modulo two to $\overline\Lambda\le\mathbb F_2^{n+1}$, $\dim\overline\Lambda=d_0$; signed equality becomes ordinary coset equality. Translating the binary reductions by $A$ sends $A\mapsto0$, $B_i\mapsto u_i'$, $C_i\mapsto u_i'+u_{i+1}'$, where $u_i'=e_0+e_i$ ($1\le i\le n$) form a basis of the even-weight hyperplane $E\le\mathbb F_2^{n+1}$, and two translated members lie in one $\overline\Lambda$-coset exactly when their difference lies in $W=\overline\Lambda\cap E$, $\dim W\le d_0$. Identifying $E$ with $\mathbb F_2^n$ through the basis $u_i'$, (36) gives $k_{D_n}(R)\ge|\mathcal S_n/W|\ge2n+1-3d_0\ge2n+1-3d$ (tag 37). Notes: Proof of (36): the images $u_i+W$ span $\mathbb F_2^n/W$, which has dimension $n-w$, so some $n-w$ of them, indexed by $Q$, form a quotient basis, and zero and these $n-w$ singleton images are distinct cosets. For $n\ge3$ the cycle $C_n$ is a simple graph in which every vertex has degree two, so removing the other $w$ cycle vertices destroys at most $2w$ cycle edges and at least $n-2w$ edges keep both endpoints in $Q$; their images are sums of two distinct basis vectors, hence distinct from each other, from zero and from the singleton images. This gives $1+(n-w)+(n-2w)=2n+1-3w$ occupied cosets when $w\le n/2$; when $w\ge n/2$ the first two terms alone give $1+n-w\ge2n+1-3w$. The coefficient 3 is exact: for $w\le n/2$, $W=\langle u_j:j\in P\rangle$ with $P$ a set of $w$ pairwise non-adjacent cycle vertices meets exactly $2n+1-3w$ cosets. The source states the lemma under its standing assumption $n\ge4$; the proof needs only $n\ge3$. The REAL-to-$\mathbb F_2$ passage (saturated lattice mod 2) is the reusable trick; it is what makes a real residual bound follow from a binary counting bound.

body:
Let X be a real random variable with mean mu and finite variance sigma^2. For every a > 0, P(X - mu >= a) <= sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + a^2), and by symmetry P(X - mu <= -a) <= sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + a^2). For sigma^2 > 0 this is strictly smaller than the bound min(1, sigma^2 / a^2) that Chebyshev's inequality gives for the one-sided tail; at sigma^2 = 0 both are 0. The bound is attained for every sigma^2 > 0 and a > 0: the law that puts mass sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + a^2) at mu + a and mass a^2 / (sigma^2 + a^2) at mu - sigma^2 / a has mean mu, variance sigma^2 and P(X - mu >= a) = sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + a^2).
X is a real random variable

[Proposition 27 (Cofinality of the two filtrations) of arXiv:2608.29585, '2608.29585'] The two filtrations
$\{\mathcal S_m\}_{m\ge0}$ and
$\{\mathcal C_N^{\mathrm{sym}}\}_{N\ge0}$ are cofinal.  More precisely:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item for every $N$ there is $m(N)$ such that
$\mathcal S_{m(N)}\subseteq\mathcal C_N^{\mathrm{sym}}$;
\item for every $m$ there is $N(m)$ such that
$\mathcal C_{N(m)}^{\mathrm{sym}}\subseteq\mathcal S_m$.
\end{enumerate}

[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] Assume $\Omega=\R$, $q,V\in C_b(\R)$ and $q\ge q_0>0$. For every $\alpha>0$,
\[
\Lambda_D^\R(\alpha)=\sup_{\psi\in C^1(\R)}\inf_{x\in\R}\mathfrak H_\alpha[\psi](x).
\]
The supremum is attained at $\psi_\alpha=-\log\phi_\alpha$, where $\phi_\alpha$ is a positive principal eigenfunction, and $\mathfrak H_\alpha[\psi_\alpha]\equiv\Lambda_D^\R(\alpha)$. Moreover,
\[
\Lambda_D^\R(\alpha)\ge\sup_{s\ge0}\left\{\inf_{x\in\R}(q(x)s-V(x))-\alpha d(M(s)-1)\right\}
\ge\alpha d\,\cH\!\left(\frac{q_0}{\alpha d}\right)-\sup_\R V,
\]
and the maximizing affine slope is unique. The kernel Hamiltonian satisfies
\[
\cH(v)=\frac{v^2}{2D_2(J)}-\frac{D_4(J)}{24D_2(J)^4}v^4+O(v^6)\qquad(v\to0)
\]
and
\[
\frac{\cH(v)}{v\log v}\longrightarrow\frac1{R_+}\qquad(v\to+\infty).
\]
If $J(R_+-t)=Kt^\nu(1+o(1))$ as $t\downarrow0$ for some $K>0$ and $\nu>1$, with $p=\nu+1$ and $A=K\Gamma(p)$, then
\[
\cH(v)=\frac v{R_+}\left[\log v+p\log\log v-p\log R_+-\log(R_+A)-1+o(1)\right].
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 6 of arXiv:2609.02416

For unit-sphere population mean-field flow with 1-Lipschitz C1 activation, |sigma(0)|<=1, M0=E[1+a0^2+||w0||^2+b0^2] finite and R=||f0-y||2, every positive-degree projection satisfies ||Pi_k f_t||2<=M0*exp(6Rt)/(2sqrt(d)). For the concrete a0=b0=0,w0=u initialization and a unit-energy zonal target, fixed-fraction q residual crossing has t >= log(sqrt(d)*(1-sqrt(q)))/6. The same projection estimate implies any measure already fitting a unit-energy degree-1 component to fraction q must have E[a^2+||w||^2]>=2sqrt(d)*(1-sqrt(q)). This separates knowing an axis from acquiring feature scale. It does not disprove O(1) fitting from a previously trained dimension-scaled law. No novelty or independent audit asserted. [Lemma 3 (No duality gap for the equality-constrained measure programs) of arXiv:2608.21496, '2608.21496'] Take a compact Hausdorff space $X$ and view the finite signed regular Borel
measures as $\mathcal M(X)=C(X)^*$ with the weak-star topology. Let
$\mathcal K\subset\mathcal M(X)$ be nonempty, convex, and weak-star compact,
and let $b_0,b_1,\ldots,b_m\in C(X)$.
Writing $\mathcal C=\mathcal K-\mathcal K$ and
$h_{\mathcal K}(z)=\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal K}\int z\,d\mu$, one has
\begin{align}
&\sup_{\substack{\nu\in\mathcal C\\
\int b_j\,d\nu=0,\ j=1,\ldots,m}}
\int b_0\,d\nu \nonumber\\
&\quad=\inf_{a\in\mathbb R^m}
\left\{h_{\mathcal K}\!\left(b_0-\sum_{j=1}^ma_jb_j\right)
+h_{\mathcal K}\!\left(-b_0+\sum_{j=1}^ma_jb_j\right)\right\}.

\end{align}
Because $\mathcal C$ is symmetric, the left side also equals the largest
absolute separation subject to the equality constraints. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: No duality gap for the equality-constrained measure programs

[Corollary c.U-FME of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Consider a marked point process $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}$ having fast $\mathbb{B} $-mixing correlations 
as in Definition~(B-omega-mixing of the paper)(Bmixing of the paper) and~(Bmixing-fast of the paper).
Let the score function be a {\em local $U$-statistic} of the form
\begin{equation}
\xi(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}) = \xi_{h}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}) := \frac{1}{k!} \sum_{\bk \tilde{x}1{k-1} \in \tilde{\mathcal{P}}^{(k-1)}}h(\tilde{x},\tilde{x}_1,\ldots,\tilde{x}_{k-1}), 
\end{equation}
for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and a symmetric, bounded  function
$h : (\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{K})^{k} \to \mathbb{R}$,
satisfying $h(\tilde{x}_0,\tilde{x}_1 \ldots, \tilde{x}_{k-1}) = 0$ whenever either 
$\max_{1 \le i \le k-1} |x_i - x_0| > r$ for some $r>0$, 
or $x_i = x_j$ for some $i \neq j$, $i,j\in\{0,\ldots,k-1\}$.
Then the marked point process
\(
\tilde{\raisebox{0pt}[0.85\height]{$\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$}} := \sum_{x_i \in \mathcal{P}} \delta_{(\tilde{x}_i, \xi_h(\tilde{x}_i, \tilde{\mathcal{P}}))}
\)
has fast $\mathbb{B} $-mixing correlations. Consequently, 
with $
 \mu_n^\xi: = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{P}_n} \xi( \tilde{x}, \tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n ) \delta_{ n^{-1/d}x }$, all statements in 
Theorems~(t:cltmarkedpp of the paper) and~(t:multcltmarkedpp of the paper), 
as well as in Propositions~(expvar of the paper) and~(t:clt_linear_marks_new of the paper), 
hold  under their respective moment, variance, and stationarity conditions.

Let d>=1 and pi(dx)=Z^(-1) exp(-V(x)) dx be a smooth strictly positive probability density on R^d. Let k be a continuous symmetric positive-definite, integrally strictly positive-definite kernel, with integral k(x,x) pi(dx)<infinity. Assume k is C^{1,1} on R^d times R^d (the first derivatives in both arguments and the mixed derivatives below are continuous). Suppose integral sum_{i=1}^d [(partial_i V(x))^2 k(x,x) - partial_i V(x)(partial_i^1 k(x,x)+partial_i^2 k(x,x)) + partial_i^1 partial_i^2 k(x,x)] pi(dx) < infinity. Define (T_{k,pi}g)(x)=integral k(x,y)g(y) pi(dy) and the nonnegative self-adjoint Stein operator L by the Friedrichs extension of L phi=-sum_i exp(V) partial_i(exp(-V) T_{k,pi} partial_i phi) on smooth compactly supported functions. Then there is no lambda>0 such that <phi,L phi>_{L^2(pi)} >= lambda ||phi||_{L^2(pi)}^2 for every mean-zero smooth compactly supported phi. Equivalently, the local Stein curvature bound in Definition 32 has no positive constant. This is the failure of exponential convergence near equilibrium in the paper's stated sense.

body: Let (Omega, F, (F_t)_{0 <= t <= T}, P) be a filtered probability space and let N^1, N^2 be Poisson processes on [0, T] with rates lambda_1, lambda_2 >= 0 with respect to this one filtration: each N^i is cadlag and adapted with N^i(0) = 0, and for 0 <= s <= u <= T the increment N^i(u) - N^i(s) is independent of F_s and Poisson distributed with mean lambda_i (u - s). Then N^1 and N^2 are independent if and only if almost surely they have no common jump time in [0, T]. For the 'if' direction it suffices that each N^i be a cadlag adapted counting process with N^i(0) = 0 and jumps of size 1 such that N^i(t) - lambda_i t is an (F_t)-martingale. The common filtration cannot be dropped: processes that are only marginally Poisson can have no common jump and still be dependent.

A Poisson process in the sense above is almost surely a counting process with jumps of size 1, and each M_i(t) = N^i(t) - lambda_i t is an (F_t)-martingale, because the increments are independent of F_s with mean lambda_i (u - s). Fix 0 <= s < u <= T and z_1, z_2 in (0, 1], and put Y_r = z_1^(N^1(r) - N^1(s)) z_2^(N^2(r) - N^2(s)) for r in [s, u]. A jump of N^i multiplies Y by z_i and no jump is common, so Y_u = 1 + int_(s,u] Y_(r-) (z_1 - 1) dN^1(r) + int_(s,u] Y_(r-) (z_2 - 1) dN^2(r). The integrands are predictable and bounded by 1 and N^i(u) is integrable, so with dN^i = dM_i + lambda_i dr the dM_i integrals have mean 0 on every event A in F_s. Hence, for A in F_s, h(u) = E[Y_u 1_A] satisfies h(u) = P(A) + a int_s^u h(r) dr with a = lambda_1 (z_1 - 1) + lambda_2 (z_2 - 1) (Y_(r-) = Y_r for all but finitely many r), and the only bounded solution is h(u) = P(A) exp(a (u - s)). Applying this on the intervals of a partition 0 = t_0 < ... < t_n = T and conditioning successively, all increment pairs are independent with product laws, so the finite-dimensional laws of (N^1, N^2) factor and N^1, N^2 are independent Poisson processes. Why the filtration matters (group04/B14; B15 checked it). With P a rate-lambda Poisson point measure on [0, T], N^1(t) = P((0, t]) and N^2(t) = P([T - t, T)): N^2 is the first process for the reflected measure x -> T - x, so each is a cadlag rate-lambda Poisson process in its own filtration; a common jump needs atoms x, y with x + y = T, an event of probability 0; and N^1(T) = N^2(T) = P((0, T)) almost surely, so Cov(N^1(T), N^2(T)) = lambda T > 0. [Lemma L:spine-complex-freedman of arXiv:2607.15966, 'Canonical Mandelbrot Cascades on Curves Are Rajchman'] Let \(N\in\mathbb{N}\), and let \((M_j,\mathcal{G}_j)_{j=0}^{N}\) be a complex-valued martingale 
with \(M_0=0\) and differences \(\Delta_j:=M_j-M_{j-1}\), \(1\leq j\leq N\).
Assume that there exist deterministic constants \(R,V>0\) such that,
almost surely,
\[
        |\Delta_j|\leq R
        \quad(1\leq j\leq N),
        \qquad
        \sum_{j=1}^{N}
        \mathbb{E}
        \left[
        |\Delta_j|^2\mid\mathcal{G}_{j-1}
        \right]
        \leq V.
\]
Then, for every \(t>0\),
\[
        \mathbb{P}
        \left(
        \max_{0\leq j\leq N}|M_j|>t
        \right)
        \leq
        4\exp
        \left(
        -\frac{t^2}{8(V+Rt)}
        \right).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma L:spine-complex-freedman of arXiv:2607.15966

body: Phi(s) = int dp sup_{|A| = 1} int_A W(x, p) dx bounds the single-hub density at every eps (a hub that sees P). Its histogram estimate keeps the top noisy bins of each P-column and is biased upward; running the same estimator with P permuted across the samples, where a hub that sees P can gain nothing, measures that bias, and net Phi is Phi minus it. On the 8-coordinate spread frame: fine combs (N = 4, 8, 16) and two-scale combs (N = 3, 5) gain at most about 2 per cent; combs at the integers gain a factor 1.06, 1.14, 1.27, 1.32 at N = 4, 6, 10, 12 (s = 0, beta = 0) and 1.66 at N = 12 with s = 2, beta = 0.5, while Phi itself falls with N. On the two-class frame of Example 5.2 (where the maximal functional M_2 grows like N) the gain is 1.10, 1.11, 1.01 at N = 4, 8, 16; at N = 16 the raw excess equals the shuffled one. Lesson: any estimator that takes a maximum over many noisy bins needs a null control built from the same samples.

body:
Let Omega be a BOUNDED open subset of R^n and let L u = a^{ij}(x) D_{ij} u + b^i(x) D_i u + c(x) u with a^{ij} = a^{ji}, L locally uniformly elliptic in the sense that a^{ij}(x) xi_i xi_j >= lambda(x)|xi|^2 with lambda(x) > 0 for every x in Omega, and with |b^i(x)|/lambda(x) bounded on Omega. Let u be in C^2(Omega) intersect C^0(closure of Omega). (i) If c is identically 0 and L u >= 0 in Omega, then max over the closure of u = max over the boundary of u (and if L u <= 0, min over the closure = min over the boundary). (ii) If c <= 0 in Omega and L u >= 0 in Omega, then max over the closure of u <= max over the boundary of u^+, where u^+ = max(u, 0); if L u <= 0 then min over the closure of u >= -max over the boundary of u^-. (iii) If c <= 0 and L u = 0, then max over the closure of |u| = max over the boundary of |u|. Nothing is assumed about continuity of the coefficients, and no sign condition is placed on a^{ij} beyond positive definiteness. WHERE IT FAILS: (a) the sign condition c <= 0 cannot be dropped - on Omega = (0,pi) x (0,pi) the function u(x_1,x_2) = sin(x_1) sin(x_2) satisfies Laplacian(u) + 2u = 0 (so c = 2 > 0), vanishes on the whole boundary and is strictly positive inside; (b) with c <= 0 but not identically 0 the positive part in (ii) is necessary: on Omega = (0,1) with L = d^2/dx^2 - k^2 the function u(x) = -cosh(k(x - 1/2))/cosh(k/2) solves L u = 0, equals -1 at both endpoints and equals -1/cosh(k/2) > -1 at the midpoint, so max over Omega of u strictly exceeds max over the boundary of u, while remaining below max of u^+ = 0; (c) boundedness of Omega cannot be dropped - u(x) = x_n is harmonic on the half-space {x_n > 0}, vanishes on its boundary and is unbounded above; on unbounded domains one needs a Phragmen-Lindelof growth restriction; (d) |b|/lambda must be bounded and lambda > 0 - degenerate ellipticity or unbounded drift relative to lambda destroys the auxiliary-function step. The conclusion is a bound by boundary values only, with no gradient information; the strong maximum principle (Hopf) is a separate statement requiring connectedness and local uniform ellipticity.
Omega is bounded and open in R^n
L is locally uniformly elliptic: a^{ij} symmetric with a^{ij} xi_i xi_j >= lambda(x)|xi|^2, lambda(x) > 0 in Omega
|b^i|/lambda is bounded on Omega
c <= 0 in Omega (identically 0 for the sharper form (i))
u is in C^2(Omega) and continuous up to the closure of Omega
the differential inequality L u >= 0 holds pointwise in Omega

body:
Measured 2026-09-05 on two stacking pools with the same protocol (test rows split 40/60 by a fixed permutation into calibration and evaluation, per-sample relative $L_2$ metric, paired gains): EMIT (10 seeds x 4 components = 40 cells; 23 members, 285 outputs, 932 calibration rows) and OCO-2 (10 seeds x 3 bands = 30 cells; 18 members, 40 outputs, 800 rows). The cross-validation-free estimator - error covariance in the relative metric, centred with an intercept, long-only minimum-variance weights, no cleaning constant - against the pool's best heuristic (per-output least squares shrunk toward the pooled simplex weights by a cross-validated amount): EMIT $+4.6$ percent at full calibration (33 of 40 cells; $+8.8$ over least squares; $+9.3$ on the physical radiance metric, 10 of 10 seeds), $+4.6/+5.1/+4.9$ at $n = 60/120/240$ calibration rows on the same draws, sign preserved under a second split ($+2.5$ mean); OCO-2 $-1.3$ percent at full calibration (0 of 30 cells; $-0.3$ against least squares) and $-4.4/-2.2/-1.3$ at $n = 60/120/240$, sign preserved under a second split ($-1.5$, correlation 0.89). The two corpora differ in the way the loss-mismatch analysis predicts: on EMIT the pooled shrink is worth $+4.5$ percent over least squares (a large objective mismatch), the members are heterogeneous and the outputs many, so a per-output fit in the right metric with the collinear duplicates pruned by the constraint is what helps; on OCO-2 the pooled shrink is worth $+0.9$ (almost no mismatch), every stack lands within two percent of every other, and pooling across the forty outputs is the regulariser that matters, so the per-output fit pays about one percent for its extra freedom. The two regularisers are complementary: the pooled cross-validated shrink applied on top of the long-only stack reads $-0.5$ on OCO-2 and $+4.9$ on EMIT. Tempering the metric weighting ($\|y\|^{-2\gamma}$, $\gamma < 1$) does not help either corpus: at full calibration $\gamma = 1$ is best or within $0.5$ percent on the median cell, on the ten EMIT cells with effective sample size below 20 at $n = 60$ the oracle $\gamma$ is worth $+0.5$ percent on average, and a rule choosing $\gamma$ by the effective sample size loses $4.4$ percent - the reported metric's weighting is right at every calibration size and its small effective sample size is a diagnostic, not a lever.
members fitted on training rows only; calibration and evaluation rows are disjoint subsets of the test rows
paired comparisons cell by cell; small-calibration arms use the same subsample draws for every estimator

body: FIRES WHEN you have answered an open question affirmatively in its smallest nontrivial case and are about to record the question as settled. WHAT HAPPENED: 'is there a trajectory with a periodic itinerary?' is YES at m = 3, and the witness is an operator already in the literature. But the m = 3 triangle admits only ONE route around its boundary, so every itinerary there is periodic once it starts - the affirmative answer is a property of the geometry of the 2-simplex, not of the dynamics the question is about. At m = 4 the same simulation produces the mixed itinerary 1,4,3,2,1,4,2,1, so itineraries need NOT be periodic. CONDITION OF FAILURE: a smallest case whose combinatorics is degenerate. WHAT THE QUESTION SHOULD HAVE BEEN, and this is the useful output: is every itinerary EVENTUALLY periodic, or which coefficient matrices force it? Ganikhodjaev and Zanin's 2012 route analysis (arXiv:1205.3841, Theorem 5), which lists the m = 4 routes 1-4-3-2-1, 1-4-2-1 and 1-4-3-1, is the starting point.

[Theorem 3 (Stochastic rounding) of arXiv:2604.27119, '\Large Applied Random Matrix Theory\relatedversion'] Consider a matrix $\mtx{A} 
\in \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$.
For $p \in \{1,2\}$, define the norms
\[
\norm{\mtx{A}}_{\max} \coloneqq \max\nolimits_{ij} \abs{a_{ij}}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\norm{ \mtx{A} }_{{\rm rc}, p} \coloneqq
(\max\nolimits_i \norm{\mtx{A}(i,:)}_p) \vee (\max\nolimits_j \norm{\mtx{A}(:,j)}_p ).

\]
Form a random matrix $\textup{\texttt{sr}}(\mtx{A}) \in \set{F}^{d_1 \times d_2}$
by independently rounding each entry of $\mtx{A}$, honoring the rule~\eqref{eqn:stoch-rounding}. 
Then
\[
\Expect \norm{ \mtx{A} - \textup{\texttt{sr}}(\mtx{A}) }

	\leq \textup{\texttt{u}} \cdot \left[ \sqrt{2 \norm{\mtx{A}}_{{\rm rc}, 2}^2 \log(d_1 + d_2)} + \frac{1}{3} \norm{\mtx{A}}_{\max} \log(d_1 + d_2) \right].
\]
In contrast, the deterministic rule~\eqref{eqn:float-rounding} only guarantees that
$\norm{ \mtx{A} - \textup{\texttt{float}}(\mtx{A}) } \leq  \textup{\texttt{u}} \cdot \norm{ \mtx{A} }_{{\rm rc},1}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Prop 29 of arXiv:2609.02561, 'NON-NEF LOCI IN MIXED CHARACTERISTIC'] Let $f: X \rightarrow S$ be a projective surjective morphism of integral Noetherian schemes with $X$ normal.

For any $\Q$-Cartier $\Q$-divisor $D$ on $X$,
\begin{enumerate}
\item $ \B (D/S) = \emptyset$ if and only if $D$ is $f$-semiample, and
\item $ \B (D/S) \subsetneq X$ if and only if $D$ is $f$-$\Q$-effective.
\end{enumerate}

For any $\R$-Cartier $\R$-divisor $D$ on $X$,
\begin{enumerate}[resume]
\item $ \Bp (D/S) = \emptyset$ if and only if $D$ is $f$-ample,
\item $\Bp (D/S) \subsetneq X$ if and only if $D$ is $f$-big,
\item $ \Bm (D/S) = \emptyset$ if and only if $D$ is $f$-nef, and
\item $\Bm (D/S) \subsetneq X$ if and only if $D$ is $f$-pseudo-effective.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop 29 of arXiv:2609.02561

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:6fab0195fdd85dd134310b94ef6776c2b47f22768066f931fb16ff8de3e62940","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/6f/6fab0195fdd85dd134310b94ef6776c2b47f22768066f931fb16ff8de3e62940.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:8ad30b8a1104b62c5be3d02bfaebfa86767727f95afa1eb266ce776a93917169","bundle_entry_key":"concave-derivatives-l1-stability-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-integrated-mmse-all-aspects-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:concave-derivatives-l1-stability-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Quantitative L1 stability of derivatives of concave functions

Supporting calculus lemma for Target 2; proof draft, unaudited.
This elementary smoothing argument is not claimed as a new general theorem.

Let S,h be positive real numbers and L>=0. Let f,g be concave Lipschitz functions
on [0,S+h], whose almost-everywhere derivatives lie in [0,L]. Suppose

    sup_(0<=t<=S+h) |f(t)-g(t)| <= epsilon.

Then

    integral_0^S |f'(t)-g'(t)| dt <= L*h+2*S*epsilon/h.    (1)

The derivatives in this formula are the almost-everywhere derivatives;
their values at the finitely or countably many corners are immaterial.
Lipschitz functions are absolutely continuous, so the fundamental theorem
and the following uses of Fubini are valid. No limit differentiation is used.

Define D_h f(t)=[f(t+h)-f(t)]/h for 0<=t<=S. Concavity gives
f'(t)>=D_h f(t) at each differentiability point, and

    integral_0^S [f'(t)-D_h f(t)] dt
      = (1/h) integral_0^h {
          integral_0^u f'(t) dt - integral_S^(S+u) f'(t) dt
        } du
      <= (1/h) integral_0^h L*u du
      = L*h/2.                                        (2)

The equality follows by writing each forward difference as an average of
the derivative and canceling the overlapping integrals. It remains valid
when h>S: the signed integral identity still holds. The integrand on the
left is nonnegative by concavity. The same bound holds for g.

The uniform error gives |D_h f(t)-D_h g(t)|<=2*epsilon/h.
Therefore, almost everywhere,

    |f'(t)-g'(t)|
      <= [f'(t)-D_h f(t)] + 2*epsilon/h
                           + [g'(t)-D_h g(t)].

Integrating and applying (2) twice proves (1). The essential assumptions
are concavity, the common derivative bound, and availability of f,g up to
S+h; a small function error alone does not control real derivatives.

The accompanying exact-rational script tests the inequality on finite

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Attempt the second-moment bound on the overlap via Gaussian interpolation. Result: In the nonnegatively correlated case the source bounds E[R(I_0,I_t)^2] using FKG-type positivity; in general the overlap between the argmax at time 0 and at time t is a function of the field and its noised copy, and its second moment can be written through the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup: E[R(I_0,I_t)^2] = E[R(I_0,I_t)] + Var-type terms involving four copies of the field (two pairs). The needed inequality is E[R^2] <= C (E R)^2 + o(1), a 'concentration of the overlap' statement; without positivity one can attempt Gaussian interpolation between the four-copy system and an independent system, whose derivative is a sum of covariance terms of mixed sign, which is exactly where positivity was used. A weaker statement is available: chaos (E R(I_0,I_t) -> 0) gives, by Markov, P(R > delta) -> 0, and multiple peaks in the WEAK sense (existence of a near-maximiser with small overlap) follows from that with the near-maximum condition replaced by the maximum of the noised field, which is a near-maximum of the original field with deficit of order sqrt(t) times the field's variance scale; so 'chaos implies multiple peaks' holds in the sense where the deficit delta_n is of order sqrt(t_n) sigma_n for the chaos time scale t_n, without any second-moment bound; the source's stronger version with the deficit o(m_n)... this weak version I can defend; the second-moment strengthening remains open. Key identity: Noised-field maximiser is a near-maximiser of the original field with deficit O(sqrt(t) sigma_n); chaos gives small overlap in probability, hence weak multiple peaks without positivity. Obstruction: Second moment of the overlap without positive correlations.

[Theorem thm33 of arXiv:2605.16160, 'Revisiting Toeplitz and Hankel random matrices via $*$-convergence of circulant-type matri'] Let $L_n$ be an $n\times n$ random left skew-circulant matrix. Then 
    
    \vskip5pt

    \noindent (i)  If the entries satisfy Assumption I, then $n^{-1/2}L_n$, as an element of 
    
    $(\mathcal{M}_n,\varphi_n=n^{-1}\mathbb{E}\text{Tr})$, converges to a self-adjoint variable whose odd moments vanish and $(2m)$th moment equals $m!$ for each $m\ge1$. 
    \vskip5pt

    \noindent (ii)  If the entries are iid with mean $0$ and variance $1$, then the ESD of $n^{-1/2}L_n$ converges weakly a.s.~to the symmetrized Rayleigh distribution.
title: Theorem thm33 of arXiv:2605.16160

body: In mathematics, the Radon–Nikodym theorem, named after Johann Radon and Otto M. Nikodym, is a result in measure theory that expresses the relationship between two measures defined on the same measurable space. A measure is a set function that assigns a consistent magnitude to the measurable subsets of a measurable space. Examples of a measure include area and volume, where the subsets are sets of points; or the probability of an event, which is a subset of possible outcomes within a wider probability space.

Let Omega in R^n be a bounded open set, A measurable with lambda|xi|^2 <= A(x)xi.xi and |A(x)xi.eta| <= Lambda|xi||eta| (A need not be symmetric), and c in L^infinity(Omega) with c >= 0 a.e. For every f in H^{-1}(Omega) (in particular f = f_0 + sum_i D_i f_i with f_0, f_i in L^2(Omega)) there is exactly one u in H^1_0(Omega) with integral ( A grad u . grad phi + c u phi ) dx = <f, phi> for all phi in H^1_0(Omega), and ||grad u||_{L^2} <= ||f||_{H^{-1}}/lambda, where the H^{-1} norm is dual to ||grad phi||_{L^2}. For inhomogeneous boundary data g in H^1(Omega) there is exactly one u with u - g in H^1_0(Omega) solving the same identity (apply the result to w = u - g and the right-hand side f - Lg in H^{-1}). Remark: with a bounded drift b added the form need not be coercive, but the problem is still uniquely solvable when c >= 0, by the Gaarding inequality plus the Fredholm alternative plus the weak maximum principle.

[Definition 31 of arXiv:2605.03236, 'Stochastic It\^o Equations and Parabolic Second-Order Equations with singular Drift'] The system $\{\Pi_{x}\}$ of families $\Pi_{x}$ of probability measures is called Markovian relative  to $(\frT,\frM_{t})$ provided the following three conditions are satisfied:

1) $\{\Pi_{x}\}$ is a $\bB(E)$-system and 
$P(x_{0}=x)=1$ for any $x\in E$ and $P\in \Pi_{x}$.

2) For any $x\in E$, $P\in \Pi_{x}$,
$\tau\in\frT$, and $f\in C_{0}$
$$
E^{P}\Big\{ \int_{0}^{\infty}
e^{-t}f(x_{\tau+t})\,dt\mid \frM_{\tau}\Big\}
\leq v(f,\Pi_{x_{\tau} })\quad P-(\rm a.s.),
$$
where
$$
v(f,\Pi_{x }):=\sup_{P\in\Pi_{x}}E^{P}
\int_{0}^{\infty}
e^{-t}f(x_{t})\,dt.
$$

3)   For any $x\in E$, $P\in \Pi_{x}$,
$\tau\in\frT$, and $f\in C_{0}$
\begin{equation}
                                
E^{P}\Big[\int_{0}^{\tau}e^{-t}f(x_{t})\,dt
+e^{-\tau}v(f,\Pi_{x_{\tau }})\Big]\leq v(f,\Pi_{x })
\end{equation}
(as we will see below, $v(f,\Pi_{x })\in\bB(E)$ so that the left-hand side is meaningful).

body:
[Definition def:wn of arXiv:2608.05089, 'Correlation decay in area-tilted line ensembles'] The set $\mathcal{W}_N$ consists of all collections $\mathbf{W}$ of $n$ random walk trajectories $\mathbf{W} = (W^i : i \in \{1,\dotsc,n\})$,
where each $W^i$ is a function $[\ell,r]_N \to \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \mathbb{Z}$, such that $\mathbf{W}$ satisfies the following conditions.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For each $i \in \{1,\dotsc,n\}$ and all $t_1, t_2 \in [\ell,r]_N$ with $|t_1 - t_2| = \frac{1}{N}$, we have
    $\mleft| W^i(t_1) - W^i(t_2) \mright| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}$, so that $W^i$ is a diffusively rescaled random walk trajectory.
    \item For each $t \in [\ell,r]_N$, we have the nonintersection constraint $W^1(t) > \dotsb > W^n(t)$.
    \item For each $i \in \{1,\dotsc,n\}$, the trajectory $W^i$ has appropriate boundary conditions, which we now explain.
    We would like to have $W^i(\ell_N) = x^i + O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}})$ and $W^i(r_N) = y^i + O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}})$,
    but some care is needed here.
    First, if $x^i$ and $x^{i+1}$ are very close (or equal), then choosing arbitrary discrete approximations of the boundary conditions
    may violate the strict ordering of the random walk trajectories.
    Furthermore, since the parity of the two boundary conditions must be compatible in order for $W^i$ satisfying the above conditions to exist,
    we will need to correct this issue if it arises.
    So we will impose the boundary conditions
    \begin{equation}
        W^i(\ell_N) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \mleft( \mleft\lfloor \sqrt{N} x^i \mright\rfloor + 2 (n-i) \mright)
        \qquad \text{ and } \qquad
        W^i(r_N) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \mleft( \mleft\lfloor \sqrt{N} y^i \mright\rfloor + 2(n-i) + \epsilon^i \mright),
    \end{equation}
    where $\epsilon^i \in \{0,1\}$ is chosen (depending on $x^i, y^i$, and $N$) to mitigate the parity issue,
    and the term $2(n-i)$ is added to ensure strict ordering of the boundary conditions.
    \item For each $t \in [\ell,r]_N$ and each $i \in \{1,\dotsc,n\}$ we have the floor and ceiling constraints.
    To state these constraints, we introduce the linear interpolation $\widetilde{\mathbf{W}} = (\widetilde{W}^i)_{i=1}^n$ of $\mathbf{W}$, which is a continuous function
    $[\ell,r] \to \mathbb{A}_+^n$ obtained by interpolating $\mathbf{W}$ linearly between points of $[\ell,r]_N$, and extending by a constant
    in $[\ell,r] \setminus [\ell,r]_N$ (i.e.\ at the edges).
    The floor and ceiling constraint is then that $\widetilde{W}^i(t) \in (f^i(t), g^i(t))$ for all $t \in [\ell,r]$. 
\end{enumerate}
This completes the definition of our set of possible states $\mathcal{W}_N$ in the
discrete model of a line ensemble. Note that due to our choices of boundary
conditions,
$\mathcal{W}_N$ is nonempty as long as $N$ is large enough and the
boundary conditions are compatible with the floors and ceilings.

For example,
to construct one element $\mathbf{W} \in \mathcal{W}_N$, we may first let $W^n_\ell$ take
downwards steps away from the left boundary, only taking upwards steps when a
downwards step would intersect $f^n$.  Similarly, we may let $W^n_r$ take
downwards steps away from the right boundary, and set $W^n =
\max\{W^n_\ell,W^n_r\}$.  Then we may inductively construct $W^i$ in the same
way, ensuring that it also does not intersect $f^i$ or $W^{i+1}$.  As long as
$N$ is large enough, the ceiling constraint will also be satisfied since there
is some constant minimum amount of room between $f^i$ and $g^i$ as $\mathbf{f} \prec
\mathbf{g}$ and these functions are continuous on a compact interval.
title: The space $\cW_N = \cW_{n,\ell,r,\f,\g}^{\x,\y}(N)$

body:
[Lemma 4 (Uniform Pigato-type inverse covariance estimate) of arXiv:2607.19752, 'Weak Equilibrium Measures and Capacity--Hitting Identities\\ for the Hypoelliptic Third-Or'] Fix $\eps>0$.  For the cutoff regularized family of
Lemma~\ref{lem:chain-compatible-cutoffs}, use the block order
\[
    X^1=r,\qquad X^2=p,\qquad X^3=\theta .
\]
Let $J_{t,s}^{\delta,\mathsf O}$ be the Jacobian flow from time $s$ to time
$t$ along the full cutoff regularized process.  The three constant noise
matrices in the block order $(r,p,\theta)$ are
\begin{equation}
    \Sigma_r=
    \begin{pmatrix}
        \sqrt{2\gamma\eps/L}\,I_d\\ 0\\ 0
    \end{pmatrix},
    \qquad
    \Sigma_p^\delta=
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0\\ \sqrt{2\eps\delta}\,I_d\\ 0
    \end{pmatrix},
    \qquad
    \Sigma_\theta^\delta=
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0\\ 0\\ \sqrt{2\eps\delta}\,I_d
    \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Each matrix in \eqref{eq:regularized-noise-blocks} belongs to
$\R^{3d\times d}$.  Define the Malliavin covariance contribution generated
only by the $r$-Brownian motion by
\[
    \mathcal M_{t,r}^{\delta,\mathsf O}
    =
    \int_0^t
    J_{t,s}^{\delta,\mathsf O}
    \Sigma_r\Sigma_r^\top
    \left(J_{t,s}^{\delta,\mathsf O}\right)^\top\,ds.
\]
Set
\[
    T_t=\operatorname{diag}\left(t^{1/2}I_d,t^{3/2}I_d,t^{5/2}I_d\right).
\]
Then, for every $q\ge1$, every $M<\infty$, and every compact
$K_0\subset\mathsf O$,
\[
    \sup_{\substack{
        0\le\delta\le1\\
        z\in K_0\\
        0<t\le M}}
    \mathbb E_z\left[
        \lambda_{\min}\left(
            T_t^{-1}\mathcal M_{t,r}^{\delta,\mathsf O}T_t^{-1}
        \right)^{-q}
    \right]
    <\infty .
\]
The same estimate holds for the adjoint cutoff family.  All constants are for
fixed $\eps$ and may depend on $\eps$.

  := \sum_{x\in S}\mu(x)\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(P(x,\cdot)\,\|\,\mu P\bigr),

where $\mu P$ is the marginal of $Y$. This equals the standard Shannon
mutual information between $X$ and $Y$ under the joint distribution
$\mu(x)P(x,y)$.

DRAFT; author proof, independent mathematical review pending. Let two disjoint finite chamber graphs L and R be joined only by a simple k-edge path from u in L to v in R. Its interior vertices have degree two. Under independent Bernoulli(p) bonds, 0<p<1, and without external or cross-chamber identifications, terminals S in L and T in R satisfy P(S connects T)=p^k P_L(S connects u) P_R(v connects T)<=p^k. The bound is attained when S={u} and T={v}. Every path edge is a separating bridge; the three necessary and sufficient events use disjoint independent edge families. This is an auxiliary finite-graph result and does not solve square-lattice conformal invariance.

If f is in L^p(mu) and g in L^q(mu), then fg is in L^1(mu) and integral |f g| dmu <= ||f||_p ||g||_q. For sequences this reads sum |a_i b_i| <= (sum |a_i|^p)^(1/p) (sum |b_i|^q)^(1/q). For 1 < p < infinity, equality holds if and only if |f|^p and |g|^q are proportional almost everywhere (one of them may vanish). The case p = q = 2 is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.

[Proposition prop:quadratic_chaos_mixed_tail of arXiv:2609.01576, '\normalfont Pointwise Majorization for sub-Weibull and Mixed Tail Processes with Applicati'] If $\max_{1\le i\le n}\|\xi_i\|_{\psi_2}\le M_0$, set $C_{HW}=2c_{HW}$, where $c_{HW}$ is the universal constant in Lemma (lem:tool_lamperski_hanson_wright of the paper). Define two metrics
\[
d_1(B_s,B_t):=C_{\mathrm{HW}}M_0^2
\|B_s-B_t\|_{\mathrm{op}},\ d_2(B_s,B_t):=C_{\mathrm{HW}}M_0^2
\|B_s-B_t\|_{\mathrm F},
\]
and set $\rho=d_1+d_2$. Then, the maps $d_1$ and $d_2$ are finite-valued,
jointly Borel pseudo-metrics, and $(T,\rho)$ is separable. 
For every $s,t\in T$ and every $u\ge0$, we have that
\begin{align*}
\PP_\xi\cbr{
|C_s(\xi)-C_t(\xi)|
>
u\,d_1(s,t)
+\sqrt{u}\,d_2(s,t)
}
\le2e^{-u}.
\end{align*}
The process is jointly measurable and has almost surely
$\rho$-continuous sample paths. Consequently,
$\cbr{C_t(\xi)}_{t\in T}$ is an anchored mixed-tail process
with order $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=(1,2)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop:quadratic_chaos_mixed_tail of arXiv:2609.01576

[Corollary 23 (Concrete torus sieve consistency) of arXiv:2609.02196, 'Schr\"odinger Bridges on Lie Group Manifolds for Probabilistic Intrinsic Generation'] Let \(\G=\T^m\), \(\mathcal O_0=\mathcal O_T=g\), and let the reference process be Eq.~\eqref{eq:intro-reference-process} with the Ornstein--Uhlenbeck specialization \eqref{eq:tdm-ref}. Assume that the source, target, and reference group-marginal densities are \(C^2\), strictly positive, and bounded above and below with respect to normalized Haar measure. Let \(\kappa_{\varepsilon}\) be the periodic heat kernel on \(\T^m\), with \(\varepsilon_N\rightarrow0\).

For endpoint calibration, let \(\mathcal B_N\) be the doubly centered trigonometric-polynomial sieve with frequencies \(\|k\|_\infty\le K_N\), restricted to a fixed bounded Lipschitz ball containing the Fej\'er approximants of the exact endpoint potentials. For direct control regression, let \(\mathcal U_N\) be a clipped tensor-product sieve, restricted to a common Lipschitz/linear-growth envelope, built from periodic trigonometric functions in \(g\), splines in \(t\), and polynomials in \(\bm\xi\) on \(\{\|\bm\xi\|\le R_N\}\), with \(R_N,B_N\to\infty\). Denote
\[
d_N=\dim(\mathcal B_N),\qquad p_N=\dim(\mathcal U_N),
\]
and let
\[
M_N:=1+\E_{\mathfrak M^{\beta^*,\varepsilon_N}}
       \bigl[\|\bm v^{Z,\varepsilon_N}\|^4\bigr].
\]
Choose the sieve growth and mollification schedule slowly enough that
\[
\frac{d_N\log N}{N}\to0,\qquad
\frac{M_N B_N^4 p_N\log N}{N}\to0,
\qquad
B_N^2 e^{-cR_N^2}\to0
\]
for some \(c>0\). Use the canonical mollified teacher law, available from the wrapped kernel, so that replay importance weights are identically one; use exact empirical optimization over the compact finite-dimensional sieves; form the calibrated self-normalized initial pool from \(N\) independent reference samples; and let the Lie--Trotter step satisfy \(\Delta t_N\rightarrow0\).

Then Assumptions~\ref{ass:rcm-calibration}, \ref{ass:rccbm-conditional-kernel}, \ref{ass:rccbm-teacher-consistency}, \ref{ass:rccbm-mollification-regularity}, and~\ref{ass:rccbm-statistical-stability} hold for this torus sieve regime. Consequently,
\[
d_{\rm BL}\!\left(P^{\rm SB},P_{N,\Delta t_N}^{\theta_N}\right)
\longrightarrow0
\qquad\text{in probability}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Concrete torus sieve consistency

body: [Prop alephfilling of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a $\Phi$-horizontal foliation such that $\partial_i \mathcal{F}$ is $\aleph$ type along some boundary component $\partial_i M$. Then $\mathcal{F}$ is monotone equivalent to a $\Phi$-horizontal foliation $\mathcal{F}'$ which has the same generalized fine boundary multislope as $\mathcal{F}$ and which extends to a foliation $\mathcal{F}'(s)$ on the Dehn filling of $\partial_i M$ along any slope $s\in \mathbb{Q}$. Moreover, $\mathcal{F}(s)$ is transverse to an extension $\Phi(s)$ of $\Phi$ to the Dehn filling. Every leaf of $\mathcal{F}'(s)$ is a leaf of $\mathcal{F}'$; hence, if $\mathcal{F}'$ is taut then so is $\mathcal{F}'(s)$.
title: $\aleph$ filling

[Definition def:family.Fktd of arXiv:2609.02588, 'Ramsey-type results for Maker-Breaker games'] Given positive integers $k,t,d,s$ with $t\geq d\geq 2$ and $k\geq s$
we define $\mathcal{F}_s(k,t,d)$ to be the family of all $d$-uniform hypergraphs
$\mathcal{H}$ that satisfy the following property:
There exists a partition of the vertex set $V(\mathcal{H}) = V_1\cup \ldots \cup V_t$
such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $|V_i| = k$ for every $i\in [t]$,
\item[(ii)] $|e\cap V_i| \leq 1$ for every $i\in [t]$ and $e\in E(\mathcal{H})$,
\item[(iii)] for every $i\in [t]$, every vertex $v\in V_i$, 
every index set $J\in \binom{[t]\setminus [i]}{d-1}$ and every choice of sets
$A_j\in \binom{V_j}{s}$ for $j\in J$, we have 
$e_{\mathcal{H}}\big( \{v\}\cup \bigcup_{j\in J} A_j\big) \neq 0.$
\end{enumerate}
title: Definition def:family.Fktd of arXiv:2609.02588

The particular clipped covariance-repair oracle in C03 has absolute L2 score error at least e0^4/(65536 a_d^2) at sigma=2t_d=8a_d/e0 for every hidden instance. This is superpolynomial for inverse-polynomial e0. It remains a valid relative-error oracle but cannot be relabeled as uniformly absolute-accurate. The naive conversion e<=2 epsilon_abs*tau is incompatible with the certified endpoint tau<=h_d(e)/(100d).
d>=3 sufficiently large
Kou-Wang equation (9) and B.1 with e0=e/4, M>=100d
C03 fixed public Gaussian contamination and B,eta exactly as defined there
0<e<=1 inverse polynomial
No claim about every possible oracle or a different family

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:4efe66e8ff37a3b643d82b1dca5ecd298329fb86a329115962654ac00d645178","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/4e/4efe66e8ff37a3b643d82b1dca5ecd298329fb86a329115962654ac00d645178.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:93ac30a22b72fe72b997e7244b04598998e5b69a59caadef670fb8f8dcfa3b42","bundle_entry_key":"absolute-error-obstruction-for-box-oracle","bundle_id":"population.t306-absolute-score-transfer-and-obstruction-002","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"diffusion sampling and statistical query lower bounds","draft":"w720/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.diffusion:draft-absolute-error-obstruction-for-box-oracle","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"Own-work; C05 v1 independently checked by urn:mb-agent:7a4f9e38007c2a28; no Target 2 exponent move. 
The archival proof below retains its historical draft status line. The exact-version PASS above governs.

# The transferred box oracle does not satisfy uniform absolute score error

Status: proof (unaudited). Target 2 route failure, not a lower bound for a
different oracle model and not an impossibility theorem about every oracle.

The particular clipped oracle of C03 has exponentially large absolute
mean-square error at a fine noise level. Thus C03's relative error promise
must not be silently replaced by a uniform absolute error promise.

## Statement and fixed parameters

Use the Kou--Wang boxes and gated oracle a from C03, with d>=3 sufficiently
large, integer per-round budget P>=1, 0<e<=1 inverse polynomial, and
e0=e/4. Let M=ceil(100(dP+1)), q=100Md/e0,
a_i=q^{-(i-1)}/4, h_i=a_i/(100M), and t_i=4a_i/e0.
Set B=4(d+1)/e, eta=e^2/[4(B+d)^2], L^2=1/(eta d),
H=N(0,L^2 I), Q=(1-eta)P_box+eta H, and
f_sigma=projection_{ball(B/sigma)} a_sigma.
The parameter a_d below is the scalar location scale, not the oracle field.

At sigma_*=2t_d=8a_d/e0, for EVERY hidden box instance,

E_{Q*Gaussian(sigma_*^2 I)} ||f_{sigma_*}-s_{Q,sigma_*}||^2
 >= e0^4/(65536 a_d^2).

For inverse-polynomial e0, the right side grows faster than any polynomial
in d, because a_d=q^{-(d-1)}/4 and q>=10000d^2/e0.

## Proof

1. The source's equation (9), Section 4, discards coordinate d's posterior
mean correction whenever sigma>t_d. Hence at sigma=sigma_*,
a_{sigma,d}(x)=-x_d/sigma^2, while the true box score is
s_{P,sigma,d}(x)=-x_d/sigma^2+m_{d,sigma}(x_d)/sigma^2,
where m_{d,sigma}(x_d)>=a_d. Thus at every x,
|a_{sigma,d}(x)-s_{P,sigma,d}(x)|>=a_d/sigma^2=e0/(8sigma).
This uses the source oracle itself, not merely its upper error bound.

2. The Gaussian denoising identity gives
E_Psigma||s_P||^2<=d/sigma^2. Source legality gives
E_Psigma||a-s_P||^2<=e0^2/sigma^2. Thus
E_Psigma||a||^2<=2(d+e0^2)/sigma^2.
Consequently the probability of clipping is at most
2(d+e0^2)/B^2<=1/[8(d+1)]<=1/16.

3. Couple X=Y+sigma Z, Y uniform on the box, Z standard Gaussian.
Let E be the intersection of the following events:
||Z||<=2sqrt(d), ||s_P(X)||<=4sqrt(d)/sigma,
and ||a(X)||<=B/sigma. By Markov and the preceding estimates their
failure probabilities are at most 1/4, 1/16, and 1/16. A union bound
gives Pr(E)>=5/8. No independence between these events is used.
E is an event of this joint (Y,Z) coupling; it need not be an event of X alone.

4. At this noise level, sigma<=h_1 sqrt(d) and sigma<=1/(2sqrt(d)).
To check this, use d>=3 and q>=1 to bound
sigma=2q^{-(d-1)}/e0<=2e0/(10000M^2d^2), with h_1=1/(400M).
The two desired inequalities follow from e0<=1/4, M>=100d and d>=3.
All denominators are positive. In particular ||X||<=1+2sigma sqrt(d)<=2
on E, since the source boxes are in the unit ball.

5. A lower bound for the box's smoothed density p_sigma at such X:
take an independent uniform box point Y'. The fraction of each interval
within distance sigma/sqrt(d) of Y_i is at least
min(1,sigma/(2h_i sqrt(d)))>=sigma/(2h_1 sqrt(d)),
where the last term is <=1/2 by Step 4. Product structure of the uniform
box (here independence really is present) gives probability at least
[sigma/(2h_1 sqrt(d))]^d that ||Y'-Y||<=sigma.
On that event ||X-Y'||<=sigma(2sqrt(d)+1)<=3sigma sqrt(d).
The Gaussian convolution integral therefore yields

p_sigma(X) >= [1/(2h_1 sqrt(2pi d))]^d exp(-9d/2).

6. The Gaussian component density g_sigma is at most
(2pi L^2)^(-d/2). Its posterior weight at X satisfies

w_H(X)=eta g_sigma(X)/[(1-eta)p_sigma(X)+eta g_sigma(X)]
 <= 2eta [2h_1 d sqrt(eta) exp(9/2)]^d.

Here 1/(1-eta)<=2. Also eta<=1/324, h_1=1/(400M), M>=100d,
and exp(9/2)<256 (exp(1)<3 and 9/2<5 suffice). Hence the bracket
is at most 256/360000<1/1000, so w_H(X)<=2eta/1000^d.
Since 2eta/e0=2e/(B+d)^2<=2/81<1/40 and
1000^d>=4sqrt(d) for d>=1, we obtain w_H(X)<=e0/(160sqrt(d)).

7. The exact mixture-score identity is
s_Q=(1-w_H)s_P+w_H s_H. This identity is used only to analyze the
oracle; the sampler is never given a density oracle or posterior weights.
On E, ||s_P||<=4sqrt(d)/sigma and
||s_H||=||X||/(L^2+sigma^2)<=2eta d<=sqrt(d)/sigma,
using Step 4 and eta<=1. It follows that
||s_Q-s_P||<=5sqrt(d)w_H/sigma<=e0/(32sigma).

8. On E clipping is inactive, so f=a. The triangle inequality and Step 1
give ||f-s_Q||>=e0/(8sigma)-e0/(32sigma)>=e0/(16sigma).
Since Q_sigma dominates (1-eta)P_sigma and eta<=1/2,

E_Qsigma||f-s_Q||^2
 >= (1-eta) E_{Y,Z}[1_E ||f(X)-s_Q(X)||^2]
 >= (1/4) e0^2/(256sigma^2)
 = e0^4/(65536a_d^2).

The coupling in Step 3 makes this expectation argument valid even though
E depends on Z. This establishes the claimed lower bound.

## Consequence for the endpoint and the other normalization route

C03 permits endpoint smoothing 0<tau<=h_d/(100d). Since sigma_*>tau,
the same error occurs if one regards R=Q*Gaussian(tau^2 I) as the base
target and queries its shifted oracle at additional noise
sqrt(sigma_*^2-tau^2)>0. A uniform absolute-error promise therefore fails
for this supplied shifted oracle as well. Under OU rescaling, the squared
score error is further multiplied by exp(2t)>=1, so this finding also
prevents calling that oracle uniformly absolute-accurate in OU coordinates.

There is also a short obstruction to repairing the upper certificate by
choosing e proportional to the endpoint. Suppose 0<epsilon_abs,tau<=1,
d>=2, and one chooses 0<e<=2 epsilon_abs tau. The box endpoint constraint
requires
tau <= [1/(40000Md)] [e/(400Md)]^{d-1}.
Dividing by tau>0 gives
1 <= 2^{d-1} epsilon_abs^{d-1} tau^{d-2}
     /[40000Md(400Md)^{d-1}] < 1,
a contradiction. Thus the usual sufficient precision conversion and the
fine endpoint certificate cannot both be met, even with constant-factor
slack. This is a failure of that conversion, not a proof that no different
oracle construction could satisfy an absolute error promise.

[Theorem 12 of arXiv:2608.30752, '2608.30752'] Assume that the homotopy class of $u_0$ satisfies the filling hypothesis
stated above. Then there exists $K_E\ge1$, depending only on
$(M,g,u_0,\mathfrak F)$ and $S$, such that, for every Teichm\"uller geodesic
$\gamma\colon\mathbb R\to\mathcal T(S)$ and every $s<t<r$,
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal E_{u_0}(\gamma(t))
  \le
  K_E
  \max\left\{
    \mathcal E_{u_0}(\gamma(s)),
    \mathcal E_{u_0}(\gamma(r))

\end{equation}
In particular, the conclusion holds if $(u_0)_*$ is surjective.

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.03819, 'Stochastic damped wave and Euler-Bernoulli equations with singular locally H\"older...'] Let $U$ and $H$ be two separable Hilbert spaces and $T>0$. We consider a stochastic differential equation which evolves in the Hilbert space $H$ of the form \begin{align} dX(t)=AX(t)dt+B(t,X(t))dt+GdW(t), \quad t\in[0,T], \quad X(0)=x \in H, \end{align} where $A:D(A)\subseteq H\to H$ is the infinitesimal generator of a strongly continuous semigroup $(e^{tA})_{t\geq0}$, $W=(W(t))_{t\geq0}$ is a $U$-cylindrical Wiener process defined on a normal filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t\in [0,T]},\mathbb{P})$, $G:U\to H$ is a linear bounded operator and $B:[0,T]\times H\to H_\beta$ is a locally $\theta$-H\"older continuous function with respect to the second variable, uniformly with respect to the first one, for some suitable $\theta\in(0,1)$. Here, $H_\beta$ is a Hilbert space which contains $H$ with continuous embedding, so that the drift term is singular: it is not well-defined from the ambient space $H$ into itself. The coefficient $\beta\geq0$ measures the order of such a singularity and the case $\beta=0$ corresponds to a drift term with values in $H$. We prove that, under suitable assumptions on the coefficients, weak and pathwise uniqueness hold true for equation \eqref{SDEa}. In particular, the conditions assumed on the coefficients cover the stochastic damped wave equation in dimension $1$ and the stochastic damped Euler--Bernoulli beam equation up to dimension $3$, even in the hyperbolic case.

body: [Thm 8 of arXiv:2607.21759, 'Marchenko--Pastur law for tensor powers of exchangeable unconditional vectors'] Assume the sequence of base vectors $\mathbf X^{(n)} \in \R^n$ satisfies the conditions of \cref{thm:finite-case} for fixed $d$, or \cref{thm:the-norm-cond} for $d = o(\sqrt n)$. Suppose that $\binom{n}{d} / m \to c$ for some constant $c > 0$, and $\mathbf x^{(1)},\dotsc,\mathbf x^{(m)}$ be i.i.d.\ according to $\PowerT(n,d,\mathbf X)$. Then it holds with probability $1$ that \[\frac{1}{\binom{n+d-1}{d}}\sum_{j=1}^{\binom{n+d-1}{d}} \delta_{\lambda_j / d!} \wkconv \mu_{\MP(c)}.\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Recall $\mu_\bG(\bx)$ defined in \eqref{eq:proj-pursuit-def}. For any fixed $\mu \in \cP_2(\R)$ and $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$, abbreviate $\bx\equiv\bx_N\equiv \cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)$ as before, and define the random variables
	\begin{align*}
	X&\equiv X_N
	\equiv X(\bG,\bg^\aux)
	\equiv \bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\bx_N),\mu\Big)\,,\\
	J&\equiv J_N
	\equiv J(\bG,\bg^\aux)
	\equiv

	\EmpDist(\bx_N),\cP(\{\pm1\})
	\Big)\,.
	\end{align*}

\begin{align}

			|X_N - \E X_N|
			\le \delta

		& \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,,\\	
		\bbE\Big[
			(X_N - \E X_N)^2
		\Big] 
		&= o_N(1)\,,\\
		
		\bbP\Big(
			|J_N - \E J_N|
			\le \delta
		\Big)
		& \ge 1-e^{-cN}\\

		\bbE\Big[
			( J_N - \E J_N)^2
		\Big] 
		&= o_N(1)\,.
	\end{align}
where $o_N(1)$ denotes a term tending to $0$ as $N\to\infty$, which may depend on $\alpha,L,\mu$.

	Throughout this proof, $c$ denotes a constant that depends on $\alpha,L,\delta$, which can change line by line.
	Let $C = C(\alpha)$ be given by Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}. As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound}, let
	\[\bar{\bx}
	\equiv\bar\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux) 
		\equiv \bx \min \bigg\{
			1, \frac{2N^{1/2}}{\|\bx\|}\bigg\}\,.\]

	\[\bar\bG = \bG \min\bigg(1,\frac{CN^{1/2}}{\|\bG\|_{\op}}\bigg)\,.\]

	\[

		\equiv \frac{1}{M} \sum_{a=1}^M \delta\bigg\{
		\frac{(\bar\bg^a, \bar{\bx})}{N^{1/2}}\bigg\}\,,
	\]
	By  the bound \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.tail} from Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}, the event

	\[

	\]
	Note also that on event $\cE$, $X=Y$. Thus, for each $\fp \in \{1,2\}$, we have

				+ (\|\mu\|_{L^2})^\fp
			\bigg)

		+ 4\P(\cE^c)

[Lemma SnikfeatFy of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] Let $n$ be a positive integer and $P \subseteq \{(a, b)
  \in \mathbb{N}^2 : 1 \leq a < b \leq n\}$. Moreover, let $f (z_1, \ldots,
  z_n)$ be a function and consider its symmetrization with respect to $P$,
  \[ f_P (z_1, \ldots, z_n) := \frac{1}{n!} \sum_{\pi \in S (n)} \frac{f
     (z_{\pi (1)}, \ldots, z_{\pi (n)})}{\prod_{(a, b) \in P} (z_{\pi (a)} -
     z_{\pi (b)})} . \]
  Then, the following holds:
  \begin{enumerate}
    {\item If $f$ is an analytic function in a neighborhood of $0^n$,
    then $f_P$ is also an analytic function in a neighborhood of $0^n$.}{\item
    If $(f^{(m)} (z_1, \ldots, z_n))_{m \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a sequence of
    analytic functions converging to zero uniformly in a neighborhood of
    $0^n$, then so is the sequence $f_P^{(m)}$.}
  \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma SnikfeatFy of arXiv:2412.09290

body:
Fix a finite irreducible continuous-time Markov generator Q and an initial probability law eta. For nonzero nonnegative killing-rate vectors d, let D=diag(d) and f(d)=eta(D-Q)^(-1)1. Then f is jointly convex in d. No reversibility or stationary initial law is required. This concerns variation of the killing rates, not variation of the modulation speed. The latter convexity can fail. The proof answers the final rate-convexity question in He2021 section4.3 directly; historical priority is unverified.
Q is fixed and finite irreducible
The initial law eta is fixed independently of d
Killing-rate vectors are nonnegative and nonzero

[Corollary 511 of arXiv:2411.15485, '\bf\Large Stochastic Volterra Equations for Local Times of Spectrally Positive L\'evy Proc'] For any $p\geq 1$,  there exists a constant $C>0$ independent of $n $ and $t $ such that 
 \begin{eqnarray*}
  \int_0^\infty  \big|R_n(nt,y)\big|^{p} \cdot \boldsymbol{e}_{c}(y)\, dy   \leq C 
  \quad \mbox{and}\quad 
  \frac{\theta_n}{n^{p-2}}  \int_0^\infty  \big|R_n(nt,y)\big|^{p} \cdot   \boldsymbol{e}_{c}*d\Lambda_n(y)\, dy 
  \leq C\cdot (1+t)^p. 
 \end{eqnarray*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
