[Theorem 76 of arXiv:2605.03236, 'Stochastic It\^o Equations and Parabolic Second-Order Equations with singular Drift'] For any $p\geq d_{0}$  we have
$$
\|g_{\cA}\|_{L_{p/(p-1)}(\bR^{d})}
 \leq N(\delta,d )
\lambda ^{d/(2p)-1}.
$$
In particular, for any Borel $f\geq0$ given on $\bR^{d}$ \(and $\lambda\geq \varkappa_{0}^{2}\rho_{b}^{-2}$\),
on $\{\tau<\infty\}$ we have
\begin{equation}
                               
E_{\cF_{\tau}}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}f(x_{\tau+t})\,dt
\leq N(\delta,d )
\lambda ^{d/(2d_{0})-1}\|f\|_{L_{d_{0}}(\bR^{d})}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Problem 5 of arXiv:2608.25164, 'A time-fractional Kalman filter'] Find the best estimate of the signal $X(t)$ at time $t$, given the observations
$Y(s)$ up to time $t$. This best estimate $\widehat{X}(t)\in\mathbb{Y}_t$ is
defined by
\begin{align}
\E[|X(t)-\widehat{X}(t)|^2]
=\inf_{H\in\mathbb{Y}_t}\E[|X(t)-H|^2], 
\end{align}
where $\mathbb{Y}_t$ denotes the set of $\Y_t$-measurable random variables in
$L^2(\P)$, and $\E$ denotes expectation under the probability law $\P$ of the
two-dimensional Brownian motion $(B_1,B_2)$. (Stated as a problem by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)

body:
[Lemma lem:pseudohybrid of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Fix $L,\eta<\infty$.  There is $C_0=C_0(L,\eta)$ such that, whenever
$T\ge C_0n\log^3n$, every polynomial $p$ of degree at most
$d\le L\log n$ on $\mathrm{SO}(n)$ satisfies, uniformly in the starting
point $x$,
\[
 \left|\mathbb E_xp(X_T)-\mathbb E_Hp\right|
 \le n^{-\eta\log n}\|p\|_\infty.
\tag{3.1.5}
\]
For a polynomial of independent separator blocks, replacing $b$ blocks
one at a time costs at most $b$ times the right side, with the supremum
norm taken after the other blocks are frozen.

[Lemma 5 (Tempered cumulative sums) of arXiv:2608.01674, '\textbf{Limit Theorems for Tempered Linear Processes with Innovations in the Domain of Att'] Let
\[
 A_N(x):=\sum_{j=1}^{\floor{Nx}}
 \e^{-\lambda_Nj}\frac{\ell(j)}{j}.
\]
Under \cref{ass:filter,ass:tempering}, for every $x>0$,
\[
 \frac{A_N(x)}{A_N(1)}\longrightarrow1, ~~~~\text{as} ~~N\to \infty.
\]
If $\lambda_*<\infty$, then $A_N(1)\sim L(N)$.  If
$\lambda_*=\infty$, then
$A_N(1)\sim L(1/\lambda_N)$.

body:
[Lemma lem:walk1 of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] Let $\mathbb{P}^W_{n}$ be the probability measure on simple random walks $(S_k)_{k\geq 0}$ starting from $n$. 
\begin{itemize}
\item Consider the infinite measure $\mu^A := \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{P}^W_n$. Then $\mu^A(S_{k} = 0) = 1$ for all $k \geq 0$.
\item Consider the infinite measure $\mu^E := \sum_{n \in 2\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{P}^W_n$. Then $\mu^E(S_{2k} = 0) = 1$ and $\mu^E(S_{2k+1}=0) = 0$ for all $k \geq 0$ .
\item Consider the infinite measure $\mu^O := \sum_{n \in 2\mathbb{Z}+1} \mathbb{P}^W_n$. Then $\mu^O(S_{2k+1} = 0) = 1$ and $\mu^O(S_{2k}=0) = 0$  for all $k \geq 0$. 
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

WHY IT IS A SEPARATE QUANTITY: the non-random fluctuation E T - n mu is not the variance and is not bounded by it. A campaign that quotes a variance bound has said nothing about this gap, and vice versa.
SUPERSEDING BOUND, NOT A CONTRADICTION: the current best is mu(x) <= E T(0,x) <= mu(x) + C (|x| log|x|)^{1/2} (see the Alexander-method state-of-the-art node). Kesten's n^{5/6} log n remains historically correct; it is simply weaker.

VERIFICATION STATUS: survey-claim. Lane P4 did not read Kesten (1993) itself.
title: Kesten (1993), Theorem 1: the NON-RANDOM fluctuation in first-passage percolation obeys E T(0,ne_1) <= n mu(e_1) + C n^{5/6} log n. This is the first upper bound on the gap between the mean passage time and the time constant, and it has since been improved to n mu(e_1) + C (n log n)^{1/2}.

body:
Let X in R^(m by d) have independent standard Gaussian entries, let A1 in R^(k1 by m) be a random matrix, and let Z1,Z2 be random seeds, with (X,A1,Z1,Z2) mutually independent. Let A2=h2(A1 X,Z2) take values in R^(d by k2), and Y=h1(A1 X,X A2,Z1), where h1,h2 are deterministic measurable maps. Write P1 for the orthogonal projector onto the row space of A1 in R^m and P2 for the orthogonal projector onto the column space of A2 in R^d. Then there exists a coupled matrix X_tilde with independent standard Gaussian entries, independent of Y, such that X=(I-P1)X_tilde(I-P2)+(I-P1)XP2+P1X(I-P2)+P1XP2 almost surely. No full-rank or invertibility hypothesis on A1 or A2 is needed. The independence asserted is X_tilde independent of Y; X_tilde generally shares the retained unobserved block with X and is not asserted independent of X.
All matrix dimensions are finite and compatible
X has iid N(0,1) entries
X,A1,Z1,Z2 are mutually independent
A2 may depend on X only through A1X and the independent seed Z2
Y is measurable from A1X,XA2,Z1
P1 projects onto rows of A1; P2 onto columns of A2

[Lemma de Moivre-Laplace of arXiv:2507.10294, 'Guessing Strategies for Shelf-Shuffling Machines'] Suppose 
\[\frac{k_n-np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}\to x\in\mathbb{R}\]
or, equivalently, $k_n=np+O(\sqrt{n})$.
Then,
\[\binom{n}{k_n}p^{k_n}(1-p)^{n-k_n}\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi np(1-p)}}e^{-\frac{x^2}{2}}\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Extreme hopcounts for general random-graph degree and weight laws structural reduction Result: On a graph with maximum degree Delta, there are at most n*Delta*(Delta-1)^(k-1) oriented simple k-edge paths. With iid weights Y, the chance any such path has total weight at most t is at most this count times exp(a*t)*(E exp(-aY))^k for every a>0. Check: After the first edge there are at most Delta-1 nonbacktracking choices. Independence along a simple path and exponential Markov inequality bound its lower-tail cost. The union bound needs no independence between different paths. Obstruction: The bound is too crude when a few hubs make Delta large and does not automatically constrain minimizing paths with unknown total cost. Degree-biased branching and extreme endpoint selection require sharper control.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0149-extreme-hopcounts-for-general-random-graph-degree-and-weight-laws
No independent review
title: Attempt on Extreme hopcounts for general random-graph degree and weight laws

[Lemma lem:hyperbolic-boundary of arXiv:2609.00777, 'Universal murmuration and Hecke augmentation'] Let
\[
R_1=\frac{2P^{k/2}}{\sqrt X}.
\]
The contribution of
\[
R_0\leq r\leq\frac{2P^{k/2}}{\sqrt N},
\qquad
N\in[X,X+Y],
\]
together with the extension of the main term in Corollary~(cor:hyperbolic-interior of the paper) from $R_0$ to $R_1$, after
multiplication by $\zeta(2)\pi/(XY)$, is
\[
O_{k,\varepsilon}\left(
(P^kX)^\varepsilon
\left(
\frac{P^kY^{3/2}}{X^{5/2}}
+
\frac{P^{k/2}Y^{1/2}}{X}
\right)
\right).
\]

$V_{1}(t,\kappa)=w_1+w_2=\lambda_0+\lambda_2+\lambda_4\kappa$, where
$\lambda_0=\lambda_4(c^4+k_2c^2)$, $\lambda_2=\lambda_4(k_2-2c^2)$.

[Proposition 32 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] Let $m>2$ be fixed.  Assume $J\in C_c^2(\R)$ is even, nonnegative, normalized and
positive on a neighborhood of the origin, and assume
\[
q\in C^2([-L,L]),\qquad a\in C^2([-L,L]),\qquad q\ge q_0>0.
\]
Set
\[
\varepsilon_\sigma:=\sigma^{m-2},
\qquad
\mu_\sigma:=\varepsilon_\sigma\Lp(\cA_{\sigma,m,L}),
\qquad
\mu_D:=d_J\frac{\pi^2}{4L^2}.
\]
Then $\mu_\sigma\longrightarrow\mu_D$.
If $\phi_\sigma>0$ is normalized by $\|\phi_\sigma\|_{L^2(-L,L)}=1$, then, after zero
extension,
\[
\widetilde\phi_\sigma\longrightarrow
e_1:=L^{-1/2}\cos\frac{\pi x}{2L}\,\mathbf 1_{[-L,L]}
\quad\hbox{strongly in }L^2(\R),
\]
and $E_\sigma(\phi_\sigma)\longrightarrow\mu_D$.
In addition,
\[
\varepsilon_\sigma\phi_\sigma(-L)^2\longrightarrow0.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\Lp(\cA_{\sigma,m,L})
=
\frac{D_2(J)\pi^2}{8L^2}\,\sigma^{2-m}
+o(\sigma^{2-m}).
\]

body: Certificate (campaign status: proved): Selector basis (S12 sec.3). Orient the cycle; for a length-two gap u-v-u' select B_v, C_v; for a length-three gap u-v-w-u' select B_v, C_v, C_w. Let B_U = {A} together with all gap-selected forms; every gap of length g contributes g forms so |B_U| = 1 + sum_gaps g = n+1 = r. Independence: in a putative dependence the coordinate B_{u'} occurs in exactly one selected form of the preceding gap (its final C-form), so that coefficient vanishes; moving backwards through the gap kills the rest, then A. Representatives modulo R = span{L_u}: A and the selected forms represent themselves; B_u = -A for u in U; in a length-three gap B_w = C_w (C_w-B_w = L_{u'}); the edge form leaving u in U obeys C_u = B_v (C_u-B_v = L_u). These cases exhaust D_n, so d_cb(A_n) <= dim R = ceil(n/3). Notes: Explains the three-at-a-time quotient mergers of the binary lower bound: a length-three gap is paid by ONE residual direction while retaining a genuine coordinate-basis transversal. This is the basis implemented by the S13 checker.

body: In functional analysis, a branch of mathematics, a compact operator is a linear operator that behaves, in several important respects, like a finite-dimensional operator such as a matrix. In infinite-dimensional spaces, bounded sets are usually not compact, and bounded sequences need not have convergent subsequences. Compact operators partly restore this finite-dimensional behavior by sending bounded sets to sets whose closures are compact, or equivalently, in normed spaces, by sending bounded sequences to sequences with convergent subsequences.

[Theorem 3 ($k$-Random-to-Top) of arXiv:2605.19084, 'Limit Profiles for Separation Distance'] For a sequence $k_n$, let $s_{n,k_n}$ be the separation distance of the shuffle which chooses $k_n$ cards uniformly without replacement and moves them to the top, preserving their relative order. If $k_n\log n/n\to0$, then for every fixed $c\in\mathbb R$,
$$s_{n,k_n}\left(\left\lfloor\frac{n}{k_n}(\log n+c)\right\rfloor\right)\to 1-e^{-e^{-c}}(1+e^{-c}).$$
If instead $k_n/n\to\alpha\in(0,1)$, set $q_{n,k_n}:=(\binom{k_n}{2}+\binom{n-k_n}{2})/\binom{n}{2}$. For any sequence of integer times $t_n$ such that
$$t_n=\frac{2\log n+c+o(1)}{-\log q_{n,k_n}},$$
we have
$$s_{n,k_n}(t_n)\to 1-\exp\left(-\frac12e^{-c}\right).$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

satisfy the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[i)]
\item Diffeomorphism invariance: Let $(D_1, g_1)$ and $(D_2, g_2)$ be two Riemann surfaces with boundary and $\psi: D_1 \to D_2$ a diffeomorphism such that $g_1 := \psi^*g_2$. Then 
$$\sigma_{\rm tw}^{D_1, g_1}(z_1, \dots, z_n) 
= \sigma_{\rm tw}^{D_2, g_2}(\psi(z_1), \dots, \psi(z_n)). 
$$ 
\item Weyl scaling: Let $\Omega: D \to \mathbb{R}_+$. Then 
$$\sigma_{\rm tw}^{D,g\Omega^2}(z_1, \dots, z_n) 
= 
\Big(\prod_{j=1}^{n} \Omega(z_j)^{-1/8}\Big)
\sigma_{\rm tw}^{D, g}(z_1, \dots, z_n). $$
\item Conformal covariance: Let $D_1$ and $D_2$ be two simply connected domains,
$D_1,D_2\neq\mathbb{C}$.
Take a conformal mapping
$\psi:D_1\rightarrow D_2$.
Let $z_1,z_2,\dots,z_n\in D_1$ be
two by two distinct.
Then,
\begin{equation}

\sigma_{\rm tw}^{D_2}(\psi(z_{1}), \psi(z_{2}),\dots, \psi(z_{n}))
=
\Big(
\prod_{j=1}^{n} \vert\psi'(z_j)\vert^{-1/8}
\Big)
\sigma_{\rm tw}^{D_1}(z_{1}, z_{2},\dots, z_{n}).
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 38 (Nil diameter bound and blowdown) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(g(t)\), \(t\geq0\), be an immortal Ricci flow on the orientable total
space \(M\) of a \(\TT^2\)-bundle over \(S^1\) with nontrivial unipotent
monodromy, under the
\hyperref[par:working-cover-convention]{working-cover convention}.  Then there
is a constant \(C<\infty\) such that
\[
        \diam(M,g(t))\leq C\sqrt t,
\]
for all sufficiently large \(t\).  In addition,
\[
        \lim_{t\to\infty}(M,t^{-1}g(t))=\pt
\]
in the Gromov--Hausdorff sense.  On every compact \(\tau\)-interval in
\((0,\infty)\), the lifted blowdown flows on the universal cover converge as
\(s\to\infty\) in the pointed Cheeger--Hamilton sense to a pointed flow
isometric to
\[
        \left(\RR^3,0,
        \frac{1}{3\tau^{1/3}}
        \left(dx+\frac12 y\,dz-\frac12 z\,dy\right)^2
        +\tau^{1/3}(dy^2+dz^2)
        \right).
\]

[Definition 34 of arXiv:2609.02105, 'Contact fundamental forms and \\ adjoint varieties'] Let $\fn_-=\fn_{-1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\fn_{-d}$
be a negatively graded nilpotent Lie algebra, and let
$\fn_0\subset{\rm Der}_{\rm gr}(\fn_-)$ be a Lie subalgebra such that
$\fn_-\oplus\fn_0$ is a graded Lie algebra.  For $i>0$, after the spaces
$\fn_j$ for $j<i$ and their brackets with $\fn_-$ have been constructed,
define $\fn_i$ to be the space of degree-$i$ linear maps
$$
\phi:\fn_-\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{j<i}\fn_j,\qquad
\phi(\fn_{-k})\subset\fn_{i-k},
$$
satisfying
$$
\phi([u,v])=[\phi(u),v]+[u,\phi(v)]\qquad (u,v\in\fn_-).
$$
Here brackets involving $\fn_0$ and the previously constructed positive
components are the recursively defined evaluation brackets on $\fn_-$.  The
graded Lie algebra
$$
\operatorname{prol}(\fn_-,\fn_0):=\bigoplus_{i\ge-d}\fn_i
$$
is called the {\em universal prolongation} of $(\fn_-,\fn_0)$.

[Lemma 18 (Maximum entropy quadruply augmented double hive) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{lem:double-maxent}
Let \(\bar a,\bar b,\bar d>0\).  Assume either
\[
\bar f \geq 0,
\]
or
\[
\bar f^2<0,
\qquad
T:=\bar a^2+\bar b^2+\bar d^2+\bar f^2<0.
\]
Let \(\mathbb D^4\) be the cone of double hives
augmented on the four exterior boundary components:
\[
\mathbb D^4
=
\bigcup_{\alpha,\beta,\eta,\phi,\nu}
GT(\alpha)\times GT(\beta)\times GT(\eta)\times GT(\phi)
\times H_n(\alpha,\beta;\nu)
\times H_n(\eta,\phi^\vee;\nu^\vee),
\]
where
\[
\alpha,\beta,\eta,\phi\in \Spec_n+\mathbb R\one,
\qquad
\sum_i\alpha_i+\sum_i\beta_i+\sum_i\eta_i-\sum_i\phi_i=0,
\]
and
\[
\nu^\vee=(-\nu_n,\ldots,-\nu_1),\qquad
\phi^\vee=(-\phi_n,\ldots,-\phi_1).
\]
Thus the fiber volume over
\((\alpha,\beta,\eta,\phi,\nu)\) contains the exterior factor
\[
\frac{V_n(\alpha)V_n(\beta)V_n(\eta)V_n(\phi)}
     {V_n(\tau_n)^4}
|H_n(\alpha,\beta;\nu)|\,|H_n(\eta,\phi^\vee;\nu^\vee)|
\]

Define a density \(p_{\mathrm{dbl}}\) on \(\mathbb D^4\), with respect to
Lebesgue measure on this cone, by
\[
p_{\mathrm{dbl}}(x)
=
Z_{\mathrm{dbl}}^{-1}
\exp\left[
-\frac12
\left(
\frac{|\alpha(x)|^2}{\bar a^2}
+
\frac{|\beta(x)|^2}{\bar b^2}
+
\frac{|\eta(x)|^2}{\bar d^2}
+
\frac{|\phi(x)|^2}{\bar f^2}
\right)
\right].
\]
Then \(p_{\mathrm{dbl}}\) is the unique probability density on
\(\mathbb D^4\) maximizing differential entropy among all densities \(q\)
such that
\[
\mathbb E_q|\alpha|^2=\mathbb E_{p_{\mathrm{dbl}}}|\alpha|^2,\qquad
\mathbb E_q|\beta|^2=\mathbb E_{p_{\mathrm{dbl}}}|\beta|^2,
\]
\[
\mathbb E_q|\eta|^2=\mathbb E_{p_{\mathrm{dbl}}}|\eta|^2,\qquad
\mathbb E_q|\phi|^2=\mathbb E_{p_{\mathrm{dbl}}}|\phi|^2.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Maximum entropy quadruply augmented double hive

Let F_q be a finite field of characteristic p and let f_1, ..., f_r in F_q[x_1, ..., x_n] be polynomials whose degrees satisfy deg f_1 + ... + deg f_r < n. Then the number N of common zeros of f_1, ..., f_r in F_q^n is divisible by p (Warning). In particular, if the system has one common zero - for instance when every f_i has zero constant term - then it has at least two (Chevalley). Warning's second theorem: if N > 0 then N >= q^{n - (deg f_1 + ... + deg f_r)}.

[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2608.03497, 'Connective Constants on Nested Fractal Graphs'] Let \(N\ge3\) and \(4\nmid N\).  The crossing vector of the regular
polygonal \(N\)-gasket satisfies a closed finite-dimensional polynomial
recursion.
Define its \emph{crossing critical inverse temperature} by
\[
  \beta_{\mathrm c,N}^{\mathrm{cr}}
  :=
  \inf\left\{
    \beta\ge0:
    \sup_{m\ge0}\|\mathbf C_m^{(N)}(\beta)\|_\infty<\infty
  \right\}.
\]
Then \(\mu_N=e^{\beta_{\mathrm c,N}^{\mathrm{cr}}}\).

For \(N\in\{6,9\}\), put
\(\tau=(\sqrt5-1)/2\) and \(d_N=N/3\).  Then
\begin{equation}
  \mu_N
  =
  \left(
    \frac{\sqrt{1+4\tau^{1/d_N}}-1}{2}
  \right)^{-1/d_N}.
  
\end{equation}
In particular, \(\mu_6\) and \(\mu_9\) are algebraic numbers. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

If no representatives remain both trajectories are zero. Otherwise let m be their number and d the largest sign-class multiplicity. The first deterministic postactivation correlation has smallest eigenvalue rho1>0. With B=10^14 and A=3*10^8*m+48*B^2*exp(2016+7200*m)*m^2/rho1, for every positive n,L there is a coupling to the joint independent-layer GP trajectory with expected sum of preactivation squared Frobenius errors divided by n at most d*A*L/n, and single-layer error at most d*A/n uniformly in depth. Including postactivations at most doubles the bound. Thus normalized joint W2 is at most sqrt(d*A*L/n), including L<=n^(1-epsilon). The constant is uniform over the deterministic activation sequence apart from its stated first-Gram stability parameter.
Fresh independent Gaussian weights with variance 1/n; zero biases; deterministic activation sequence indexed by probability measures on [1,2]; finite input covariance with diagonal in [0,1].

Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: narrowed. Target: T250(a). Novelty is unverified. This is a whole infinite-dimensional activation family, not a claim about arbitrary Tensor Programs.

## 1. Statement and indexing

For a probability measure nu supported on [1,2], define

    g_nu(t)=integral_[1,2] (1-exp(-s t))/s dnu(s), t>=0,
    Phi_nu(x)=sign(x)*sqrt(g_nu(x^2)), Phi_nu(0)=0.

Fix any DETERMINISTIC sequence nu_0,nu_1,... of such measures. All neurons within transition l use Phi_{nu_l}; the measure may change between layers. There are no biases. Every hidden layer has width n, and fresh independent layer weights have independent N(0,1/n) entries. Equivalently, and also defining the initial Gaussian layer without input-dimension restrictions, start with a positive semidefinite p-by-p covariance K_0 with diagonal in [0,1]. Conditional on K_l, the n rows of h_{l+1} are independent N_p(0,K_l), and K_{l+1}=n^{-1}sum_i Phi_{nu_l}(h_{l+1,i})Phi_{nu_l}(h_{l+1,i})^T. The initial K_0 is deterministic. This conditional construction is the exact law of the fresh-Gaussian-weight network, not a limit or an SDE.

Define the GP recursion bar K_0=K_0 and bar K_{l+1}=E[Phi_{nu_l}(Z)Phi_{nu_l}(Z)^T], Z~N_p(0,bar K_l). Its joint preactivation trajectory has independent Gaussian layers with these deterministic covariances. Let K_0=VV^T. Delete zero rows v_j of V and retain one representative of each class v_j=+-v_k. Let m be the number retained. If m=0 all finite and GP trajectories are identically zero. Otherwise let d be the largest class multiplicity, and rho_1 the smallest eigenvalue of the normalized correlation of the FIRST deterministic postactivation Gram on the m representatives. Then rho_1>0, and, with

    B=10^14,
    A(m,rho_1)=3*10^8 m +48 B^2 exp(2016+7200m)m^2/rho_1,

there is a coupling, for every positive integer n,L, such that

    E sum_{l=1}^L ||h_l-bar h_l||_F^2/n <= d A(m,rho_1) L/n.      (1)

Each individual layer has expected normalized squared error <=d A(m,rho_1)/n, uniformly in its depth. Including the corresponding postactivations at most doubles (1). Thus normalized joint W_2<=sqrt(d A L/n), in particular for L<=n^(1-epsilon). L counts Gaussian layers; recording their activations uses at most 2L variable-producing lines. The constants are uniform over the entire deterministic activation sequence except for the stated first-Gram stability parameter rho_1. No uniform positive lower bound on rho_1 over inputs and nu_0 is asserted.

The hardest new pieces are uniform normalized-feature estimates and strict positivity of the first activation Gram for arbitrary, possibly nonatomic, nu_0. The stochastic error estimate is written out below to expose its conditioning and constants.

## 2. Uniform activation and scalar-kernel estimates

Write R_nu(t)=g_nu(t)/t=integral integral_0^1 exp(-s t u) du dnu(s), with R_nu(0)=1. For t>=0,

    t/(1+2t)<=g_nu(t)<=min(t,1),
    0<g_nu'(t)<=1,   |R_nu'(t)|<=1.

The lower bound follows from 1-exp(-a)>=a/(1+a); the upper bounds use s>=1 and 1-exp(-a)<=a. Concavity gives t g_nu'(t)<=g_nu(t). Hence, for x!=0,

    Phi_nu'(x)=|x|g_nu'(x^2)/sqrt(g_nu(x^2)),
    0<=Phi_nu'(x)<=sqrt(g_nu'(x^2))<=1,
    Phi_nu'(x)>=g_nu'(x^2)>=1-2x^2.

The last lower bound uses g_nu(t)<=t and exp(-a)>=1-a. Together these show 0<=1-Phi_nu'(x)<=2x^2. The representation Phi_nu(x)=x sqrt(R_nu(x^2)) proves smoothness at zero and Phi_nu'(0)=1, so these are critical, odd, bounded, 1-Lipschitz activations. Derivatives of R_nu are bounded on t>=0 by finite powers of 2, and R_nu(t)>=(1+2t)^{-1}; differentiation therefore gives at most polynomial growth for every derivative of Phi_nu. This also supplies the Gaussian integrability used below.

For standard Gaussian Z, set F_nu(q)=E Phi_nu(sqrt(q)Z)^2. Gaussian integration gives the exact expression

    F_nu(q)=integral_[1,2] [1-(1+2s q)^(-1/2)]/s dnu(s).

This map is increasing and concave, vanishes at zero, and is positive for q>0. Jensen under the probability measure Z^2 dgamma gives, for 0<=q<=1,

    F_nu(q)>=q E[Z^2/(1+2qZ^2)]>=q/(1+6q)>=q/7.

Since (1-exp(-s t))/s=integral_0^t exp(-s u)du decreases in s, F_nu(q)<=1-(1+2q)^(-1/2)=:F_1(q). On [0,1],

    1-F_1'(q)=1-(1+2q)^(-3/2)>=2q/(1+2q)>=(2/3)q.

Integration yields q-F_nu(q)>=q^2/3, and we use only the weaker bound q-F_nu(q)>=q^2/6. If Y=Phi_nu(sqrt(q)Z)^2, then 0<=Y<=1, Y<=qZ^2, and Var(Y)<=3q^2<=147F_nu(q)^2.

At transition l use F_l=F_{nu_l}. For a positive marginal chain Q_l and its deterministic iteration s_{l+1}=F_l(s_l), Q_0=s_0 in (0,1], conditional sampling gives E[Q_{l+1}|past]=F_l(Q_l), Var(Q_{l+1}|past)<=147F_l(Q_l)^2/n. Every state lies in [0,1]. Concavity and monotonicity imply that S_l=F_l(Q_l)/F_l(s_l) lies between Q_l/s_l and 1. Therefore v_l=E(Q_l/s_l-1)^2 satisfies

    v_{l+1}<=(1+294/n)v_l+294/n,
    v_l<=588l/n if 294l/n<=1.

All relative moments at finite l exist since Q_l<=1 and s_l>0. For mu_l=E Q_l, Jensen and the quadratic drift give mu_{l+1}<=mu_l-mu_l^2/6. The same holds for s_l. Taking reciprocals when positive gives mu_l,s_l<=6/l for l>=1; a zero state stays zero. Telescoping gives sum_l s_l^2<=6s_0. Splitting at l=n/294, using (sqrt(r)-1)^2<=(r-1)^2 in the early window and (sqrt(a)-sqrt(b))^2<=a+b afterwards, proves

    E(sqrt(Q_l)-sqrt(s_l))^2<=3528/n for every l.          (2)

This argument permits varying F_l because all bounds hold separately at each transition; it does not silently apply a fixed-map lemma to a varying map.

## 3. Uniform feature sensitivity and random-product moments

For q>0 put u_{nu,q}(z)=Phi_nu(sqrt(q)z)/sqrt(F_nu(q)), a unit Gaussian-L2 vector. Its continuous extension at q=0 is z. Let h_q(z)=Phi_nu(sqrt(q)z)/sqrt(q)=z sqrt(R_nu(qz^2)). Then

    |partial_q h_q(z)|<=|z|^3 sqrt(1+2z^2)/2, q<=1,
    ||partial_q h_q||_2^2<=(15+2*105)/4=225/4,
    ||h_q||_2>=1/sqrt(7).

Differentiating a normalized Hilbert-space vector gives an orthogonal projection of its derivative divided by its norm. Thus ||partial_q u_{nu,q}||_2<=15sqrt(7)/2<20, uniformly in nu. The displayed Gaussian-integrable envelope justifies differentiation and the extension at zero. For jointly standard Gaussian (X,Y) with correlation c, define H_nu(q,r,c)=E[u_{nu,q}(X)u_{nu,r}(Y)]. Cauchy-Schwarz gives

    |H_nu(q,r,c)-H_nu(s,t,c)|<=20(|q-s|+|r-t|).          (3)

Gaussian integration by parts, justified by bounded Phi_nu and Phi_nu', gives E Phi_nu'(sqrt(q)Z)=E[Z Phi_nu(sqrt(q)Z)]/sqrt(q). Weighted Jensen and the lower activation bound imply

    E Phi_nu'(sqrt(q)Z)>=E[Z^2/sqrt(1+2qZ^2)]>=1/sqrt(1+6q)>=1/sqrt(7).

Also Var(Phi_nu'(sqrt(q)Z))<=E(1-Phi_nu')^2<=12q^2. Cauchy-Schwarz implies F_nu(q)>=q(E Phi_nu')^2. Consequently

    chi(q):=q E Phi_nu'(sqrt(q)Z)^2/F_nu(q)<=1+84q^2.

Price's covariance identity and Cauchy-Schwarz now give 0<=partial_c H_nu<=sqrt(chi(q)chi(r))<=1+42(q^2+r^2). The identity holds on (-1,1); boundedness and dominated convergence extend the Lipschitz bound to c=+-1. A primary locator for this identity is Voigtlaender, arXiv:1710.03576, Theorem 1 and Corollary 2; its smoothness/growth hypotheses hold by the first paragraph of section 2.

For any scalar marginal, put X=Y-EY, |X|<=1. For 0<=t<=1, e^(tX)<=1+tX+t^2 X^2, since the absolute Taylor remainder is at most (e-2)t^2 X^2<t^2X^2. Conditional independence within a layer yields, for a>=0 and n>=36a,

    E[exp(a Q_{l+1})|past]<=exp(aF_l(Q_l)+3a^2Q_l^2/n)
      <=exp(aQ_l-aQ_l^2/12).

With a=12b, the process exp(b sum_{t<l}Q_t^2+12bQ_l) is a nonnegative supermartingale when n>=432b. Thus E exp(b sum_{t<L}Q_t^2)<=exp(12bQ_0), for every finite L. Holder across two input marginals, requiring no independence between them, implies for

    P_L=product_{l<L}[1+42(Q_{j,l}^2+Q_{k,l}^2)]

that E P_L^r<=exp(504r(Q_{j,0}+Q_{k,0})) when n>=36288r. In particular ||P_L||_4<=exp(1008) when n>=145152. This estimate alone does not permit treating P_L as independent of propagated noise.

## 4. Early-window fourth moments and empirical correlation noise

Set N=10^7. Conditional on the past, xi=Q_{l+1}/F_l(Q_l)-1 is the mean of centered iid W=Y/F_l(Q_l)-1. Since |W|<=7Z^2+1,

    E W^4<=E(7Z^2+1)^4=273596,
    E[xi^2|past]<=147/n,
    E[xi^4|past]<=338423/n^2,
    E[|xi|^3|past]<=10000/n^(3/2).

The fourth moment uses the exact iid centered-average formula; 338423=273596+3*147^2. Write delta=Q_l/s_l-1, S=F_l(Q_l)/F_l(s_l), a=S-1. Then delta_next=a+S xi, |a|<=|delta| and S<=1+|delta|. Expanding conditionally gives, x=|delta|,

    v4(l+1)<=v4(l)+(882/n)E[x^2(1+x)^2]
      +(40000/n^(3/2))E[x(1+x)^3]+(338423/n^2)E[(1+x)^4].

Use x^2(1+x)^2<=2x^2+2x^4, (1+x)^4<=8(1+x^4), x/n^(3/2)<=x^2/(2n)+1/(2n^2), 3x^3/n^(3/2)<=3(x^2+x^4)/(2n), and n>=1 for the remaining terms. The coefficients of v4/n, v2/n, and 1/n^2 are at most 2809148, 201764, and 2727384 respectively, hence at most N. Unrolling, for 1<=l<=n/N, gives

    v4(l)<=N e*589 l^2/n^2<400^4 l^2/n^2,
    ||Q_l-s_l||_4<=2400/(sqrt(n)sqrt(l)).                 (4)

For the two-input noise, let U=u_{nu,q}(X), V=u_{nu,r}(Y), with correlation c and n independent paired rows. Write A=n^{-1}sum U_i^2, D=n^{-1}sum V_i^2, T=n^{-1}sum U_iV_i, h=E UV. The empirical correlation is c'=T/sqrt(AD). All denominators are positive almost surely, including at c=+-1 and n=1. Also |c'|<=1.

Since U^2<=7X^2 and V^2<=7Y^2, each centered single-row coordinate among U^2,V^2,UV has variance <=147 and fourth moment <=851000. For the product coordinate, use |UV-h|<=(7/2)(X^2+Y^2)+1 and (a+b+c)^4<=27(a^4+b^4+c^4), giving 6807051/8<851000; the square coordinates have the smaller bound 273596. Thus each centered sample mean has fourth moment <=915827/n^2<10^6/n^2.

On the event E={A,D in [1/2,3/2]}, the line segment from (1,1,h) to (A,D,T) has |T|<=3/2. The gradient coordinates of T/sqrt(AD) are bounded by 3 and its Hessian entries by 9. Markov gives P(E^c)<=32*10^6/n^2. Therefore

    E|c'-h|^4 <=(3^4*27*3*10^6+16*32*10^6)/n^2<10^10/n^2.

The Taylor remainder on E has expected magnitude <=(9/2)*3*(3*147)/n<6000/n. The full linear Taylor term has mean zero; its expectation restricted to E has magnitude <=9sqrt(147*32*10^6)/n^(3/2)<10^6/n^(3/2). The actual error on E^c contributes <=64*10^6/n^2. Thus, beta=E c'-h and zeta=c'-E c' satisfy, with B=10^14,

    |beta|<=B/n, E zeta=0, E|zeta|^k<=B n^(-k/2), k=2,3,4. (5)

For the last claim use E zeta^4<=16*10^10/n^2 and Lyapunov. These are uniform conditional estimates, so they apply given the complete network past and the current deterministic nu_l.

## 5. Adapted correlation error

Assume n>=N. For a pair j,k let e_l=C_{l,jk}-bar C_{l,jk}, with e_0=0. Equations (3)-(5) and the correlation Lipschitz estimate give

    e_{l+1}=A_l e_l+d_l+zeta_{l+1},
    0<=A_l<=a_l:=1+42(Q_{j,l}^2+Q_{k,l}^2),
    ||d_l||_4<=96000/(sqrt(n)sqrt(l))+B/n for 1<=l<=n/N,
    ||d_0||_4<=B/n.

A_l is the difference quotient of H_{nu_l} at the random variances (set it to zero when e_l=0); d_l is the variance-parameter difference plus beta_l. They are measurable before the next sample. Put P_0=1, P_{l+1}=P_l a_l, gamma_l=A_l/a_l in [0,1], y_l=e_l/P_l. Split y=z+w, both starting at zero, by

    z_{l+1}=gamma_l z_l+eta_{l+1}, eta=zeta_{l+1}/P_{l+1},
    w_{l+1}=gamma_l w_l+d_l/P_{l+1}.

The denominator P_{l+1} is past measurable and at least one. Thus eta retains the centered conditional moment bounds (5). Conditional expansion gives E z_l^2<=Bl/n and

    E z_{l+1}^4<=E z_l^4+(6B/n)E z_l^2+(4B/n^(3/2))E|z_l|+B/n^2.

Summing with E|z_l|<=sqrt(Bl/n) yields E z_L^4<=12B^2 L^2/n^2 and ||z_L||_4<=2sqrt(B)sqrt(L/n). Pathwise contraction gives |w_L|<=sum_{l<L}|d_l|, so ||w_L||_4<=192000sqrt(L/n)+BL/n. For L<=n/N, ||y_L||_4<=2B sqrt(L/n). The random-product bound and unconditional Holder, without independence, give

    ||e_L||_2<=||P_L||_4||y_L||_4<=2B exp(1008)sqrt(L/n). (6)

No future random product was used as a martingale weight. Only the increment's predictable normalization is used inside conditional expectations.

## 6. Deterministic spectral gap, including singular inputs

The first postactivation Gram is positive definite on the reduced representatives. To prove this, fix nu=nu_0, A=integral 1/s dnu(s), J(x)=integral exp(-s x^2)/s dnu(s). For b!=0 and t>0,

    Phi_nu(bt)=sign(b)[sqrt(A)-D_b(t)],
    D_b(t)=J(|b|t)/(sqrt(A)+sqrt(A-J(|b|t)))>0.

Let s_*=inf supp(nu). If 0<a<b, choose epsilon>0 such that (s_*+epsilon)a^2<s_*b^2. The measure mu(ds)=dnu(s)/s has positive mass on [s_*,s_*+epsilon]. Consequently

    J(bt)/J(at) <= [A/mu([s_*,s_*+epsilon])]
       *exp(-[s_*b^2-(s_*+epsilon)a^2]t^2) ->0,

and D_b(t)/D_a(t)->0 as well, since their denominators differ by at most a factor two.

For distinct nonzero v_j modulo sign, a finite union of proper hyperplanes can be avoided to find w with b_j=v_j.w nonzero and all |b_j| distinct. A Gaussian-L2 identity sum_j c_j Phi_nu(v_j.Z)=0 holds everywhere on their span by continuity and the full support of its standard Gaussian. Restrict to z=tw, take t to infinity to get sum c_j sign(b_j)=0, subtract this identity, and divide by the strictly positive D_{b_*}(t) for the smallest |b_j|. The tail-ratio limit forces c_*=0. Induction proves all coefficients zero. Thus the feature Gram and its normalized correlation are positive definite, proving rho_1>0. This feature-independence fact is not claimed as a novel identifiability theorem.

For subsequent layers let u=u_{nu_l,q}, a_nu(q)=E Zu(Z). The bounds above show 1>=a_nu(q)>=1/sqrt(7)>1/3. From ||partial_q u||_2<20 and u_0=Z we have 1-a_nu(q)=||u_q-Z||_2^2/2<=200q^2. Therefore -log a_nu(q)<=600q^2. For a Gaussian vector of correlation bar C_l, decompose u_{nu_l,s_j}(Z_j)=a_j Z_j+v_j(Z_j). Gaussian conditioning and E[Z_j v_j]=0 annihilate all cross terms. Hence bar C_{l+1}=D_a bar C_l D_a+V, with V positive semidefinite. Iterating from layer 1 and using sum_l s_{j,l}^2<=6q_{j,0} gives

    lambda_min(bar C_l)>=rho_1 exp(-7200m), l>=1.        (7)

The varying deterministic activation causes no difficulty because the estimates for a_nu are uniform at each layer. At state l=0, actual and GP covariance frames coincide, so no initial spectral gap is needed.

## 7. Joint coupling and all-depth split

On the m representatives, let Q_l be the random diagonal variances, C_l the empirical correlations, and D_l=diag(sqrt(Q_l)). Couple each next layer using a fresh n-by-m iid Gaussian matrix G_{l+1}:

    h_{l+1}=G_{l+1} C_l^(1/2)D_l,
    bar h_{l+1}=G_{l+1} bar C_l^(1/2)bar D_l.

Conditional row covariance is K_l in the actual chain. The GP frames are deterministic, so the independent G give the correct entire GP joint law. For PSD C and positive definite bar C with lambda_min>=rho, the Sylvester identity for X=C^(1/2)-bar C^(1/2), namely C^(1/2)X+X bar C^(1/2)=C-bar C, gives ||X||_F<=||C-bar C||_F/sqrt(rho) by Frobenius inner product and Cauchy-Schwarz. This remains valid for singular empirical C.

Split the frame difference as C_l^(1/2)(D_l-bar D_l)+(C_l^(1/2)-bar C_l^(1/2))bar D_l. Its expected squared Frobenius norm, which is the per-neuron next-layer coupling cost, is at most

    7056m/n +2(max_j s_{j,l})rho^{-1}E||C_l-bar C_l||_F^2.

For n>=N and 1<=l<=n/N, insert s<=6/l, (6), and rho=rho_1 exp(-7200m) from (7). This gives at most

    [7056m+48B^2 exp(2016+7200m)m^2/rho_1]/n.

At l=0 the cost is zero. For late states l>n/N, use instead cost<=2E[tr K_l+tr bar K_l]<=24m/l<24mN/n. For n<N, the state variances <=1 give cost<=4m<=4mN/n at every state. Both alternatives and 7056m/n fit inside 3*10^8 m/n. Summing costs gives (1) on the representatives without any independence requirement between errors at different layers.

Finally, zero initial vectors stay zero. Sign-identical initial vectors yield sign-identical preactivations and activations at every layer, because every Phi_nu is odd and weights are shared across input columns. The GP law obeys the same exact constraints. Extend the representative coupling by these signs and zeros: each representative error is counted at most d times. Every activation is 1-Lipschitz, giving the factor two for pre- plus postactivations.

## Audit and literature status

Primary context: Agazzi, Mosig Garcia, Trevisan, arXiv:2607.06290, Theorem 1.2 and Section 4.1 (fixed-program constants). Price identity: Voigtlaender, arXiv:1710.03576, Theorem 1 and Corollary 2. This proof builds on the structure of C002-C007 but reproduces the needed estimates for the new family; in particular it proves the varying-kernel extension rather than invoking a fixed-kernel statement outside its assumptions. C002 v2, C003 v1, C004 v1 have reviewer PASS; C005-C007 remain unaudited. C008 itself is unaudited, and no literature novelty finding is claimed. Review especially sections 4-5 and the essential-support tail ratio in section 6. Let X be a nonempty set and let L be a vector lattice of real-valued functions on X: L is a real vector space of functions X -> R, and f, g in L implies max(f,g) and min(f,g) are in L. Assume STONE'S CONDITION: f in L implies min(f, 1) in L. Let I : L -> R satisfy (i) linearity; (ii) positivity: f >= 0 pointwise implies I(f) >= 0 (equivalently f <= g implies I(f) <= I(g)); (iii) the DANIELL CONTINUITY CONDITION: whenever f_n in L decrease pointwise to 0 at every point of X, I(f_n) -> 0. Granted (i) and (ii), condition (iii) is equivalent to: f_n in L increasing pointwise to f with f in L implies I(f_n) -> I(f). CONCLUSION (Daniell-Stone): there is a measure mu on sigma(L), the smallest sigma-algebra on X making every member of L measurable, such that every f in L is mu-integrable and I(f) equals the integral of f with respect to mu. If moreover there exist f_n in L increasing pointwise to the constant function 1 (an exhaustion, i.e. sigma-finiteness along L), then mu is unique on sigma(L). WHERE IT FAILS: (a) condition (iii) is the whole content and cannot be dropped. On X = (0,1] take L to be the set of restrictions to (0,1] of the continuous functions on the closed interval [0,1] - a vector lattice satisfying Stone's condition - and let I(f) be the limit of f(x) as x decreases to 0, which exists for every member of L. This I is linear and positive, but f_n(x) = max(0, 1 - n x) lies in L and decreases pointwise to 0 on (0,1] while I(f_n) = 1 for every n, and I is not integration against any Borel measure on (0,1]: the 'missing' representing measure is a unit mass at the point 0, which does not lie in the space. A positive linear functional on a lattice always yields a finitely additive set function; (iii) is exactly what upgrades finite additivity to countable additivity. (b) Stone's condition is what manufactures indicator functions: for f in L and c > 0 the functions min(n (f - c)^+, 1) lie in L and increase pointwise to the indicator of {f > c}, which is how the measure of a generating set is defined. Without it one still gets a representation, but on a lattice of sets rather than on a sigma-algebra. (c) Without the exhaustion hypothesis uniqueness can fail: sets that no member of L 'sees' are unconstrained. Example: X = {p} union (0,1] with L the continuous compactly supported functions on (0,1] extended by the value 0 at p; then {p} lies in sigma(L) but its measure may be chosen freely without changing any I(f). (d) The theorem produces a measure on sigma(L) only; regularity (inner or outer) of mu is NOT part of the conclusion and needs topological hypotheses, which is where Riesz-Markov-Kakutani differs from Daniell-Stone.
L is a vector lattice of real-valued (finite everywhere) functions on a set X
Stone's condition: f in L implies min(f,1) in L
I : L -> R is linear
I is positive: f >= 0 implies I(f) >= 0
Daniell continuity: f_n in L with f_n decreasing pointwise to 0 implies I(f_n) -> 0
for the uniqueness clause only: there are f_n in L increasing pointwise to the constant 1
no topology on X is assumed, and no regularity of the resulting measure is claimed

Let the rows of Z be independent centered vectors conditional on an environment F, with E(||z_i||^2 | F)=v<infinity. Write X=Z+mu 1_n e^T, Q=(X^T X+aI)^(-1), zbar=Z^T 1_n/n, q=mu e+zbar, J=I_n-1_n 1_n^T/n, and A=Z^T J Z+aI. Deterministically X^T X+aI=A+n q q^T and q^T Qq<=1/n, giving e^T Qe <=(2/mu^2)(1/n+||zbar||^2/a). Therefore mu^2 E(e^T Qe | F)<=(2/n)(1+v/a), without independence between A and zbar or between coordinates of a row. For an independent Gaussian teacher w_*~N(0,s_*^2 I_p), noise epsilon~N(0,sigma^2 I_n), y=Xw_*+epsilon, and ridge error delta=QX^T y-w_*, E[(mu e^T delta)^2 | F]<=(2/n)(s_*^2 a+sigma^2)(1+v/a). This controls both the mean-direction predictive uncertainty and realized-teacher error. In random features e=p^(-1/2)1_p and mu is the activation mean; the raw population second-moment matrix has a rank-one spike mu^2 p ee^T even though its weighted predictive traces have the same limit as the centered model. For an arbitrary finite positive-mass aligned scale law, bounded nonzero output weights and biases, and a uniformly bounded exponential reference approximation with error <=sqrt(q)/4, ordinary all-parameter exponential population mean-field flow fits a unit-norm target to full residual energy q in dimension-independent time. Explicit constants depend on the minimum atom mass and initial bounds, not on d. Separately, any scale law dominating positive Lebesgue density on an interval has the requisite bounded-coefficient approximation property for every fixed-degree norm-one polynomial in the sphere coordinate, uniformly for all sufficiently large d. The finite-atomic flow assumes |a_i(0)|<=A, |b_i(0)|<=B, min atom mass p_min>0, bounded aligned scales, and reference coefficients |c_i|<=C with L2 approximation error <=sqrt(q)/4 for a unit-norm target. The potential uses kappa_i=b_i(0)-a_i(0)^2/2 and F_i(a)=a^2-2 exp(-kappa_i)c_i integral_0^a exp(-s^2/2)ds. Its weighted derivative is exactly -2<r,f-g_t>. An interval-density law has the approximation property but no general continuous-flow theorem is inferred from an averaged potential. No novelty claim or independent certification.

body: In computational complexity theory, the polynomial hierarchy is a hierarchy of complexity classes that generalize the classes NP and co-NP. Each class in the hierarchy is contained within PSPACE. The hierarchy can be defined using oracle machines or alternating Turing machines. It is a resource-bounded counterpart to the arithmetical hierarchy and analytical hierarchy from mathematical logic. The union of the classes in the hierarchy is denoted PH.
title: Polynomial hierarchy

body: In computational complexity theory, a probabilistically checkable proof (PCP) is a type of proof that can be checked by a randomized algorithm using a bounded amount of randomness and reading a bounded number of bits of the proof. The algorithm is then required to accept correct proofs and reject incorrect proofs with very high probability. A standard proof, as used in the verifier-based definition of the complexity class NP, also satisfies these requirements, since the checking procedure deterministically reads the whole proof, always accepts correct proofs and rejects incorrect proofs. However, what makes them interesting is the existence of probabilistically checkable proofs that can be checked by reading only a few bits of the proof using randomness in an essential way.
title: Probabilistically checkable proof

Method: Controlled generators, exact finite-state diagnostic, coupling, renewal reward or capacity comparison Result: For a state with m jobs and z busy servers, the count part of the generator applied to exp(theta*m) is [Lambda*(exp(theta)-1)+mu*z*(exp(-theta)-1)]*exp(theta*m). For a discrete memoryless channel with finite input alphabet, finite output alphabet, and fixed transition probabilities p(y|x) (the output at each use depends only on the current input, independently of other uses), define the channel capacity C = max_{p(x)} I(X;Y), the maximum over input distributions p(x) of the mutual information between the channel input X and output Y. Then for every rate R < C there exists a sequence of block codes of length n and rate approximately R whose probability of decoding error tends to 0 as n -> infinity. Conversely, for every rate R > C, the probability of decoding error is bounded away from 0 for every sequence of rate-R codes, regardless of how encoding and decoding are chosen.
the channel is discrete and memoryless: each output Y_i depends on the inputs only through a fixed conditional law p(y|x) applied to X_i
block coding is used with block length n tending to infinity

[Lem 173 (eighth moment bounds for $X^{\RomIII}$, $X^{\trunc,\RomIII}$, and $X^{\frozen,\RomIII}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The bound of Lemma~\ref{l:subgaus.X.II}
also holds with $X^{\RomIII}$ in place of $X^{\RomII}$: for $N$ large enough, we have 
	\[
	\E\bigg[\bigg(
	\sum_{\ell=a}^{b-1} \Delta X^{\RomIII}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))
	\bigg)^8\bigg]
	\le L^{O(1)} (q_b-q_a)^4
	\]
for all $0\le a\le b\le \dmax$. The same bound holds 
with $\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomIII}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))$
or $\Delta X^{\frozen,\RomIII}(q_d,a^\frozen(q_{d+1}))$
in place of $\Delta X^{\RomIII}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))$.

\begin{proof}
This follows by essentially the same argument as for 
Lemma~\ref{l:subgaus.X.II}. Recalling \eqref{e:X.decomp}, we let
	\[
	\Delta X^{\RomIII}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))
	=
	\frac{\sqrt{q_d (p_{d+1}-p_d)}
		(\bmeta^{a(q_{d+1})}(q_{d+1}),
		\bar{\bx}(q_d)
		)}{N^{1/2}}\,.
	\]
In this case, $\bar{\bx}(q_d)$ is measurable with respect to $\cFt(q_d)$, while $\bmeta(q_{d+1})$ is a standard gaussian vector in $\R^N$ that is measurable with respect to
$\cFt(q_{d+1})$. We can then repeat the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:subgaus.X.II} with $\bar{\bx}(q_d)$ taking the place of $\bar{\bg}(q_d)$, and $\bmeta(q_{d+1})$ taking the place of $\by(q_{d+1})$.
In place of \eqref{e:control.norm.event} we let
	\[E_d\equiv \bigg\{
	\frac{\|\bar{\bx}(q_d)\|^2}{N} \le  L^{O(1)}
	\bigg\} \in \cFt(q_d)\,,\quad
	E_\star=\bigcap_{d=a}^{b-1} E_d\,,\]
so the events have very high probability by Lemma~\ref{l:bar.x.subgaus} (which also holds with $\cFt(q_d)$ in place of $\cG(q_d)$) and Lemma~\ref{l:sg.norm.bound}. It is again straightforward to verify that the same argument applies with $X^{\trunc,\RomIII}$ or $X^{\frozen,\RomIII}$ in place of $X^{\RomII}$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: eighth moment bounds for $X^{\RomIII}$, $X^{\trunc,\RomIII}$, and $X^{\frozen,\RomIII}$

	then $Y_r=0$ for all $r\geq R=\inf \{r>0:Y_r=0\}<\infty\ \mathbb P_{y_0\delta_0}$-a.s.

Let U ⊂ C be open and connected, let a ≠ b be two fixed complex numbers, and let F be the family of all holomorphic functions on U that take neither the value a nor the value b anywhere on U. Then F is normal in the extended sense: every sequence in F has a subsequence that either converges uniformly on compact subsets of U to a holomorphic function, or converges to ∞ uniformly on compact subsets (that is, the reciprocals converge to 0 uniformly on compact subsets). If U is not connected the dichotomy is applied separately on each connected component. Omitting only one value is not enough (see the pitfall entry), and the limit ∞ genuinely occurs, e.g. the constants f_n = n omit 0 and 1 for n ≥ 2.

[Definition 7 of arXiv:2609.00448, 'Equivariant formality and representation theory'] (\cite[p. 172]{H}, \cite{GD}). Let $A$ be a ring and $B$ an $A$-algebra. The module of K\"ahler differentials $\Omega^1_{B/A}$ of $B$ over $A$ is the quotient of the $B$-module freely generated by the symbols $\{db| b\in B\}$ by the submodule generated by the following sets
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item(Constancy of elements of $A$) $\{da| a\in A\}$, 
		\item(Linearity of $d$) $\{d(b_1+b_2)-db_1-db_2| b_1, b_2\in B\}$, and 
		\item(Derivation) $\{d(b_1b_2)-b_1db_2-b_2db_1| b_1, b_2\in B\}$.
	\end{enumerate}
	The Grothendieck differentials $\Omega^*_{B/A}$ is defined to be the exterior $B$-algebra $\displaystyle\bigoplus_{p=0}^\infty \bigwedge\nolimits_B^p\Omega_{B/A}^1$.

Let (X, Σ) be a measurable space and T: X → X a measurable map (T⁻¹(E) ∈ Σ for every E ∈ Σ). A measure μ on Σ is T-invariant (equivalently: T preserves μ, or T is a measure-preserving transformation of (X, Σ, μ)) if μ(T⁻¹(E)) = μ(E) for every E ∈ Σ, i.e. the push-forward T_*μ := μ∘T⁻¹ equals μ. Equivalent formulation for a finite measure: ∫ f∘T dμ = ∫ f dμ for every bounded measurable f; when X is a compact metrizable space with its Borel σ-algebra and T is continuous, it suffices to test f ∈ C(X), because finite Borel measures on such a space are determined by their integrals against continuous functions. Note the direction: invariance is stated with the PREIMAGE T⁻¹(E), not the image T(E); for non-injective T the image condition μ(T(E)) = μ(E) is a different (and generally false) statement, e.g. the doubling map x ↦ 2x mod 1 preserves Lebesgue measure but doubles the length of short intervals. For a flow (φ_t)_{t∈ℝ} invariance means φ_t*μ = μ for every t.
T is measurable with respect to Σ
invariance is defined through preimages T⁻¹(E), not images T(E)

\mathcal L_x\bigl((W_t)_{0\leq t\leq S}\mid \theta T+a<A_T\leq \theta T+b\bigr)
\xrightarrow[T\to\infty]{\mathrm{TV}}
\mathcal L_x\bigl((X_t)_{0\leq t\leq S}\bigr),
\]
where $X$ is the ground-state diffusion as in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.  In particular,
the limiting process is independent of the choice of $a<b$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 14 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] Let $\Omega_1\subset \Omega_2$ be intervals. Then $\Lp(\Omega_1)\ge\Lp(\Omega_2)$. If $a_1\le a_2$ on a fixed interval $\Omega$, then
\[
\Lp(d\mathcal J_\Omega+q\partial_x+a_1)\ge\Lp(d\mathcal J_\Omega+q\partial_x+a_2),
\]
where $\mathcal J_\Omega u=\int_\Omega J(x-y)u(y)\,dy-u(x)$. Moreover,
\[
|\Lp(a_1)-\Lp(a_2)|\le\|a_1-a_2\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}.
\]
If $K_1,K_2$ are nonnegative kernels on $\Omega\times \Omega$ and $K_1\le K_2$, then, with the drift and zeroth-order coefficient fixed,
\[
\Lp(dK_1+q\partial_x+a)\ge\Lp(dK_2+q\partial_x+a).
\]

[Thm aronsson-package of arXiv:2608.30847, 'An Almgren-type formula for planar $p$-harmonic functions'] Let $u$ be a nonconstant $p$-harmonic function in a planar domain $\Omega$.
\begin{enumerate}[\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item The critical set
$$
  \operatorname{Crit}(u):=\{x\in\Omega:D u(x)=0\}
$$
is discrete.  In particular, if $x_0\in\operatorname{Crit}(u)$, then there exists $\rho>0$ such that $D u\ne0$ in $B_\rho(x_0)\setminus\{x_0\}$.

\item If $x_0\notin\operatorname{Crit}(u)$, then $u$ is real analytic in a neighborhood of $x_0$.

\item Let $x_0\in\operatorname{Crit}(u)$.  Then there are an integer $N\ge1$, a number $\delta>0$, and a nonzero homogeneous $p$-harmonic function $P$ in $\mathbb R^2$ such that, after subtracting the constant $u(x_0)$,
$$
  P(r\theta)=r^{\lambda_N(p)}\Phi(\theta),
  \qquad \theta\in\mathbb S^1,
$$
and, uniformly for $\theta\in\mathbb S^1$ as $r\to0$,
$$
  u(x_0+r\theta)-u(x_0)=P(r\theta)+O(r^{\lambda_N(p)+\delta}),
$$
$$
  D u(x_0+r\theta)=D P(r\theta)+O(r^{\lambda_N(p)-1+\delta}).
$$
Moreover $|D P(\theta)|>0$ on $\mathbb S^1$, and the hodograph representation gives the logarithmic-gradient expansion
$$
  \partial_r\log |D u(x_0+r\theta)|
  =
  \frac{\lambda_N(p)-1}{r}+O(r^{-1+\delta})
$$
uniformly in $\theta$.
\end{enumerate}
Here
$$
  \lambda_N(p)=\frac{\beta_{N+1}(p)}{\beta_{N+1}(p)-1},
$$
with
$$
  \beta_{N+1}(p)
  =
  \frac{\sqrt{(p-2)^2+4(p-1)((N+1)/N)^2}-(p-2)}{2}.
$$
For $p=2$, the same statement is understood in the classical harmonic sense and gives $\lambda_N(2)=N+1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Regularity of planar $p$-harmonic functions

[Corollary Recovery constants: sharp profile for fixed

\(B_{M}\left( x_{i},\varepsilon \right)\),
\(i = 1,\ldots,m\), and let \(\Lambda_{i}\) denote the
sharp small-hole constant of Theorem D.6 (for \(d \geq 3\),
\(\Lambda_{i} = \beta\left( a_{i} \right)\) with
\(a_{i} = \lim\,\operatorname{dist}\left( x_{i},\partial M \right)/\varepsilon\)) or
Theorem D.8 (for \(d = 2\),
\(\Lambda_{i} = B\left( \theta_{i} \right)\) with
\(\theta_{i} = \lim\,\log\,\operatorname{dist}\left( x_{i},\partial M \right)/\log\varepsilon\)),
so that the killed eigenvalues satisfy
\(\lambda_{i}(\varepsilon) \sim \gamma_{d}|M|^{- 1}\Lambda_{i}\,\kappa_{d}(\varepsilon)\).
The genuinely sharp finite-family information is the missed-target
profile of Corollary 4.5,

\[\Phi_{A}(u) \sim \sum_{i = 1}^{m}\exp\left( - \frac{\gamma_{d}}{|M|}\,\Lambda_{i}\,\kappa_{d}(\varepsilon)\, u \right);\]

in particular, writing
\(\Lambda_{\min} = \min_{i}\Lambda_{i}\), the following
worst-target condition gives a clean high-probability threshold: for
failure probability \(\delta \in (0,1)\), hitting every target
with probability at least \(1 - \delta\) holds once

\[T \geq s_{0} + \frac{|M|}{\gamma_{d}\,\Lambda_{\min}}\,\kappa_{d}(\varepsilon)^{- 1}\left( \log m + \log\frac{C}{\delta} \right),\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 6 of arXiv:2606.09904, 'Non-explosion principles for branched rough differential equations with unbounded coeffici'] For a map \(\mathbf{X} : [0, T] \to G_N(\CH)\), we denote \(\mathbf{X}_{st} = \mathbf{X}^{-1}_s \curvearrowright \mathbf{X}_t\).
  For any \(\gamma \in (\frac{1}{N + 1}, \frac{1}{N}]\), we say \(\mathbf{X}\) is a \(\gamma\)-H\"older branched rough path if 
  \[\sup_{s < t \in [0, T]} \frac{|\< \mathbf{X}_{st}, f\>|} {|t - s|^{\gamma|f|}} < \infty\]
  for all \(f \in \CF_N\).

  For a branched rough path \(\mathbf{X}\), we define its path component \(X^a\) by 
  \[\delta X^a_{st} = \< \mathbf{X}_{st}, \tree<X>\>.\]

[Definition 5 of arXiv:2506.09592, 'Extremal process of the local time of simple\\random walk on a regular tree'] Given a locally-finite random point measure $\eta$ on~$\R$, a Branching Random Walk with step distribution~$\eta$ started at $x\in\R$ is a sequence
$\{\xi_k \}_{k \ge 0}$
of random locally-finite point measures on~$\R$ such that $\xi_0=\delta_x$ a.s.\ and, denoting
$\scrF_k:=\sigma(\xi_j\colon j\le k)$,
\begin{equation}

E\bigl(\texte^{-\langle\xi_{k+1},f\rangle}\,|\,\scrF_k\bigr) =\texte^{-\langle\xi_k,\tilde f\rangle}\quad\text{where}\quad\tilde f(h):=
- \log E \bigl(\texte^{-\langle \eta, f(h+\cdot) \rangle} \bigr)
\end{equation}
holds for all $k\ge0$ and all continuous $f\colon\R\to[0,\infty)$  with compact support.

Let γ: [a,b] → ℂ be a continuous closed curve (γ(a) = γ(b)) and let z₀ ∈ ℂ be a point NOT on the curve, z₀ ∉ γ([a,b]). Because γ(t) − z₀ never vanishes, there is a continuous function θ: [a,b] → ℝ (a continuous choice of argument) with γ(t) − z₀ = |γ(t) − z₀| e^{iθ(t)}; θ is unique up to adding a constant integer multiple of 2π. The winding number of γ about z₀ is n(γ, z₀) := (θ(b) − θ(a)) / (2π). It is an integer (since γ(b) = γ(a) forces θ(b) − θ(a) ∈ 2πℤ) and does not depend on the choice of θ. For piecewise C¹ curves it equals the contour integral (1/2πi) ∮_γ dz/(z − z₀). Basic properties: z₀ ↦ n(γ, z₀) is constant on each connected component of ℂ \ γ([a,b]) and equals 0 on the unbounded component; it is additive under concatenation of closed curves at a common point and changes sign when the orientation of γ is reversed; it is invariant under homotopies of closed curves that avoid z₀ (see the classification theorem). The circle t ↦ z₀ + r e^{2πikt}, t ∈ [0,1], k ∈ ℤ, has winding number k about z₀ and winding number 0 about any point with |z − z₀| > r. The winding number is NOT defined when z₀ lies on the curve, and it is not a homotopy invariant for homotopies that are allowed to cross z₀ (the circle about z₀ is null-homotopic in ℂ but has winding number 1).
γ is a continuous closed curve in ℂ
z₀ does not lie on the image of γ

Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); ROUTE DIAGNOSTIC, not a standard-initialization theorem. For scalar ordinary separately bias-corrected outside-sqrt Adam with beta1=.9,beta2=.999 and cap1/rho>38, the analytic origin stable manifold has a two-dimensional fixed-clock physical fiber. For every sufficiently large absolute time N there exist physical positive-variance states with the actual clocks b^N,d^N and nonzero positions such that X_t~C_X*r_s^(t-N),V_t~C_V*d^(t-N), where C_X is nonzero,C_V>0 and-b<r_s<0. Thus V_t/X_t^2 grows to infinity while the new squared-gradient variance contribution is negligible: carried variance and tiny position do not imply regrowth. The initial variance ratio can be arbitrarily large. This does not refute standard-zero-moment global entry; proving that the standard initialization curve avoids this stable surface remains unpaid.

After division by I=2pm, this is

H(f)/I(f) <= 4(r/m)(1-p)[1-(1-1/(2 ln(2)))/r] < 4.

Here ln(2)>1/2, for example by integrating 1/t>1/2 on (1,2), and r/m<=1. The cases r<=1 were already handled. For a fixed r>=2, H(f)>0 is fixed and I=2pm is minimized exactly at m=r. In that case U is an r-dimensional subspace of its r-coordinate support and therefore is that entire coordinate space; A fixes those r coordinates and leaves the others free. Conversely any such coordinate subcube has m=r. For coordinate subcubes the nonempty entropy term divided by I is 4(1-p)(r-1)/r ->4. The remaining nonnegative empty term is at most 2(1-p)/(r ln(2)) ->0. Thus M_r->4 and any C<4 fails for some r. body:
[Defn def:smc-prime of arXiv:2604.20629, 'Rates of forgetting for the sequentially Markov coalescent'] Let $(Y'_{\ell})_{\ell\ge0}$ be a Markov jump
process on $(0,\infty)$ with the following dynamics. When
$Y'_{\ell}=y$, recombination events occur at rate $y$. Given
that a recombination occurs at time
$r\in(0,y)$, the detached lineage recoalesces with either of the
two existing lineages at rate $1$ each (total rate $2$). If recoalescence
occurs with its own ancestral lineage before time $y$, then the recombination
is \emph{silent} and the state does not change. Otherwise---either
if recoalescence occurs with the other lineage, or if no recoalescence
occurs before time $y$---the recombination is \emph{visible}, and
the process jumps to a new TMRCA determined by the time of this coalescence
event.
The probability of a visible recombination at current TMRCA $s$ is
\begin{equation}
p_{\mathrm{vis}}(s)=\frac{2s+1-e^{-2s}}{4s},\qquad
p_{\mathrm{sil}}(s)=1-p_{\mathrm{vis}}(s).

\end{equation}

Equivalently, one may construct $(Y'_{\ell})$ from its embedded jump
chain and holding times as follows. Let $(X'_{n})_{n\ge0}$ be the
jump chain, and let $(E_{n})_{n\ge0}$ be i.i.d.\ $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$
random variables, independent of the chain. Given $X'_{n}$, define
the holding time 
\[
\Delta\ell_{n}:=\frac{E_{n}}{X'_{n} p_{\mathrm{vis}}(X_{n}')}
\]
and the jump locations $\ell_{0}:=0$, $\ell_{n+1}:=\ell_{n}+\Delta\ell_{n}$.
Then define 
\[
Y'_{\ell}:=X'_{n}\quad\text{for }\ell\in[\ell_{n},\ell_{n+1}),
\]
and $X'_{n+1}\sim q_{\mathrm{SMC}'}( \cdot \mid X_{n}'),$ where
\[
q_{\mathrm{SMC}'}(t\mid s)=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{2(1-e^{-2t})}{2s+1-e^{-2s}}, & 0<t<s,\\[10pt]
\dfrac{2(1-e^{-2s})}{2s+1-e^{-2s}} e^{-(t-s)}, & t\ge s.
\end{cases}
\]
title: Defn def:smc-prime of arXiv:2604.20629

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2605.16733, 'Concentration Inequalities for Sample Cross-Covariances'] Let \((Z_i,W_i)_{i=1}^N\) be i.i.d. copies of a centered random
vector \((Z,W)\in \mathbb R^{d_Z+d_W}\). Assume that \(Z\) and \(W\) are isotropic
sub-Gaussian random vectors with sub-Gaussian constants \(K_Z\) and \(K_W\).  Let
\(T\subset \mathbb R^{d_Z}\) and \(S\subset \mathbb R^{d_W}\) be bounded sets. For every \(u\ge 1\), it holds with probability at least  \(1-\exp(-u)\)  that
\begin{align}
&\sup_{v\in T,\, h\in S}
\left|
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N
\langle Z_i,v\rangle \langle W_i,h\rangle
-
\E \langle Z,v\rangle \langle W,h\rangle
\right| \nonumber\\
&\lesssim K_Z K_W \rad(T)\rad(S)\left(
\sqrt{\frac{d(T)+d(S)+u}{N}}+\frac{\sqrt{(d(T)+u)(d(S)+u)}}{N}\right).
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 2 of arXiv:2605.16733

Let psi_1(x) = exp(x) - 1 for x >= 0. The sub-exponential Orlicz norm of a random variable X, denoted ||X||_{psi_1}, is defined by ||X||_{psi_1} = inf { c > 0 : E[psi_1(|X| / c)] <= 1 } = inf { c > 0 : E[exp(|X| / c)] <= 2 }.
X is a real random variable

[Proposition 8 (Geometric bounds for the first perfect square reached after $N$) of arXiv:2604.23133, 'High-Precision Framework for Expected Hitting Times Analysis in the Dice-Sum Process'] Let $(S_t)$ be the cumulative-sum process defined in~\eqref{eq:S}, and fix a perfect square cutoff $N = K^2$ with $K \in \mathbb{N}$ and $K \ge 4$.  
Consider the target set $\mathcal{H} = \{n^2 : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$.

For each integer $j \ge 0$, define
\[
h_j := (K + 1 + j)^2,
\]
the $(j+1)^{\mathrm{st}}$ perfect square strictly greater than~$N$.  
Then, for every initial state $s \le N$ with $\mathbb{P}_s(A_N) > 0$, the probability that the
first perfect square reached after $N$ equals $h_j$ satisfies
\[
\biggl(\frac{5}{7} - \varepsilon_N\biggr)^{\!j}
\biggl(\frac{2}{7} - \varepsilon_N\biggr)
\;\le\;
\mathbb{P}_s(S_T = h_j \mid A_N)
\;\le\;
\biggl(\frac{5}{7} + \varepsilon_N\biggr)^{\!j}
\biggl(\frac{2}{7} + \varepsilon_N\biggr),
\]
where
\[
\varepsilon_N = \frac{5}{7}\,|w_+|^{\,2K-4},
\qquad
|w_+| = 0.7302499667.
\]

body: [Defn Downward closed of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] A subset $A \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is \textbf{downward closed} if for all $\bm{x} \in A$ we have $(\bm{-\infty}, \bm{x}] \subset A$. body:
Every simple graph G on n vertices with m edges contains at least m (4m - n^2) / (3n) triangles; the bound is informative when 4m > n^2, that is, above the Mantel threshold m > n^2/4. Equivalently, writing t(G) for the number of triangles, t(G) >= (m / (3n)) (4m - n^2). Check on the complete graph: m = n(n-1)/2 gives 4m - n^2 = n(n-2) and the bound equals n(n-1)(n-2)/6 = C(n,3), which is exact. (Revision 2026-09-11: the earlier statement displayed a second form, (n/3)(4m/n - n)(m/n^2), that simplifies to m(4m - n^2)/(3n^2), a factor n below the correct bound; the (3n) form above is the theorem.)
G is a simple graph on n vertices with m edges

body: [Definition 15 of arXiv:2608.27630, 'Oriented planar maps and \\ annular mating of trees'] Fix $\tau\in (0, \infty)$. We write $\QA_\tau$ for the law of the LQG surface $(\cA_\tau, \phi)/\mathord\sim_\gamma$ where $\phi\sim \LF_\tau$. Given an embedding  $(\cA_\tau, \phi)$ of $\QA_\tau$, we write $\cL_0^\phi$ and $\cL_1^\phi$ for the LQG length measure induced by $\phi$ on $C_0 = \{|z|=1\}$ and $C_\tau = \{|z|=e^{-2\pi\tau}\}$, respectively. We further weight the law of $\phi$ by  $\|\cL_0^\phi\|$, the LQG length of the outer circle, and sample a point $x\in C_0$ according to the probability measure proportional to the LQG length measure   $\nu_\phi$. We write $\QA_\tau^1$ for the law of the resulting LQG surface   $(\cA_\tau, \phi,x)/\mathord\sim_\gamma$.

\[
\kappa=(\kappa_{1,1},\dots,\kappa_{1,\nu_1};\dots;\kappa_{d,1},\dots,\kappa_{d,\nu_d}),
\qquad \kappa_{j,j'}>0~~\text{for all}~~j=1,\cdots,d~~\text{and}~~ 1\le j^\prime\leq\nu_j.
\]
Define the local sets
\[
\Omega_{\delta,\boldsymbol{n}} =
\Bigl\{ \omega \in \Omega :
|g_{\boldsymbol{n}}(\omega)|
>
{\delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\tnorm{\boldsymbol{n}}_\kappa
\Bigr\},
\]
where
\[
\tnorm{\boldsymbol{n}}_\kappa
= \prod_{j=1}^d \prod_{j'=1}^{\nu_j} (1 + |n_{j,j'}|)^{\kappa_{j,j'}},
\]
and the global set
\[
\Omega_\delta = \bigcup_{\boldsymbol{n} \in \mathbb{Z}^\nu} \Omega_{\delta,\boldsymbol{n}}.
\]
Then we have
\[
\mathbb{P}(\Omega_\delta) =\mathcal O( e^{-\delta^{-1}}).
\]

OWNER RESULT DRAFT: proof (unaudited), T336-w727-C011 v1; no novelty claim. Let k and k_p be real symmetric PSD kernels on X, with k(x,x)<=1. Suppose h=k-k_p is PSD and sup_x h(x,x)<=eta, eta>=0. Let s>0 be observation noise variance. For every fixed context of length l<=n (n a nonnegative integer), labels |y_i|<=B (B>=0), and query x_*, let N(m,v) and N(m_p,v_p) be the noisy-query GP conditioning distributions computed from k and k_p on the same locations and labels. For l>0 these are m=u^T(K+sI)^{-1}y and v=s+k(x_*,x_*)-u^T(K+sI)^{-1}u, with K_ij=k(x_i,x_j) and u_i=k(x_i,x_*), and analogously for k_p; empty contexts have mean zero and noisy prior variance. Define C_mu=nB/s+n^2 B/s^2 and C_v=1+2n/s+n^2/s^2. Then |m-m_p|<=C_mu eta, 0<=v-v_p<=C_v eta, and s<=v_p<=v<=s+1, uniformly over these contexts. For eps>0, if eta<=min(1/2,sqrt(s eps)/(2(1+C_mu)),s sqrt(2eps)/(2C_v)), any predictor (mhat,vhat) satisfying s<=vhat<=v_p, |m_p-mhat|<=sqrt(s eps)/2, and v_p-vhat<=s sqrt(2eps)/2 has forward KL(N(m,v)||N(mhat,vhat))<=eps. The PSD tail premise, rather than an absolute entrywise error alone, proves the variance ordering through a joint-kernel variational formula. These are pointwise fixed-design conditioning formulas; a posterior interpretation assumes an exogenous design, zero-mean GP prior and independent Gaussian observation noises. This statement supplies no RBF rank-tail certificate, raw-input encoder, or training guarantee.

s>0; fixed contexts of length<=n with labels bounded by B; noisy-query Gaussian conditioning

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:0ede06f3692e3038c4ba7c22962c47f338f7d10e91475181413be989d65aeb79","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/0e/0ede06f3692e3038c4ba7c22962c47f338f7d10e91475181413be989d65aeb79.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:5dc013e697cd629fbd40ddf7b02f7b0d5cee7442f9a7dae5c7eeaca3b264d76f","bundle_entry_key":"t336-w727-c011","bundle_id":"population.w727-t336-psd-kernel-tail-006","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian processes; kernel approximation; Bayesian prediction","draft":"w727/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.transformers:draft-t336-w727-c011-psd-kernel-tail-gp-kl","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C011 v1: a PSD kernel-tail interface for noisy GP prediction

Kind: bound. Target: none (reviewer-authorized kernel-truncation continuation).
Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claim. This is a conditional interface;
it does not supply an RBF rank-versus-error theorem or a raw-input encoder.
The solver corollary depends on unaudited C010 v1. The kernel perturbation
lemma below is independent of that construction. C004's accepted feature
perturbation argument is background, not re-audited here.

## 1. Statement and hypotheses

Let k and k_p be real symmetric PSD kernels on X. Assume k(x,x)<=1 and
h=k-k_p is also a PSD kernel with sup_x h(x,x)<=eta, eta>=0. These conditions
imply 0<=k_p(x,x)<=1 and |h(x,z)|<=eta by PSD Cauchy-Schwarz.
Let the observation noise variance be s>0. Fix any context of length l<=n,
with arbitrary locations, a query x_*, and labels |y_i|<=B. Here n is a
nonnegative integer and B>=0. These are pointwise GP conditioning formulas;
a probabilistic interpretation assumes an exogenous design and the stated GP
prior and independent Gaussian observation noise, not arbitrary adaptive design.

Let (m,v) and (m_p,v_p) be the noisy-query posterior mean and variance for
k and k_p respectively, conditioning on the same context labels. Then

    |m-m_p| <= C_mu eta,
    0 <= v-v_p <= C_v eta,
    s <= v_p <= v <= s+1,
    C_mu = n B/s + n^2 B/s^2,
    C_v = 1 + 2n/s + n^2/s^2.

The lower bound on v-v_p requires h PSD, not merely entrywise error control.
The constants deliberately use n even when l<n.

## 2. Mean and absolute variance perturbation

For l>0 write K=(k(x_i,x_j)), u=(k(x_i,x_*)), a=k(x_*,x_*),
A=K+sI, and similarly K_p,u_p,a_p,A_p. PSD gives A,A_p>=sI.
Kernel Cauchy-Schwarz and the tail bound imply

    ||u||,||u_p|| <= sqrt(l), ||y||<=sqrt(l)B,
    ||u-u_p||<=sqrt(l)eta, ||K-K_p||_op<=l eta,
    ||A^{-1}||,||A_p^{-1}||<=1/s.

The matrix norm bound follows from the Frobenius norm (l^2 entries).
The resolvent identity, with its sign explicit, is

    A^{-1}-A_p^{-1}=A^{-1}(A_p-A)A_p^{-1},
    ||A^{-1}-A_p^{-1}||<=l eta/s^2.

Split m-m_p as

    (u-u_p)^T A^{-1}y + u_p^T(A^{-1}-A_p^{-1})y.

Cauchy-Schwarz gives (l B/s+l^2 B/s^2)eta <= C_mu eta.
For the quadratic posterior correction use the exact decomposition

    u^T A^{-1}u-u_p^T A_p^{-1}u_p
      =(u-u_p)^T A^{-1}u
       +u_p^T A^{-1}(u-u_p)
       +u_p^T(A^{-1}-A_p^{-1})u_p.

Its absolute value is at most (2l/s+l^2/s^2)eta.
Since |a-a_p|<=eta and v=s+a-u^T A^{-1}u, this proves the absolute
variance error bound. When l=0, m=m_p=0 and v-v_p=a-a_p; the assertions
follow directly without zero-dimensional inverse conventions.

## 3. Why the variance is ordered

For w in R^l define

    F_k(w)=a-2w^T u+w^T(K+sI)w.

Completing the square gives min_w F_k(w)=a-u^T A^{-1}u=v-s.
Also F_k(w) is the sum of the nonnegative joint-kernel quadratic form
(-w,1)^T K_joint (-w,1) and s||w||^2. Thus v>=s, and w=0 gives v<=s+a.
The same statements hold for k_p. For every w,

    F_k(w)-F_{k_p}(w)=(-w,1)^T h_joint (-w,1)>=0.

Taking minima preserves this inequality: v-s>=v_p-s. Combined with
Section 2 and a<=1 this proves every variance assertion in Section 1.
This argument also covers the empty context directly. It does not infer
posterior ordering solely from an ordering of the context covariance block.

For necessity of the tail-PSD premise for this ordering argument, on a
singleton domain choose constant kernels k=1/2 and k_p=1. Both are PSD and
their uniform difference is 1/2, but the empty-context noisy variances are
s+1/2 and s+1, in the reverse order. This example violates h PSD.

## 4. Joint forward-KL allocation

Let eps>0. Choose a PSD tail certificate satisfying

    eta <= min(1/2, sqrt(s eps)/(2(1+C_mu)),
                      s sqrt(2 eps)/(2 C_v)).

Suppose a finite-kernel predictor outputs (mhat,vhat) with

    s<=vhat<=v_p,
    |m_p-mhat|<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    v_p-vhat<=s sqrt(2 eps)/2.

The preceding bounds imply

    |m-mhat|<=sqrt(s eps),
    0<=v-vhat<=s sqrt(2 eps).

Write z=(v-vhat)/vhat>=0. The exact forward Gaussian KL is

    KL(N(m,v)||N(mhat,vhat))
      = (z-log(1+z))/2 + (m-mhat)^2/(2 vhat).

For all z>=0, z-log(1+z)<=z^2/2: the difference of right minus left
vanishes at zero and has derivative z^2/(1+z)>=0. Consequently

    KL <= (v-vhat)^2/(4s^2)+(m-mhat)^2/(2s) <= eps.

No triangle inequality for KL is used.

## 5. Conditional transformer corollary and remaining obstruction

If k_p has a supplied p-dimensional feature map with norm at most one,
C010 v1 at accuracy eps_c=eps/4 supplies the two error inequalities in
Section 4 and s<=vhat<=v_p. Indeed its residual delta budget implies
|m_p-mhat|<=sqrt(s eps_c) and
v_p-vhat<=s sqrt(2 eps_c). Its exact-output boundary cases also satisfy them.
Its token and size claims remain those of C010: p fixed auxiliary tokens,
width 9p+4, at most four heads, depth 2T+3. This is a dependency on that
unaudited construction, not a new independent audit or an architecture change.

The hardest remaining step for an explicit RBF result is a primary-source
certificate giving a finite p with uniform PSD diagonal-tail <=eta on the
specified compact domain, followed by the intended input-encoding choice.
A Mercer L1 tail or an average-case kernel error alone does not meet this
uniform hypothesis. [Thm 206 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\cA_N=\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)$ be a sequence of $L$-Lipschitz algorithms, as in Definition~\ref{d:Lip}. Let $\chi^N\equiv \chi_{\cA_N}$, and assume further that
    \[
    \frac{1}{L^2} \le (\chi^N)'(p) \le L^2
    \]
for all $0\le p\le 1$. Consider a Brownian bridge terminating at $(\bG,\bg^\aux)$, and let $\vX^N\equiv (\vX^{\RomI:\RomIII},X^\Ising)^N$ be the resulting $\R^4$-valued process defined by \eqref{e:X.decomp}--\eqref{e:vX}. Let $\vX^{\trunc,N}$ be the truncation given by Definitions~\ref{d:trunc}--\ref{d:buckets.Ising}, and let $\vY^N$ be the spatial rerandomization of $\vX^{\trunc,N}$ from Definitions~\ref{d:rerand} and \ref{d:rerand.Ising}. Let $\vD^N$ and $\vQ^N$ denote respectively its discrete-time drift and covariation with respect to the filtration given by the buckets --- see Definitions~\ref{d:D} and \ref{d:Q} below ($\vD^N$ is $\R^4$-valued, while $\vQ^N$ is $\R^{10}$-valued).

We make
$(\vY,\vD,\vQ)^N$ into continuous-time $\R^{18}$-valued processes by taking the linear interpolation on each time interval $[q_d,q_{d+1}]$. We also denote the piecewise constant variants $(\vY,\vD,\vQ)^{\bullet,N}$, so for example $\vY^{\bullet,N}(t)=\vY^N(q_d)$ for all $[q_d,q_{d+1})$. Let $\mu_{\bG^N}$ be the law of $(\vY,\vD,\vQ)^N$ conditional on the disorder $\bG^N$, and let $\Q_N$ be the law of $\mu_{\bG^N}$. Let $\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}$ be the law of $(\vY,\vD,\vQ)^{\bullet,N}$ conditional on the disorder $\bG^N$, and let $\Q_{\bullet,N}$ be the law of $\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}$. Note that 
$\mu_{\bG^N},\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}$ are probability measures on the space of $\R^{18}$-valued paths equipped with the uniform topology, and we equip the space of such measures with the topology of weak convergence.

If $N\to\infty$ with parameters satisfying Assumption~\ref{a:params}, then the measures $\Q_N$ are tight, with respect to the weak convergence topology described above. If $\Q_N\to\Q$ along an integer subsequence $N\to\infty$, then we have $\Q_{\bullet,N}\Rightarrow\Q_N$ along the same subsequence. For any subsequential limit $\Q$, if $\mu\sim\Q$ and $(\vY,\vD,\vQ)\sim\mu$, then $\vY$ is a semimartingale with drift $\vD$ and covariation $\vQ$. Moreover, $Y^\RomI$ is a finite-variation process while $Y^{\RomII}$, $Y^{\RomIII}$, and $Y^{\Ising}$ are martingales: this means $D^\sigma\equiv0$ for $\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$, and $Q^{\RomI,\sigma}\equiv0$ for all $\sigma$. We also have $Q^{\sigma,\Ising}\equiv0$ for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$. 

All the analogous statements hold with $\vY^{\frozen,N}$, $\vY^\frozen$, $\vD^\frozen$, $\vQ^\frozen$ in place of $\vY^N$, $\vY$, $\vD$, $\vQ$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem MVT of arXiv:2411.11759, 'Milstein-type schemes for McKean--Vlasov SDEs driven by Brownian motion and Poisson random'] Let $f:\mathbb R^d\times \mathscr P_2(\mathbb R^d)\to\mathbb R$ be a function having  measure derivative $\partial_\mu f:\mathbb R^d\times \mathscr P_2(\mathbb R^d)\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$.
		Then, for any $z,x^j,y^j\in\mathbb R^d$
		\begin{align*}
			f\Big(z,\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} \delta_{x^{j}}\Big) \hspace{-0.04cm}- \hspace{-0.04cm}f\Big(z,\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} \delta_{y^{j}}\Big)
			\hspace{-0.03cm}=\hspace{-0.03cm} \frac{1}{N}\int_0^1\sum_{\widehat j=1}^{N}\partial_{\mu}f\Big(z,\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} \delta_{y^j+\theta(x^j-y^j)},y^{\widehat j}+\theta(x^{\widehat j}\hspace{-0.02cm}-\hspace{-0.02cm}y^{\widehat j})\Big)(x^{\widehat j}\hspace{-0.02cm}-\hspace{-0.02cm}y^{\widehat j}) d\theta.
		\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Theorem thm:uniqueness-geodesics of arXiv:2609.04140, 'The conformally invariant metric on $\CLE_4$ III:\\ uniqueness'] Almost surely, for each $\SCL_1, \SCL_2 \in \Gamma_\BH$, there is a unique $D_{\Gamma_\BH}^\BH$-geodesic connecting $\SCL_1$ and $\SCL_2$, in the sense that if $P_1$ and $P_2$ are $D_{\Gamma_\BH}^\BH$-geodesics connecting $\SCL_1$ and $\SCL_2$, then $\{\SCL \in \Gamma_\BH : \SCL \cap P_1 \neq \emptyset\} = \{\SCL \in \Gamma_\BH : \SCL \cap P_2 \neq \emptyset\}$. A similar statement holds with a deterministic connected arc of $\partial\BH$ (resp.\ two deterministic disjoint connected arcs of $\partial\BH$) in place of $\SCL_1$ (resp.\ $\SCL_1$ and $\SCL_2$). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Uniqueness of geodesics

body: In differential geometry, a Riemannian manifold is a geometric space on which many geometric notions such as distance, angles, length, volume, and curvature are defined. Euclidean space, the -sphere, hyperbolic space, and smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space, such as ellipsoids and paraboloids, are all examples of Riemannian manifolds. Riemannian manifolds take their name from German mathematician Bernhard Riemann, who first conceptualized them in 1854.
title: Riemannian manifold

body:
Own work, proof (unaudited), W719-T295-C013 v1; conditional method record, no specialist novelty asserted. For arbitrary time-varying symmetric positive definite H_t, fixed real vector a, b_t>0, mu_t>=0, eta_t>0 with H_t>=mu_t I+b_t aa^T and eta_t H_t<=I, the recursion d_(t+1)=(I-eta_t H_t)d_t-eta_t a u_t, y_t=a^T d_t, obeys ||d_T||^2+sum_(t<T) eta_t mu_t||d_t||^2+sum_(t<T) eta_t b_t y_t^2 <=||d_0||^2+sum_(t<T) eta_t u_t^2/b_t. In particular, equal-start input u_t=beta r_t, constant b_t=beta>0 and constant step give temporal l2 gain at most one. No commutativity or positive scalar response products are required. Proof: eta_t H_t<=I gives H_t^(-1)>=eta_t I. Expanding the new squared norm and using this inequality cancels the mixed input/state terms, giving ||d_next||^2<=||d||^2-eta d^T H d+eta u^2 a^T H^(-1)a. The directional lower bound gives a^T H^(-1)a<=1/b and d^T H d>=mu||d||^2+b(a^T d)^2. Sum over time. This implication is pathwise, even when matrices depend on the trajectory. For phase retrieval the exact full-gradient secant Q_t=(1/m)sum_j[p_j^2+p_j q_j+q_j^2-g_j^2]a_j a_j^T and scalar input u_t=((q_i^2-g_i^2)q_i)/m fit the recursion, with p_j=a_j^T x_t, q_j=a_j^T z_t, g_j=a_j^T x_*. The required directional curvature/smoothness of Q_t at linear m and the weighted input budget are unproved. The temporal l2 estimate does not supply a temporal supremum bound or all-time relative incoherence; a bounded input alone gives only a sqrt(T) pointwise estimate from this inequality. No actual nonlinear GD convergence is established.
strictly positive definite symmetric H_t at each step; common direction a; arbitrary scalar input
pathwise directional lower bound H_t>=mu_t I+b_t aa^T and smoothness eta_t H_t<=I
actual nonlinear phase-retrieval secants have not been proved to satisfy these hypotheses at linear m

[Lemma 32 (Control of the geometry-matter tensor) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Given a Navier--Stokes potential~$\chi$ as in \autoref{def-pot-hyperbolic}, one has the following inequalities: for $a,b\in\{0,1\}$,
\bel{Tchi-DEC-M}
|\Mbf_\chi^{ab}| \leq \Mbf_\chi^{00} , \qquad
-2 \Mbf_\chi^{00} \leq \frac{1}{2} \Msource^\chi - \frac{3}{4}(\Mbf_\chi^{00} - \Mbf_\chi^{11}) \leq \Mbf_\chi^{00} .
\ee
For the Euler stress-tensor the last lower bound is improved to $-\Mbf_\chi^{00}$.

body: [Definition def:semi-adaptive of arXiv:2608.20480, 'When Clean Data Hurts: Learning with Monotone \\ Corruptions Beyond Binary Classification'] Fix $m\le n$. An \emph{\textbf{$m$-semi-adaptive adversary}} is shown $m$ clean labeled examples, whose indices are selected independently of their values, and may choose its additions as an arbitrary function of these visible examples. The remaining $n-m$ clean examples are hidden.

[Proposition Strandabove3 of arXiv:2604.07227, 'Transition probabilities of step-reinforced random walks'] Let $S$ be a generalized SRRW on a Euclidean space with reinforcement parameter $\alpha \in [0,1)$ and step distribution $\mu$ being genuinely d-dimensional. Then for any $r>0$, there exists a positive constant $C=C(r,\mu,\alpha)$ such that for all $n\geq 1$,
    $$
\mathbb{P}( \|S_n\| < r ) \leq C n^{-\frac{d}{2}}.
    $$
In particular, $S$ is transient if $d\geq 3$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition Strandabove3 of arXiv:2604.07227

body:
[Definition 1 ($q$-Demazure product) of arXiv:2604.06532, 'Random permutations from $q$-Demazure products'] Fix $q \in [0,1]$.
The \emph{$q$-Demazure product} of a simple transposition $s_i$ and a permutation
$\sigma \in S_n$ is the random permutation
\[
  s_i \cdot_q \sigma \;:=\;
  \begin{cases}
    s_i\sigma, & \text{if } \ell(s_i\sigma) > \ell(\sigma),\\[6pt]
    \begin{cases}
      s_i\sigma & \text{with probability } q,\\
      \sigma    & \text{with probability } 1-q,
    \end{cases}
    & \text{if } \ell(s_i\sigma) < \ell(\sigma),
  \end{cases}
\]
where $\ell(\sigma) = \#\{(a,b) : a < b,\, \sigma(a) > \sigma(b)\}$ is the number of
inversions of $\sigma$.
The $q$-Demazure product of a word $s_{i_1}\cdot_q \cdots \cdot_q s_{i_k}$ is defined by applying the rule
left-to-right with independent randomness at each step.
At $q=0$ this reduces to the \emph{Demazure product}; at $q=1$ it is the ordinary
group multiplication in $S_n$.
title: $q$-Demazure product

[Corollary 26 (Descent-wise cancellation polynomials) of arXiv:2609.01882, '\textbf{Coxeter Descents and Parabolic Homotopy Colimits}\\[2mm] \large A Hochster-type de'] For every $0\le d\le r$ there is a polynomial $\Theta_{r,d}(z)\in\mathbb N[z]$ such that
\[
\Psi_{r,d}(z)=
\begin{cases}
1+(1+z)\Theta_{r,0}(z),&d=0,\\
(1+z)\Theta_{r,d}(z),&0<d<r,\\
z^{r-1}+(1+z)\Theta_{r,r}(z),&d=r.
\end{cases}
\]
The coefficients of $\Theta_{r,d}$ count matched unit pairs by lower bar degree for the matching of Lemma~\ref{lem:booleanmatching}.
